lost_or_transferred_material: CoS: Arthur physically throwing himself at Lucius Malfoy—film has him restrained before initiating, not launching himself as in the book
CoS: Arthur's principled furious confrontation with Fred and George over the Engorgement Toffee (book scene; film shows only Howler aftermath)
CoS: The extended 'loophole' confrontation with Molly over the enchanted car, showing Arthur's self-aware rule-bending humor
PoA: The overheard argument between Arthur and Molly about whether to tell Harry the truth about Sirius Black—a key scene of independent moral judgment and marital friction
OotP: The full texture of Arthur's Ministry office (windowless, littered with Muggle objects, cramped beside Perkins)—showing his dignified endurance of professional marginalization
OotP: The St Mungo's Christmas scene where Arthur attempts Muggle stitching on his snake-bite wounds—showing his incorrigible Muggle enthusiasm even while recovering from near-death
OotP: Arthur's extended running commentary on Ministry colleagues at the World Cup campfire (book GoF scenes), compressed to brief exchanges in the film
DH Part 1: Potterwatch radio scene (confirmed cut)—Arthur quietly building communication radios for Order members on the run, showing wartime agency and initiative

comparative.key_observations: Arthur Weasley is one of the better-adapted supporting characters in the Harry Potter film series. His core personality—Muggle enthusiasm, warm paternal inclusiveness, principled values, mild-mannered competence with occasional flashes of real anger—is consistently and recognizably present across all eight films. The performances and screenplay selections correctly identify what is most essential about him. The losses are real but concentrated: the PoA overheard argument is the single most significant omission, as it is the scene where Arthur most clearly acts as an independent moral agent against institutional and familial pressure; its compression into a unilateral warning reduces his characterization from principled advocate to dutiful informer. The Engorgement Toffee confrontation and the St Mungo's stitches scene, both cut, together remove the most revealing examples of his contradictory nature. The confirmed-cut Potterwatch radio scene loses his quiet wartime initiative. What remains is an Arthur Weasley who is warm, funny, genuinely Muggle-obsessed, and clearly good—but somewhat less complex, less contradictory, and less agentive than his book counterpart. The score of 75 reflects a faithful but meaningfully simplified adaptation.

personality_voice.book_baseline: Umbridge's defining trait in the books is the sustained, deliberate gap between her surface presentation and her inner cruelty. Her voice is high-pitched, breathy and girlish ('hem, hem'); she speaks with excessive sweetness ('dear', 'kindly', 'I'm sure we'll be very good friends'); she smiles constantly, including a wide toad-like smile that appears precisely when she is inflicting harm. Her tone shifts are observable and meaningful: sweetness evaporates into cold bureaucratic precision when challenged, and into barely restrained rage when authority is defied. She is methodical and controlling — the repeated classroom rituals ('Good afternoon, Professor Umbridge'), the structured course aims on the blackboard, the insistence on hand-raising — all reveal someone who uses petty proceduralism as an instrument of dominance. Her cruelty is not impulsive; it is deliberate and pleasurable. She explicitly savours Trelawney's public humiliation ('Harry was revolted to see the enjoyment stretching her toadlike face'), examines Harry's bleeding hand with calm satisfaction ('Ah. Good. That ought to serve as a reminder'), and plans her Cruciatus attack with the excited manner of someone who has wanted to do it for a long time ('There was a nasty eager, excited look on her face that Harry had never seen before'). Her confession in the office — 'He never knew I ordered Dementors to go after Potter last summer... I was the one who actually did something about it' — reveals cold self-congratulation and a sense of personal mission. The books also show her insecurity: she name-drops 'Cornelius' before correcting herself to 'the Minister', she petulantly contacts Fudge when McGonagall bypasses her authority, and she screams accusations of ambition at McGonagall in a loss of composure. Her speech patterns include memorised bureaucratic language ('let us preserve what must be preserved, perfect what can be perfected and prune practices that ought to be prohibited'), falsely maternal diminutives toward children she is simultaneously harming, and an inability to modulate her language when genuinely enraged.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The film captures the core of Umbridge's personality very effectively. Imelda Staunton's performance delivers the girlish high pitch, the persistent smile, the saccharine classroom rituals ('Good afternoon, Professor Umbridge'), the 'hem, hem' cough, and the sharp shift from sweetness to threat. Key line deliveries — 'Oh, you won't need any ink', 'Yes? That's right. Because you know, deep down, you deserve to be punished' — preserve her controlled, pleasurable cruelty in the detention scenes. The film also preserves her bureaucratic proceduralism through the course-aims blackboard, the wands-away instruction, and her clipboard presence during inspections. The Deathly Hallows courtroom scene captures the predatory enjoyment in her prosecution of Muggle-borns and the Patronus detail (warmth for the accusers, cold for the accused) correctly translates her self-satisfaction. Her visual presentation — pink cardigan, velvet bow, kitten plates — is faithfully reproduced in both films.
personality_voice.difference: Several layers of personality texture are absent or reduced. The books' Umbridge has a demonstrable insecurity that surfaces through her correction of 'Cornelius' to 'the Minister', her tantrum when Hogwarts' Headmaster office seals itself against her, and her near-hysteria when Marietta refuses to confirm the DA's activities. The film does not show these moments of composure cracking under institutional failure. The Cruciatus scene, which is the most explicit proof in the books of her willingness to commit illegal violence on a child while justifying it as Ministry necessity, is present in the film but abbreviated: in the books she shifts her wand around Harry's body 'apparently trying to decide where it would hurt most' before the confession about the Dementors bursts out — the confession is preserved in the film but the prior physical build-up and deliberate self-justification ('You are forcing me, Potter... I am sure the Minister will understand') are compressed. The books also show Umbridge's contempt for 'half-breeds' as a distinct and sustained trait (anti-werewolf legislation, her 'extremely dangerous half-breeds' comment in the first lesson, her treatment of Hagrid), which appears in the film but only briefly and without the legislative background that makes it a conviction rather than an insult. The four scenes excluded per the non-theatrical note include her speech to students and the Trelawney inspection scene; the Trelawney inspection in particular contained extended evidence of her cold proceduralism and calculated humiliation technique. Without it, the film's Umbridge inspection characterisation rests almost entirely on the Hagrid scene.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The core personality — sweetness-as-mask, bureaucratic sadism, physical and verbal menace beneath the girlish surface — is well established in both films with specific, observable evidence. The losses are real but constitute secondary texture: the insecurity reveals, the full range of her anti-half-breed conviction, and the fine-grained procedural cruelty of the Trelawney inspection (excluded). These do not alter recognition of the character but do reduce the depth of what is shown. Score: 20 out of 25.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: Umbridge's structural function in Order of the Phoenix is multiple and interlocking: she is simultaneously the Ministry's instrument of institutional control over Hogwarts, the primary disciplinary antagonist for Harry personally (detentions, torture via quill, attempts to expel and incarcerate), the High Inquisitor who dismantles teacher autonomy and student freedom, the agent who manufactures the conditions that make the DA necessary, and the person who ultimately triggers the Ministry confrontation by pursuing Harry and Hermione into the Forest. She drives significant plot movement: she creates the Inquisitorial Squad, passes decree after decree, fires Trelawney, attempts to sack Hagrid, intercepts Harry's communications with Sirius, attempts Veritaserum interrogation, attempts the Cruciatus Curse, and is the direct cause of Harry and Hermione walking into the Forest — which leads to the centaur confrontation and Harry's decision to go to the Ministry. In Deathly Hallows she is the institutional face of Voldemort's purge of Muggle-borns, running the Muggle-Born Registration Commission with dementors present, and she possesses the Horcrux locket, which is the objective of the Ministry infiltration. Her agency is consistently active: she initiates, decides, enforces, searches, interrogates, threatens, and punishes.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: In Order of the Phoenix, the film preserves Umbridge's role as Ministry enforcer, classroom oppressor, and institutional antagonist. She passes Educational Decrees (shown via montage), fires Trelawney (Entrance Hall scene preserved), attempts to interrogate Harry about Sirius, accompanies Harry and Hermione into the Forest and is taken by centaurs. In Deathly Hallows Part 1 she is present in the Atrium, runs the Muggle-Born Registration Commission courtroom, possesses the locket, and is Stunned by Harry. These are the essential plot functions and they are present.
narrative_role_agency.difference: Several significant acts of agency are removed or curtailed. The film does not show Umbridge's attempt to use Veritaserum on Harry and Snape's active refusal to supply more — a scene in which both characters' agency is defined and their antagonism is vivid. The books' Umbridge attempts the Cruciatus Curse and is stopped only by Hermione's intervention; the film preserves this but with less textual preparation and without the full exchange in which Umbridge confesses to sending the Dementors — this confession does appear in the film, but it arrives with less dramatic weight because the lead-up (her wand moving across Harry's body, her self-justification speech) is compressed. The book's Umbridge also intercepts Harry's mail, attacks Hedwig, uses Willy Widdershins as an informant, deploys her network of surveillance across the school in ways that are shown in montage in the film but not as specific agentic acts. The Inquisitorial Squad scene (cut per non-theatrical note) removed her act of recruiting students as enforcers. More significantly, the books show Umbridge as the proximate cause of Fred and George's departure — she attempts to physically restrain them and they escape past her — while the film presents this as a spectacle with Umbridge reacting rather than actively pursuing. Her attempted sacking of Hagrid with Ministry Aurors during the Astronomy exam (books: she directs the assault, gives the order, fires Stunning Spells) is glimpsed in the film but Umbridge's personal command role in that scene is less visible. In Deathly Hallows, her courtroom role is partially transferred in focus: the film makes the Horcrux locket the primary visual and narrative focus of the scene rather than Umbridge's institutional brutality, and her prosecution of Mrs Cattermole receives less dialogue and buildup than in the book.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: The core narrative functions — institutional oppressor, DA antagonist, communications interceptor, Ministry courtroom figure, locket holder — are present. But several specific agentic moments are removed (Veritaserum confrontation with Snape, the full Cruciatus sequence, the Hagrid night assault) or compressed to montage (the decree-passing campaign). The transfer rule applies to the Veritaserum scene: in the books Snape actively undermines Umbridge by lying about having no more Veritaserum; the film shows this scene but truncates it significantly, reducing Umbridge's agency in the interrogation and Snape's counter-agency. Score: 15 out of 20.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Umbridge's motivations are layered. At the surface level she is acting on Ministry orders — Fudge wants Hogwarts controlled and any mention of Voldemort's return suppressed. But the books establish that her motivations go beyond obedience: she personally volunteered to act when others were merely talking ('They were all bleating about silencing you somehow — discrediting you — but I was the one who actually did something about it'). She has genuine ideological convictions about blood purity (the anti-werewolf legislation, her contempt for 'half-breeds') that precede and exceed her Ministry role. She derives personal pleasure from authority and from the suffering of those she punishes — this is an internal drive, not simply professional conduct. She experiences something close to joy during Trelawney's humiliation and during Harry's detentions. Her internal conflict, such as it is, is visible in the Cruciatus scene: she shifts her weight, talks herself into it, justifies it repeatedly ('You are forcing me, Potter'), suggesting that even she recognises the line she is crossing — though she crosses it anyway. In Deathly Hallows her motivation is to advance within the new regime by demonstrating zealous enforcement of its ideology.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The film preserves the Ministry-as-motivation clearly and establishes her personal investment through the detention scenes and the 'you deserve to be punished' line. Her Dementor confession preserves the personal initiative motivation. In Deathly Hallows, the courtroom scene shows her enforcing blood-purity ideology actively, and the detail of her claiming the locket as a 'family heirloom' (in the book) appears to be streamlined in the film — the locket is simply around her neck without the dialogue about Selwyn ancestry. The Patronus detail (her cat Patronus, bright because she is happy in her element) is a strong, economical translation of her self-satisfaction motivation.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The blood-purity ideology as a sustained personal conviction is underweighted in the film. In the books, the anti-werewolf legislation and her 'half-breed' contempt across multiple scenes establish this as a deep conviction; the film shows it briefly in her treatment of Hagrid and in the Muggle-Born Registration Commission but without the legislative backstory that makes it a revealed character motivation rather than incidental cruelty. The self-justification arc in the Cruciatus scene — where she works herself up and talks herself through the moral threshold — is compressed in the film. The books show her motivation for the Dementor attack as genuinely self-initiated action, and this is preserved in the film's dialogue, though the weight of the revelation is reduced by the scene's pacing.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: Core motivations (Ministry enforcement, personal pleasure in authority, genuine ideological conviction) are present and recognisable. The ideology motivation is underexplained relative to the books but not absent. The self-justification texture of the Cruciatus scene is simplified but the essential motivation is intact. Score: 11 out of 15.

character_arc.book_baseline: Umbridge's arc in Order of the Phoenix is a rise-and-fall structure: she arrives as an unknown quantity, rapidly accumulates institutional power (High Inquisitor, then Headmistress), reaches her apex when Dumbledore flees and she effectively controls Hogwarts, and then collapses — her office seals against her, the school resists her en masse (Peeves, Skiving Snackboxes, Nifflers), Fred and George humiliate her publicly, the teachers passively undermine her, and she is ultimately carried away by centaurs in a scene of complete loss of control and dignity. Her return to the hospital wing — silent, unable to speak, trembling at hoof-sounds — and her final departure (chased by Peeves) completes the humiliation. In Deathly Hallows she has a smaller but coherent arc within the infiltration sequence: she is in institutional power, conducting interrogations from a position of authority, and is Stunned and stripped of the Horcrux. The arc is flat in the sense that she does not change internally — she remains what she is — but her external trajectory is a clear rise-and-fall.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The film follows the same rise-and-fall structure in Order of the Phoenix: establishment, accumulation of power (decree montage), Headmistress appointment, resistance from students and staff, Forest scene and centaur removal. The Deathly Hallows arc (institutional authority → Stunned) is preserved. The post-Forest hospital wing scene, which shows the depth of her psychological collapse (the hoof-sound trigger), is present in the film.
character_arc.difference: The peak of Umbridge's power is less fully dramatised in the film than in the books. The books show her Headmistress period as a time of sustained, escalating institutional dominance — new decrees appearing daily, teachers being systematically undermined, Hagrid's attempted sacking with Aurors, the Niffler incidents, Peeves's campaign against her. The film compresses this into a montage and selected scenes, which means the depth of her reach and the scale of the resistance it provokes are both underrepresented. The specific arc beat of Hogwarts sealing its office against her (a moment of institutional rejection that is particularly humiliating given her power-accumulation arc) is mentioned in the books but not shown in the film. The hospital wing collapse is shown but briefly. These are compression losses rather than arc alterations.
character_arc.penalty_logic: The structural arc — rise, apex, collapse, humiliation — is intact and faithfully rendered in both films. The compression of the Headmistress period slightly reduces the peak of the arc, which in turn slightly reduces the impact of the fall, but the arc's shape and trajectory are correct. Score: 13 out of 15.

key_relationships.book_baseline: The books establish several key relationships. With Harry: it is a sustained, escalating personal antagonism in which she specifically targets him, uses his detentions as a method of psychological attrition, and takes evident pleasure in his suffering. The relationship is personal, not merely professional — she notes his scars with satisfaction, tries to trap him repeatedly, and he carries the physical reminder of her cruelty (the hand scars) throughout the rest of the series. With Fudge: she is his instrument but also his initiative — she acts before he asks, she contacts him directly when McGonagall bypasses her, she name-drops him in ways that reveal both dependence and a sense of personal alliance ('Cornelius just sent it'). With McGonagall: the relationship is one of sustained institutional conflict and open contempt on both sides; their confrontations (the careers meeting, the Quidditch ban, the Trelawney dismissal) are among the most vivid relationship dynamics in the book. With Dumbledore: she cannot touch him directly and is visibly diminished every time he acts — his appointment of Firenze, his response to her Trelawney dismissal, his escape — and her impotent fury in these moments is a key character beat. With teachers generally: she uses inspections as instruments of humiliation, particularly toward Trelawney and Hagrid, and is actively resisted by the rest of the staff in ways that demonstrate their collective judgment of her.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The Harry/Umbridge relationship is well preserved through the detention scenes, the classroom confrontations, and the Forest sequence. The McGonagall/Umbridge relationship is shown in the Quidditch ban scene and the careers meeting (truncated) and the Trelawney dismissal scene. The Fudge/Umbridge relationship is established but not explored in depth — in the film Fudge is more of a principal and Umbridge more of a subordinate, whereas the books show her as genuinely self-initiating. The Dumbledore/Umbridge dynamic is present (she cannot act against him directly, he outmanoeuvres her over Trelawney and Firenze, he escapes from her office) but the sustained quality of her impotent fury around Dumbledore is underrepresented. The Hagrid/Umbridge relationship is shown in the hut scene and the Thestral lesson, which is present in the theatrical cut (unlike the Trelawney inspection, which is excluded).
key_relationships.difference: The Trelawney inspection (excluded per non-theatrical note) was the primary source of the Umbridge/Trelawney relationship dynamic, which in the books is a sustained campaign of professional humiliation across multiple inspection visits. Its removal means that the Trelawney dismissal scene in the film arrives without the gradual build-up that makes it a culmination of a relationship rather than a single event. The Umbridge/Snape relationship — in which she suspects him, questions him about his career history, and eventually tries to use him as a tool in the Veritaserum interrogation — is present in the film but significantly abbreviated; the inspection of his class and her probing questions about why Dumbledore won't appoint him (a moment of subtle cruelty toward Snape that also reveals her intelligence as an interrogator) is compressed to a brief exchange. The Fudge/Umbridge relationship loses the nuance of her self-initiative relative to him. The McGonagall/Umbridge relationship is the best-preserved of the secondary relationships, with the Quidditch ban confrontation and Trelawney dismissal scene both present.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: The Harry/Umbridge relationship is faithfully rendered. The McGonagall/Umbridge relationship is substantially preserved. The Trelawney/Umbridge relationship loses its gradual dimension due to the excluded inspection scene. The Snape/Umbridge and Fudge/Umbridge relationships are compressed in ways that remove important dynamic texture. Score: 7 out of 10.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: Umbridge's complexity in the books derives from several sources. First, the gap between her surface and interior is maintained at a very fine grain — even small moments (her correction of 'Cornelius' to 'the Minister', her tantrum at the sealed office, her near-hysteria when Marietta refuses to cooperate) reveal insecurity beneath the authoritarian performance. Second, her blood-purity ideology is given legislative specificity (anti-werewolf legislation) that makes it a conviction rather than incidental cruelty. Third, her capacity for institutional intelligence is shown: she plants informants (Willy Widdershins), monitors communications through multiple channels (mail, fires, the school floo), uses Filch's knowledge of the school, recruits the Inquisitorial Squad, places stealth-sensing spells on her office, and ultimately identifies and exploits the weak link in the DA (Marietta). This makes her a genuinely formidable antagonist rather than simply a bully. Fourth, her relationship with pleasure is specific and disturbing: she enjoys her work. The books show her in moments of 'gloating enjoyment', 'callous pleasure', and a 'nastily eager, excited look' before the Cruciatus attempt. Fifth, her self-deception — framing her torture of a child as being 'for their own good', framing the Dementor attack as 'doing what had to be done' — adds a layer of ideological self-justification that makes her more than a simple villain. In Deathly Hallows, her claiming the Horcrux locket as a 'Selwyn family heirloom' reveals her blood-purity pretension and social climbing as additional character texture.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The film preserves the core contradiction (sweetness/cruelty) and the pleasure-in-authority trait visibly. The detention scenes, the Trelawney dismissal, and the courtroom sequence all show her enjoying her work. Her institutional intelligence is partially shown (stealth sensing spells referenced in the film's forest sequence setup, the interception of mail referenced by Sirius). The Deathly Hallows courtroom scene with dementors and the Patronus detail preserves the ideological self-satisfaction effectively.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The Trelawney inspection sequence (excluded per non-theatrical note), which was the most extended demonstration of her precision as a bureaucratic tormentor — the clipboard notes, the impossible demands, the condescending questions calibrated to humiliate — is entirely absent from the theatrical film. This removes a layer of her professional competence and the specific pleasure she takes in systematic institutional cruelty as distinct from physical cruelty. The full Marietta sequence — in which Umbridge loses composure when her witness refuses to cooperate, physically shakes her, is restrained by Kingsley, and then has to recover her poise — is present in the books but absent from the film (the DA discovery is handled differently, with Umbridge using Bombarda Maxima on the Room of Requirement rather than an informant). This removes both a moment of vulnerability/loss of control and the specific texture of her operating through informants and procedural manipulation. The Hagrid night assault — where she personally commands Ministry Aurors in a midnight attack — is glimpsed but Umbridge's personal command role in it is not prominent in the film. The locket Selwyn dialogue from Deathly Hallows (in the book she claims it as a family heirloom) is absent from the film, removing a revealing moment of social pretension. The anti-werewolf legislation background, which explains her half-breed contempt as ideological rather than incidental, is mentioned by Sirius in the book but not in the film.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: The most significant complexity losses are: (1) the Trelawney inspection material (excluded, removing her most detailed demonstration of bureaucratic precision as sadism); (2) the Marietta interrogation sequence (absent from film, removing vulnerability and a specific intelligence-based method of operation); (3) the blood-purity legislative backstory (absent, reducing her ideology from conviction to behaviour); (4) the Selwyn locket dialogue (absent, removing social pretension detail). Together these constitute a noticeable simplification: the film's Umbridge is recognisably the same character but without the full texture of her institutional intelligence, her specific ideological architecture, and her moments of composure-cracking failure. Score: 9 out of 15.

score_caps_applied: Cap 3 (score not above 75 if a core book function, decision, or act of agency is transferred or removed) — applied: the Marietta informant sequence, which is Umbridge's most sustained exercise of intelligence-based agency in the books, is entirely absent from the film (replaced by Bombarda Maxima on the Room of Requirement wall); the Trelawney inspection is excluded; the Veritaserum interrogation scene is significantly compressed. These collectively constitute removal of core agentic functions. Total held at 75.
comparative.key_observations: The film adaptation of Umbridge is substantially faithful — the core character (sweetness-as-mask, bureaucratic sadism, institutional cruelty, pleasure in authority, blood-purity ideology) is well preserved and Imelda Staunton's performance carries the personality with high fidelity. The detention scenes, the Trelawney dismissal, the Forest sequence, and the Deathly Hallows courtroom are all effective translations. The losses are real but concentrated in specific areas: the excluded Trelawney inspection removes her most precise demonstration of professional sadism; the absent Marietta sequence removes her most complex exercise of institutional intelligence; and the blood-purity ideology loses its legislative specificity. The result is a character who is fully recognisable and effectively menacing, but slightly simplified — the film's Umbridge is a bully who enjoys power, while the book's Umbridge is additionally a competent, ideologically motivated institutional operator who uses procedure itself as an instrument of cruelty. The total of 75 reflects this: faithful in the essentials, reduced in the texture that made her one of the most precisely drawn antagonists in the series.

personality_voice.book_baseline: In the books, Madam Pince is established through repeated, consistent behavioral patterns across multiple novels. She is described physically as 'thin, irritable' and 'like an underfed vulture,' with 'sunken cheeks,' 'skin like parchment,' and a 'long hooked nose.' Her dominant traits are extreme territorial protectiveness over her books, chronic suspicion of students, and a hair-trigger temper. She interrogates students ('What are you looking for, boy?'), drives them out without cause ('You'd better get out, then. Go on -- out!'), holds notes up to the light to detect forgeries, 'stalks' between shelves, extinguishes lamps to chase students out, and — most dramatically — uses her wand to make Harry's books and bag chase and whack him out of the library when she finds chocolate near them. Her voice and manner are consistently hostile, bureaucratic, and contemptuous. She also has a comic undertone: the aside that she and Filch might be 'secretly in love' gives her a faint grotesque-romantic dimension. She 'prowls the aisles menacingly, breathing down the necks of those touching her precious books' and squeaks slightly as she walks.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: In the film corpus, Madam Pince appears in only two meaningful moments. In Chamber of Secrets (Film Scene 2), she is referenced indirectly: Ron relays her message to Hermione in the hospital wing — 'Madam Pince asked that we relay a message to you, Hermione: She'd appreciate it if you'd leave a few books for the rest of the school.' In Film Scene 2 (the library scene in CoS), she is briefly shown at her desk and described only in the stage direction as someone Harry notices eyeing him from her desk. In the Half-Blood Prince film corpus (Scene 3), she does not appear at all. The corpus provides no direct film dialogue from Pince herself and no active scene in which her personality is expressed through her own behavior.
personality_voice.difference: The core personality traits — aggressive territorial protectiveness, suspicion, hostility, the vulture-like physical presence, the capacity for dramatic punitive action — are established in the books through repeated direct scenes. The film corpus contains no scene where Pince herself speaks, acts, or displays these traits directly. The single reference to her (the relayed message about books) is broadly consistent with her character — it implies she complained about Hermione borrowing too many books — but it is a secondhand account delivered by Ron, not a direct portrayal. The vivid behavioral texture (wand-chasing students, holding notes to the light, stalking aisles, squeaking shoes) is entirely absent from this film corpus.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The personality conveyed by the indirect reference is not wrong — it is plausibly consistent with book Pince. However, the corpus provides no direct evidence of her voice, behavior, or emotional tone in the films. The relayed message preserves one surface trait (possessiveness over books) but does not constitute a full portrayal of her personality. Per the scoring rubric, the main personality is preserved in outline but there is significant loss of secondary traits, tone, and behavioral texture. A score in the 18–22 range is appropriate: the trait that is shown is correct, but most of her defining voice and manner is absent from this corpus. Score: 18.
personality_voice.evidence_status: Directly evidenced (book baseline across multiple scenes); Reasonably inferred for film (the relayed message implies book-consistent protectiveness, but her actual voice and behavior are not shown in this corpus).

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: In the books, Pince serves several consistent narrative functions: (1) she is an environmental obstacle — her presence prevents characters from researching freely, raises stakes of library scenes, and forces characters to be covert; (2) she is a gatekeeper of restricted knowledge — she must be shown signed notes, she controls access to restricted section books, and she can help or obstruct research; (3) she occasionally provides mild comic relief through her extreme reactions; (4) she is a minor atmospheric anchor for the library as a dangerous, policed space. She has limited but real agency: she drives Harry out, she evaluates Lockhart's note, she extinguishes lamps to end research sessions, she wields her wand against students who violate library rules. She also plays a small but noted role at Dumbledore's funeral, standing beside Filch in a black veil.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: In the film corpus, Pince's narrative function is reduced to a single indirect reference (Ron relaying her complaint about books) and one visual appearance at her desk in a library scene where she is not described as doing anything consequential. She does not act as a gatekeeper, does not obstruct research, does not appear as an active environmental presence. Her funeral appearance is not evidenced in the film corpus provided.
narrative_role_agency.difference: The environmental obstacle and gatekeeper functions are not demonstrated in this corpus. The one moment where she is referenced is consistent but passive — her complaint is relayed through Ron rather than enacted directly. She does not drive anyone out, evaluate notes, restrict access, or otherwise exercise the minor but real agency she has in the books.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: Her role is recognizable in principle — the relayed complaint implies she still monitors book borrowing — but her active gatekeeper and obstacle functions are absent from this corpus. Per the rubric, role and agency are reduced but recognizable. Score: 14.
narrative_role_agency.evidence_status: Directly evidenced (book role across multiple scenes); Not enough evidence to confirm or deny full film role from this corpus alone.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Pince's motivations in the books are simple but consistent: an intense, almost pathological attachment to the library's books as objects to be protected from students. This manifests as suspicion (assuming students will damage or steal), territoriality (enforcing closing times, demanding notes), and punitive action (chasing students out with bewitched objects). There is no significant internal conflict — her motivation is one-dimensional but clearly established. The comic hint of a romantic attachment to Filch adds a faint personal dimension but is not developed.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The relayed message ('She'd appreciate it if you'd leave a few books for the rest of the school') is consistent with the same motivation — possessiveness over the library's collection. No internal conflict is shown, which is consistent with the books where none exists meaningfully.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The motivation is consistent with what the books establish. No change is detectable. The simplicity of her motivation means there is not much to lose here.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: The motivation preserved in the film reference matches the book baseline. The simplicity means this dimension is inherently limited in scope. A score of 12 reflects that the motivation is consistent but the evidence is too thin to score higher with confidence. Score: 12.
motivations_internal_conflict.evidence_status: Reasonably inferred for both book and film; the motivation is consistent but the film corpus is too limited to confirm fully.

character_arc.book_baseline: Pince has no character arc across the series. She is intentionally flat — the same irritable, book-protective librarian in book 1 as in book 6. The one slight development is the hint in HBP that she may have a personal relationship with Filch, and her appearance at Dumbledore's funeral in a black veil. These are not arc developments but texture additions. A flat arc, if intentionally flat, should not be penalized.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The corpus provides no evidence of any change or development, which is consistent with a flat arc.
character_arc.difference: No arc in the books; no arc in the films. This is consistent.
character_arc.penalty_logic: Per the scoring rule, a character whose arc is flat in the books and flat in the films scores full points. Score: 14.
character_arc.evidence_status: Directly evidenced (book baseline consistently flat across all corpus scenes; film corpus consistent with this).

key_relationships.book_baseline: Pince's most notable relationship in the books is her dynamic with students — specifically as an authority figure defined by hostility and suspicion toward them. The books also plant a comic suggestion (treated as school gossip by Harry and Hermione) that she and Filch may be 'secretly in love.' This is not developed narratively but gives her a minor relational texture. Her relationship with Filch — two bitter, rule-obsessed servants of the school — is tonally coherent. She also has a functional relationship with teachers, accepting signed notes from them as validation for restricted access.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: No direct relationship dynamic with any character is shown in the film corpus. The relayed message involves Ron passing on her words to Hermione, which is not a direct relationship scene. The Filch connection is not evidenced in this corpus.
key_relationships.difference: The Filch relationship and the student-hostility dynamic are not shown in the film corpus. The note-authority relationship with teachers is also absent.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: The relationships are not present in the film corpus, but for a very minor character, their absence is partly a function of reduced presence rather than active alteration of the dynamic. What little is shown (possessiveness toward students' use of books) is directionally consistent with the book dynamic. However, the Filch connection — a small but humanizing note in the books — is entirely absent from this corpus. Score: 7.
key_relationships.evidence_status: Directly evidenced in books; Not enough evidence from film corpus.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: Pince is not a complex character, but the books give her specific texture: the vulture-like physicality, the wand-wielding punitive action against students who bring food near books, the shoe squeak as she patrols, the way she holds notes to the light suspecting forgery, the closing-time ritual of extinguishing lamps, and the comedy of the Filch romantic speculation. These details create a vivid minor character who is more than just 'strict librarian.' Her appearance at Dumbledore's funeral in a thick black veil is a small but humanizing detail suggesting she had genuine feeling for Dumbledore or the institution.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: None of this texture is present in the film corpus. The single reference reduces her to her most basic trait (book possessiveness) without any of the behavioral specificity, physical description, or comic dimension.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The punitive wand use, the forgery-suspecting note inspection, the closing-time lamp extinguishing, the shoe squeak, the Filch speculation, and the funeral appearance are all absent from this corpus. What remains is one surface-level consistent trait delivered secondhand.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: For a minor character, the standard is not to penalize merely for less material unless it changes characterization. The material that is present is consistent, not contradictory. However, the removal of the behavioral specificity that makes her a vivid minor character — particularly the wand-chasing scene which is her most memorable and defining book moment — represents a real loss of nuance. The character is reduced to a name and a single implied trait rather than a living minor presence. Score: 10.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.evidence_status: Directly evidenced in books; film corpus too limited for full assessment.

lost_or_transferred_material: Pince's wand-chasing scene (HBP, chasing Harry and Ginny out of the library for bringing chocolate) — her most dramatically vivid book moment — is absent from the film corpus
Physical description as 'underfed vulture' / 'shrivelled face' / 'skin like parchment' / shoe-squeaking patrol — atmospheric texture absent from film corpus
Scene of Pince holding Lockhart's signed note up to the light to detect forgery — gatekeeper function not shown
Pince extinguishing lamps to force Harry out of the library during Triwizard research — active obstacle function absent
Pince's appearance at Dumbledore's funeral in a thick black veil beside Filch — humanizing detail absent from film corpus
Comic speculation by Harry and Hermione that Pince and Filch may be secretly in love — relational texture absent
comparative.key_observations: Madam Pince is a minor recurring character whose book portrayal is defined less by plot importance than by consistent behavioral texture: the vulture-like physicality, the punitive wand use, the forgery-suspecting gatekeeping, and the comic Filch relationship hint. The film corpus provides almost no direct portrayal — a single relayed secondhand complaint and one background visual appearance. The one piece of film evidence is directionally consistent with her book characterization (book possessiveness intact), preventing a lower score, but the vivid behavioral specificity that makes her a memorable minor character is entirely absent. Confidence is Medium overall because the character is minor enough that her limited film presence is partly expected, but the corpus is too thin to fully assess whether her characterization was actively altered or merely compressed. The score of 75 reflects a character whose core trait survives in outline form but whose defining texture, agency, and relational dimension are unconfirmed or absent in the available film material.

personality_voice.book_baseline: The Basilisk in the books is defined almost entirely through behavioral and physical description rather than interiority. Its 'personality' is that of an apex predator: relentless, methodical, and obedient to Parseltongue command. It does not hesitate, does not retreat except from roosters, and pursues Harry with heavy, deliberate movement. The book conveys its presence through sound (the slithering, the weight of its body on the floor), physical scale (fangs long as sabers, mouth wide enough to swallow Harry whole), and the visceral danger it radiates. It snaps furiously at Fawkes, lunges with precision, and when blinded continues to hunt by sound and smell. It is not malevolent in a thinking sense - it is an instrument of destruction, but one with animal persistence and ferocity.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The film preserves the core behavioral identity: the Basilisk is large, lethal, obedient to Riddle's Parseltongue commands, and hunts Harry after being blinded by Fawkes. It hisses in pain, thrashes, and strikes blindly. The film adds a roar when blinded, which is not in the books, and the physical confrontation is rendered as a more dynamic action sequence (Harry climbing the statue, sliding down the serpent's back). The fundamental behavioral pattern - predatory, relentless, instrument of Riddle - is intact.
personality_voice.difference: The film adds a roar to the Basilisk when blinded, which is a minor addition not in the books. The book's Basilisk is described as hissing and snapping, not roaring. The film also compresses the hunt sequence, removing the moment where Harry hides in an alcove and the snake nearly finds him by smell alone - a scene that emphasizes the creature's sensory hunting rather than brute force. The book's emphasis on the weight and sound of the creature ('heavy body slithering heavily across the dusty floor') is partially lost in the film's more visually kinetic presentation.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The Basilisk has no true personality in the human sense - it is an animal. Its 'voice' is physical presence and behavioral pattern. The film preserves the essential pattern (predatory, obedient, lethal) but adds a roar and shifts emphasis from slow dread to kinetic action. This is a minor change that slightly alters the creature's texture without fundamentally changing what it is. A small penalty is warranted for the roar addition and the loss of the alcove scene's sensory-hunting emphasis.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: The Basilisk's narrative role is threefold: (1) it is the instrument of Slytherin's will, the weapon that has been petrifying and threatening to kill students; (2) it is the climactic physical antagonist Harry must defeat; (3) its venom and fang become plot-critical tools - the fang kills Harry in book 7's terms (via Horcrux destruction) and the venom nearly kills Harry in book 2. Its agency is entirely reactive - it acts only when called - but within that constraint it is the primary physical threat of the entire book.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: The film preserves all three functions. The Basilisk is still the weapon behind the attacks, still the climactic antagonist Harry fights, and its fang is still used to destroy the diary Horcrux. In Deathly Hallows Part 1 and Part 2 (film corpus scenes 2-4), the basilisk fang's role as a Horcrux-destroying tool is preserved, with Hermione explaining the sword's impregnation with basilisk venom and the fang being used to destroy the diadem.
narrative_role_agency.difference: In the books, the basilisk fang used to destroy the diary in book 2 is the same fang Harry pulls from his own arm - a moment of desperate improvisation. In the film this beat is preserved. However, in Deathly Hallows, the book has Ron retrieve basilisk fangs from the Chamber himself (with Hermione), which is a significant act of agency and initiative for Ron. The film corpus (scene 2) shows Hermione explaining the basilisk venom connection, and scene 3 shows Hermione tossing Harry a basilisk fang to destroy the diadem - the retrieval of the fangs by Ron and Hermione from the Chamber is present in the film (DH Part 2) but the corpus here only partially captures it. The Basilisk's own narrative role is not diminished.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: The Basilisk's own role and agency are preserved. The minor penalty reflects that the film's action-sequence framing slightly reduces the creature's function as a source of slow, inescapable dread (which is part of its narrative role in building tension) in favor of a more conventional monster-fight structure. This is a compression that modestly affects function.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: The Basilisk has no internal conflict and no motivation beyond obedience to Parseltongue command. It is an animal. Its 'motivation' is purely instinctual: it kills what it is told to kill, flees from roosters, and is driven by predatory instinct when hunting. There is no internal contradiction or moral dimension to evaluate.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The film portrays the same absence of internal motivation - the Basilisk acts on Riddle's commands and hunts by instinct when blinded. This is fully consistent.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: No meaningful difference. The Basilisk has no motivations or internal conflict in either medium.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: No penalty. A creature with no internal motivation in the books cannot be penalized for lacking internal motivation in the films. The score reflects the ceiling imposed by the character's nature rather than any adaptation failure. A score in the 11-13 range is appropriate because the motivations that exist (pure obedience/instinct) are correctly preserved, but the dimension is inherently limited for this character.

character_arc.book_baseline: The Basilisk has no character arc in the traditional sense. It enters the story as a weapon, functions as a weapon, and dies as a weapon. Its trajectory is flat by design: it does not change, learn, or develop. The only 'arc' is its physical journey from the Chamber to death at Harry's hands, which is a plot arc rather than a character arc.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The film preserves this flat trajectory exactly. The Basilisk appears, hunts, is blinded, continues to hunt, and is killed. No arc is invented or removed.
character_arc.difference: No difference. The arc is flat in both, intentionally.
character_arc.penalty_logic: No penalty. Per the scoring rules, a character with an intentionally flat arc in the books scores full points if the arc is equally flat in the films. The score reflects the inherent ceiling for a non-developing creature rather than any adaptation failure.

key_relationships.book_baseline: The Basilisk has two meaningful relational dynamics in the books. First, its relationship with Riddle/Voldemort: it is an instrument of his will, called by Parseltongue, and this relationship defines its entire existence in the story. Second, its relationship with Harry as antagonist: the fight between them is the climax of book 2, and the creature's venom nearly kills Harry, creating a physical and symbolic bond (the fang later destroys Horcruxes). The book also establishes the Basilisk's relationship with spiders (mortal enemies who flee it) and roosters (fatal to it), which are narratively important clues.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The Riddle-Basilisk relationship is preserved: Riddle calls it in Parseltongue and commands it to kill Harry. The Harry-Basilisk antagonist dynamic is preserved through the fight sequence. The spider-fleeing detail is referenced in the film corpus (the paper Hermione left mentions 'spiders flee before it') and the rooster detail is mentioned. However, the film does not show the roosters being killed by the Heir of Slytherin to prevent the Basilisk from being harmed - this is only referenced in the book corpus as a deduction Harry makes. The film compresses the relational texture between the Basilisk and its ecological enemies.
key_relationships.difference: The rooster-killing subplot (Hagrid's roosters being killed to protect the Basilisk) is absent from the film as an active plot element, though the rooster detail is mentioned in the paper. The spider-fleeing relationship is referenced but not dramatized. These are minor compressions. The core relationships (Riddle's instrument, Harry's antagonist) are intact.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: Minor penalty for the loss of the rooster subplot as an active relational element - in the books this is a clue that reveals the Heir of Slytherin's protective relationship with the Basilisk, adding a layer to how Riddle manages and protects his weapon. The film reduces this to a passing reference. The core dynamics are preserved.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: The Basilisk's complexity in the books is primarily physical and atmospheric rather than psychological. Key nuances include: (1) the creature's vulnerability - it can be killed by a rooster's crow, it flees spiders, it can be blinded; (2) the sensory hunting after blinding - it tracks Harry by sound and smell, creating a specific kind of dread distinct from visual threat; (3) the alcove scene where Harry hides and the snake nearly detects him, emphasizing the creature's sensory acuity; (4) the physical cost of killing it - the fang that kills Harry is the same fang that nearly kills Harry, creating a symmetry of destruction; (5) the creature's role as a centuries-old being ('may live many hundreds of years') that has been dormant and is now unleashed.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The film preserves the vulnerability (blinding by Fawkes, killed by the sword), the physical cost (fang in Harry's arm), and the sensory hunting in a compressed form. The alcove scene is present in the film corpus (Harry hides in a side tunnel, the snake's head enters and withdraws). The centuries-old nature is not emphasized. The film adds kinetic spectacle (Harry climbing the statue, sliding down the snake) that replaces some of the book's atmospheric dread with action-movie energy.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The most significant loss is the atmospheric texture of the book's hunt sequence - the slow, heavy, sound-based dread of a blinded creature tracking by smell and hearing. The film's version is more visually dynamic and faster-paced, which changes the emotional register from horror to action. The alcove scene is present but compressed. The rooster subplot's nuance (the Heir actively protecting the Basilisk) is reduced. The creature's ancient nature is not conveyed.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: The shift from atmospheric dread to kinetic action is a meaningful change in how the Basilisk functions as a source of terror - the book's version is more psychologically unsettling (the creature that can kill you without you seeing it, that hunts by sound in the dark) while the film's is more conventionally monstrous. This is a noticeable simplification of the creature's horror register, warranting a moderate penalty. The core physical facts are preserved but the texture that makes the Basilisk specifically frightening in the books is partially lost.

lost_or_transferred_material: The slow, atmospheric dread of the blinded Basilisk hunting Harry by sound and smell is compressed into a faster action sequence
The alcove scene where the Basilisk's head enters inches from Harry's face and withdraws is present in the film but significantly compressed
The roosters being killed by the Heir of Slytherin to protect the Basilisk is reduced from an active plot clue to a passing reference
The book's emphasis on the Basilisk's weight and sound ('heavy body slithering heavily across the dusty floor') as primary horror elements is replaced by visual spectacle
The Basilisk's centuries-old nature ('may live many hundreds of years') is not conveyed in the film

The specific detail that Hermione deduced the Basilisk's identity and wrote 'Pipes' on the page is preserved in the film but the full chain of Hermione's reasoning (given to Harry in the film) slightly redistributes the deductive agency
comparative.key_observations: The Basilisk is a non-psychological character whose faithfulness is measured primarily through behavioral pattern, physical presence, narrative function, and atmospheric register. The film preserves all core functions - instrument of Riddle, climactic antagonist, source of plot-critical venom and fangs - and the essential behavioral identity (predatory, obedient, lethal, vulnerable to blinding and roosters). The primary adaptation loss is tonal: the book constructs the Basilisk as a source of slow, sensory, atmospheric horror (a creature that kills without being seen, that hunts by sound in darkness), while the film renders it as a more conventional action-movie monster. This shift in register is real but does not fundamentally alter what the Basilisk is or does. The score of 75 reflects a faithful but tonally compressed adaptation of a character whose complexity was always more atmospheric than psychological.

personality_voice.book_baseline: Fudge in the books is a portly, bowler-hat-wearing bureaucrat defined by a cluster of observable traits: fatherly warmth toward Harry in early books (buttering crumpets, smiling 'like an uncle'), political anxiety expressed through fidgeting with his bowler and sweating, a tendency to bluster and defer to pressure rather than principle, clipped officiousness when acting under Ministry mandate, and a capacity for genuine cruelty when his power is threatened. His speech patterns shift across the series: early on he is jovial, verbose, and slightly pompous ('Oh, my dear boy, we're not going to punish you for a little thing like that!'); by GoF and OotP he becomes defensive, snarling, and paranoid ('YOU SEE? roared Fudge'). He is capable of warmth, pettiness, cowardice, and self-deception simultaneously. His voice is distinctively that of a small man who has convinced himself he is a large one.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The films preserve the core surface traits: the lime-green bowler, the portly figure, the pinstriped cloak, the fatherly early manner with Harry at the Leaky Cauldron (PoA film), the clipped officiousness when sending Hagrid to Azkaban (CoS film), the bluster and paranoia in the OotP hearing and confrontation with Dumbledore. Robert Hardy's performance captures the shift from jovial to defensive. The Leaky Cauldron scene in PoA preserves the nervous evasiveness about Sirius. The OotP hearing preserves the snarling, supercilious tone ('I'm sorry to interrupt what I'm sure would have been a very well-rehearsed story'). The confrontation with Dumbledore at the end of OotP preserves the outrage and bluster.
personality_voice.difference: The films compress or omit several voice-defining moments. The extended Three Broomsticks conversation in PoA — where Fudge holds court, tells the story of Pettigrew's death with emotional weight, shudders at the memory of the crime scene, and shows genuine complexity — is heavily truncated in the film, with McGonagall taking over much of the narrative function. The HBP chapter where Fudge visits the Muggle Prime Minister — one of the richest characterisation passages in the books, showing his self-importance, his nervous energy, his diminished state after being sacked, and his bitter final line — is entirely absent from the films. The GoF hospital wing confrontation, where Fudge's obstinacy is shown in granular detail across many exchanges, is compressed but the essential beats survive. The film Fudge is slightly more one-dimensionally pompous and slightly less capable of the fatherly warmth that makes his later betrayal of Harry more pointed.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The core personality — pompous, cowardly, politically self-serving, capable of warmth that curdles into hostility — is preserved. The shift from jovial to paranoid is present. The bowler-fidgeting, the bluster, the sweating are all there. The loss of the Prime Minister scenes removes a significant register of his voice (the self-important explainer, the man who has convinced himself he is doing fine), and the truncation of the Three Broomsticks scene reduces his emotional texture. These are real losses but not transformative ones. The character remains recognisable and largely faithful. Minor simplification warrants a score in the 18–22 range.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: Fudge serves multiple structural functions across the books: (1) institutional obstacle — he represents the Ministry's failure to act, and his decisions directly shape the plot (sending Hagrid to Azkaban, suspending Dumbledore, refusing to believe Voldemort has returned, placing Umbridge at Hogwarts, holding the rigged hearing against Harry); (2) information conduit — the Three Broomsticks scene in PoA is the primary vehicle by which Harry (and the reader) learns the full backstory of Sirius Black and the Potters; (3) antagonist-by-cowardice in OotP — his campaign against Harry and Dumbledore drives the entire institutional conflict of that book; (4) witness to Voldemort's return at the end of OotP, which forces the plot turn into HBP. He initiates, decides, and changes events throughout.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: The films preserve his role as institutional obstacle and his function as the Ministry's face of denial. The CoS scene (sending Hagrid to Azkaban) is intact. The PoA Leaky Cauldron scene preserves his role as the nervous authority figure managing Harry. The OotP hearing preserves his role as antagonist-prosecutor. The end of OotP preserves his role as the man who finally sees Voldemort and is forced to acknowledge the truth. The GoF hospital wing confrontation preserves his refusal to act.
narrative_role_agency.difference: The Three Broomsticks scene in PoA is significantly restructured in the film: Fudge's role as the primary narrator of the Pettigrew/Black backstory is transferred largely to McGonagall. In the book, Fudge leads the conversation, provides the most detail, and delivers the emotionally resonant account of the crime scene. In the film, McGonagall carries most of the exposition. This is a direct transfer of a narrative function. Additionally, the HBP Prime Minister scene — where Fudge's role as the man who failed and must now introduce his successor is a key structural beat — is absent from the films entirely, removing his final narrative function. His role in GoF as the man who refuses to act after Cedric's death is compressed but present.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: The transfer of the Three Broomsticks narration from Fudge to McGonagall is a clear agency transfer under the transfer rule. Fudge still appears in the scene in the film, but his role as the primary explainer and the emotional weight of his account ('I still dream about it sometimes') is given to McGonagall. This warrants a penalty. The absence of the HBP scene removes his final narrative function entirely. However, his role as institutional obstacle and antagonist across CoS, PoA, GoF, and OotP is substantially preserved. The penalty is real but not catastrophic.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Fudge's motivations are clearly established across the books: (1) love of office and fear of losing power — explicitly stated by Lupin, Tonks, and Dumbledore in OotP ('he's become fond of power'); (2) fear of Dumbledore as a rival — he believes Dumbledore wants to be Minister and is destabilising him; (3) self-deception as a coping mechanism — he genuinely convinces himself that Voldemort has not returned because accepting it would mean his comfortable world is over; (4) political cowardice — he acts under pressure from figures like Lucius Malfoy rather than from principle. His internal conflict is between knowing something is wrong and refusing to accept it because acceptance would destroy him. By HBP, the books show him as a broken man who knows he was wrong.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The films preserve the core motivations: his love of office, his fear of Dumbledore, his self-deception about Voldemort. The OotP scenes — both the hearing and the hospital wing confrontation — make his denial and his paranoia about Dumbledore explicit. The GoF hospital wing scene preserves his refusal to act even when presented with evidence. His final acknowledgment ('He's back') at the end of OotP is present.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The films do not show the gradual psychological portrait of why Fudge is the way he is. The OotP book provides extensive off-screen context through Lupin, Tonks, and Sirius explaining Fudge's psychology in detail. The films compress this but the essential motivation — denial driven by self-interest — is present in the scenes that survive. The HBP Prime Minister scene, which shows Fudge's motivations in their most fully realised form (the bitter, diminished man who knows he was wrong), is absent. However, the core motivations are not changed or replaced; they are simplified.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: Motivations are simplified but correct. The films do not invent different motivations; they compress the explanation of existing ones. The self-deception, the love of office, the fear of Dumbledore are all present in observable film behaviour. The loss of the HBP scene means the final stage of his motivation — the reckoning — is absent, but this is a loss of completeness rather than a change of substance. Score in the 11–13 range.

character_arc.book_baseline: Fudge's arc across the series is: (1) well-meaning but weak bureaucrat (PS/CoS); (2) nervous but still functional authority figure managing a crisis (PoA); (3) beginning of denial and political self-interest hardening (GoF); (4) full antagonist driven by paranoia and self-deception, campaign against Harry and Dumbledore (OotP); (5) forced acknowledgment of the truth, public humiliation, sacking, diminished advisory role (HBP). The arc ends with a broken man who knows he was wrong and must live with the consequences. Key turning points: the GoF hospital wing refusal, the OotP campaign, the Ministry confrontation, the sacking.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The films cover the arc from CoS through OotP. The progression from fatherly authority figure (PoA Leaky Cauldron) to paranoid antagonist (OotP hearing) to forced acknowledgment (OotP finale) is present. The arc is compressed but the major beats survive.
character_arc.difference: The HBP arc — the sacking, the diminished state, the bitter advisory role, the final scene with the Prime Minister — is entirely absent from the films. This is the resolution of Fudge's arc: the man who denied everything finally confronting what his denial cost. Without it, the arc ends at the moment of acknowledgment ('He's back') rather than at the full reckoning. The arc is incomplete. Additionally, the gradual hardening in GoF is somewhat compressed, though the hospital wing scene preserves the key moment.
character_arc.penalty_logic: The arc is present through OotP but missing its resolution. The HBP material is not a minor detail — it is the culmination of everything Fudge has been building toward. The arc ends at acknowledgment rather than consequence. This is a meaningful incompleteness. However, the major steps of the arc through OotP are present and faithful. Score in the 11–13 range for a compressed but recognisable arc missing its final stage.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Fudge's key relationships are: (1) Dumbledore — begins as dependent (pelting him with owls for advice) and ends as paranoid adversary; the dynamic is one of a lesser man who resents his dependence on a greater one; (2) Harry — begins as fatherly protector and ends as institutional persecutor; (3) Lucius Malfoy — a relationship of corrupt influence, with Malfoy effectively steering Fudge's decisions; (4) the Muggle Prime Minister — a relationship that reveals Fudge's self-importance and his ultimate failure.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The Dumbledore relationship is preserved in its essential dynamic — the OotP confrontation shows the paranoid adversary phase clearly. The Harry relationship arc (fatherly to persecutor) is present across PoA and OotP. The Malfoy relationship is shown in CoS (Malfoy arriving at Hagrid's hut) and briefly in OotP (Fudge seen talking to Lucius in the Ministry corridor). The Prime Minister relationship is entirely absent.
key_relationships.difference: The Prime Minister relationship is completely absent from the films, removing the most revealing external relationship Fudge has — the one that shows his self-importance, his condescension, and ultimately his humiliation. The Malfoy relationship is present but underdeveloped; the books make explicit that Malfoy is effectively buying influence with Fudge, which the films only gesture at. The Dumbledore and Harry relationships are substantially preserved.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: The loss of the Prime Minister relationship removes a significant emotional and dramatic dimension. The Malfoy relationship is present but its corrupt depth is underplayed. The two most important relationships (Dumbledore, Harry) are preserved in their essential dynamics. The losses are real but the core relational characterisation survives. Score in the 7–8 range.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: Fudge's complexity in the books comes from several sources: (1) the genuine warmth he shows Harry in early books, which makes his later persecution more pointed and morally complex; (2) the Three Broomsticks scene where he shows emotional depth — shuddering at the memory of the crime scene, speaking with genuine weight about Pettigrew's death; (3) the HBP Prime Minister chapter, which is the richest single characterisation passage for Fudge in the entire series — showing his self-importance, his nervous energy, his gradual diminishment, his bitterness, and his final self-aware admission that he was wrong; (4) the contradiction between his genuine belief that he is doing the right thing and his actual cowardice and self-interest; (5) his relationship with Lucius Malfoy as a portrait of institutional corruption.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The films preserve the surface complexity — the shift from warm to hostile, the bluster, the cowardice. The OotP scenes are reasonably faithful to the book's portrayal of his paranoia and self-deception. The CoS and PoA scenes preserve his early characterisation.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The HBP Prime Minister chapter is entirely absent. This is the single greatest loss of nuance for Fudge in the adaptation. It is the scene where his complexity is most fully realised: the self-important man who has been wrong about everything, now diminished and bitter, still trying to maintain dignity. The Three Broomsticks scene is truncated and his emotional weight in it is transferred to McGonagall. The gradual portrait of his psychology — built across OotP through multiple characters explaining his fears and self-deceptions — is compressed to a few lines. The result is a Fudge who is recognisable but flatter: more straightforwardly pompous and obstructive, less the genuinely tragic figure of a small man destroyed by his own limitations.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: The loss of the HBP material is significant. The loss of the Three Broomsticks emotional depth is real. The character is simplified from a figure with genuine tragic dimensions into a more straightforwardly comic-antagonist bureaucrat. This is noticeable simplification that removes important nuances. Score in the 8–10 range.

lost_or_transferred_material: Three Broomsticks narration (PoA): Fudge's role as primary narrator of the Pettigrew/Black backstory transferred largely to McGonagall in the film
