comparative.key_observations: The film Fudge is a faithful but simplified version of the book character. The core identity — pompous, cowardly, self-deceiving bureaucrat who shifts from fatherly authority to paranoid antagonist — is preserved across all films in which he appears. The major plot functions (sending Hagrid to Azkaban, the rigged hearing, the GoF refusal, the OotP confrontation) are substantially intact. The primary losses are: the Three Broomsticks narration transferred to McGonagall, the entire HBP Prime Minister chapter absent, and the gradual psychological portrait of his self-deception compressed. These losses flatten a character who in the books has genuine tragic dimensions — a small man destroyed by his own limitations — into a more straightforwardly comic-antagonist figure. The adaptation is recognisable and largely functional, but the richest material that made Fudge more than a plot obstacle is largely absent.

personality_voice.book_baseline: In the books, Luna is defined by a constellation of traits that are consistent and layered: she is dreamy and unhurried in speech ('said Luna dreamily', 'said Luna vaguely', 'said Luna serenely'), speaks uncomfortable truths with complete guilelessness ('People expect you to have cooler friends than us'; 'It was like having friends'), holds eccentric beliefs with absolute sincerity and defends them with mild but genuine sharpness when mocked ('said Luna, her voice losing its dreamy quality'; 'There are plenty of eye-witness accounts'), possesses unexpected emotional groundedness when discussing loss and death ('Yes, it was rather horrible... I still feel very sad about it sometimes. But I've still got Dad'), and displays a capacity for explosive, disproportionate laughter (the scene where she laughs so hard at Ron's Goyle impression that she slides off her seat). She is not passive — she initiates conversations, makes observations others avoid, delivers tactical practicality at unexpected moments ('We'll have to fly, won't we?'), and shows bravery without drama. Her voice is marked by a floating, unhurried cadence interrupted by sudden sharpness or unexpected earnestness. She is also conspicuously undefended: she does not perform hurt when mocked, acknowledges she is called 'Loony' with complete equanimity, and never seeks approval.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The films preserve the most visible surface features: the dreamy cadence, the belief in Nargles and Wrackspurts, the Spectrespecs, the radishes, the upside-down Quibbler, the matter-of-fact delivery of bizarre statements ('Wrackspurts. Your head's full of them'), and isolated moments of emotional directness (the Dobby scene at Shell Cottage, which is excluded from scoring per instructions, and the Thestrals scene in OotP). Evanna Lynch's performance is faithful to the unhurried, floating quality. The film Luna correctly defends herself against the Ravenclaw boys dismissing her diadem idea ('The lost diadem of Ravenclaw? Hasn't anyone ever heard of it? It's quite famous'). The OotP film gives her the Thestrals conversation with emotional resonance. In HBP, she spots the Felix Felicis bottle, calls out Harry on the bridge with unexpected assertiveness ('HARRY POTTER! YOU LISTEN TO ME RIGHT NOW!'), and her Quidditch commentary is preserved in the screenplay though only partially in the film.
personality_voice.difference: Several important personality textures are absent or reduced. The books show Luna's capacity for explosive, unguarded laughter — a vivid, physical response that makes her surprising and real. This is entirely absent from the films, which present her as consistently serene. Her book-voice includes a micro-register of sharpness when her father or beliefs are attacked directly (the Rita Skeeter scene: 'I'll have it back, thank you,' said Luna coldly; the Rita negotiation scene where she participates actively and speaks up for her father with pointed dignity). The Rita Skeeter scene — where Luna is present, speaks several lines, and actively contributes to the negotiation about the interview — is completely absent from the films, removing one of her most complex and characterful book appearances. Her book habit of making quietly devastating social observations repeatedly — 'He says funny things sometimes, doesn't he? But he can be a bit unkind. I noticed that last year' — is reduced to a single such moment in HBP ('It was like having friends'). The film also removes her commentary role during the Gryffindor-Hufflepuff Quidditch match (partially present in the HBP screenplay, unclear in theatrical cut) and the detail of her posting signs for stolen possessions, which produces one of the book's most important emotional beats. The film Luna is more uniformly serene and less capable of the sudden sharpness or laughter that defines the book character's full range.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The core traits — dreamy delivery, eccentric beliefs held with sincerity, emotional directness about death and loss, unexpected courage, uncomfortable honesty — are preserved in the films. This earns a strong baseline. The penalties apply to: (1) the complete absence of her disproportionate explosive laughter, which is a distinctive and repeated book trait; (2) the removal of her Rita Skeeter scene participation, which is the clearest book example of her voice sharpening under provocation while remaining herself; (3) the reduction of her pattern of uncomfortable social observations to only one or two instances. These are secondary traits rather than core ones, so the penalty is moderate rather than severe. Score: 20.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: In the books, Luna serves multiple distinct narrative functions across five novels: (1) She is the first character to openly believe Harry about Voldemort's return, doing so publicly and explicitly in OotP ('I believe He Who Must Not Be Named is back and I believe you fought him'). (2) She is an active and capable participant in the Department of Mysteries battle — she helps Ginny walk, manages Neville when he is incapacitated, bewitches doors alongside Neville, casts Patronuses, and is only taken down when directly overpowered. (3) She is a structurally important figure in the Hogwarts resistance — with Ginny and Neville, she is one of the three leaders of the DA under Snape's regime. (4) In DH, she actively helps Harry escape Malfoy Manor, works the ropes while Hermione is being tortured, and after arrival at Shell Cottage, speaks for Dobby at his funeral and provides emotional grounding. (5) She solves the key narrative problem in DH Part 2 by identifying the need to speak to someone dead, calling out Harry on the bridge and redirecting his search to the Grey Lady. (6) She provides the crucial information about the lost diadem in the Room of Requirement. Her agency is consistent: she initiates, decides, solves, challenges, and changes the course of scenes.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: The films preserve several of these functions. In OotP, Luna is included in the DA, participates in the DoM battle (casts Levicorpus, is shown fighting), and her Patronus is shown in the DA training scene. In DH Part 2, she directly solves the diadem problem on the bridge — this is one of her best film moments, where she calls Harry out with genuine authority and provides the solution ('We have to talk to someone who's dead'). She then leads him to the Grey Lady's corridor and identifies Helena Ravenclaw. In the Room of Requirement, she correctly names the lost diadem. The cellar rescue is preserved. In HBP, her Quidditch commentary is retained in the screenplay.
narrative_role_agency.difference: Significant agency losses occur across the adaptation. In OotP, her public, proactive declaration of belief in Harry ('I believe He Who Must Not Be Named is back') is removed; in the film she merely says 'You're just as sane as I am' in a private carriage scene, which is less active and less public. The Rita Skeeter negotiation scene — in which Luna participates as an active presence, contributes pointed remarks about her father's editorial standards, and is the reason the interview gets published in The Quibbler — is entirely absent from the films, removing a scene of genuine agency. Her role as one of three DA leaders under Snape's regime is stated in the books (she is taken off the Hogwarts Express; Phineas Nigellus confirms she is punished along with Neville and Ginny) but is not dramatized or given meaningful screen presence in DH Part 1. The cellar rescue (working the ropes while Ron and Harry are bound) is present but compressed. The funeral speech for Dobby — where Luna speaks for everyone, says what Harry cannot say, and Harry acknowledges 'Luna had said it all for him' — is absent from the theatrical cut (excluded per instructions), removing a key moment of emotional agency. The DoM battle gives her some presence but her specific actions (bewitching doors with Neville, caring for injured friends) are less individuated than in the book.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: The DH Part 2 bridge scene and the Grey Lady identification represent genuine, preserved agency — this is arguably Luna's most important single act in the series and the films render it well. The diadem identification in the Room of Requirement is also preserved. However, the Rita Skeeter scene agency is entirely lost; the Dobby funeral speech is lost (excluded scene); the public OotP declaration is privatized and made passive; the Hogwarts resistance leadership is absent from the screen. Per the transfer rule: no specific transfer to another character occurs for most of this material — it is simply removed. The agency losses are real but the film preserves the most plot-critical agency moments. Score: 14.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Luna's motivations in the books are consistent and clear, even if lightly stated: she is motivated by genuine loyalty and friendship (she fights at the DoM not because she was asked but because she decides to go; she says 'Harry, we want to help you' in the cellar); by a deep, settled grief and love for her mother that shapes her relationship to death and loss; by a sincere, unironic belief in her father's journalism and worldview; and by a quiet desire for connection and friendship that she almost never expresses directly, making it more powerful when it surfaces ('It was like having friends'). She experiences no significant internal conflict in the conventional sense — her internal life is unusually integrated. The closest she comes to internal conflict is the scene with Harry at the end of OotP, where she reveals the depth of her loneliness (possessions stolen, called 'Loony') without complaint, suggesting a private world of quiet endurance. Her motivation in DH when choosing to return to Hogwarts and fight is clearly loyalty — she was taken because of her father's support for Harry, and she immediately returns to the cause.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The films preserve the core motivations: loyalty and friendship (the OotP film includes the Thestrals scene, where she explains her mother's death and explicitly states her belief in Harry; the HBP scene with 'It was like having friends'); genuine belief in her father and his work; settled grief for her mother rendered as equanimity rather than trauma. Her motivation in DH Part 2 to return and fight is consistent with the books, even without explicit dialogue explaining it.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The primary loss is the depth of her loneliness and the quiet endurance that accompanies it. The end-of-OotP scene (posting signs for stolen possessions, the conversation with Harry about Sirius and the voices behind the veil, the revelation of her mother's death) is partially preserved in the film in a compressed form, but the specific detail of her possessions being taken and her equanimous response to it — which reveals the texture of her daily life at Hogwarts and the motivation behind her self-contained manner — is reduced in the film. The film's Luna appears less lonely and more simply eccentric. The motivation of 'finding her way to connection on her own terms' is suggested but not established with the same texture. The Rita Skeeter scene, which shows her defending her father and his work with real investment, is absent, reducing the evidence for her motivation of loyalty to her father's worldview.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: Motivations are simplified but not changed. The films correctly establish: love of her mother, settled grief, loyalty to friends, belief in her father's work, desire for friendship. The simplification is mostly in texture and evidence rather than in the motivations themselves. The loneliness dimension is present but less supported by evidence. Score: 12.

character_arc.book_baseline: Luna's arc across the books is a gradual integration into a chosen family after a life of isolation and mockery. She begins in OotP as an eccentric figure most characters (including Harry) are embarrassed to be seen with, associated with the nickname 'Loony', her possessions stolen, her beliefs mocked. By GoF/HBP she is a genuine friend — Harry invites her to Slughorn's party as a friend, stands up for her when Romilda Vane excludes her, defends her to Ron. By DH she is part of the inner circle: she fights at the DoM, she is taken hostage because of her father's support for Harry, she is freed from Malfoy Manor and becomes part of the Shell Cottage community, she returns to Hogwarts as one of the resistance leaders. Her arc ends with her ceiling painting — five portraits of Harry, Ron, Hermione, Ginny, and Neville linked by the repeated word 'friends... friends... friends...' — which is the single most complete expression of her inner life and the culmination of her arc. It is discovered by Harry during the Lovegood visit. She is also the one who speaks at Dobby's funeral, suggesting that others now trust her emotional wisdom. There is no dramatic transformation — her personality is stable — but her social integration and the recognition she receives from others deepens continuously.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The films broadly follow this arc. In OotP, she is fringe and mocked (the carriage scene, the film Hermione calling her 'Loony Lovegood' before catching herself). By HBP she is clearly a friend: the party scene, the 'It was like having friends' moment. In DH, she is part of the fight. The scene at Shell Cottage where she plants sea lavender at Dobby's grave is in the theatrical cut and preserves her as someone who honours the dead. The Room of Requirement return in DH Part 2 shows her welcomed back as part of the group.
character_arc.difference: The ceiling painting — the single most important visual expression of Luna's arc and her inner life — is entirely absent from the theatrical film (it exists in no film corpus scene). This is the culmination of her arc in the books: the discovery that she has painted her five friends on her ceiling, linked by the word 'friends', reveals retrospectively the depth of her longing throughout the series and the meaning of those relationships to her. Its absence is a significant loss. The Dobby funeral speech (excluded per instructions) is also absent, removing the moment where her emotional wisdom is most explicitly recognised. The arc is still traceable in the films (fringe → friend → fighter) but the interior dimension — the private depth of her attachment — is substantially lost. The OotP end-scene conversation where Harry feels genuine pity and connection with Luna (and she speaks about the voices behind the veil) is present in the film but compressed.
character_arc.penalty_logic: The arc's broad shape — social integration and recognition — is preserved. However, the most important single piece of evidence for what the arc means to Luna herself (the ceiling painting) is absent, and the culminating emotional beat (Dobby funeral speech) is excluded. The arc is compressed and the interior dimension is missing important steps. Score: 11.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Luna's key relationships in the books are: (1) Harry: a gradually deepening friendship based on shared experience of loss, mutual recognition, and Harry's growing respect for her. The dynamic moves from Harry being embarrassed by her to defending her to treating her as a genuine friend and confidante (the end-of-OotP conversation; inviting her to Slughorn's; defending her to Ron and Romilda Vane). (2) Ginny: a warm, protective friendship; Ginny is the one who stops boys calling her 'Loony', who speaks up for her when Harry invites her to the party ('She's so excited'). (3) Neville: a parallel outsider figure with whom she has quiet rapport; they fight together at the DoM and in DH. (4) Her father Xenophilius: a deep, loving bond in which she shares his worldview and defends him without blindness to his limitations. (5) The wider DA: she is a genuine member, not merely a peripheral figure. The relationship with Harry is the most narratively significant: it is built across five books through specific scenes of mutual recognition.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The Harry-Luna relationship is partially preserved in the films. The Thestrals scene in OotP establishes mutual recognition through shared loss. The HBP 'It was like having friends' exchange is present and effective. The DH bridge scene shows Luna trusting Harry enough to shout at him, which implies established intimacy. The Ginny friendship is gestured at but barely present in the films. The Neville connection is effectively reduced to a brief exchange in the DH Part 2 courtyard scene where he stuns a Death Eater who was about to get Luna and she thanks him, plus Neville's line about being 'mad for her'. The father-daughter relationship is present in both DH films — she defends him at the wedding, the Lovegood visit shows her as his reason for existing, the discussion after Malfoy Manor shows Harry understanding why Xenophilius acted as he did, in part because of the kind of person Luna is.
key_relationships.difference: The most important losses are: (1) The end-of-OotP conversation between Harry and Luna — in the film it is shortened and loses the specific detail of the stolen possessions and the extended conversation about the voices behind the veil, which is the scene that most deeply establishes the emotional texture of their friendship. (2) The Rita Skeeter scene, where Luna is present while her father's work is negotiated and mocked, and she defends it with dignity — this scene shows the father-daughter relationship and Luna's independence of voice simultaneously. (3) The Ginny-Luna friendship is almost entirely absent from the films as a dramatised relationship; it is mentioned (Ginny says she's been nice to Luna in HBP) but never shown. (4) The ceiling painting, which is the most complete expression of what her friendships mean to her and what kind of relationship she has with the core group, is absent. The Harry-Luna dynamic in the films is warmer than zero but significantly less developed than in the books, particularly the mutual recognition and growing respect that builds across OotP and HBP.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: The Harry-Luna relationship is preserved at a functional level but loses depth in the OotP end scene and the Rita Skeeter scene. The Ginny friendship is essentially absent as a dramatised relationship. The Neville relationship gains a moment of romantic framing (Neville declaring he is 'mad for her') that does not exist in the books, which is a minor addition but not a serious distortion. The father-daughter relationship is reasonably preserved. Overall the key relationships are simplified and several important dynamics are weakened or absent. Score: 7.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: Luna's complexity in the books arises from the interplay of: (1) her sustained equanimity about her own social marginalisation, which is neither performed stoicism nor obliviousness but a genuinely unusual psychological settlement; (2) her capacity for sudden sharpness or anger when her beliefs or her father are directly attacked; (3) her disproportionate, physical laughter that makes her unpredictable and vivid; (4) her emotional intelligence about others, displayed quietly and accurately ('He can be a bit unkind. I noticed that last year' about Ron); (5) the ceiling painting as the single richest piece of evidence for her inner life; (6) the Rita Skeeter scene, in which she is present in a negotiation between adults and participates with unexpected authority; (7) the end-of-OotP conversation, which is the scene most responsible for Harry (and the reader) understanding who Luna actually is beneath the eccentricity. The combination of surface eccentricity with genuine emotional intelligence, suppressed loneliness, and unexpected sharpness is what makes her a complex character rather than a simple eccentric.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The films preserve: the surface eccentricity, the Thestrals/death scene emotional resonance, the 'It was like having friends' moment, the DH bridge assertiveness, the cellar grace, and the general quality of her being more perceptive than others expect. The HBP film gives her the moment where she spots the Felix Felicis, which is a subtle indicator of her perceptiveness. The DH Part 2 film gives her the Grey Lady navigation, which is one of her best moments of quiet capability.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The major losses are: (1) the ceiling painting — the single richest expression of her inner life and the depth of her feeling for her friends; (2) the Rita Skeeter scene — the clearest demonstration of her sharpness when provoked, her defence of her father, and her presence as a participant in adult-level negotiation; (3) her explosive, disproportionate laughter (the Goyle impression scene); (4) the pattern of quiet, accurate social observations that runs through OotP and HBP as a repeated texture; (5) the Dobby funeral speech (excluded per instructions) where her emotional wisdom is made explicit and Harry acknowledges 'Luna had said it all for him'; (6) the detail of her possessions being stolen and her equanimous, non-complaining response to it, which is the key evidence for the quality of her daily endurance. The film Luna is recognisably Luna but significantly flattened — the eccentricity is preserved but the emotional intelligence, the sharpness, and the interiority are substantially reduced.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: The absent material — particularly the ceiling painting, the Rita Skeeter scene, and the Dobby funeral speech — is not decorative but constitutive of what makes Luna complex rather than merely quirky. The ceiling painting is the culmination of her arc's interior dimension. The Rita Skeeter scene shows a register the film never accesses. The laughter scene shows an emotional range the film never establishes. These losses reduce the character's depth from layered to primarily surface. Score: 10.

score_caps_applied: Cap 3 (score above 75 if a core book function is transferred or removed): Luna's ceiling painting — the interior culmination of her arc — is absent. The Rita Skeeter scene agency is entirely removed. The Dobby funeral speech (her most important moment of emotional agency being recognised by Harry) is absent from theatrical cut. These constitute core book functions removed without replacement. Cap applied at 75.

Cap 1 (score above 85 if films remove a major part of complexity): The ceiling painting, the laughter scene, the Rita Skeeter scene, and the pattern of social observations together constitute the major part of Luna's book complexity beyond her surface eccentricity. Their removal prevents a score above 85. Already covered by cap 3.
comparative.key_observations: The films capture Luna Lovegood's most visible surface features with genuine fidelity: the dreamy cadence, the eccentric beliefs, the emotional directness about death, the Spectrespecs, the courage in battle, and the unexpected assertiveness at key moments. Evanna Lynch's performance is consistently faithful to the book's register. The DH Part 2 bridge scene — where Luna calls Harry out and redirects his search to the Grey Lady — is one of the best Luna moments in the film series and preserves a critical piece of her agency. However, the adaptation loses a significant layer of interior complexity: the ceiling painting (the richest expression of her inner life and the culmination of her arc), the Rita Skeeter negotiation scene (her sharpest and most adult moment in the books), her disproportionate explosive laughter (a vivid and distinctive book trait), and the pattern of quiet accurate social observations that builds her as an emotional intelligence across OotP and HBP. The Dobby funeral speech, where Harry explicitly acknowledges that Luna said what he could not, is absent from the theatrical cut. The result is a Luna who is recognisable and consistently played, but meaningfully flattened — her eccentricity is faithfully preserved while the emotional intelligence, suppressed loneliness, sharpness, and interiority that make the book character genuinely complex are substantially reduced.

personality_voice.book_baseline: Wood is defined by obsessive, single-minded Quidditch fanaticism expressed through manic energy, pre-dawn training sessions, multi-board tactical diagrams, pre-match speeches the team knows by heart, and a capacity to subordinate almost everything else — including Harry's physical safety — to winning. He is earnest, intense, occasionally comic in his excess, and capable of genuine emotion (sobbing at the Cup win). His voice is direct, commanding, and prone to outbursts ('I booked the field!'). He has a specific flaw: his priorities are visibly skewed — he tells McGonagall he doesn't care if the Firebolt throws Harry as long as Harry catches the Snitch first, and he tells Harry to 'get the Snitch or die trying.' He is not cruel, but his obsession produces moments of genuine moral blindness.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The films preserve the core of Wood's personality well. His pre-dawn training call in CoS ('We're going to train earlier, harder, and longer!'), his outrage at Flint's note, his 'Save it for the match' restraint of Fred and George, and his tactical intensity are all present. The actor conveys the manic gleam. The brief exchange before the first match ('I took a Bludger to the head two minutes in. Woke up in the hospital a week later') captures his self-aware but undeterred fanaticism. His 'Cancelled! They can't cancel Quidditch—' reaction is faithful.
personality_voice.difference: The films omit the most extreme expressions of his skewed priorities: the Firebolt conversation with McGonagall where he explicitly says he doesn't care if Harry is thrown as long as he catches the Snitch, and the extended PoA arc of obsessive pre-match preparation (five practices a week, constant corridor ambushes of Harry with tactical tips, the three-board pre-dawn briefing that puts the team to sleep). The film CoS training scene is compressed. The PoA Cup-winning emotional breakdown (sobbing into Harry's shoulder) is absent from the corpus. His voice is preserved but the most comedically extreme and morally revealing moments are reduced.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The main personality traits — obsessive, intense, earnest, commanding — are preserved and recognizable. The penalty is for the loss of the most distinctive expressions of his flaw (the Firebolt/McGonagall exchange, the sleep-inducing tactical briefings, the corridor ambushes) which are what make him more than a generic sports captain. These are not merely comic — they reveal the specific texture of his obsession. Minor-to-moderate simplification warrants a score in the 18-22 range.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: Wood's narrative function across books 1-3 is: (1) introduce and explain Quidditch to Harry and the reader; (2) serve as the primary driver of Quidditch plot tension across three years; (3) provide comic relief through his excess; (4) act as a pressure source on Harry; (5) embody the stakes of the Quidditch Cup. He initiates training schedules, makes tactical decisions, confronts Flint, negotiates with McGonagall, and is the emotional center of the Cup victory. In GoF he appears briefly as a professional player. In OotP he is referenced as a benchmark. In DH he appears carrying Colin Creevey's body — a small but dignified moment of agency.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: The films preserve his role as Quidditch explainer (PS training scene), team captain, and source of pre-match pressure. The Flint confrontation in CoS is present. His 'Cancelled!' reaction is present. The DH body-carrying moment is present. His GoF cameo (introducing himself to Harry at the World Cup) is present in the corpus.
narrative_role_agency.difference: The PoA arc — where Wood is the emotional engine of the entire Quidditch Cup storyline across multiple matches, the Hufflepuff match disaster, the Ravenclaw match triumph, and the Slytherin Cup win — is substantially compressed. The Cup win itself, where Wood sobs and passes Harry the trophy, is absent from the film corpus provided. The extended tactical agency (five practices a week, the Firebolt negotiation with McGonagall, the constant corridor briefings) is removed. His role as a recurring pressure source across PoA is reduced to brief appearances.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: His core function as Quidditch captain and explainer is preserved. However, his role as the primary emotional and tactical driver of the PoA Quidditch arc — the most sustained narrative function he has across the books — is significantly compressed. The Cup win moment, his most important single scene, is absent from the film corpus. This is a meaningful reduction in agency and narrative weight, though not a transfer to another character. Score in the 14-17 range.
narrative_role_agency.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for what is present; reasonably inferred for what is absent based on corpus gaps

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Wood's motivation is transparent and consistent: win the Quidditch Cup before he leaves Hogwarts. In PoA this becomes explicitly urgent — it is his seventh and final year, he has never won, and the desperation in his voice is noted by the narrator ('a quiet sort of desperation'). His internal conflict is minor but real: he genuinely cares about his team but his obsession causes him to prioritize the Cup over Harry's safety (Firebolt conversation, 'get the Snitch or die trying'). He is not unaware of this — he looks awkward when approaching Harry about the dementor problem.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The films convey his desire to win clearly. The CoS scene establishes his intensity. His PoA motivation (final year, must win) is present in the film but compressed. The awkwardness around Harry's safety versus winning is partially present in the 'get the Snitch or die trying' line referenced in the book corpus and the Bludger match scene.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The explicit PoA framing — 'This is my last chance, I'll never get another shot at it,' the 'quiet sort of desperation,' the dejectedness when speaking about past failures — is present in the book but the film does not give it the same weight or screen time. The Firebolt conversation, which most clearly shows the internal tension between caring for Harry and wanting to win, is absent from the film corpus.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: The core motivation is preserved and recognizable. The loss of the Firebolt conversation removes the clearest expression of his internal conflict. The PoA urgency is present but compressed. Motivations are simplified but still correct — score in the 11-13 range.
motivations_internal_conflict.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for core motivation; reasonably inferred for degree of compression

character_arc.book_baseline: Wood's arc across books 1-3 is: eager fifth-year captain who discovers a prodigy Seeker → increasingly obsessed sixth-year who drives his team relentlessly → desperate seventh-year who finally wins the Cup and breaks down in tears. The arc culminates in the PoA Cup win, which is his resolution. Post-Hogwarts, he is signed to Puddlemere United (GoF), confirming his trajectory. The arc is not one of internal transformation but of sustained pursuit finally rewarded.

comparative.key_observations: Oliver Wood's film portrayal is recognizable and captures his dominant trait — obsessive Quidditch fanaticism — with reasonable fidelity. The core personality, motivation, and narrative function are preserved across PS and CoS. However, the PoA arc, which is the emotional and narrative climax of his book characterization, is substantially compressed in the films: the three-book escalation of his desperation, the most extreme and revealing expressions of his skewed priorities (the Firebolt conversation), the Cup win breakdown, and the extended tactical obsession that gives him his specific comic and dramatic texture are all reduced or absent. The result is a character who is broadly faithful but flattened — recognizable as 'intense Quidditch captain' without the specific nuances that make him memorable in the books. The DH cameo carrying Colin Creevey's body is faithfully preserved and adds quiet dignity. Total of 74 reflects a character whose broad identity is intact but whose most distinctive material has been significantly compressed.

personality_voice.book_baseline: In the books, Lupin is defined by a distinctive combination of warmth and restraint. He is measured, calm under pressure, and gently ironic — he responds to Peeves with mild patience, deflects Snape's provocations with cool composure, and even in moments of crisis (the Shrieking Shack confrontation) maintains a degree of controlled formality. His voice is notably careful: he rarely raises it, prefers understatement ('I have not been helping Sirius'), and uses precise, slightly formal diction. His emotional life is consistently suppressed — he acknowledges guilt, cowardice, and shame through indirect confession rather than outburst. He is also capable of dry humor ('I was just trying to make you feel better. Honeydukes' sweets are the best in the world') and of warm intimacy with those he trusts. Crucially, his dominant personality flaw — a deep-seated tendency toward self-abnegation, avoidance, and rationalizing cowardice as responsibility — is always present beneath the composure. His sharpness emerges rarely but memorably: 'Enough of this. There's a steely note in his voice Harry had never heard before.' He is also notably intellectually engaged as a teacher: enthusiastic, encouraging, inventive. His self-loathing over his werewolf condition is a running undercurrent rather than an explicit complaint.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The films capture the core of Lupin's personality with considerable accuracy. David Thewlis plays him as measured, warm, and quietly authoritative. The Boggart lesson shows his encouraging pedagogy, his patience with Neville, and his deflection of Snape's contempt with dignified calm. The train scene establishes his composed competence under threat. The Patronus lessons show his gentleness and intellectual engagement. His dry wit survives: the bridge scene in PoA ('No. I was just trying to make you feel better') is a direct preservation of his book voice. His emotional restraint is consistent. In DH Part 1, his eruption at Grimmauld Place when Harry challenges him about abandoning Tonks is one of the few moments the film captures his internal fracture — his 'Don't you understand what I've done?' speech is faithful to the book's portrait of a man whose self-loathing is barely contained. The Battle of Hogwarts scene on the battlements ('It's the quality of one's conviction that determines success, not the number of one's followers') adds a line not in the books but is tonally consistent with his character. His line at Hogwarts' arrival in DH2 — identifying himself in full to Harry — is slightly comedic but captures his precision and self-awareness.
personality_voice.difference: Two meaningful gaps exist. First, several of Lupin's most characteristic speech patterns from the books — hesitation followed by directness, the interplay of warmth and self-reproach, the careful threading between honesty and deflection — are compressed or simplified in the films. The extended tea-room conversations (PoA book chapters) where his personality emerges through small gestures, oblique humor, and measured candor are largely absent; the bridge scene in the film is a partial but incomplete substitute. Second, the film's Lupin is occasionally more declarative than the book version. In the books, his self-disgust and social shame emerge gradually and obliquely; in the films they tend to surface in single concentrated scenes (the Grimmauld confrontation) without the accumulated texture of smaller moments. His tendency to rationalize cowardice as wisdom is present in HBP (he tells Harry 'You are blinded by hatred') but does not land with the same moral complexity as in the books, where it is part of a sustained pattern. The Shrieking Shack scene is well-handled but compressed, and Lupin's 'I am no longer your teacher' dignity at his departure is reduced to a brief farewell without the full emotional resonance of the book scene.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The core personality — measured warmth, dry wit, suppressed guilt, composed authority, intellectual enthusiasm — is preserved. The main losses are in texture and accumulation rather than in fundamental characterization. His dominant flaw (self-abnegation as a mask for cowardice) is present but less fully developed because the scenes that build it up over time are reduced. A minor penalty is appropriate: this is 'main personality preserved, but there is minor simplification, softening, or loss of secondary traits' — specifically the loss of the repeated small-scale texture that builds his self-awareness and irony in the books.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: In the books, Lupin is structurally active across four major narrative functions: (1) as teacher and mentor in PoA, where he is the primary agent of Harry's Patronus training and the key figure in the Boggart/Dementor education arc; (2) as a pivotal agent in the Shrieking Shack revelation — he is the one who correctly reads the Marauder's Map, understands Pettigrew's true identity, restrains Sirius, insists on explanation, and manages the confrontation; (3) as an active intelligence-gatherer and strategist for the Order in OotP and HBP (living among werewolves, providing political analysis to Harry, pressing Snape on Occlumency); (4) as a moral presence and advisor across books 5–7, where he delivers key contextual information (the political situation, Voldemort's strategy, Ministry's corruption) and challenges Harry directly. In DH he also independently investigates the betrayal (Grimmauld Place identity check), serves as a named battle leader at Hogwarts, and provides the emotional beat of Teddy's birth. His agency is consistently active: he initiates, explains, challenges, and decides.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: Most of Lupin's book functions are preserved in the films, though with some compression. The PoA film faithfully shows him discovering the Dementor on the train, teaching the Boggart lesson, conducting Patronus training, and managing the Shrieking Shack scene. His role as the one who reads the Marauder's Map and pieces together Pettigrew's identity is preserved. In OotP (film), his role in the Order briefing is reduced to a few lines but he retains his function as a contextualizing voice. In HBP (film), the Weasley house scene gives him a meaningful scene where he defends Snape's trustworthiness and challenges Harry's judgment — preserving his role as a voice of hard-headed realism. In DH Part 1, his Grimmauld Place identity-check is intact, his political briefing (Ministry's fall, Muggle-borns, Voldemort's strategy) is preserved, and his offer to accompany Harry and the subsequent confrontation about Tonks is fully retained. The Battle of Hogwarts role (DH Part 2) shows him as a named battle commander alongside Shacklebolt. His death and the image of him and Tonks in the Great Hall are present.
narrative_role_agency.difference: Several agency losses occur. (1) In the books, Lupin is much more agentically involved in OotP political discussions — he is a named voice in multiple strategy sessions, delivers extended analysis, and explicitly corrects/challenges multiple characters. In the film these are compressed into brief group scenes where his lines are reduced. (2) The Tonks scene at the Battle in DH2 where she arrives and they fight together (cut scene per non-theatrical exclusion list) removes a beat of his agency. (3) His role in recovering Moody's body (books: he goes out with Bill to retrieve it) is absent in the films. (4) In the books, his briefing of Harry at Grimmauld Place in DH is longer and more substantive — he provides page-level political analysis. The film condenses this significantly. (5) His challenge to Harry about Expelliarmus ('You behaved a little too kindly to Stan Shunpike') is absent in the films, which removes one of his most active moral interventions.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: Core functions (teacher, Shrieking Shack agent, Order member, DH advisor) are preserved. The losses are real but mostly involve compression of supporting agency rather than elimination or reassignment of primary functions. The missing Expelliarmus challenge is a meaningful agency loss — in the books it is one of his sharpest direct challenges to Harry's judgment. The condensed OotP political role is a real but moderate loss. Score is in the 'role and agency are reduced but recognizable' range.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Lupin's central motivation across all books is survival — specifically, the continuous negotiation between his desire to live a meaningful life and the shame and self-imposed limitations of his werewolf condition. His primary internal conflict is between self-abnegation (he believes he is a danger, an embarrassment, and a burden) and his genuine desire for connection, purpose, and love. In PoA, this manifests as his suppressed loyalty to his friends (Sirius, James, Lily) and his cowardice in not telling Dumbledore about Sirius being an Animagus. In OotP, it is his marginalization and poverty while still actively serving the Order. In HBP/DH, the conflict becomes acute: he genuinely loves Tonks but believes his condition makes him wrong for her and dangerous to their child. His offer to abandon Tonks and join Harry's mission is not presented as heroic in the books — it is explicitly identified by Harry (and by Lupin himself, implicitly) as a form of cowardice, an attempt to recapture something of his old adventurous life rather than face his terrifying domestic responsibilities. His motivations in the DH confrontation scene are explicitly fear-based: fear of what he has done to Tonks, fear that his child will inherit his condition, fear of shame. His return to Tonks after Harry's rebuke, and his final sacrifice, represent his resolution of this conflict.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The film preserves the core motivations. In PoA, his motivation to protect Harry and explain the truth about Pettigrew is intact. The Grimmauld Place DH confrontation ('I made a grave mistake in marrying Tonks... I am too old for you, too poor, too dangerous') directly captures his self-abnegating motivation. His anguished 'What have I done to my wife and unborn child?' speech is a faithful rendering of the book's internal conflict. The HBP Weasley house scene shows his conflicted loyalty to Dumbledore's judgment over his personal distaste for Snape.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: Some important texture is lost. The books show the gradual development of Lupin's guilt over his PoA cowardice (failing to tell Dumbledore about Sirius) through his own words: 'I always managed to forget my guilty feelings... And I haven't changed.' This self-diagnosis — that he is a habitual rationalizer of his own cowardice — is present in the films only implicitly, through the DH confrontation. The PoA film does not include his explicit self-reproach about having failed Dumbledore's trust. Additionally, his motivation during the werewolf mission (living among werewolves for the Order) and the complex self-awareness this produces ('I bear the unmistakable signs of having tried to live among wizards') is largely absent from the films. The HBP conversation about Greyback ('It was Greyback who bit me... My father had offended him') — which contextualizes his entire condition and deepens his motivation — is completely missing.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: The primary motivations (shame, love for Tonks, desire for purpose, self-abnegation) survive in the films, primarily through the DH confrontation scene. But the supporting motivational texture — the accumulated self-knowledge, the Greyback backstory, the habitual rationalizing — is absent, making his motivations slightly simplified. 'Motivations are simplified but still correct' applies.

character_arc.book_baseline: Lupin's arc across all seven books is one of the more complete secondary character arcs in the series. Starting point: a damaged, marginalized man who has learned to suppress his desires and live defensively. PoA arc: rediscovers connection and purpose through teaching, confronts his past cowardice (regarding Sirius, regarding Dumbledore's trust), and is forced to resign — demonstrating that his position in society remains precarious regardless of his merit. OotP–HBP: serves the Order while continuing to marginalize himself; his relationship with Tonks begins but he resists it. DH arc: marries Tonks against his better judgment, panics and tries to abandon her when the child is coming, is confronted by Harry and forced to acknowledge his cowardice, returns to Tonks and his responsibility, and ultimately dies fighting for the world his son will inhabit. The resolution of his arc is explicit: he tells Harry in the Forest 'I was trying to make a world in which he could live a happier life.' The arc moves from defensive self-suppression to a terrified attempt at connection, a near-retreat, a confrontation with cowardice, and a final act of purpose. Key turning points: PoA resignation, Tonks relationship, DH abandonment attempt, Harry's rebuke, Teddy's birth, death in battle.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The PoA arc is faithfully compressed: teaching, mentoring, forced resignation, farewell. The DH arc is largely preserved: resistance to Tonks, DH Part 1 confrontation scene, apparent resolution, death at the Battle. The arc's beginning and end are present. The wedding scene in DH Part 1 (Lupin announcing the godfather offer while looking 'rather unhappy') is a faithful capture of his unresolved conflict at that point. The Grimmauld confrontation is a direct rendering of the book's key turning-point scene. His death in the Great Hall with Tonks is shown.
character_arc.difference: Several arc steps are absent or reduced. The OotP–HBP period — during which Lupin's isolation, poverty, and marginalisation are developed at length, and during which his resistance to Tonks is dramatised — is almost entirely absent from the films. The films jump from PoA resignation to DH Grimmauld Place without dramatising the intermediate arc. The book's HBP Christmas scene at the Burrow, where Tonks confronts him and he resists ('I am too old for you, too poor, too dangerous') is not present in the films — the same sentiment appears in the DH Grimmauld scene, but as a compressed single encounter rather than a sustained pattern. The Teddy's birth scene at Shell Cottage (DH1) where 'he seemed dazed by his own happiness' and 'looked years younger' is absent from the theatrical films, which removes the emotional resolution of his arc prior to his death. The HBP werewolf mission material (his self-awareness about his condition and his complex position among other werewolves) is entirely absent. These are significant arc steps that the film compresses or skips.
character_arc.penalty_logic: The arc's key turning points (PoA teaching/resignation; DH abandonment/confrontation; death in battle) are present. But the intermediate arc — years of marginalisation, the sustained Tonks resistance pattern, the Teddy birth resolution — is missing, making the arc feel incomplete and somewhat rushed in the DH section. The DH abandonment-confrontation scene lands harder in the books because the prior arc has established the pattern clearly. Without the OotP–HBP bridge material and the Teddy birth scene, the arc is 'incomplete, rushed, or missing important steps.' The Teddy birth absence is a particularly significant loss as it represents the emotional resolution before death.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Lupin's most important relationships are: (1) Harry — a mentoring relationship with genuine paternal warmth, defined by Lupin's ability to see James and Lily in Harry and to offer Harry the kind of support he was unable to give the parents; (2) Sirius — a deep friendship defined by shared grief, loyalty, and mutual recognition, complicated by years of believing the other was a traitor; (3) James Potter (in memory) — foundational to Lupin's identity and motivation; (4) Tonks — a romantic relationship defined by Lupin's resistance, shame, and ultimately painful love; (5) Snape — a relationship of suppressed mutual hostility, complicated by genuine debt (the Wolfsbane potion) and old grudges. Each of these relationships reveals key traits: the Harry relationship reveals his nurturing warmth and his lingering connection to his dead friends; the Sirius relationship reveals his loyalty and the depth of his grief; the Tonks relationship reveals his shame and self-abnegation; the Snape relationship reveals his capacity for grudging fairness.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The Harry mentoring relationship is well-preserved in PoA and present in OotP, HBP, and DH. The emotional warmth, paternal quality, and connection to James are all maintained — the bridge scene ('They lived. Every moment of every day') is a strong filmic rendering of the book dynamic. The Sirius relationship is compressed but the fraternal recognition at the Shrieking Shack and the shared grief over James are present. The Tonks relationship is shown: the DH Part 1 Grimmauld scene preserves the resistance-shame dynamic, and the wedding scene shows his ambivalent affection. The Snape relationship is present in the Shrieking Shack scene (film) and the HBP Weasley house scene, where Lupin defends Snape's trustworthiness as an expression of grudging fairness.
key_relationships.difference: The Sirius-Lupin relationship suffers most. In the books, it is an extremely rich relationship — decades of friendship, years of separation and mutual suspicion, the complexity of their reunion, the easy intimacy they re-establish, and Lupin's grief at Sirius's death (collapsing in a chair, 'he had never seen Lupin lose control before'). The films show the reunion and the brotherly embrace but almost none of the depth: the scene of Lupin collapsing at Sirius's death is present but brief. The book's extended portrayal of their dynamic (the PoA aftermath, the OotP headquarters scenes where their old friendship resurfaces) is much reduced. The Tonks relationship is shown but the HBP sustained resistance pattern is collapsed into the DH scene, removing the accumulated emotional weight. The relationship with James (in memory) is present but less developed — the books give multiple scenes where Lupin connects Harry to James with genuine grief and joy; the films give this in the Patronus training but not elsewhere. The Snape debt is present in HBP film but the full complexity (Lupin acknowledging Snape kept him healthy despite the betrayal) is reduced to a brief assertion of trust.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: Most key relationships are recognizable but several are meaningfully compressed. The Sirius relationship specifically loses emotional depth — the film shows the dynamic but not the grief and intimacy that define it in the books. The Tonks relationship is present but missing the sustained prior arc that makes it emotionally coherent. This is 'relationships mostly faithful, with some compression or simplification' rather than full alteration, but the Sirius loss is significant enough to bring it below the top range.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: Lupin is one of the more internally complex adult characters in the series. His complexity rests on several pillars: (1) a fundamental contradiction between his intelligence, morality, and warmth on one hand, and his habitual cowardice and self-sabotage on the other — he explicitly recognises that he rationalises cowardice as wisdom; (2) his dark capacity for violence, visible in the Shrieking Shack ('I think so. Yes, I think so') when he and Sirius prepare to kill Pettigrew, and in his near-abandonment of his pregnant wife; (3) his intellectual life as a teacher, which is rich in the books and shows genuine enthusiasm, creativity, and pedagogical care; (4) the werewolf mission material in DH, which gives him an unusual form of institutional critique and self-awareness about his double life; (5) the Greyback backstory — 'It was Greyback who bit me. My father had offended him' — which contextualises his entire condition and complicates easy sympathy; (6) his capacity for sharp moral intervention (the Expelliarmus challenge; the rebuke of Harry about his father in the Pensieve; the firm correction of Harry's over-trust of his friends); (7) the sustained pattern of small kindnesses that define his texture (chocolate on the train, chocolate frogs after Patronus training, butterbeer in the classroom, the wry twinkle about tea leaves).
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The films preserve Lupin's intellectual enthusiasm in the teaching scenes, his warmth, and his dark capacity (the preparation to kill Pettigrew is present in the Shrieking Shack film scene). The small kindnesses are visible — chocolate on the train, the chocolate frog in Patronus training. The DH Part 1 confrontation captures his contradictions. The battlements scene in DH2 ('It's the quality of one's conviction...') suggests his ironic self-awareness.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: Significant complexity is lost. (1) The Greyback backstory is entirely absent, removing a crucial layer that complicates his condition from something he merely endures to something that was deliberately done to him as punishment to his family. (2) The werewolf mission material — his complex double position among marginalised werewolves, his self-awareness about 'bearing the unmistakable signs of having tried to live among wizards,' his critique of his own ineffectiveness against Greyback's appeal — is absent. This material makes him genuinely morally complex in a way the films do not show. (3) His explicit self-diagnosis as a habitual rationalizer ('I always managed to forget my guilty feelings... And I haven't changed') is absent from the films. (4) The Expelliarmus challenge in DH1 books — one of his most pointed moral interventions — is cut. (5) The Pensieve response to Harry's horror about James ('Did I ever tell you to lay off Snape? Did I ever have the guts to tell you I thought you were out of order?') — a moment of genuine moral self-criticism — is absent. (6) The Teddy birth scene, with its emotional release and its portrait of a man who has resolved his internal conflict, is absent from theatrical releases. (7) The OotP Christmas scene and multiple small moments that show his poverty, isolation, and maintenance of dignity are absent. These are not decorative losses — they collectively remove the book's portrait of a man who is simultaneously admirable, self-aware, and deeply flawed in ways he cannot fully overcome.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: The films preserve Lupin's surface complexity but lose much of the material that makes him genuinely contradicted and uncomfortable. The lost Greyback backstory, the werewolf mission arc, the explicit self-diagnosis of cowardice, the Expelliarmus challenge, the Pensieve moral self-criticism, and the Teddy birth scene together constitute a meaningful reduction in nuance. The character remains recognizable and sympathetic, but several of the specific contradictions and vulnerabilities that define him in the books are absent or only implied. This is in the 'noticeable simplification; important nuances, relationships, agency, or contradictions are missing' range.
