Cap 3 not strictly triggered (no single core action clearly transferred to another character — the Ron-aggression scenes are simply removed rather than reassigned), but the absence of those scenes produces a similar functional result.
comparative.key_observations: Demelza Robins is a minor character whose book presence is modest but humanly textured: she is a skilled Chaser, a functional social actor, and a sympathetic victim of Ron's aggression who is defended by a smaller teammate. The film retains her name, her athletic skill, and a single functional role in the tryout scene, but removes every layer of human texture the books provide — her voice, her emotional responses, her relationships with Ron and Peakes, and her structural role as the evidence of Ron's deteriorating behaviour. What remains is essentially a background Quidditch extra with a name card. The score of 67 reflects that the film is recognisable in the most superficial sense but has stripped the character of almost everything that made her a minor human presence rather than pure scenery. Confidence is medium throughout because the corpus is limited on both sides, but the gap between what the books give and what the film delivers is clear enough to evaluate with reasonable certainty.

personality_voice.book_baseline: In the books, Goyle is established as physically large, thuggish, and almost entirely non-verbal. His dominant traits are dimness (described as 'almost as stupid as he was mean'), brute physical menace, sycophantic laughter at Malfoy's insults, and a kind of passive, reflexive obedience to Malfoy. He rarely speaks independently; his contributions are grunts, sniggering, cracking knuckles, and flexing arms. He is greedy (falls for the sleeping-draught cakes), and described with consistent animal/gorilla imagery: 'gorilla-ish arms,' 'gorilla-like,' 'low grunt.' His 'voice' in the handful of book lines he does have is minimalist and dull. He also shows small flickers of separate will late in the series — in Deathly Hallows he has opinions and speaks several lines independently ('We 'ung back, Potter... We decided not to go'), and he casts an Avada Kedavra, showing he has absorbed real Dark Arts training under Voldemort's regime. Ron's comment that impersonating Goyle requires acting 'less intelligent' reinforces his stupidity as a defining and comedic trait.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The films preserve Goyle's physical bulk, his near-silence, and his role as a laughing presence at Malfoy's side. He sniggering at Malfoy's jokes, lumbers alongside him, and his few lines of dialogue are consistent with his dull, slow speech. In Deathly Hallows Part 2, the film gives Goyle the pivotal line 'C'mon, Draco. Don't be a prat. Just do 'im' and his use of Avada Kedavra and Fiendfyre are retained. His greedy swallowing of cakes is absent from the theatrical cut. His sycophantic reactions to Malfoy and his near-total silence across most films match the book baseline. One notable addition is that Blaise Zabini replaces Crabbe for much of the sixth and seventh films, which slightly dilutes the Goyle-specific presence, but what remains of Goyle's on-screen behaviour is faithful to type.
personality_voice.difference: The films largely preserve Goyle's surface personality — thuggishness, near-silence, sycophancy, physical menace. What is partially lost is the specific texture of that stupidity as rendered through narration (the book repeatedly emphasises his dimness through free indirect description and others' observations in ways the film cannot replicate). His late-series independent voice in Deathly Hallows — surprisingly speaking in full sentences, showing he has made a deliberate choice to stay behind and capture Harry — is present in the film, which is faithful. The cut Polyjuice preparation scene removes one small characterisation beat (greedily eating cakes without suspicion), but this is a minor loss. No traits are added that contradict the books.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The core personality is preserved: dull, large, threatening, obedient to Malfoy, minimally verbal, capable of sycophantic laughter. The book's dense descriptive texture of his stupidity cannot transfer fully to film, but the observable behaviours that encode it largely do. A modest penalty is appropriate for the compression of this texture and the loss of a few minor greed/stupidity beats, but the character remains recognisable in all major traits. Score sits in the 14–17 range.
personality_voice.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for most traits; reasonably inferred for the degree of loss from book narration.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: In the books, Goyle's structural function is threefold: (1) physical intimidation and bodyguard alongside Crabbe for Malfoy; (2) a foil/comedic object whose stupidity is mined for humour; (3) a plot-functional role in Book 2 (his body is used for Polyjuice) and Books 6–7 (he acts as a lookout for Malfoy's Room of Requirement project and takes independent action in the Battle of Hogwarts). In Deathly Hallows he becomes briefly agentive: he decides independently to stay behind with Malfoy at Hogwarts rather than evacuate, he casts Avada Kedavra at Hermione (an act of genuine lethal aggression), and he sets off Fiendfyre, which kills him. These are the most plot-consequential things Goyle ever does and they are causally significant: the Fiendfyre destroys the diadem Horcrux and kills Goyle, driving the emotional beat of the scene. He also physically blocks Harry and serves as the main combat threat in the Room of Requirement.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: In the theatrical films, Goyle's bodyguard/intimidation function is preserved across multiple films. The Polyjuice plot in Chamber of Secrets loses the scene of Harry and Ron hiding and waking the real Crabbe and Goyle (cut), but the use of his body (hair) for the transformation is retained in context. In Half-Blood Prince and Deathly Hallows, Goyle appears as a lookout and then as a combatant. In Deathly Hallows Part 2, his 'Just do 'im' line, his Avada Kedavra, his triggering of Fiendfyre, and his death are all present. However, in the film it is Goyle (not Crabbe as in the book) who casts the Fiendfyre and dies, due to the recasting caused by Jamie Waylett's real-life legal issues. This transfer from Crabbe to Goyle is actually an increase in Goyle's agency relative to the books, not a decrease. His role as lookout in Book 6 is partially shown.
narrative_role_agency.difference: The primary agency-related loss is the cut Polyjuice scene (unconscious Crabbe and Goyle being dragged and stored), which removes a beat where Goyle's body is literally appropriated as a prop — a minor humiliation that adds texture. The transfer of Fiendfyre from Crabbe to Goyle in the films technically preserves the overall plot function and actually elevates Goyle's agency and narrative consequence. His role as Malfoy's lookout in Book 6 is present but compressed. The bodyguard intimidation function is consistent across both media.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: Goyle's role and agency are largely preserved. The Crabbe-to-Goyle transfer in Deathly Hallows means Goyle's film role is, if anything, slightly elevated in consequence. The cut Polyjuice staging scene is a minor loss. No major action of Goyle's is given to another character — the Fiendfyre transfer goes to Goyle from Crabbe, not away from Goyle. A moderate score is appropriate: role and agency are recognisable and mostly intact, with some compression, scoring in the 10–13 range.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Goyle has almost no explicitly stated motivations in the books. His behaviour is entirely conditioned by: (1) following Malfoy's lead without question through most of the series; (2) implicit pure-blood supremacist ideology absorbed from his Death Eater father (his father is named as a Death Eater at the graveyard in Goblet of Fire); (3) in Deathly Hallows, a nascent independent motivation emerges — he wants to be 'rewarded' by Voldemort and deliberately positions himself to capture Harry, speaking with the simplistic avarice of 'a small child promised a large bag of sweets.' There is no genuine internal conflict in the books; Goyle has no moment of doubt or moral struggle. His motivations are externally driven and unreflective.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The films give almost no access to Goyle's motivations — consistent with the books. His Deathly Hallows dialogue ('We 'ung back, Potter. We decided not to go. Decided to bring you to 'im.') preserves the book's portrait of a simple, reward-seeking loyalty to Voldemort. The film does not invent motivations or complicate them beyond what the books establish.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: Almost no change. The books themselves provide very little motivational material for Goyle, and the films faithfully represent that thinness. The main gap is the absence of the book's explicit statement about his Death Eater father's influence and the slight dimming of the 'child promised sweets' characterisation in the film (it is implied rather than narrated), but neither constitutes a meaningful alteration of what motivations exist.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: The motivations are thin in both books and films. What little exists is preserved. The confidence is Low because there is simply not much to evaluate. A modest penalty for the slight loss of the explicit 'father as Death Eater' motivation context, which the books provide and the films do not foreground for Goyle specifically. Score in 8–10 range.
motivations_internal_conflict.evidence_status: Reasonably inferred; the corpus provides limited direct evidence of Goyle's inner life in either medium.

character_arc.book_baseline: Goyle has a flat arc for most of the series: he is Malfoy's silent, thuggish follower from Book 1 through Book 6. In Book 7, there is a micro-arc: he makes an independent choice (to stay at Hogwarts and capture Harry for Voldemort), demonstrates genuine Dark Arts capability (Avada Kedavra, Fiendfyre), and dies as a direct consequence of his own action. This is a minimal but real arc — from passive follower to independently agentive Death Eater-in-training who dies by his own magic. It is not a moral arc but a functional one: he becomes genuinely dangerous and pays with his life.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The film preserves this micro-arc faithfully. Goyle is a passive follower for most of the series, then in Deathly Hallows Part 2 he speaks independently, casts lethal spells, triggers Fiendfyre (with the Crabbe-to-Goyle transfer noted above), and dies. The arc endpoint — death by Fiendfyre he himself unleashed — is intact.
character_arc.difference: The arc is compressed (the Book 6 section where Goyle serves as Malfoy's lookout and is part of the Room of Requirement surveillance is less developed in the film), but the critical narrative beats — passive follower → briefly independent and dangerous → dead — are all present. The transfer from Crabbe to Goyle for the Fiendfyre beat actually strengthens Goyle's arc in the film relative to the books.
character_arc.penalty_logic: Arc is compressed but faithful. The key turning point (Deathly Hallows independent agency and death) is preserved. Minor compression in Book 6 beats. Score in 11–13 range.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Goyle's primary relationship is with Malfoy: total, unthinking subordination and loyalty. He does whatever Malfoy does, laughs when Malfoy laughs, flexes muscles when Malfoy needs intimidation. There is no warmth or genuine friendship in the books — it is hierarchical follower-leader with Goyle as a near-object. His relationship with Crabbe is one of identical pairing — they are often indistinguishable, described as a unit. By Deathly Hallows, a small fracture appears: Goyle's independent decision-making (staying behind, casting lethal spells) suggests a shift toward self-directed loyalty to Voldemort rather than purely to Malfoy.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The Malfoy-Goyle dynamic is preserved as hierarchical subordination throughout the films. The Crabbe-Goyle unit is partially disrupted in the later films by Blaise Zabini's presence, which dilutes the Goyle-Crabbe pairing but does not misrepresent Goyle's relationship with Malfoy. The Deathly Hallows dynamic where Goyle shows mild independence from Malfoy ('Just do 'im') while still orbiting him is present. The emotional flatness of the relationship — no affection, no genuine loyalty, just proximity and use — is preserved.
key_relationships.difference: The main loss is the Crabbe-Goyle unit being partially broken up across the later films by Zabini's substitution. This does reduce the specific texture of their identical-pair function. The Malfoy-Goyle dynamic's key quality (total subordination) is intact. The Deathly Hallows scene where Goyle pushes past Malfoy to act independently (in the Room of Requirement, he steps into the breach when Malfoy hesitates) is present in the film.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: Key relationship with Malfoy is substantially faithful. The Crabbe-Goyle pairing is partially diluted in later films. A small penalty for the loss of the specific unit-pairing texture. Score in 7–8 range.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: Goyle is not a complex character, but the books give him specific texture that goes beyond generic thug: (1) his stupidity is carefully calibrated — Ron mimes writing as Goyle in Book 5 ('I must not look like a baboon's backside') as a specific comedy beat; (2) the Polyjuice sequence in Book 2 gives him unusual centrality — Harry literally inhabits his body, observes his appearance from the inside, and the narration generates specific physical detail (bristly hair, dull deep-set eyes, thick wrists, boatlike shoes, low rasp of voice); (3) his cowardice/fear under the Invisibility Cloak mud-attack in Book 3 (he hops in pain, tries to rub mud from his small dull eyes) shows vulnerability; (4) he attempts to steal leprechaun gold in Book 4 (Hagrid calls him out); (5) he genuinely attempts to harm Harry and Hermione with Avada Kedavra in Deathly Hallows — the most morally definitive act the books give him; (6) the description of Crabbe and Goyle at the Slytherin table after Malfoy's departure in Half-Blood Prince ('oddly lonely without the tall pale figure of Malfoy between them, bossing them around') is a rare moment of pathos.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The films preserve his physical presence and intimidation function. The Deathly Hallows combat scenes give him genuine menace. What is lost: (1) the Polyjuice interior-view of Goyle's body (the cut scene removes the most intimate characterisation of Goyle in the series); (2) the specific comedy beats (Ron's impression, the leprechaun gold, Scabbers biting his finger) are absent; (3) the brief pathos of the lonely Crabbe-Goyle image in HBP is not present; (4) the mud-throwing vulnerability sequence from PoA is condensed — Crabbe and Goyle's knees go out (film) rather than Goyle hopping and rubbing mud from his eyes (book), losing the specific physical comedy.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The film retains Goyle's broad identity but loses most of the specific textural material that made him more than a generic thug: the Polyjuice intimate characterisation, the comedy beats, the pathos moment, and several small humiliation/vulnerability scenes. The films keep the functional outline but drop the detail. This is a noticeable simplification.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: The character is simplified but not unrecognisably so. The most significant single loss is the Polyjuice cut scene (excluded per instructions), which contained the richest characterisation of Goyle's physicality in the entire series. The remaining lost material (comedy beats, pathos moment, mud humiliation) cumulatively reduces the texture meaningfully. Score in 8–10 range.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for losses; reasonably inferred for cumulative effect.

lost_or_transferred_material: Polyjuice preparation scene cut (theatrical): Harry inhabiting Goyle's body — the most detailed physical characterisation of Goyle in the series, including his dull deep-set eyes, bristly hair, thick wrists, boatlike shoes, and low rasp voice
Scabbers biting Goyle's finger on the Hogwarts Express (Book 1) — not depicted in film
Goyle greedily eating sleeping-draught cake (Book 2, cut scene) — greed/stupidity beat lost
Real Crabbe and Goyle encountering their Polyjuiced doubles (Book 2, cut scene)
Ron's impression of Goyle struggling to write ('I must not look like a baboon's backside') — Book 5 comedy beat absent
Goyle attempting to steal leprechaun gold in Care of Magical Creatures (Book 4) — absent
Goyle hopping and rubbing mud from his small dull eyes during invisible mud-throw (Book 3) — compressed in film
Pathos moment of Crabbe and Goyle looking oddly lonely at Slytherin table without Malfoy (Book 6) — absent
Goyle's potion shattering and setting his robes on fire in Book 5 Potions — mentioned by Hermione in book but not depicted
Crabbe (book) → Goyle (film) transfer for Fiendfyre casting and death in Deathly Hallows (noted as transfer from Crabbe, not a loss for Goyle — actually an elevation)
score_caps_applied: Cap 4 considered (score above 70 only if films preserve more than broad identity): Films do preserve specific behaviours and key plot beats beyond broad identity — Deathly Hallows agency is faithfully rendered — so cap 4 does not strictly apply, but the cumulative texture loss from cut and absent scenes keeps the score naturally below 75.
comparative.key_observations: Goyle is a minor character whose book characterisation is already thin, so the films have relatively little to preserve or lose. The surface identity — large, dull, silent, thuggish, obedient to Malfoy — is consistently maintained across all films. The most significant faithfulness concern is the loss of the Polyjuice body-inhabitation sequence (cut from theatrical release per instructions), which contained the series' richest physical and comedic characterisation of Goyle. Several smaller comedy and humiliation beats from the books are absent. Conversely, the adaptation of the Deathly Hallows Room of Requirement scene is largely faithful, and the transfer of the Fiendfyre role from Crabbe to Goyle actually strengthens Goyle's narrative consequence in the film. The character scores moderately: the broad strokes are right, the specific texture is meaningfully reduced, and the confidence is Medium throughout due to the limited dialogue corpus available for Goyle in both media.

personality_voice.book_baseline: In the books, Griphook is defined by several consistent traits: cold pride in goblin identity and craftsmanship, contempt for wizards as a class ('wand-carriers'), a transactional and calculating intelligence, malicious humor (laughing at the idea of a Death Eater trapped in a vault, smugly withholding information from them), and a deep-seated resentment rooted in genuine political grievance. He is not simply villainous — he is ideologically motivated. His speech is measured, formal, and often cutting. He uses silence and delay as power tools ('I shall... think about it'). He is unexpectedly bloodthirsty during planning, laughs at pain in lesser creatures, and eats raw meat separately from the group — behavioral details that establish him as genuinely alien and unsettling rather than merely unpleasant. He is also capable of grudging respect: he acknowledges Harry as unusual, notes that he would believe Harry seeks no personal gain, and is visibly moved by the burial of Dobby. His betrayal at the vault is not impulsive — it is the logical conclusion of a character who never trusted wizards and always intended to reclaim what he considered rightfully goblin property.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The film preserves the core of Griphook's transactional nature, his goblin pride, his contempt for wizard ownership of goblin-made objects, and his ultimate betrayal. His line 'I said I'd get you in. I never said anything about getting you out' is a clean distillation of his book character. His observation that Harry buried the elf and is 'a very unusual wizard' is retained. His refusal of gold, his insistence on the sword, and his ideological framing ('This is a wizard's war. I take no side') are present. However, several defining vocal and behavioral traits are absent or compressed. The malicious humor — his delight in having deceived the Death Eaters about the fake sword, his roaring laughter with Gornuk — is entirely absent from the film. The bloodthirsty planning-phase behavior, the raw meat, the deliberate social isolation, and the sustained menace of his presence at Shell Cottage are all cut. His speech in the film is functional and efficient but lacks the formal, measured cadence and the ideological elaboration of the books. The wand-rights speech — his most politically articulate moment — is absent. In the film he is sharp and untrustworthy, but not the ideologically complex, quietly menacing figure of the books.
personality_voice.difference: The film retains the transactional core and the betrayal logic, but removes the malicious humor, the ideological voice, the behavioral alienness (raw meat, isolation, surveillance of Harry), and the formal speech patterns that give book-Griphook his texture. He becomes a functional antagonist-ally rather than a character with a coherent worldview expressed through behavior and voice.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The main traits are recognizable — calculating, proud, ultimately treacherous — but the secondary traits that make him distinctive (malicious glee, ideological articulation, behavioral alienness, formal measured speech) are substantially reduced. This warrants a score in the 14–17 range: recognizable but with important traits reduced.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: In the books, Griphook serves multiple narrative functions: he is the intelligence source who reveals the fake sword (overheard by Harry and Hermione), the negotiating partner whose terms Harry must navigate, the tactical expert who guides the Gringotts break-in, and the agent of betrayal who seizes the sword at the critical moment. He also functions as a moral and ideological counterweight — his arguments about goblin rights force Harry, Ron, and Hermione to confront the limits of their own assumptions. His agency is high throughout: he withholds information strategically, sets the terms of the deal, monitors Harry for signs of deception, provides tactical guidance inside Gringotts, and executes his betrayal with deliberate timing. He is also the one who spots the cup on the sword's blade and lunges for it — the act that triggers the betrayal.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: The film preserves Griphook's role as negotiator, tactical guide, and betrayer. He identifies the Thief's Downfall, explains the Gemino and Flagrante curses, manages Bogrod, and executes the betrayal. His agency in the vault sequence is largely intact. However, his role as intelligence source — the campfire scene where he reveals the fake sword to Harry and Hermione — is entirely absent. In the film, Griphook simply tells Harry about the fake sword during their Shell Cottage negotiation, which compresses his function but does not eliminate it. More significantly, the film transfers the Imperio curse on Bogrod from Harry to Ron, and the key moment of spotting the cup on the sword's blade — which in the books is Griphook's act that precipitates the betrayal — is restructured so that Harry retrieves the cup independently and Griphook simply holds the sword afterward. The betrayal line is rewritten: in the books Griphook never promised to get them out; in the film he explicitly states this as his justification, which is faithful in spirit.
narrative_role_agency.difference: The campfire intelligence function is removed (compressed into the Shell Cottage scene). The cup-retrieval moment — where Griphook's lunge for the sword is what causes the cup to fly free, making his betrayal the direct mechanism of Harry's success — is restructured so Harry retrieves the cup himself and Griphook's betrayal is more passive. The Imperio transfer to Ron is a minor agency loss.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: The core role is preserved — negotiator, guide, betrayer — but the campfire function and the structural importance of his betrayal as the mechanism of Harry's success are reduced. The golden rule applies: the cup-retrieval moment is transferred to Harry. Score in the 14–17 range.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Griphook's motivations are layered and coherent. He helps Harry not out of loyalty or sympathy but because he wants the sword — which he believes is rightfully goblin property, stolen by Gryffindor from Ragnuk the First. This is not mere greed; it is a principled claim rooted in goblin law and history. His resentment of wizards is ideological: they deny goblins wand rights, they keep goblin-made objects without returning them, they treat goblins as servants. His betrayal is the logical expression of this worldview — he never trusted wizards to keep their word, and he acts on that distrust the moment he can. There is also a secondary motivation: he left Gringotts because he 'recognized no Wizarding master,' which establishes his independence and pride as genuine rather than performative. The internal conflict is subtle: he is capable of acknowledging Harry's unusual decency, yet this does not change his fundamental distrust of wizards as a class.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The film preserves the transactional motivation (he wants the sword) and the ideological framing ('This is a wizard's war. I take no side'). His reason for leaving Gringotts is simplified to 'Soon the Death Eaters will control it. That was unacceptable to me' — which is faithful in substance. The sword-as-rightful-goblin-property argument is absent from the film's Shell Cottage scene; Griphook simply wants the sword without the historical justification (Ragnuk the First, the claim that Gryffindor stole it). This removes the principled dimension of his motivation and makes his desire for the sword look more like acquisitiveness than a rights claim. The internal conflict — his grudging acknowledgment of Harry's decency coexisting with his fundamental distrust — is present but compressed.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The historical and ideological basis for wanting the sword (Ragnuk the First, goblin ownership law) is absent. The wand-rights argument is absent. His motivation is simplified from a principled political claim to an unexplained desire for a valuable object. The internal conflict is present but underexplained.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: The motivations are partially altered and flattened. The transactional core is intact, but the principled dimension that makes his betrayal coherent rather than merely villainous is removed. Score in the 8–10 range.

character_arc.book_baseline: Griphook's arc is not a redemption arc or a growth arc — it is a confirmation arc. He begins as a calculating, resentful goblin who distrusts wizards. He is persuaded to help Harry through a combination of Harry's unusual decency (burying Dobby, rescuing Griphook) and a deal he intends to exploit. Throughout the planning phase, he monitors Harry for signs of deception, grows more comfortable in his role as tactical expert, and waits for the right moment. His betrayal at the vault is the arc's resolution: he never changed, never trusted, and acts exactly as his worldview predicted he would. The arc is flat in the sense that Griphook does not transform, but it is dramatically complete — the reader understands why he does what he does, and the betrayal feels earned rather than arbitrary.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The film follows the same arc: initial wariness, negotiation, tactical cooperation, betrayal. The key beats are present. However, the planning phase — weeks at Shell Cottage, the growing unease, Griphook's surveillance of Harry, Bill's warning — is entirely absent. The arc jumps from negotiation to Gringotts with no intermediate development. This means the betrayal, while logically consistent, lacks the accumulated tension and the sense that Griphook has been waiting and watching. The film's betrayal line ('I said I'd get you in. I never said anything about getting you out') is sharp and effective, but it arrives without the buildup that makes it feel inevitable rather than convenient.
character_arc.difference: The arc's shape is preserved but the middle is missing. The planning phase, the surveillance, the growing mutual distrust, and Bill's warning are all absent. The betrayal is present but compressed to the point where it reads as a plot twist rather than a character conclusion.
character_arc.penalty_logic: The arc is compressed but still faithful in its trajectory. The starting point, the deal, and the betrayal are all present. The missing middle reduces the arc's dramatic weight but does not change its direction. Score in the 11–13 range.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Griphook's most important relationship is with Harry, which is defined by mutual wariness, strategic calculation, and asymmetric trust. Harry needs Griphook and treats him with unusual respect; Griphook acknowledges this but never extends genuine trust in return. The relationship is a negotiation that both parties know is adversarial beneath the surface. Secondary relationships include his dynamic with Ron (whom he dismisses and corrects), Hermione (whose Mudblood status he acknowledges as a point of solidarity, though he remains unmoved), and Bill (whose warning about goblin notions of ownership frames the relationship's stakes). The relationship with Fleur is one of mutual irritation. The campfire relationship with Gornuk and Ted Lupin establishes Griphook's social world among his own kind — he is more relaxed, more openly malicious, and more politically articulate in that context.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The Harry-Griphook relationship is preserved in its essential dynamic: mutual wariness, the deal, the betrayal. The Shell Cottage scene captures the sizing-up quality of their interaction. However, the relationship with Ron is reduced to a single sharp exchange in Diagon Alley. The relationship with Hermione — her appeal to goblin solidarity, her display of Bellatrix's cut — is entirely absent. The campfire relationships with Gornuk and Ted are absent. Bill's warning scene is absent, removing the external framing of the relationship's danger.
key_relationships.difference: The Harry-Griphook dynamic is mostly preserved. The Hermione solidarity moment is lost. The campfire social context is lost. Bill's warning is lost. The relationship is narrowed to Harry alone, which simplifies Griphook's social and political positioning.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: The primary relationship is mostly faithful. The loss of the Hermione solidarity moment and Bill's warning simplifies the relational texture but does not fundamentally alter the Harry-Griphook dynamic. Score in the 7–8 range.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: Book-Griphook is one of the series' most ideologically coherent minor characters. His complexity comes from the coexistence of genuine political grievance (goblin rights, wand access, ownership law) with personal malice and bloodthirstiness. He is not simply a villain — his critique of wizard society is largely correct — but he is also not sympathetic in the conventional sense. He laughs at pain, eats raw meat, surveils Harry obsessively, and plans his betrayal from the moment he shakes hands. The campfire scene establishes him as part of a community of displaced magical beings, capable of camaraderie and malicious humor. The planning phase at Shell Cottage reveals his alienness in domestic detail. His acknowledgment of Harry's decency is genuine but does not change his behavior — this contradiction is the character's most interesting quality.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The film retains the transactional intelligence, the betrayal, and the goblin-pride framing. It loses the ideological elaboration (wand rights, Ragnuk the First), the malicious humor, the behavioral alienness (raw meat, isolation, surveillance), the campfire community, the Hermione solidarity scene, and the planning-phase tension. What remains is a functional version of Griphook: untrustworthy, sharp, effective. The complexity that made him more than a plot device — the genuine political grievance, the coexistence of correct critique and personal malice, the domestic alienness — is largely absent.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The film removes most of the material that distinguishes Griphook from a generic untrustworthy ally. The ideological dimension, the behavioral texture, the social context, and the moral ambiguity of his position are all reduced or absent.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: Noticeable simplification. Important nuances — the ideological voice, the behavioral alienness, the campfire community, the Hermione moment — are missing. The character is reduced toward a single function (untrustworthy guide) without the contradictions and texture that made him complex. Score in the 8–10 range.

lost_or_transferred_material: Campfire scene: Griphook reveals the fake sword to Harry and Hermione (overheard) — compressed into Shell Cottage negotiation, losing the intelligence-source function and the malicious humor with Gornuk
Wand-rights argument: Griphook's articulation of goblin political grievance about wand access is entirely absent from the film
Ragnuk the First: the historical basis for Griphook's claim to the sword (Gryffindor stole it) is absent, reducing his motivation from principled claim to unexplained desire
Hermione's solidarity appeal: her display of Bellatrix's cut and her claim of shared oppression as a Mudblood — absent from the film
Bill's warning scene: his explanation of goblin notions of ownership and the danger of any bargain with Griphook — absent
Planning phase at Shell Cottage: weeks of cohabitation, Griphook's surveillance of Harry, his raw meat diet, his social isolation, his bloodthirstiness during planning — all absent
Malicious humor: Griphook's delight in deceiving Death Eaters, his laughter with Gornuk, his smug withholding of information — absent

Cup-retrieval moment: in the books, Griphook lunges for the sword and the cup flies free as a direct result of his betrayal act; in the film Harry retrieves the cup independently before Griphook takes the sword
Imperio on Bogrod: transferred from Harry to Ron in the film
Campfire community: Griphook's social world among Gornuk, Ted Lupin, Dean, and Dirk — establishing him as part of a displaced magical community — entirely absent
score_caps_applied: Cap 3 (score above 75 if a core book function, decision, or act of agency is transferred to another character): cup-retrieval moment restructured so Harry acts independently; Imperio on Bogrod transferred to Ron — cap considered but total falls below 75 naturally
Cap 1 (score above 85 if films remove a major part of complexity, agency, contradiction, or narrative function): applies — total falls well below 85
comparative.key_observations: The film preserves Griphook's functional identity — calculating, transactional, ultimately treacherous — and the key beats of his arc (negotiation, deal, betrayal). The betrayal line is sharp and faithful in spirit. However, the film strips away almost everything that made book-Griphook more than a plot device: his ideological voice, his historical grievance, his malicious humor, his behavioral alienness, his social context among displaced magical beings, and the accumulated tension of the Shell Cottage planning phase. What remains is a recognizable but substantially simplified version of the character — untrustworthy and effective, but without the political coherence and domestic texture that gave his betrayal moral weight rather than mere narrative convenience. The score reflects a character who is faithfully sketched in outline but significantly hollowed in substance.

personality_voice.book_baseline: In the books, Mafalda Hopkirk exists solely through three written letters — formal, bureaucratic, impersonal, and procedurally correct. Her voice is that of an institutional functionary: she cites specific decrees and statutes by name and paragraph, enumerates offenses with clinical precision, and closes with the performatively cheerful 'Enjoy your holidays!' — a jarring incongruity that reveals an oblivious or indifferent bureaucratic personality rather than any malice. She never speaks directly. Her personality is entirely mediated through the register of official correspondence: rule-citing, impersonal, procedurally dutiful, and tone-deaf to emotional context. In the infiltration scene (Book 7), she is unconscious and passive — a body used as a disguise — and has no observable personality at all beyond what her ID card and Ministry tokens convey.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: In the OotP film (Scene 1), Mafalda's letter is read aloud in voice-over as a direct address to Harry. The wording is condensed and simplified: the statute citations, paragraph references, and the jarring 'Enjoy your holidays!' are removed. The letter retains its expulsion threat but loses its bureaucratic texture. In the DH1 film (Scenes 2–6), Hermione impersonates Mafalda and speaks as her. The lines given to 'Mafalda Hopkirk/Hermione' — 'You're somebody. Be careful,' 'Muggles. In their rightful place,' 'Try Finite Incantatem,' 'I don't like him being on his own down there,' 'You really have horrible teeth, you know that' — are all Hermione's character speaking through Mafalda's body. These lines reflect Hermione's concern, wit, and moral indignation, not anything derivable from the book Mafalda.
personality_voice.difference: The book Mafalda has a precise, identifiable bureaucratic voice — formal register, statute citation, procedural cheerfulness. The film removes this texture in the OotP letter and then replaces her personality entirely in DH1 with Hermione's voice. There is no film moment where the real Mafalda's voice or personality is independently expressed.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The loss of the statute citations and 'Enjoy your holidays!' removes the only observable personality markers the book Mafalda has. This is a minor but real simplification. More significantly, all of the 'Mafalda' dialogue in DH1 is Hermione speaking, which means the film audience has no access to Mafalda's personality at all beyond the condensed letter. This warrants a score in the 14–17 range: the character remains recognizable as a Ministry functionary, but her defining voice texture is reduced (letter) or entirely absent (DH1).
personality_voice.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for book baseline (letter text in corpus); directly evidenced for film OotP simplification (voice-over wording in Scene 1); reasonably inferred that DH1 dialogue is Hermione's rather than Mafalda's, based on the corpus stage directions explicitly labeling speakers as 'MAFALDA HOPKIRK/HERMIONE.'

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: In the books, Mafalda Hopkirk serves two distinct narrative functions. First, as author of the expulsion/warning letters (Books 2, 5), she is the bureaucratic arm of the Ministry's surveillance apparatus — she is the mechanism by which the Ministry asserts control over underage magic. This function drives plot (the letters create stakes, expulsion threats, and institutional pressure). Second, in Book 7, she is a passive instrument: her identity is stolen so Hermione can infiltrate the Ministry. She has no agency in this scene; she is stunned and used.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: In OotP (Scene 1), the letter retains its plot-driving function — it triggers Harry's expulsion threat, which is a key story beat. The film preserves this role. In DH1 (Scenes 2–6), Mafalda's role as the identity stolen for infiltration is preserved structurally. However, once Hermione assumes her form, all agency in those scenes belongs to Hermione. The real Mafalda is unconscious and offscreen.
narrative_role_agency.difference: The core narrative roles — Ministry enforcer via letter, and infiltration vehicle — are both present in the films. However, the DH1 book scene has Mafalda stunned backstage near a theater, while the film relocates the ambush to a street corner (Whitehall). This is a setting change with no meaningful impact on narrative function. The agency picture is the same in both media: Mafalda has none in the infiltration sequence.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: The letter role is preserved with minor compression (one letter in OotP film vs. two letters across Books 2 and 5 in the books — the Book 2 letter is absent from the film corpus but that film handles the Dobby hover-charm scene differently and is outside this corpus). The infiltration role is structurally preserved. No agency is lost because Mafalda had no agency in the DH scene to begin with. Minor penalty for the OotP letter being the only surviving instance of the Ministry enforcement function, and for some compression of the letter's procedural detail that weakens the institutional weight of the role.
narrative_role_agency.evidence_status: Directly evidenced: both letter and infiltration functions appear in corpus. Directly evidenced: Mafalda is stunned and passive in both book and film infiltration scenes.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: The books offer no insight into Mafalda Hopkirk's internal motivations beyond what is implied by her role: she is a Ministry bureaucrat doing her job. There is no evidence of personal investment, ideological commitment, fear, ambition, or moral conflict. Her letters suggest procedural compliance rather than any discernible inner life. In Book 7, she is an unconscious body — motivations are entirely inaccessible.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The film provides no additional motivation. The letter is delivered and the character is stunned. No internal life is added or removed because none existed in the source material.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: No meaningful difference. Neither medium provides access to Mafalda's internal motivations.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: Since the books establish no motivations or internal conflict for this character, the films cannot be penalized for failing to show them. Full score would be inappropriate because the absence of motivation evidence means we cannot confirm faithfulness — only absence. The score reflects the neutral position: nothing to preserve, nothing lost, but also nothing to confirm. A middling score acknowledges the structural limitation.
motivations_internal_conflict.evidence_status: Not enough evidence in either corpus to evaluate internal motivation. Score is based on the shared absence of motivational material.

character_arc.book_baseline: Mafalda Hopkirk has no arc. She appears in three letters across two books and is unconscious in her only physical appearance. There is no starting point, evolution, turning point, or resolution. Her arc is intentionally flat — she is a functional character, not a developmental one.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The film similarly presents no arc. She appears in a letter voice-over and is stunned for an infiltration sequence. No arc is introduced or implied.
character_arc.difference: No difference. Both book and film present a flat, arc-free character.
character_arc.penalty_logic: Per the scoring rules, a character can score full marks if their arc is flat in the books and flat in the films. This applies here. The score reflects the faithful preservation of flatness. Minor deduction only because the film's compression of the letter (OotP) removes one data point that might, in aggregate, have contributed to a slightly more textured institutional presence — but this does not constitute an arc change.
character_arc.evidence_status: Directly evidenced: no arc present in either corpus.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Mafalda's only book relationships are institutional: she is in correspondence with Harry Potter (as a Ministry official addressing a rule-violator) and implicitly with the Ministry hierarchy she serves. There is no personal relationship, no emotional dynamic, no power balance of note beyond bureaucrat-to-subject. In Book 7, she has no relationship with the trio — she is a stranger they ambush.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: In OotP, the letter relationship (Ministry-to-Harry) is preserved in function. In DH1, Hermione speaks as Mafalda and interacts with Harry and Ron — but these interactions express Hermione's relationships, not Mafalda's. The real Mafalda has no relationship with the trio in either medium.
key_relationships.difference: The institutional relationship (Ministry enforcer to Harry) is preserved in OotP. In DH1, the film adds dialogue between 'Mafalda' and the trio, but this is Hermione speaking, not Mafalda — so no genuine relationship is added for the character herself. The DH1 book does not give Mafalda any dialogue or relationship with the trio either; she is simply stunned.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: The only meaningful relationship — Ministry bureaucrat writing to Harry — is functionally preserved in OotP. The DH1 'relationship' dialogue belongs to Hermione, not Mafalda, so it neither adds nor subtracts from Mafalda's relational faithfulness. Minor penalty for the removal of the Book 2 letter, which was an additional instance of the same bureaucratic relationship but is absent from the film record in this corpus.
key_relationships.evidence_status: Directly evidenced: institutional relationship preserved in OotP letter. Reasonably inferred: DH1 dialogue is Hermione's, not Mafalda's, based on corpus labeling.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: Mafalda's complexity in the books is minimal but specific: the tonal incongruity of the bureaucratic letter — citing statutes by exact paragraph, threatening expulsion, and then signing off with 'Enjoy your holidays!' — is a subtle piece of characterization. It renders her not as a villain but as an oblivious institutional agent: someone so embedded in procedure that she cannot perceive the human cost of her correspondence. This is a small but texturally interesting detail. In Book 7, she contributes to the world-building of the Ministry as a place where individuals are reduced to tokens and ID cards.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The film removes 'Enjoy your holidays!' and the statute citations from the OotP letter. This eliminates the tonal incongruity that gave the book Mafalda her only distinctive nuance. In DH1, all dialogue attributed to her is Hermione's, so no book nuance survives. The Ministry infiltration scene preserves the ID card / tokens detail (corpus scenes 14–17 in books, scene 2–3 in films), which maintains some of the dehumanizing institutional texture.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The tonal incongruity ('Enjoy your holidays!') is lost. The statute citations that convey bureaucratic thoroughness are lost. What remains is functional identification of the character as a Ministry employee — recognizable but stripped of its only distinctive texture.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: The loss of 'Enjoy your holidays!' and the statute detail is a genuine nuance loss: it was the one element that made Mafalda more than a plot device and gave her a faint but real personality. This is not a major flattening (the character was already simple), but it is the loss of the only material that complicated her. Score reflects noticeable simplification without major characterization damage.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.evidence_status: Directly evidenced: 'Enjoy your holidays!' and statute citations present in book corpus, absent from film corpus. Directly evidenced: ID card and tokens detail preserved in both corpora.

lost_or_transferred_material: Statute citations with specific paragraph references (Decree for the Reasonable Restriction of Underage Sorcery, 1875, Paragraph C; Section 13 of the International Confederation of Warlocks' Statute of Secrecy) removed from the OotP film letter
The closing 'Enjoy your holidays!' — the only tonal marker suggesting bureaucratic obliviousness — removed from the OotP film letter

All DH1 dialogue attributed to 'Mafalda Hopkirk' in the film is spoken by Hermione in disguise — none of it reflects the real Mafalda's voice, personality, or agency; it is effectively transferred to Hermione's characterization
score_caps_applied: Cap 4 considered (films preserve only broad identity, removing most of what defines book characterization): applied implicitly — the 'Enjoy your holidays!' tonal detail and statute citations are the defining book texture; their loss contributes to a score below 75

No hard cap mechanically applied because the character's book presence is so minimal that the remaining faithful material (institutional role, identity theft function) represents a substantial proportion of what was available to adapt
comparative.key_observations: Mafalda Hopkirk is a minor functional character whose book presence consists of three bureaucratic letters and one unconscious physical appearance. The films preserve her structural roles — Ministry enforcement letter and infiltration vehicle — but strip out the only nuance she possesses: the tonal incongruity of 'Enjoy your holidays!' and the precise statute citations that rendered her a recognizable type of oblivious institutional functionary rather than a mere name on a page. All DH1 dialogue ostensibly in her voice is actually Hermione's, meaning the film audience receives no independent characterization of the real Mafalda beyond a condensed and smoothed-over letter. The score of 67 reflects a character who is structurally recognizable and functionally preserved, but whose sole distinguishing textual texture has been removed. Confidence is medium throughout because the source material is so thin that evaluation requires interpretation of small details rather than broad behavioral patterns.

personality_voice.book_baseline: Across all seven books, Ron's personality is defined by a consistent and recognizable cluster: loyal, brave, and genuinely warm, but also insecure, reactive, prone to jealousy, and capable of petty cruelty toward those he loves. His voice is colloquial, direct, and emotionally unguarded — short sentences, rhetorical questions, blunt assessments, self-deprecating humor, and occasional unexpected tenderness. He deflects anxiety with jokes, expresses jealousy clumsily, and shows moral clarity in moments of crisis. Crucially, he is not simply comic relief: he is a co-investigator, a strategist, and an emotional anchor who is also capable of sustained unpleasantness. His personality across the series is defined as much by his flaws — weeks of cold-shouldering Hermione in HBP and GoF, petty cruelty about girls at the Yule Ball, the departure in DH, sustained aggression during the GoF estrangement — as by his virtues. The insecurity of being the sixth Weasley son, perpetually in Harry's shadow, is the foundational psychological texture confirmed structurally by the Mirror of Erised in PS.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The films preserve Ron's core personality markers consistently across all eight entries: his humor is present throughout (the spider butterflies line in CoS, 'kill us faster' in PS, 'Wankers' in HBP, 'That's unfortunate' in DH); his loyalty is unwavering and well-performed; his bluntness survives in multiple exchanges ('She's a nightmare, honestly'; 'Piss off' to Percy; 'Not bloody likely'); his bravery in crisis is preserved (chess chamber, Shrieking Shack, Department of Mysteries, Horcrux destructions). The love-potion sequence in HBP, the Deluminator speech in DH, and the spider-fear sequences in CoS and PoA all represent the films at their most characterologically faithful to Ron's voice.
personality_voice.difference: The films systematically remove the sustained unpleasantness that is one of Ron's defining characteristics in the books. The weeks-long cold-shouldering of Hermione in HBP, the extended GoF estrangement, the sustained pettiness in OotP's Quidditch Keeper arc — all compressed into single scenes or removed entirely. The foundational insecurity about being the sixth Weasley son, the texture that the Mirror of Erised confirms, is largely absent from the theatrical films (the Mirror scene is cut from PS theatrical release). His wit is sharper and more inventive in the books; the film Ron is funnier in broad strokes but less verbally precise. Across the series, the film consistently prioritizes Ron's warmth and humor at the expense of his capacity for petty cruelty, prolonged dysfunction, and the specific social anxiety of perpetual secondness. Books 5 and 6 represent the worst failures: in OotP virtually every subplot that gives Ron complexity (Quidditch Keeper arc, prefect badge, Percy's letter) is absent; in HBP the weeks of emotional deterioration are replaced by episodic comedy. The most important books for Ron's series-wide arc — GoF (jealousy/estrangement), OotP (insecurity/triumph), HBP (romantic arc), and DH (maturation/co-protagonist status) — all show meaningful personality compression.
personality_voice.evidence_status: Directly evidenced across all seven per-book scorings
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The per-book scores ranged from 17 (GoF, OotP) to 20 (PoA), with most clustering at 17–18. The two most important books for Ron's series-wide personality — OotP and HBP, where his flaws and complexity are most fully dramatized — both scored 17, reflecting significant simplification. PoA's 20 is the high-water mark because that film happened to preserve his voice most densely. The synthesis score of 17 reflects: core personality consistently present and well-performed; secondary layer of sustained unpleasantness, insecurity texture, and wit systematically stripped; no major trait inverted but the defining psychological architecture (the sixth-son insecurity) largely absent from theatrical films. The 17 sits at the lower end of the 'main personality preserved, notable simplification of secondary traits' band, weighted toward GoF and OotP losses.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: Across the series, Ron is an active co-protagonist whose narrative agency is substantial and varied. He is the character who knows the wizarding world and explains it to Harry (and the reader). He is the chess sacrifice in PS, the Polyjuice co-architect in CoS, the Scabbers/Pettigrew link in PoA, the investigative co-theorist across GoF, the Quidditch Keeper arc center in OotP, the Horcrux-planning leader in DH, the Chamber-of-Secrets-entry originator in DH. He initiates plans (ghoul plan, Norbert-to-Charlie, Ministry infiltration), provides intelligence others lack (Unbreakable Vow consequences in HBP, Magical Maintenance uniforms, Potterwatch), and performs decisive actions at key turning points (Expelliarmus alongside Hermione against Snape in PoA, Imperio on Bogrod in DH, Parseltongue entry into Chamber in DH). His absence during estrangement in GoF is itself narratively significant — Harry is genuinely weakened without him.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: The films preserve Ron's most dramatically visible acts of agency: the chess sacrifice (PS), the forest drive and rockfall guard (CoS), the Shrieking Shack sacrifice (PoA), the Yule Ball scenes (GoF), the Umbridge distraction (OotP), the Horcrux destructions and Chamber entry (DH). His role as Harry's companion and emotional validator is consistently maintained. The Polyjuice participation (CoS), the Imperio casting (DH), and the Parseltongue entry (DH) are all preserved and represent the films' most faithful renderings of his agency.
narrative_role_agency.difference: The films systematically strip Ron's intellectual and investigative agency, transferring much of it to Hermione. The Flamel discovery (PS), the Riddle award deduction (CoS), the Buckbeak defense research (PoA), the cave-scene analysis and Bagman/leprechaun-gold theorizing (GoF), the Potterwatch discovery and sustained leadership during Harry's Hallows obsession (DH), and the ghoul plan (DH) are all absent or reduced. The Joint Expelliarmus against Snape (PoA) is cut, Harry acting alone. Ron's entire Quidditch Keeper arc (OotP), which is the book's primary narrative spine for his character, is largely absent from the theatrical film. The climactic DA defense of Hogwarts (HBP) is cut. His role as theorist, planner, and intelligence-gatherer is the single most consistently lost dimension across all seven films. What remains is primarily his role as emotional validator and brave combatant — important functions, but a substantial reduction from the books.
narrative_role_agency.evidence_status: Directly evidenced across all seven per-book scorings
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: Per-book scores ranged from 13 (PS, CoS, HBP, GoF, OotP, DH) to 14 (PoA, DH). The narrow range reflects a consistent pattern: his dramatic agency is preserved, his intellectual and investigative agency is systematically transferred or removed. The synthesis score of 13 reflects: dramatic role intact and well-performed in most films; intellectual co-protagonist function substantially diminished across the entire series; multiple specific acts of initiative transferred to Hermione (the Transfer Rule penalizes this consistently); OotP's near-total absence of his Quidditch arc and DH's absence of the ghoul plan and Potterwatch as the worst individual failures. Weighted toward the most agency-critical books (GoF, OotP, DH), 13 is the appropriate synthesis.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Ron's motivations are layered throughout the series but have a consistent core: love for Harry and Hermione as chosen family; terror of being inadequate — as a friend, a Keeper, a son, a wizard; the deep insecurity of being the sixth Weasley, always in Harry's shadow; family loyalty coexisting with family shame about poverty. His internal conflicts are specific: jealousy of Krum (GoF, OotP) that is really displaced romantic feeling for Hermione; the estrangement from Harry in GoF driven by years of accumulated secondness; the departure in DH where real insecurities are amplified by the Horcrux. His motivations are almost always correct in the books but rarely stated — they are dramatized through sustained behavior across chapters.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The films preserve the correct motivational direction consistently. Loyalty to Harry and Hermione, family love, insecurity about adequacy — all are present in every film in some form. The departure scene in DH explicitly names his jealousy and family fear. The Deluminator speech names his redemptive guilt. The GoF confrontation scene ('Ron Weasley, Harry Potter's stupid friend') articulates his shadow-anxiety more directly than any single book passage. The family fear motivation is present in every appearance of the Weasley family.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The films state motivations more bluntly and less through accumulated evidence. In the books, Ron's motivations are built across weeks of observable behavior — the sustained estrangement in GoF, the weeks of Quidditch dysfunction in HBP and OotP, the Potterwatch obsession in DH — that make the motivations feel lived-in rather than declared. The film versions tend to compress motivation to a single confrontation scene per book that explicitly names the conflict, losing the texture of motivation expressed behaviorally over time. The insecurity about being the sixth Weasley son — confirmed by the Mirror of Erised, built across dozens of small moments in PS — is substantially absent from theatrical films. His complicated family-loyalty conflict (Percy in OotP, the ghoul plan logic in DH) is largely absent. The internal conflict about adequacy in the Quidditch Keeper arc (OotP) is unfilmed.
motivations_internal_conflict.evidence_status: Directly evidenced across all seven per-book scorings
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: Per-book scores ranged from 10 (OotP) to 12 (PoA, DH), with most at 11. OotP's 10 reflects the most severe simplification — the Quidditch Keeper arc's entire motivational architecture is absent. The synthesis score of 11 reflects: core motivational direction consistently correct; specific texture of insecurity-as-behavior largely absent; motivations stated rather than dramatized; the most important motivational vehicle (the sixth-son insecurity across the full series) substantially underexplained in theatrical films. Weighted toward OotP and GoF as the books where motivation is most richly dramatized and most compressed in film.

character_arc.book_baseline: Ron has both a book-level arc in each volume and a series-level arc across all seven. The series arc is a maturation from insecure, reactive boy into a co-equal hero who chooses his loyalties deliberately. Key arc stages: PS (recognition by Dumbledore, first individual triumph); CoS (tested loyalty, courage under pressure); PoA (sacrifice, moral clarity about betrayal); GoF (estrangement and reconciliation, incomplete emotional growth); OotP (failure and triumph as Quidditch Keeper, first independent recognition via prefect badge); HBP (romantic arc with Hermione, commitment to the Horcrux hunt); DH (departure, return, maturation, co-protagonist status in the final battle). The series arc is explicitly resolved when Ron stands at Voldemort's defiance and fights alongside Harry and Hermione as an equal, having chosen them over safety.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The films preserve the arc's major endpoints and most emotionally visible pivot points: the chess sacrifice recognition (PS), the Shrieking Shack sacrifice (PoA), the GoF reconciliation, the HBP hospital scene and commitment to accompany Harry, the DH departure and return, the Horcrux destructions, the Chamber of Secrets initiative, and the final battle. The series ends with Ron in the right place emotionally and narratively. Rupert Grint's performance consistently conveys warmth, growth, and deepening commitment across the eight films.
character_arc.difference: Almost every individual book arc is missing important developmental steps. PS's arc lacks its starting-point texture (sixth-son insecurity). GoF's arc compresses the weeks of estrangement into one scene, making the reconciliation feel less earned. OotP's primary arc (Quidditch Keeper arc) is entirely absent — the film Ron has no arc in OotP, entering and exiting in the same condition. HBP's arc is present in emotional peaks but missing the sustained low points that give the recovery its weight. DH's arc is missing the middle section where Ron proves himself through sustained daily leadership rather than single dramatic acts. The series-level arc's connective tissue — the slow accumulation of Ron growing from boy to man across seven years of tested loyalty — is significantly thinned because so many of the intermediate steps in individual books are absent. What survives is a series of emotional high points without the sustained groundwork.
character_arc.evidence_status: Directly evidenced across all seven per-book scorings
character_arc.penalty_logic: Per-book scores ranged from 9 (HBP, OotP) to 11 (PS, PoA, DH), with CoS and GoF at 10. OotP's 9 is the worst failure — no discernible arc in the theatrical film. HBP's 9 reflects the missing low points. The synthesis score of 10 reflects: series arc's major endpoints and dramatic pivot points preserved; individual book arcs consistently missing important developmental steps; the series-level maturation arc readable but significantly thinned; OotP and HBP as the worst individual failures weighted appropriately. The 10 sits at the upper boundary of the 'incomplete, missing important steps' band — recognizable arc, destination correct, but too many rungs of the ladder removed to score higher.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Ron has three defining relationships across the series: (1) Harry — equal co-protagonist friendship defined by mutual loyalty, complementary skills, and the specific dynamic of Ron knowing the wizarding world while Harry knows the non-magical one; the relationship includes estrangements (GoF, DH), genuine tension (OotP when Harry considers withholding Order information), and ultimately co-equal standing; (2) Hermione — the most emotionally complex and sustained relationship arc in the series, moving from hostility through bickering partnership to romantic love, expressed through jealousy, protectiveness, banter, and tenderness; (3) his family — particularly the weight of being one of seven, the Weasley family warmth, the poverty-and-pride tension, and specific family dynamics (Percy's betrayal in OotP, the ghoul plan logic of protecting his family in DH, Fred's death). Secondary: Sirius (GoF), Hagrid (consistent warmth across all books), Ginny (protective dynamic).
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The Harry-Ron friendship is the most faithfully preserved relationship across all films — the warmth, the ease, the mutual backing, and the estrangement-and-reconciliation beats are consistently rendered. The Hermione-Ron relationship is present in every film in its jealousy and banter dimensions and reaches its emotional peaks (hospital scene in HBP, Deluminator speech in DH, reunion in DH). The Weasley family warmth is consistently present. The most important Hermione-Ron emotional beats (hospital scene, the kiss implied in the Horcrux destruction, the final commitment) survive.
key_relationships.difference: The Hermione-Ron relationship loses its nurturing-warmth dimension in almost every film — the handkerchief scene in DH, the multiple book-moments of Ron comforting Hermione, the sustained quiet protectiveness — are largely absent, leaving the relationship skewed toward jealousy and banter. The relationship's full emotional complexity is therefore underrepresented. The Harry-Ron relationship loses its 'Ron as anchor when Harry is passive' dynamic (most significant in DH) and the daily-texture of co-equal partnership across OotP and GoF. The family relationships are most significantly diminished in OotP (Percy's betrayal arc entirely absent) and DH (Potterwatch obsession — the visceral daily terror for his family — absent). The Sirius relationship in GoF (cave scene) is entirely absent. The reconciliation mechanisms in PoA (Hagrid-mediated hug rather than organic) and GoF (Ron retroactively claiming credit) slightly alter the emotional honesty of those relationship dynamics.
key_relationships.evidence_status: Directly evidenced across all seven per-book scorings
key_relationships.penalty_logic: Per-book scores were uniformly 7 across all seven books — a remarkably consistent finding reflecting the same pattern repeated: Harry-Ron core intact, Hermione-Ron emotional texture compressed toward jealousy/banter at the expense of warmth, family dynamics significantly thinned, and specific secondary relationships (Sirius in GoF, Percy in OotP) entirely absent. The synthesis score of 7 directly reflects this consistent finding — relationships are functionally present and emotionally recognizable in their core dynamics, but consistently missing the sustained texture and secondary dimensions that give them their book richness.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: Ron's complexity across the series derives from the coexistence of contradictory traits that are never fully resolved: simultaneously loyal and capable of petty cruelty; brave and anxious; funny and morally perceptive; warm and sometimes unkind; smart in practical ways and dismissive of intellectual effort. His class anxiety (poverty, secondhand things, being the sixth Weasley) gives his reactions consistent subtext. His capacity for emotional intelligence — comforting Hermione in DH, the tea-for-Hagrid instinct in PoA, his tact about Mad-Eye's death — surprises even attentive readers because it coexists with frequent clumsiness. His intellectual contributions (Unbreakable Vow deduction in HBP, Riddle award connection in CoS, Chamber entry in DH, ghoul plan in DH) reveal a practical intelligence that the books never fully acknowledge as intelligence, making it more authentic. The sustained unpleasantness — weeks of coldness to Hermione in HBP and GoF, the extended departure in DH, the aggression of the GoF estrangement — is where his complexity is most visible.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The films preserve Ron's broad contradictions: he is brave and insecure, funny and occasionally cruel, loyal and jealous. Individual nuanced moments survive: the Deluminator speech in DH, the 'I let you sleep in my bed' disgust in PoA, the dormitory skin conversation in HBP, the love-potion sequence. Rupert Grint's performance consistently conveys more nuance than the scripts give him — his physical comedy, his timing, and his warmth add texture that the written dialogue alone would not generate.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The films systematically lose the accumulated small-moment texture that makes book-Ron complex rather than merely likeable. The socioeconomic subtext (secondhand things, family poverty anxiety) is present in at most one scene per film and absent from most. The sustained unpleasantness — the defining feature of Ron in HBP's middle section and GoF's estrangement — is consistently compressed to single scenes, removing the behavioral patterns that demonstrate genuine character complexity. Ron's nurturing emotional intelligence is almost entirely absent from the films. His intellectual contributions that are most revealing of his character (the ghoul plan as love, the Potterwatch obsession as daily terror, the Buckbeak research as moral reparation) are largely absent. OotP's entire complexity architecture — the Quidditch Keeper arc, the prefect badge, Percy's letter, the dormitory conversations — is absent. The result is a film Ron who is consistently more likeable and less uncomfortable than the book Ron, which is precisely the wrong direction for a character whose complexity depends on being sometimes genuinely difficult.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.evidence_status: Directly evidenced across all seven per-book scorings
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: Per-book scores ranged from 8 (OotP) to 10 (PoA), with most at 9. OotP's 8 is the worst individual failure — virtually all nuance absent. PoA's 10 is the best — the most density of preserved complexity. The synthesis score of 9 reflects: broad contradictions preserved and Grint's performance adding texture; systematic loss of socioeconomic subtext, nurturing intelligence, sustained unpleasantness, and small-moment accumulative texture across all seven films; OotP and HBP as the worst failures weighted appropriately. The 9 sits in the 'noticeable simplification; important nuances, relationships, agency, or contradictions are missing' band — the character is recognizable but substantially flatter than the source.
