comparative.key_observations: The synthesis score of 67 reflects a consistent and coherent pattern across all seven books: the films preserve Ron Weasley's emotional core with genuine fidelity but systematically simplify the character in every dimension that requires sustained behavioral development rather than single-scene dramatic payoff. Rupert Grint's performance is frequently better than what the scripts give him, and the warmth, loyalty, humor, and bravery that define Ron most visibly are well-served by the adaptations. The chess sacrifice, the Shrieking Shack protection, the Horcrux destructions, the departure-and-return in DH, the Chamber of Secrets initiative — the films' Ron has real dramatic moments that honor the character. The failure is systematic rather than random: every dimension shows the same compression pattern. The most important books for Ron's series-level arc — GoF (estrangement and jealousy), OotP (insecurity and triumph), HBP (romantic arc maturation), and DH (co-protagonist coming of age) — all show meaningful simplification in multiple dimensions. The single worst individual book adaptation for Ron is OotP, where virtually his entire arc (Quidditch Keeper triumph, prefect recognition, Percy's letter) is absent from the theatrical film, leaving him as a functional but almost characterless supporting presence. The second worst is HBP, where the weeks of sustained emotional dysfunction that are Ron's defining characterization in that book are compressed to episodic comedy beats. The core finding is directional rather than distortive: the films never portray Ron as something he is not, but they consistently prioritize his warmth and humor at the expense of his capacity for petty cruelty, prolonged dysfunction, and the specific social anxiety of perpetual secondness. The result is a Ron who is pleasant to watch across eight films but who lacks the full complexity, contradiction, and hard-earned growth of his book counterpart — a character rendered in two dimensions when the source material offers three.

personality_voice.book_baseline: Sirius's personality across the books is consistent and rich: volatile, fiercely loyal, darkly humorous, impulsive, contemptuous of authority and of Snape, emotionally raw about James, prone to bitterness under confinement, capable of genuine tenderness, and carrying a schoolboy cruelty that never fully matured. His voice is urgent, direct, impatient, and laced with gallows humor. PoA establishes this in full; OotP develops the psychological damage of confinement; GoF shows his analytical intelligence; DH preserves his arrogant wit in the train scene and his calm courage in the Resurrection Stone scene.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The film across all books (primarily PoA and OotP, where Sirius is an active character) preserves the most visible surface traits: volatility, loyalty, urgency, recklessness, and warmth toward Harry. Gary Oldman's performance carries the emotional register. But the films systematically lose the secondary and darker traits: the deliberate murder-planning coldness of PoA's Shrieking Shack; the progressive bitterness and sullenness under confinement in OotP; the analytical intelligence and dark wit of GoF; the 'You're less like your father than I thought' taunt; the young Sirius dialogue on the Hogwarts Express in DH. The farewell speech in PoA adds invented heroic composure the book character lacks.
personality_voice.difference: The core personality is recognizable and the films avoid active distortion. What is lost is the darker, more morally textured edge: the deliberate planning of murder, the adolescent cruelty toward Snape (present but softened), the psychological damage made visceral, the analytical sharpness, and the most revealing voice moments. The invented PoA farewell speech is the most egregious addition — it imposes a composed nobility that contradicts the book character's emotional state at that point.
personality_voice.evidence_status: Directly evidenced across PoA, OotP, GoF, and DH corpora.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: PoA is the foundational book for Sirius's personality and the film is broadly faithful there. OotP adds more personality material and the film is roughly recognizable. GoF and DH show meaningful voice compression. The PoA farewell addition and the consistent softening of his darker traits across all films prevent a higher score. Score anchored at 18: recognizable character, important secondary traits reduced, one significant addition distorting his composure.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: Sirius is agentive across multiple books: in PoA he is the primary agent driving the Pettigrew revelation; in GoF he is Harry's investigative partner, independently returning to Britain at personal risk, providing intelligence on Crouch/Karkaroff/Bagman, advising on the dragon task, and being activated by Dumbledore to rebuild the Order; in OotP he advocates for Harry, provides intelligence, gives the two-way mirror, confronts Snape, defies orders, and dies at the DoM; in DH the mirror shard drives plot to Aberforth, his Regulus knowledge enables the R.A.B. identification, and his spirit actively guides Harry into the forest.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: PoA preserves his core agency. OotP preserves his most dramatic acts but neutralizes the two-way mirror's narrative function and compresses fireplace intelligence scenes. GoF is severely cut — the cave scene, the dragon advice, the systematic investigation, and the end-of-book activation are all absent, leaving only a single fireplace warning. DH preserves the mirror shard function and Resurrection Stone guidance but removes the Kreacher moral function and reduces R.A.B. informational agency.
narrative_role_agency.difference: GoF represents the worst agency failure: his entire function as Harry's investigative partner is reduced to one reactive scene. The two-way mirror in OotP is present but its narrative function is neutralized. The Kreacher moral consequence in DH removes a posthumous agency vector. Across the series, agency is consistently compressed from active initiator to reactive warner.
narrative_role_agency.evidence_status: Directly evidenced across all relevant books.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: PoA agency is mostly intact. OotP agency is clearly but not severely altered. GoF is a severe failure — his central function is nearly eliminated. DH losses are real but the core plot functions survive. GoF's severity drags this dimension down significantly. Score of 13 reflects the OotP/PoA partial preservation offset by the GoF near-elimination and DH reductions.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Sirius's motivations are layered: obsessive drive to avenge/protect Harry from the real traitor (PoA); guilt over suggesting Pettigrew as Secret-Keeper and thereby causing the Potters' deaths (PoA); love for James expressed through fierce protectiveness of Harry; desperate need to feel useful rather than imprisoned (OotP/GoF); willingness to risk freedom and life for Harry (GoF); recklessness rooted in Azkaban damage that makes inaction unbearable (OotP). His central internal conflict is between genuine protective love and reckless compulsion to act — the tension that kills him.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The films preserve the protective motivation clearly and the recklessness is present ('What's life without a little risk?'). The love for Harry/James and the urgency of the godfather duty survive. But the guilt over the Secret-Keeper suggestion — the most morally interesting dimension, making him complicit rather than purely victimized — is entirely absent across all films. The psychological weight of confinement as the root cause of his death is present but underdeveloped, lacking the multi-week deterioration that makes it causally credible.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The guilt admission (PoA: 'I as good as killed them... I persuaded Lily and James to change to Peter') is removed in every relevant adaptation, flattening Sirius from a partly responsible man to a pure victim of betrayal. The internal conflict between self-preservation and duty is present but lacks the concrete sacrifice (cave scenes, rat diet) that makes it visible. Confinement's psychological toll is gestured at but not built up sufficiently to explain the DoM recklessness as inevitable rather than coincidental.
motivations_internal_conflict.evidence_status: Directly evidenced across PoA and OotP; reasonably inferred for GoF and DH.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: The most morally interesting motivation (guilt, self-implication) is consistently absent across all films. Core motivations (love, duty, recklessness) survive. Score of 11 reflects correct broad motivations with meaningful complexity removed.

character_arc.book_baseline: Sirius's arc across the series: monstrous threat → revealed innocent and godfather (PoA); fugitive maintaining agency as Harry's investigator (GoF); psychologically eroding under confinement → reckless death that is the product of his own damage (OotP); posthumous legacy shaping Harry's arc and moral reckoning (HBP, DH). The PoA and OotP arcs are the most important — PoA establishes him, OotP completes him with a tragedy that flows directly from his character.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The PoA arc is present and broadly faithful in shape. The OotP arc captures key beats but loses the multi-stage psychological deterioration that makes the death feel earned rather than arbitrary — the progressive sullenness is absent, so his DoM recklessness reads as consistent personality rather than culmination of a specific decline. The GoF arc (fugitive to Order soldier) is almost entirely absent. The posthumous arc in HBP/DH is compressed but the Resurrection Stone scene correctly treats his arc as complete.
character_arc.difference: The PoA arc is adequately served. The OotP arc is the critical failure: without the intermediate deterioration stages, Sirius's death loses its tragic logic — the film presents him as someone who dies because he's reckless, rather than someone whose specific psychological disintegration under unjust confinement produces the exact recklessness that kills him. The GoF arc endpoint (activation to rebuild the Order) is entirely absent.
character_arc.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for PoA and OotP; directly evidenced for GoF absence; reasonably inferred for posthumous arc handling.
character_arc.penalty_logic: PoA arc is intact. OotP arc is incomplete at its crucial middle stages, weakening the tragic logic. GoF arc is absent. Score of 10 reflects the partial preservation of the most important arc (PoA) against the incomplete execution of the second most important (OotP).

key_relationships.book_baseline: The primary relationships: (1) Sirius-Harry — godfather/surrogate son, complicated by Sirius sometimes seeing James instead of Harry, ranging from warmth to unintentional harm; (2) Sirius-Lupin — deep old friendship conveyed with remarkable economy ('Together?'/'I think so'); (3) Sirius-Pettigrew — contempt and righteous fury; (4) Sirius-Snape — unresolved school-era mutual hatred with real dramatic history; (5) Sirius-Kreacher — the relationship that most complicates his heroism, his cruelty to Kreacher being causally linked to his death; (6) Sirius-James — the organising loyalty of his entire psychology.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The Sirius-Harry relationship is preserved in emotional core across PoA and OotP. The Sirius-Lupin friendship loses its most resonant moment ('Together?'). The Sirius-Pettigrew dynamic is broadly preserved. The Sirius-Snape antagonism is present in PoA and OotP but loses the Pensieve/fireplace confrontation dimension. The Sirius-Kreacher relationship — across OotP, HBP, and DH — is consistently reduced to negligible or absent, removing his most morally complicating relational dynamic. The Sirius-James relationship is referenced but not dramatized.
key_relationships.difference: The most consistent relationship failure is Sirius-Kreacher: the contempt, the consequences, and Hermione's moral indictment linking his cruelty to his death are absent across all films. The Sirius-Harry relationship loses its central complication ('You're less like your father than I thought') in OotP. The Sirius-Lupin relationship loses its most precise emotional beat. These are not trivial compressions — they remove the dimensions that make Sirius's relationships morally complex rather than simply warm.
key_relationships.evidence_status: Directly evidenced across PoA, OotP, GoF, and DH corpora.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: The basic dynamics are present and recognizable for the most important relationships. The Kreacher failure is consistent and severe across multiple films. The Harry relationship's central complication is removed. Score of 7 reflects functional preservation of primary relationships against meaningful loss of moral texture.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: Sirius's complexity across the series rests on: his guilt over the Secret-Keeper suggestion making him complicit rather than purely victimized; his physical attack on Harry in PoA showing he is dangerous even to those he loves; the Snape prank revealing adolescent cruelty never fully outgrown; his cruelty to Kreacher as a moral blind spot with fatal consequences; his progressive psychological deterioration under confinement as the engine of his death; his conflation of Harry with James revealing a love that is partly projection; his epilogue generosity (Firebolt, owl) revealing a thoughtful self-aware man beneath the fugitive; his bedroom as a self-portrait of deliberate rebellion; Hermione's posthumous moral indictment.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: What survives: recklessness, warmth, the Snape contempt (partial), the DoM fight, the Shrieking Shack confrontation (compressed). What is consistently absent: the guilt admission; the physical attack on Harry; the Snape prank backstory; the Kreacher moral dimension (across OotP, HBP, DH); the multi-week psychological deterioration; the James conflation ('You're less like your father'); the Firebolt epilogue; the bedroom psychological texture; Hermione's Kreacher indictment. The PoA farewell speech addition imposes false heroic composure.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The pattern across all films is consistent: the film preserves the heroic, warm, reckless surface and removes the moral complications (guilt, cruelty, projection, blind spots) that make the book Sirius genuinely complex. This is not random compression — it is systematic simplification toward a more sympathetic archetype. The Kreacher dimension alone, absent across three films (OotP, HBP, DH), would be sufficient to significantly lower this score.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.evidence_status: Directly evidenced across all books in the corpus.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: This is the dimension with the most consistent failure across the series. The removed material is not incidental — it constitutes the moral and psychological substance that distinguishes the book Sirius from a straightforwardly noble figure. The PoA additions (farewell speech) actively distort. Score of 8 reflects substantial but not total loss: the recklessness and volatility that are part of his complexity do survive.

comparative.key_observations: The films deliver a recognizable and emotionally coherent Sirius Black — Gary Oldman's performance preserves the surface register of volatility, loyalty, recklessness, and warmth, and the core narrative arc from monstrous threat to wrongly-condemned godfather (PoA) is broadly faithful. PoA is the most important book for Sirius and the film handles it adequately, which anchors the overall score above the midpoint. However, across the full series the films engage in systematic simplification: they consistently remove the moral complications (the Secret-Keeper guilt, the Kreacher cruelty, the James conflation) and the psychological texture (the deterioration under confinement, the Azkaban damage made visceral) that distinguish the book Sirius from a straightforwardly noble figure. The GoF cave scenes — his most agentive and emotionally rich sustained appearance outside PoA — are entirely cut. The OotP arc loses its tragic logic because the multi-stage deterioration is absent. Across HBP and DH, where Sirius functions as a posthumous moral force, he is reduced to a name-drop and a brief spirit. The net result is a Sirius who is more sympathetic and less morally textured than his book counterpart — faithful enough at the surface level to be effective for general audiences, but missing the specific weight that made him one of the richer supporting characters in the series. The 67 total reflects a character who is recognizable and partly well-served in his defining book (PoA) but systematically simplified across his full series arc.

personality_voice.book_baseline: Pansy is defined by sharp, public cruelty delivered with gleeful energy. Her insults are targeted and specific: she mocks Hermione's appearance ('What was she judging against - a chipmunk?'), taunts Harry about dementors with theatrical shrieking, ridicules Angelina Johnson's hair, and laughs at Hagrid's speech to Umbridge's face. Her voice is loud, performative, and socially calculated - she performs cruelty for an audience, especially Malfoy's. She is not merely a bystander; she initiates mockery, leads Slytherin girls in group ridicule, and delivers lines with a specific shrieking, giggling register. She also shows a softer, fawning side exclusively toward Malfoy - 'How is it, Draco? Does it hurt much?' - which coexists with her cruelty toward others.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The films preserve the core register: she simpers over Malfoy ('Does it hurt terribly, Draco?'), strokes his hair with a smug possessiveness, and delivers the Great Hall betrayal line with urgency. In the HBP train scene she plays a calming, almost maternal role toward Draco ('Relax, boys. The lights went out is all. Come, Draco.') and reacts with indignation when he hints at leaving Hogwarts. In DH2 she calls Filch a 'filthy squib' from the dungeon cage. The shrieking, performative public cruelty toward Harry, Hermione, and others is almost entirely absent from the film corpus.
personality_voice.difference: The films retain her fawning dynamic with Malfoy and her one major public act (the Great Hall betrayal), but strip out the sustained pattern of targeted, audience-directed mockery that defines her voice in the books. The specific shrieking insults at Hermione, Harry, Angelina, and Hagrid - which collectively establish her as an active, gleeful tormentor - are absent. What remains is a quieter, more reactive Pansy. The 'filthy squib' line in DH2 shows some residual sharpness, but it is a single isolated moment.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The dominant trait of performative, targeted public cruelty is recognizable in the Great Hall scene but the sustained pattern that builds it across the books is missing. The fawning Malfoy dynamic is preserved. The character remains recognizable but the full texture of her voice - the shrieking, the specific insults, the audience-seeking cruelty - is reduced. Score sits in the 14-17 range: recognizable but with important tonal and behavioral reduction.
personality_voice.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for both book and film patterns; the absence of the shrieking insult pattern in films is directly evidenced by the film corpus.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: Pansy serves two structural functions: (1) active social tormentor of Harry, Hermione, and Gryffindors across multiple books, initiating mockery, leading Slytherin girl groups, and amplifying Malfoy's cruelty; (2) in DH, the pivotal moment where she attempts to hand Harry to Voldemort, which triggers the unified counter-response of the other Houses. She also functions as Malfoy's social satellite, amplifying his status and providing emotional support. Her agency is real: she initiates scenes, leads group behavior, and in DH makes a consequential narrative move.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: The DH2 Great Hall scene preserves her most consequential act of agency - calling for Harry to be seized - and the film handles this faithfully. The HBP train scene gives her a calming/management role with Draco. The POA scene gives her the 'Does it hurt terribly' line. The DH2 dungeon scene gives her one defiant line. Her role as active tormentor across years 3-5 is absent.
narrative_role_agency.difference: Her multi-year function as active social tormentor - which is a genuine narrative role, not mere decoration - is absent from the film corpus. The Inquisitorial Squad subplot (where she sprouts antlers as consequence), her role conducting Slytherin supporters at Quidditch, her leading the mockery of Hermione with Witch Weekly, and her participation in Umbridge's inspection of Hagrid are all absent. Her agency in the Great Hall is preserved. Her agency as tormentor is not.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: The most narratively significant act of agency (DH Great Hall) is preserved. But her sustained role as an active agent of social cruelty - which is her primary function across books 3-5 - is reduced to near-zero in the films. This is a clear role reduction, though not elimination. Score in the 10-13 range.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Pansy's motivations are not deeply explored in the books - she is not a POV character and receives no internal narration. What can be reasonably inferred: she is motivated by social status within Slytherin, loyalty/attraction to Malfoy, and a desire to perform cruelty as a form of in-group bonding. In HBP, her reaction to Malfoy's hints about leaving ('What's that supposed to mean?', 'What do you mean, you might not be at Hogwarts next year?' said Pansy indignantly) shows genuine anxiety about losing him, suggesting her attachment to Malfoy is a real motivating force. In DH, her attempt to hand Harry over is motivated by self-preservation and alignment with Voldemort's side.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The HBP film preserves her anxiety about Malfoy leaving ('What's that supposed to mean?'). The DH2 Great Hall scene preserves the self-preservation/Voldemort-alignment motivation. The social-status-through-cruelty motivation is not visible because the cruelty scenes are absent.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The core motivations that are actually shown in the books - attachment to Malfoy, self-preservation, Voldemort alignment - are present in the films. The social-performance motivation is inferrable but not directly shown in either medium. The motivations are simplified by absence of context but not changed.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: Motivations are simplified due to reduced presence but not fundamentally altered. The two most explicit motivational moments (anxiety over Malfoy, DH betrayal) are preserved. Score in the 8-10 range given the thinness of the film portrayal overall, but no direct distortion.
motivations_internal_conflict.evidence_status: Reasonably inferred for books; directly evidenced for the two preserved film moments.

character_arc.book_baseline: Pansy has a flat arc in terms of moral development - she does not grow, reform, or change her values. Her trajectory is one of escalating alignment with Malfoy and the Death Eater cause, culminating in the DH betrayal attempt. The arc is not one of internal change but of revealed allegiance: by DH she is willing to hand a student to Voldemort to save herself and her House. This is consistent with everything established earlier.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The films show the endpoint of this trajectory (DH2 Great Hall) and the mid-point anxiety about Malfoy (HBP train). The escalating pattern of cruelty and alignment that builds the arc across books 3-5 is absent, but the arc's destination is present.
character_arc.difference: The arc's destination is preserved but the steps that build it are compressed to near-invisibility. The audience sees the result without the accumulation. However, since the arc is essentially flat (no internal change, just revealed allegiance), compression is less damaging than it would be for a character with genuine internal development.
character_arc.penalty_logic: The arc is flat by design and its endpoint is preserved. Compression of a flat arc is less penalizable than compression of a developmental arc. However, the absence of the intermediate steps means the DH betrayal lacks the full weight of established pattern. Score in the 11-13 range: compressed but still faithful to the arc's nature.
character_arc.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for endpoint; reasonably inferred for the arc's flat nature.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Pansy's defining relationship is with Malfoy: she is his fawning satellite, physically attentive (stroking his hair, clutching his arm at the Yule Ball), emotionally invested, and socially dependent on his status. She is also defined relationally by her antagonism toward Hermione specifically - the Witch Weekly scene, the teeth-shrinking mockery, the 'chipmunk' comment - which is more sustained and personal than her general cruelty. Her relationship with her Slytherin girl gang is also a structural element: she leads them.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The Malfoy relationship is preserved in its physical and emotional texture: hair-stroking, the 'Does it hurt terribly' fawning, the indignant reaction to his hints about leaving, the waiting with hand outstretched (book scene 98 is referenced in the HBP film). The Hermione antagonism is entirely absent from the film corpus. The Slytherin girl gang leadership is absent.
key_relationships.difference: The Malfoy dynamic is the best-preserved element. The Hermione antagonism - which is the second most important relational dynamic and reveals specific traits (targeted cruelty, jealousy, social competition) - is completely absent from the film corpus. This is a meaningful loss: the Hermione relationship shows a different dimension of Pansy than the Malfoy fawning does.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: One key relationship (Malfoy) is substantially preserved. A second key relationship (Hermione antagonism) is absent. The loss of the Hermione dynamic removes a relational dimension that reveals important character traits. Score in the 5-6 range: important relationship dynamics are altered or weakened by absence.
key_relationships.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for both the preservation of the Malfoy dynamic and the absence of the Hermione dynamic.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: Pansy's complexity is modest but real. She is not merely a one-note villain: she shows genuine emotional investment in Malfoy (not just performance), a moment of almost-genuine delight at the unicorn foals that she suppresses ('even Pansy Parkinson had to work hard to conceal how much she liked them'), social intelligence in reading the Malfoy/Ginny dynamic on the train ('A lot of boys like her... even you think she's good-looking, don't you, Blaise'), and the capacity to be both cruel and genuinely attached. The Inquisitorial Squad subplot and the antlers consequence show she has real stakes. Her leading role among Slytherin girls gives her social agency beyond Malfoy's orbit.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The films preserve the Malfoy attachment and the DH betrayal. The unicorn foal moment, the social intelligence on the train (partially - the Ginny observation is absent from the film corpus though the train scene exists), the Inquisitorial Squad, the antlers, and the sustained Hermione mockery are all absent.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The unicorn foal moment (a rare crack in her cruelty), her social intelligence reading Malfoy's reaction to Ginny, her Inquisitorial Squad role, and the full texture of her Hermione antagonism are lost. What remains is a character who fawns over Malfoy and betrays Harry - recognizable but stripped of the small moments that gave her texture.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: The character is reduced to two functions: Malfoy satellite and DH betrayer. The nuances that complicated her - suppressed delight, social intelligence, group leadership, sustained targeted cruelty - are absent. This is noticeable simplification. Score in the 8-10 range.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for losses; reasonably inferred for the significance of the unicorn foal and train social intelligence moments.

comparative.key_observations: Pansy Parkinson's film portrayal preserves her two most structurally significant moments - the Malfoy fawning dynamic and the DH Great Hall betrayal - but strips away the sustained pattern of performative, targeted cruelty that is her primary function across books 3-5. The result is a character who is recognizable at her endpoints but hollowed of the texture that makes her more than a plot device. Her relationship with Hermione, her group leadership, her social intelligence, and the small humanizing cracks (the unicorn foal) are all absent. The Malfoy relationship is the best-preserved element. The score reflects a character whose broad identity survives but whose book characterization is substantially reduced.

personality_voice.book_baseline: Trelawney in the books is a composite of genuine eccentricity, theatrical self-promotion, fragile ego, defensive pride, and intermittent authentic gift. Her dominant voice is misty and performative — she speaks in a soft, dreamy register, uses 'my dear' as a verbal tic, and frames mundane observations as cosmic revelation. She is theatrical to the point of self-parody: she predicts doom habitually, flatters believers (Parvati, Lavender), and attacks skeptics (Hermione) with sharp, personal insults that cut through her mystical veil. She is also genuinely insecure: she flinches when McGonagall undercuts her, she is rattled by Umbridge's inspection, and she drinks cooking sherry in increasing quantities under pressure. Her emotional register includes genuine distress (the sacking scene), prickly vanity (her exchange with Firenze), and moments of sharp, unguarded anger. She is not simply a fraud — she has real Second Sight that she herself cannot access consciously, and this contradiction (the genuine prophet who performs hollow prophecy) is the heart of her character. Her speech pattern blends dreamy passivity with sudden sharpness when provoked.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The films preserve the most visible surface traits: the huge magnifying glasses, the misty dreamy voice, the dramatic entrance, the 'my dear' phrasing, the prediction of doom for Harry, the sharp dismissal of Hermione, and the crystal ball theatrics. Emma Thompson's performance captures the performative fragility and the theatrical self-importance. The sacking scene in Order of the Phoenix is emotionally present, and the second prophecy delivery in Prisoner of Azkaban is faithfully eerie. In Deathly Hallows Part 2, the line 'There's more to me than incense and tea leaves, Mr. Finnegan' conveys her defensive pride.
personality_voice.difference: Several important traits are compressed or absent. The films do not show the sustained emotional escalation of her behaviour under Umbridge's pressure — the corridor-wandering, the sherry, the hysterical classroom outburst, the tearful self-pity about 'sixteen years of devoted service' — all of which reveal that beneath the mystical persona is a frightened, wounded woman clinging to her role. The Umbridge inspection scene is excluded from theatrical release (per the non-theatrical exclusion rule), removing the most textured book portrayal of her defensiveness, pride, and stubborn resistance. The films also lose her prickly competitiveness with Firenze, her self-deluding rationalisations about her lineage, and the sustained voice pattern of someone who talks to manage anxiety rather than to communicate. The film Trelawney is recognisable but slightly flattened toward pure comedy-pathos, losing the sharp edges that appear when she feels threatened.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The core voice — misty, theatrical, vain, fragile — is preserved with reasonable fidelity. The penalty reflects the loss of her emotional escalation arc under pressure (books show a progressive breakdown; films show only two moments of distress without the texture that connects them), the loss of the sherry-drinking as a behavioral marker of deterioration, and the exclusion of the Umbridge inspection scene which was the fullest expression of her personality under challenge. The insult to Hermione is present in both versions, but the film version is slightly more cruel and polished ('your soul as dry as the pages of the books') whereas the book version shows more wounded dignity. Minor simplification, but the main personality is preserved.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: Trelawney serves three narrative functions in the books: (1) comic relief and atmosphere — her predictions of Harry's death create ironic texture and parody the genre of doom-prophecy; (2) structural plot driver — she is the source of the prophecy that caused Voldemort to kill Harry's parents, and this is directly revealed to Harry in Half-Blood Prince via her account of the interview at the Hog's Head; (3) dramatic victim of institutional cruelty — her battle with Umbridge and subsequent sacking is a major set piece in Order of the Phoenix, illustrating Umbridge's malice and Dumbledore's protective authority. In addition, in Half-Blood Prince, she is an active participant in the plot: she wanders the corridors, hides sherry in the Room of Requirement, stumbles onto evidence that someone is celebrating inside it (Malfoy), and then delivers this critical intelligence to Harry — who then relays it to Dumbledore. This is genuine agency: Trelawney is the one who provides the information that alerts Harry to Malfoy's activities, and it is her telling Harry about the eavesdropper at the Hog's Head that reveals Snape's role in the prophecy to Harry. In the Battle of Hogwarts (Deathly Hallows), she fights actively.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: The films preserve her role as comic relief/atmosphere and as dramatic victim of the sacking in Order of the Phoenix. The second prophecy in Prisoner of Azkaban is retained in a compressed but faithful form. In Deathly Hallows Part 2, she actively fights Death Eaters with crystal balls — this is drawn from the books. However, her Half-Blood Prince role is entirely absent from the films: she does not appear in the HBP film in any meaningful way. The critical scene in which she tells Harry about the Hog's Head eavesdropper — the scene that causes Harry to realise Snape overheard the prophecy and reported it to Voldemort — is cut entirely. The prophecy itself in Order of the Phoenix is heard by Harry as a recording in the Department of Mysteries, read aloud in Trelawney's voice, but this is passive archival playback, not active agency.
narrative_role_agency.difference: The most significant loss is her Half-Blood Prince function. In the books, Trelawney's chance encounter with Harry in the corridor, her account of being thrown from the Room of Requirement, and her revelation about the Hog's Head eavesdropper constitute the scene that triggers Harry's confrontation with Dumbledore about Snape. This is active, consequential agency — she changes the direction of the plot. This is entirely absent from the film. Additionally, her role in the sacking scene in Order of the Phoenix is partially preserved in the theatrical cut, but the Umbridge inspection scene (excluded per non-theatrical rule) removed a major portion of her dramatic role as an institutional victim being ground down over time. The films also omit her sustained presence as a figure of growing anxiety in the castle corridors during Order of the Phoenix.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: The transfer/loss of the Half-Blood Prince corridor scene is a clear agency loss. Trelawney's role in revealing Snape's eavesdropping to Harry — one of the most consequential pieces of information in the entire series — is removed entirely from the film. This is precisely the kind of agency transfer/removal that must be penalised. Her role as comic atmosphere and sacking victim is preserved, but the plot-driving function she serves in HBP is gone. Score reflects: role mostly preserved in PoA and OotP, partially preserved in DH2, but the consequential Half-Blood Prince agency is absent.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Trelawney's motivations are layered. She is driven by a need to be believed and valued — her entire performative apparatus (the misty voice, the predictions, the dramatic entrances) is in service of establishing her legitimacy as a Seer. This is complicated by the fact that she knows, on some level, that most of her predictions are hollow, and she defends herself by constructing elaborate frameworks (the Inner Eye cannot be commanded, one must have the Gift). She is motivated by institutional belonging — Hogwarts is her home and her identity, which is why the sacking devastates her. She is also motivated by competitive insecurity: she resents Firenze not because she dislikes him personally but because his presence implicitly questions her own standing. There is a genuine internal conflict: she is a person with real Second Sight who cannot access it voluntarily and spends her professional life performing a simulacrum of it, which means she lives in a permanent tension between authentic gift and fraudulent practice — though she does not fully consciously acknowledge this.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The films communicate her desire to be believed and her institutional attachment clearly — the sacking scene ('Hogwarts is my home') is one of the most emotionally direct moments she has in either medium. The comedy of her hollow predictions implicitly conveys that she knows they are hollow without admitting it. However, the internal conflict between genuine Seer and performed fraud is not explicitly developed in the films — it is present structurally (she delivers a real prophecy, she delivers hollow ones), but the films do not construct this as a conscious internal tension for the character. The competitive resentment of Firenze and her insecurity about her lineage (the 'three generations' rationalisation, her conversation with Harry about Dumbledore's deep impression of her) are entirely absent, as those scenes do not appear in the films.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The core motivation (need to be believed, institutional attachment) survives. What is lost is the texture of the internal conflict — particularly her defensive self-awareness about the limits of her gift, her rationalisations about lineage, and the quiet desperation that underlies the performative confidence. The Half-Blood Prince corridor scenes in the books (where she talks to Harry about Dumbledore's first interview, essentially seeking validation from a teenager) reveal a motivation of deep, ongoing anxiety about her legitimacy that the films do not capture. The sherry drinking as a behavioural expression of her internal fragility is also absent.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: Motivations are simplified but not wholly wrong. The institutional belonging motivation is faithfully rendered. The need to be believed is present but less textured. The internal conflict between real gift and performed prophecy exists structurally in the films but is not developed as a felt tension for the character. Score reflects partial preservation with meaningful flattening.

character_arc.book_baseline: Trelawney's arc across the books runs from eccentric, self-satisfied teacher (PoA) through mounting institutional anxiety under Umbridge (OotP) to public humiliation and collapse (sacking in OotP) to a kind of dignified defiance and recovery (returning to the school, fighting in the Battle of Hogwarts). There is also the retrospective revelation of her true significance — that she is the author of the prophecy that shaped the entire war, a fact she herself does not know. This arc is not a traditional growth arc; it is closer to a tragic-comic unmasking: a character who is largely a fraud who turns out to have been instrumentally central to history, without knowing it. Her HBP appearances show her still wounded, still drinking, still insecure — but also still functioning, still defending her territory against Firenze, still engaged with the world in her chaotic way. The arc ends in active heroism in DH, which is the culmination of the 'more than meets the eye' irony.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The films capture the PoA introduction, the OotP sacking (compressed), and the DH2 fight scene. This covers the starting point, the nadir, and the concluding heroism. The second prophecy in PoA is included, which is the key structural beat that establishes her genuine Sight. The sacking is emotionally present. The DH2 crystal ball fight is faithful.
character_arc.difference: The middle of the arc — the sustained deterioration under Umbridge's pressure in OotP, the corridor-wandering with sherry, the hysterical classroom, and the gradual psychological collapse — is largely absent from the theatrical cut. The inspection scene (excluded per non-theatrical rules) would have shown the arc's most textured passage. The HBP portion of the arc — her wounded, sherry-soaked, defensive but still-functioning state — is absent entirely, since her HBP appearances are cut from the film. This means the arc jumps from sacking (OotP) directly to heroism (DH2) without the intervening recovery period. The revelation of her true narrative significance (the prophecy's origin) is handled differently: in the books, this is delivered by Trelawney herself to Harry in a corridor; in the films, it is handled through Dumbledore and the Pensieve without Trelawney's direct involvement.
character_arc.penalty_logic: The arc's key structural beats are present (introduction, nadir, heroism), and the arc is compressed rather than inverted. However, the middle passage — which shows the arc's emotional texture and the sustained deterioration — is missing, and the HBP recovery stage is absent entirely. The arc is incomplete but not falsified. Score reflects a compressed but partially faithful arc with a missing middle section.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Trelawney's most important relationships in the books are: (1) Trelawney/McGonagall — a sustained professional rivalry defined by mutual disdain; McGonagall is openly dismissive, Trelawney is defensively wounded, but McGonagall comforts her at the sacking, which is a moment of complex human decency across hostility; (2) Trelawney/Hermione — a teacher-student conflict defined by Hermione's empirical skepticism challenging Trelawney's authority, culminating in Hermione's public walkout; Trelawney attacks Hermione's inner life in ways that are unusually personal and cruel; (3) Trelawney/Dumbledore — a relationship of professional debt and uncertain loyalty; Dumbledore protects her, keeps her on staff knowing she is largely a fraud, and she is aware enough to feel gratitude and insecurity simultaneously; (4) Trelawney/Harry — a persistent, somewhat parasitic relationship in which she fixates on Harry as her best 'Object' for predictions, simultaneously making his life miserable and revealing genuine concern for him at moments; (5) Trelawney/Firenze — a competitive antagonism rooted in insecurity about her own legitimacy.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The McGonagall/Trelawney dynamic is partially present: McGonagall's dismissive comment ('then you should know, Potter, that Sibyll Trelawney has predicted the death of one student a year since she arrived') and her comforting gesture at the sacking are in the theatrical films. The Hermione/Trelawney conflict is present in PoA and POA crystal ball scene (included in theatrical cut). The Dumbledore/Trelawney protection dynamic is present in the sacking scene. However, the Trelawney/Firenze antagonism is entirely absent (those scenes are not in the films). The Trelawney/Harry relationship in HBP — where she seeks validation from him, tells him about the Hog's Head, and walks to Dumbledore's office with him — is absent from the films. The sustained McGonagall/Trelawney rivalry is compressed to two moments rather than the book's running counterpoint.
key_relationships.difference: The McGonagall dynamic is present but compressed; the emotional complexity of their relationship (hostility plus surprising solidarity) is only partially visible in the films because the running counterpoint of their professional friction across years is largely absent. The Hermione relationship is preserved in its key beats (PoA dismissal, walkout) but the OotP inspection scene (which shows Trelawney rattled and defensive in a way that illuminates the dynamic further) is excluded. The Firenze antagonism is entirely absent. The HBP Harry/Trelawney dynamic — which is one of the warmest and most humanising moments in the books, showing Trelawney confiding in Harry — is absent. The Dumbledore protective relationship is present but only in one scene.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: Two of the five key relationships are substantially absent or reduced to near-nothing (Firenze, HBP Harry), one is compressed to the point of losing most of its texture (McGonagall), and two are reasonably preserved (Hermione in PoA, Dumbledore at sacking). The emotional dynamics of the most important relationship — with McGonagall — are recognisable but the book's sustained counterpoint is lost. Score reflects important relationship material missing without replacement.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: Trelawney's complexity in the books rests on several things: (1) the prophecy irony — she is a largely fraudulent prophet who made the most consequential prophecy in the wizarding world, and she does not know it; this gives her a tragic weight beneath the comedy; (2) the sherry drinking and corridor-wandering — behavioral detail that reveals a person in genuine distress, not just a comic figure; (3) the Christmas feast scene (excluded per non-theatrical rules for the film version, but present in the books as a long scene showing her social awkwardness, her passive-aggression with McGonagall, her genuine loneliness, and her misplaced predictions about Lupin); (4) her conversation with Harry in the HBP corridor — the most humanising scene she has, showing her vulnerability, her need for validation, her awareness that people doubt her, and her accidental revelation about Snape; (5) the Firenze antagonism, which adds professional dimension; (6) the sustained deterioration under Umbridge, which shows her cracking under institutional pressure in a way that is both funny and genuinely sad.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The films retain the prophecy irony (structurally), the sacking pathos, the DH2 heroism, the PoA second prophecy, and the Hermione conflict. These are not trivial — they constitute the most narratively significant moments of the character. However, they do not capture the behavioral texture, the humanising vulnerability, the professional dimension, or the sustained deterioration.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The Christmas feast scene is excluded per non-theatrical rules — this is a significant loss because it is the only sustained scene in the books where Trelawney is shown in a non-classroom social context, revealing her isolation, awkwardness, and the McGonagall dynamic in sharpest relief. The HBP corridor scene is absent. The sherry drinking as a character marker is entirely absent from the films. The Firenze antagonism is absent. The sustained OotP deterioration is absent. What remains is a character who is recognisable and whose most dramatically important moments are present, but whose texture — the repeated behavioral patterns, the humanising vulnerability, the professional anxieties — is stripped away. The film Trelawney is the outline of the book Trelawney with the interior removed.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: The lost material is substantial. The Christmas feast scene, the HBP corridor scene, the Firenze antagonism, the sherry drinking, and the sustained OotP deterioration together constitute most of what makes Trelawney a complex rather than merely eccentric character. The films keep the plot-significant moments and the most visually striking ones, but the texture that makes her simultaneously comic and sad, fraudulent and genuine, annoying and sympathetic is largely absent. A cap applies (see score_caps_applied): the removal of a major part of her complexity, key relationships, and agency triggers the cap at 85. The actual dimension scores already reflect this, but the cap is noted.

Umbridge inspection of Trelawney's classroom (OotP books) — excluded from theatrical film; the fullest expression of her personality under challenge, showing defensiveness, wounded pride, anger, and fragile dignity
Sustained OotP deterioration — corridor-wandering, sherry drinking, hysterical classroom outburst, tearful self-pity about 'sixteen years of devoted service'; entirely absent from films

score_caps_applied: Cap 1 (85): Not triggered at dimension level — overall score is already below 85 due to genuine dimension penalties.

Cap 3 (75): Applied — Trelawney's consequential agency in Half-Blood Prince (the Hog's Head eavesdropper revelation, which causes Harry to confront Dumbledore about Snape) is transferred away from her entirely; this is a core book function transferred to other delivery mechanisms. Total is held to 75 maximum under this cap. Calculated total (18+13+10+11+6+8 = 66) is already below this ceiling, so cap does not alter final score but is noted as applicable.
comparative.key_observations: The films faithfully preserve Trelawney's surface identity — her visual eccentricity, her theatrical voice, her doom-predictions, her sharp dismissal of Hermione, the sacking pathos, the second prophecy, and her DH2 heroism. Emma Thompson's performance captures the core performative fragility. However, the adaptation systematically removes the behavioral and relational texture that makes her a complex rather than merely eccentric character: the sustained deterioration under Umbridge, the humanising HBP corridor scenes, the Firenze antagonism, the sherry drinking, and — most consequentially — her active narrative agency in Half-Blood Prince, where she is the one who inadvertently reveals Snape's role in the prophecy to Harry. The film Trelawney is a faithful silhouette of the book character: the outline is correct, but the interior has been emptied. The result is a character who scores well on the most visible dimension (personality/voice) but progressively lower as the evaluation looks deeper — into agency, relationships, and the nuances that distinguish a rich secondary character from a recurring background figure.

personality_voice.book_baseline: Across all seven books, Dumbledore's voice is one of the most distinctive in the series: warmly ironic, gently eccentric, philosophically layered, and capable of cold authority without ever raising his volume. His defining traits include strategic indirection (the lemon drops deflection, the socks answer, 'three turns should do it'), controlled playfulness that coexists with genuine moral gravity (the school song, the troll joke, the chamber pot anecdote), sustained philosophical register even in crisis (the Pettigrew life-debt speech, the love-as-protection explanation, the prophecy lecture), and a private emotional texture that is never sentimental but is genuinely present (the light going out of his eyes at the Dursleys' doorstep, the tear in his beard, the weeping at King's Cross). His voice is most fully itself in private moments with Harry — the post-crisis conversations, the Pensieve sessions, the hospital wing exchanges — where his public performance relaxes into something more confessional and philosophically rich. Crucially, he never shouts; he manages crisis through calm weight rather than volume.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The films preserve the surface of Dumbledore's personality well across most books: the warm authority, the dry wit, the philosophical declarations, the calm under threat. Books 2, 3, and 6 are the strongest adaptations of his voice, with the feast speeches, the hospital wing scenes, the cave sequence, and the Astronomy Tower confrontation all landing close to the source. The King's Cross scene in DH preserves his warmth, guilt, and philosophical cadence. The hearing and arrest scenes in OotP preserve his public persona accurately. However, two systematic failures recur across all films: (1) the ironic, deflecting, quietly manipulative layer is consistently stripped — the lemon drops, the socks, the school song, the troll joke, the chamber pot, the 'temporarily deaf' moment, the Aberforth goat story are all absent, removing the mechanism by which his control and private intelligence are expressed through humor; and (2) the private philosophical voice — the extended post-crisis conversations with Harry, the multi-session Pensieve pedagogy, the King's Cross confessional passages — is consistently compressed or cut, removing the texture of his inner life. The GoF film introduces the most significant active contradiction: the raised voice at 'Harry Potter!!!' directly opposes the book's explicit characterization of a man who manages crisis through calm.
personality_voice.difference: The films deliver a Dumbledore who is recognizably himself in type but consistently thinner in texture. The ironic-deflecting mechanism is almost entirely absent across all films. The private philosophical register survives only in fragments. The most character-defining scenes in each book — the lemon drops (PS), the post-crisis Harry conversations (PoA, OotP), the Pensieve pedagogy (GoF, HBP), the King's Cross confession (DH) — are either cut or heavily compressed. The GoF raised-voice deviation is the only outright contradiction rather than compression, but it is a meaningful one. The cumulative effect is a Dumbledore who functions as a wise, warm authority figure but who loses the specific, slightly unsettling ironic intelligence that distinguishes the book character from a generic archetype.
personality_voice.evidence_status: Directly evidenced across all seven per-book assessments; the GoF contradiction is directly evidenced; compressions are directly evidenced by scene-level comparison.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The core surface traits are preserved well enough to avoid the lowest bands. The penalty reflects the systematic removal of the ironic-deflecting mechanism (across all films), the private philosophical voice (compressed in every film), and the one active contradiction (GoF raised voice). The result is a score that sits in the 'recognizable but with important traits significantly reduced' band rather than the 'clearly altered' band, because the broad identity is intact and several key scenes land well. The per-book scores range from 14 (GoF, worst) to 21 (CoS, best); the synthesis weights GoF and OotP heavily for the most consequential failures, and recognizes PS, CoS, PoA, and HBP as solid if imperfect. The floor is set by GoF's active contradiction and OotP's near-complete loss of the private voice. Final: 17.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: Dumbledore is the series' prime mover. Across all seven books he functions simultaneously as: institutional protector (setting threat parameters, managing the castle's defenses, resisting Ministry encroachment); investigative intelligence (the Pensieve sessions, the Horcrux theorization, the Moody trunk examination, the Patronus/Priori Incantatem analysis); political operator (navigating Fudge across multiple books, arguing specific policy, dispatching allies, protecting Harry from Scrimgeour); pedagogical mentor (the post-crisis conversations with Harry in PoA and HBP, the five-plus Pensieve lesson arc, the moral framing after Cedric's death); posthumous architect (the will, the Pensieve memories, the portrait network, the doe-sword subplot in DH). His agency is active and initiatory throughout: he places Harry at the Dursleys, engineers the Time-Turner solution, dispatches Snape back to the Death Eaters, confronts Fudge in the GoF parting-of-the-ways scene, orchestrates his own death to neutralize the Elder Wand. His absences are themselves agentive decisions.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: The films preserve Dumbledore's institutional and crisis-management agency consistently: the lockdowns, the tournament management, the hearing intervention, the Ministry duel, the cave mission, the Astronomy Tower resolution. The Time-Turner architecture (PoA) and the Horcrux investigation framework (HBP) are both well-handled. The posthumous agency in DH is preserved at the structural level: the will, the Pensieve, the King's Cross revelation. However, two systematic agency failures recur: the political operator function is severely compressed in every film — the GoF Fudge confrontation is reduced from a defining 30-page scene to two reactive lines; the OotP confrontation is similarly truncated; the Scrimgeour-resistance material is absent from HBP — and the pedagogical mentor function is consistently cut or compressed, meaning the post-crisis moral framing conversations (PoA, GoF) and the sustained Pensieve lesson arc (HBP) that constitute his most important active function with Harry are largely absent from the theatrical cuts.
narrative_role_agency.difference: The biggest agency failures are: (1) GoF — the Fudge confrontation, the dispatch of allies, and the full Pensieve investigation arc are reduced to fragments; (2) OotP — the explanatory and confessional function at the book's climax (the prophecy, the admission of fault for Sirius's death, the strategic accounting) is absent from the theatrical cut via the excision of Scene 10; (3) HBP — the sustained pedagogical architecture of five-plus Pensieve sessions and the Scrimgeour political dimension are both cut; (4) PS — the 'Just in case' note and the quiet proactive management of Harry's development are absent. These are not mere compressions in every case — in OotP, the core narrative function (explaining the prophecy, accepting responsibility) is structurally absent from the theatrical cut.
narrative_role_agency.evidence_status: Directly evidenced across all per-book assessments; OotP Scene 10 exclusion is directly evidenced as the source of the most consequential agency loss.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: The per-book scores range from 13 (GoF) to 17 (CoS). The most consequential failures are OotP (absent explanatory function) and GoF (radically reduced political and investigative agency). PoA, CoS, and HBP show medium compression. PS and DH are closest to intact at the structural level. The synthesis weights OotP and GoF heavily as the two books where Dumbledore's agency is most central and most reduced. The institutional and crisis-management functions consistently preserved prevent the score from falling further. Final: 14.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Dumbledore's motivations across the series build from a simple protective instinct (PS/CoS) into a philosophically layered, self-critically aware set of drives: protection of Harry and the students; commitment to truth and justice over institutional authority; loyalty to individuals others distrust (Snape, Hagrid, Lupin); a long-view reasoning about magical consequence (the Pettigrew life-debt); a philosophical belief in love and free will as the ultimate weapons against Voldemort (HBP); and, revealed in DH, a complex personal history of guilt (Ariana), self-distrust (refusing the Ministry), and the catastrophic cost of his youthful desire for glory. His internal conflict is the engine of his most important decisions throughout: the tension between protective love and strategic necessity (OotP, most explicitly) produces choices that are simultaneously caring and harmful, and this conflict is explicitly named and accepted in King's Cross. His motivation for instrumentalizing Harry — raising him 'like a pig for slaughter' while genuinely loving him — is the defining moral ambiguity of the entire series.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The films preserve the immediate motivations accurately throughout: protection, truth-telling, strategic necessity, trust in his chosen allies. The surface motivational logic of his behavior is consistently correct. However, the deeper motivational architecture — the philosophical dimension (HBP's love/free will argument), the internal conflict dimension (OotP's explicit self-indictment), the biographical dimension (DH's youth psychology and Grindelwald ideology) — is consistently underexplored or absent. In OotP, the internal conflict between protective love and strategic wisdom is the entire psychological engine of the book and is absent from the theatrical cut. In HBP, the philosophical conviction that makes his pedagogical approach coherent is stripped to almost nothing. In DH, the confession that makes his adult career comprehensible as an act of penance is heavily truncated.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The films give us the conclusions of Dumbledore's self-awareness without fully showing the inner journey. The most significant failures: OotP (the self-indicting analysis — 'I acted exactly as Voldemort expects we fools who love to act' — is absent); HBP (the philosophical argument about love and choice as the decisive weapons is absent); DH (the youth psychology, the fear of Grindelwald, the desire for power are referenced but not dramatized). The correct motivations are present throughout; the internal conflict that gives them depth and moral weight is consistently missing.
motivations_internal_conflict.evidence_status: Directly evidenced across per-book assessments; OotP Scene 10 exclusion confirmed as the primary source of the internal conflict loss for that book.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: Per-book scores range from 10 (OotP, GoF) to 13 (CoS, PoA). The synthesis recognizes that the internal conflict dimension is the most systematically underserved across the entire series — it is either absent (OotP) or reduced to surface gesture in every other major entry. The philosophical layer is lost in HBP; the biographical layer is truncated in DH; the paternalistic-withholding tension is present only in fragments throughout. The correct motivational skeleton is always present, which prevents a lower score, but the flesh of genuine internal conflict is consistently missing. Final: 10.

character_arc.book_baseline: Dumbledore's arc is a series-length revelation arc, not a transformation arc within any single book. Within books it is largely flat by design (PS through HBP), with each book's contribution being a progressive deepening of the reader's understanding: from mysterious authority (PS) to institutional anchor (CoS) to indirect mentor (PoA) to political force and prophetic strategist (GoF) to flawed, guilt-ridden protector (OotP) to philosophical teacher and willing martyr (HBP) to fully exposed, morally complex, posthumously confessing human being (DH). The arc across all seven books moves from idealization to full human complexity — and this movement is what makes the King's Cross chapter the series' emotional climax. Within each book, the arc is intentionally static except where the situation forces disclosure: OotP (forced to confront his own failure), GoF (forced from background management into foreground confrontation), DH (posthumous reckoning). The series arc is: admirable authority → complicated authority → acknowledged fallibility → full confession and integration.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The films preserve the flat-arc pattern within individual books accurately. The series arc is partially preserved: the gradual disclosure of Dumbledore's flaws, culminating in King's Cross, is legible in the films. However, critical arc steps are missing: the OotP arc's resolution (the explicit acknowledgment of failure and the turning-point conversation with Harry) is absent from the theatrical cut; the GoF arc's preparatory phase (concealed investigation, proto-Order management) is not established; the DH arc's middle phase (Harry's sustained resentment and intellectual working-through of trust) is compressed, weakening the emotional weight of the King's Cross resolution; and HBP's arc endpoint — the full philosophical handoff that completes Dumbledore's pedagogical purpose — is truncated. The series arc arrives at roughly the right destination but with missing steps that reduce its coherence and emotional impact.
character_arc.difference: The most significant arc failures: (1) OotP — the arc's resolution (reckoning and disclosure) is entirely absent from the theatrical cut; the arc ends at catastrophe without recovery, which is structurally and emotionally wrong; (2) HBP — the arc's thematic culmination (the philosophical handoff) is truncated; (3) DH — the arc's middle phase (sustained doubt, conscious choice to trust) is compressed, weakening King's Cross; (4) GoF — the arc's starting condition (concealed long-running preparation) is not established, making the response arc read as reactive rather than planned. These are not all equal: the OotP failure is the most consequential because it changes whether the audience understands that arc as Dumbledore having a reckoning or simply failing.
character_arc.evidence_status: Directly evidenced; OotP Scene 10 exclusion confirmed as the decisive arc-resolution failure.
character_arc.penalty_logic: Per-book scores range from 8 (OotP, worst — arc resolution absent) to 14 (CoS — flat arc correctly rendered). The synthesis must weigh arc importance by narrative centrality: OotP is the book where Dumbledore has his most important single arc movement (the reckoning), and its absence from the theatrical cut is the most consequential arc failure in the series. HBP and DH compressions are significant but do not wholly remove the arc's resolution. PS, CoS, PoA have correctly rendered flat arcs. GoF's compressed starting condition is a meaningful loss. The OotP failure alone would cap this dimension; combined with HBP and DH compressions, the score sits at 10. Final: 10.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Dumbledore's most important relationships across the series are: (1) Dumbledore–Harry — the series' central relationship, defined by deep mutual care, profound asymmetry of knowledge, and the painful fact that Dumbledore instrumentalizes the person he loves most; this relationship's defining scenes are the post-crisis conversations (PoA), the 'choices' speech (CoS), the King's Cross resolution (DH), and the 'Dumbledore's man' exchange (HBP); (2) Dumbledore–Snape — cold, mutually dependent, calculated trust; the books build this through repeated behavioral patterns across multiple books culminating in the full Pensieve revelation in DH; (3) Dumbledore–McGonagall — the best-drawn secondary relationship, characterized by banter, deflection-through-wit, and half-exasperated admiration (most fully present in PS); (4) Dumbledore–Fudge — a deteriorating political relationship that drives GoF and OotP; (5) Dumbledore–Lupin/Sirius/Hagrid — loyalty relationships that reveal his willingness to protect those others dismiss. The Harry relationship is the most important and the most consistently reduced across the films.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The films preserve the structural outlines of most relationships: the Harry mentorship is present in warmth and function, the Snape alliance is dramatized in the Pensieve and Astronomy Tower scenes, the Fudge antagonism is present in hearing/confrontation scenes, and the Hagrid loyalty is noted. However, the relational texture — the specific conversational dynamics that reveal how these relationships actually work — is consistently compressed or cut. The most significant individual failures: the Dumbledore–Harry relationship loses its defining emotional moments in OotP (the post-Sirius reckoning, which is the relationship's climax in the series), in HBP (the broom-shed Sirius conversation and the 'Dumbledore's man' exchange), and in PoA (the post-time-travel philosophical dialogue); the Dumbledore–McGonagall dynamic (the richest secondary relationship in PS) is severely flattened; the Dumbledore–Fudge rupture in GoF is compressed from a defining confrontation to two reactive lines; the Dumbledore–Snape relationship in DH loses the intermediate scenes that show years of deliberate management.
key_relationships.difference: The Harry relationship's most important scenes are its most consistently absent ones: the post-crisis conversations, the 'Dumbledore's man' exchange, the OotP resolution. The Snape relationship is preserved in outline but loses the behavioral texture that builds its complexity. The McGonagall relationship is severely reduced in PS. The Fudge relationship is adequately handled in OotP but badly handled in GoF. The cumulative effect across all seven books is a portrait of relationships that are functionally correct but emotionally and texturally thin.
key_relationships.evidence_status: Directly evidenced across per-book assessments; specific scene-level absences confirmed throughout.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: Per-book scores range from 6 (OotP, GoF) to 8 (CoS). No book scores above 8 in this dimension, reflecting a consistent pattern of relationship compression across the entire series. The synthesis cannot score this dimension higher than the consistent pattern allows: the Harry relationship — the most important in the series — loses its defining emotional moments in multiple films, and the other key relationships are either compressed (Snape, Fudge in GoF) or severely reduced (McGonagall in PS, Lupin/Sirius across multiple films). The structural outlines prevent the lowest score range. Final: 6.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: Dumbledore's complexity across the series rests on a set of productive contradictions that build cumulatively: he is warmly ironic and quietly manipulative; he protects those he loves by using them; he champions justice while engineering situations rather than trusting people with the truth; his greatest virtue (love) is also his greatest strategic weakness; his entire admirable adult life is an act of penance for a brilliant, selfish, ideologically dangerous youth. The specific material that builds this complexity includes: the ironic deflection mechanism (lemon drops, socks, troll joke, 'temporarily deaf' — present across PS, GoF); the private philosophical voice in post-crisis conversations (PoA, GoF, OotP); the self-indicting analysis of his own emotional weakness (OotP King's Cross); the philosophical argument about love and free will (HBP); the biographical revelation of his youth, his desire for power, and his Grindelwald ideological complicity (DH); the Pettigrew life-debt long-view reasoning (PoA); the gleam of triumph at the blood-protection revelation (GoF); the 'pig for slaughter' self-awareness (DH). None of these is incidental decoration — each is a load-bearing element of what makes the character morally complex rather than merely wise.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The films preserve the broad contours of complexity: Dumbledore is shown to be fallible (he withholds information, he makes mistakes), his love for Harry is shown to coexist with strategic use of Harry, his trust of Snape is shown to require something painful from Snape. The public persona of controlled warmth and authority is well-rendered throughout. However, the specific material that builds the productive contradictions is systematically absent: the ironic deflection mechanism is almost entirely gone; the private philosophical voice survives only in fragments; the self-indicting analysis (OotP) is absent from the theatrical cut; the philosophical love/free will argument (HBP) is absent; the full biographical confession (DH) is truncated; the gleam of triumph (GoF) is absent; the Pettigrew life-debt reasoning (PoA) is absent; the 'For the Greater Good' ideological depth (DH) is reduced to a summary reference. The films leave the sketch of complexity but remove most of the specific evidence that makes it persuasive.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The cumulative loss across all seven films is the most significant finding of this synthesis. No single film catastrophically misrepresents Dumbledore, but every film removes material from this dimension, and the removed material is consistently the most philosophically and psychologically rich content. The result is a character who is recognizably complex in type but whose specific complexity is almost entirely asserted rather than shown. A viewer who has not read the books will understand that Dumbledore is wise, caring, and fallible; they will not understand that his fallibility is the consequence of specific psychological patterns (the desire for glory, the fear of self-knowledge, the use of love as both weapon and weakness) that the books dramatize with precision. This is not compression — it is the systematic substitution of a simpler character for a more complex one while preserving enough surface features to avoid obvious misrepresentation.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.evidence_status: Directly evidenced across all per-book assessments; the cumulative pattern is directly evidenced by the consistent absence of the same categories of material across all seven films.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: Per-book scores range from 7 (GoF, OotP) to 11 (CoS). The synthesis must reflect the cumulative weight of systematic loss across the entire series. No film scores above 11 in this dimension. The most important books for character complexity are OotP (internal conflict, self-indictment), HBP (philosophical argument, emotional intimacy), and DH (biographical depth, ideological revelation) — and all three have significant complexity losses. The CoS and PoA scores are somewhat higher because their specific complexity losses are more contained. The overall pattern is one of consistent simplification of the character's most philosophically and psychologically rich material across the entire series. Final: 8.
