PoA: Post-crisis mentor conversation with Harry (Pettigrew life-debt speech; Patronus/James connection; moral framing of the night's events); backstory material about Dumbledore's role in the Fidelius Charm and offering to be Secret-Keeper; 'He's not unbalanced' line about Snape

GoF: Troll-hag-leprechaun joke; chamber pot anecdote; 'temporarily deaf' moment; Aberforth goat story; full Pensieve scene (pacing, extracting thoughts, scar theory, Neville's parents bitterness, Snape dispatch context); full Fudge confrontation including dementor/giant policy argument and formal parting-of-the-ways declaration; strategic dispatch of Sirius, Bill, McGonagall, and Snape in hospital wing; Hagrid cabin scene (Dumbledore's protective loyalty, dry humor, refusal to be moved); gleam of triumph at blood-protection revelation; raised voice at 'Harry Potter!!!' (active contradiction of book characterization)

OotP: Entire post-Sirius lost-prophecy conversation (Scene 10 excised from theatrical cut) including: full prophecy explanation, explicit admission of fault for Sirius's death, self-indicting analysis of protective love as strategic weakness ('I acted exactly as Voldemort expects we fools who love to act'), account of Occlumency delegation to Snape, Harry destroying the office, Dumbledore sitting still through Harry's rage, weeping; Sirius–Dumbledore tension arc (confinement, resentment, and its role in Sirius's fatal decision); sustained texture of Harry's experience of Dumbledore's avoidance as abandonment

HBP: Extended philosophical argument about love, free will, and the prophecy's non-compulsory nature; Scrimgeour Christmas confrontation and Dumbledore's active protection of Harry from Ministry co-option; Sirius broom-shed conversation (most emotionally intimate Harry–Dumbledore scene in HBP); 'Dumbledore's man through and through' exchange and Dumbledore's near-tears response; Voldemort-return-to-Hogwarts Pensieve memory (one of the richest Dumbledore–Voldemort scenes); five-plus Pensieve lesson architecture with cumulative pedagogical buildup; self-deprecating acknowledgment of fallibility ('my mistakes tend to be correspondingly huger'); explicit articulation of why Harry has 'earned the right' to join the cave mission; Dursley Privet Drive visit in HBP (social manipulation, humor)

DH: Extended confessional passages in King's Cross about youthful desire for glory and escape; Dumbledore's explicit fear of self-knowledge regarding Grindelwald and Ariana; five-year delay against Grindelwald explained as motivated by fear; full Grindelwald ideological letter ('FOR THE GREATER GOOD') and its moral weight for Dumbledore's complicity; Dumbledore's refusal of Ministry framed as learned self-distrust ('power was my weakness'); dark humor at his own death; portrait's active wartime role directing Snape; intermediate Pensieve scenes showing Dumbledore managing Snape over years (walking the grounds, refusing to explain sword instructions, inviting Snape to his office); full elaboration of Elder Wand succession plan to neutralize its power
score_caps_applied: No formal caps applied. OotP theatrical cut excision of Scene 10 functions as a structural constraint that caps several dimensions independently: narrative_role_agency cannot recover the explanatory function; character_arc cannot recover the resolution; motivations_internal_conflict cannot recover the self-indicting analysis; key_relationships cannot recover the Harry relationship resolution. This is treated as a confirmed structural absence rather than a capped inference.
GoF raised-voice contradiction treated as an active deviation rather than a compression, creating a ceiling effect on personality_voice for that book and weighing against the series synthesis.
comparative.key_observations: The synthesis score of 65 reflects a film portrayal that is recognizably and functionally faithful at the level of surface identity — Dumbledore's broad character type, his structural role as series architect, his warmth toward Harry, his authority, his willingness to tell the truth in public at personal cost — while systematically failing to render the specific material that makes him genuinely complex rather than archetypally wise. Two patterns explain most of the penalty. The first is the near-total removal of the ironic-deflecting mechanism: across all seven films, the scenes in which Dumbledore's intelligence and control are expressed through humor, strategic silence, and deliberate evasion (the lemon drops, the socks, the 'temporarily deaf' moment, the troll joke, the Aberforth story) are consistently cut, leaving a Dumbledore who is warm and authoritative but who no longer demonstrates the particular quality — being slightly, amusingly, deliberately in control of every conversation — that the books make central to his character. The second pattern is the compression or excision of his private voice: the post-crisis conversations with Harry, the Pensieve pedagogy, the sustained self-indicting King's Cross confession are the primary vehicles for his philosophical and emotional depth, and every film reduces or removes them. The most consequential single failure is OotP, where the theatrical cut excises the scene that contains the book's most important self-revelation — Dumbledore's explicit acknowledgment that his love for Harry caused him to act against his own strategic judgment and contributed to Sirius's death. Without this scene, the film's Dumbledore never demonstrates the defining characteristic of book-Dumbledore at his most complex: that his greatest virtue and his greatest flaw are the same thing. The GoF film adds an active contradiction (the raised voice) and removes or compresses virtually every scene — the Hagrid cabin, the full Fudge confrontation, the Pensieve, the troll joke — that builds his complexity in that book. The DH film handles the King's Cross and Pensieve sequences better than most, but truncates the biographical material (the youthful desire for glory, the Grindelwald ideological complicity) that gives those scenes their full moral weight. The result, across all seven films, is a Dumbledore who is adequate as a plot-functional wise mentor and who would be recognizable to book readers as a somewhat simplified version of the source character, but who would not, for a film-only audience, convey the specific psychological portrait the books construct: a brilliant, self-distrusting, strategically manipulative, privately guilt-ridden man whose admirable adult life is an act of penance for a dangerous youth, and whose love for Harry is simultaneously the most important thing about him and the thing that most consistently leads him to make choices that harm the people he loves.

personality_voice.book_baseline: In the books, Dean Thomas is a grounded, sociable Gryffindor with a distinct voice: he is passionate about football (West Ham), opinionated, willing to speak up in class and in public, and carries a light sense of humour. He expresses himself directly: 'Send him off, ref! Red card!' (Book 1 Quidditch); 'It was Malfoy's fault!' (Book 3); 'He's the best Defence Against the Dark Arts teacher we've ever had' (Book 3, boldly to Snape); 'Says who?' when Lockhart dismisses the danger (Book 2). He is curious ('But maybe you've got to be related to Slytherin,' Book 2), artistically talented (drawing banners, noted twice), and pragmatic about his Muggle background ('My parents are Muggles, mate. They don't know nothing about no deaths at Hogwarts, because I'm not stupid enough to tell them,' Book 5). He is neither a passive background figure nor a comic foil: he defends Lupin hotly to Umbridge across three exchanges, jokes with Seamus, and shows genuine moral courage in small moments. His voice is characterised by directness, short declarative sentences, and a willingness to challenge authority.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The films preserve some surface elements: Dean announces the post arriving in CoS ('Post is here!'), asks a sensible question in the Boggart lesson ('But what does it mean, Professor?'), performs Riddikulus successfully, comments on the Fat Lady situation ('What d'you expect? After what happened to the Fat Lady, none of the other pictures would take the job'), and speaks up in the DA meeting ('Blimey, Harry, I didn't know you could do that'). In HBP he functions as a Quidditch Chaser and Ginny's boyfriend, with one line on the pitch ('Ginny! Let's go!'). In DH he returns as a fighter, asks 'Where is it?' in the Room of Requirement and receives an instruction from Kingsley on the battlements. He laughs with Seamus in the final Great Hall scene.
personality_voice.difference: The films strip away almost all of Dean's verbal personality. His football passion is entirely absent (the West Ham argument with Ron, the 'Red card!' moment, his West Ham pyjamas and poster — all book-only material). His habit of boldly challenging authority — most clearly his three-exchange defence of Lupin to Umbridge — is absent from the film. His pragmatic, wry commentary on the Muggle/wizard divide ('My parents are Muggles, mate') is absent. His artistic talent is noted in the book twice and acknowledged zero times in the films. His longer, opinionated lines in Book 5 (Umbridge classroom) are absent. What survives is functional reaction and minimal dialogue rather than a recognisable voice.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The film retains Dean's physical presence and a handful of short correct-register lines, so he is not unrecognisable. However, the dominant traits that give him texture — football passion, directness, willingness to challenge authority, pragmatic Muggle perspective, artistic identity — are almost entirely absent. This constitutes a reduction of secondary traits sufficient to place the score in the 14–17 band rather than higher.
personality_voice.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for book baseline; directly evidenced for film portrayal; reasonably inferred that omissions constitute character flattening given the volume of absent material.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: Dean serves several distinct narrative functions across the series: (1) a grounding voice that contextualises the Muggle-wizard divide from a Muggle-born perspective; (2) a member of the DA who participates actively and asks questions that advance exposition; (3) Ginny's boyfriend in Book 6, whose relationship with her is a key driver of Harry's jealousy arc and Ginny's eventual independence; (4) a fugitive in Book 7 whose off-page flight and reappearance at Shell Cottage tracks the regime's persecution of Muggle-borns and whose question about Ginny ('What happened to Ginny and all the others?') is what prompts the crucial piece of intelligence about the sword. He initiates questions, defends positions, and his presence or absence meaningfully affects scenes.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: In the films, Dean is present but largely reactive. He appears in group scenes, receives instructions (from Kingsley on the battlements), and asks 'Where is it?' in the Room of Requirement. His Quidditch role as Chaser is shown in montage. His relationship with Ginny is depicted — they are seen kissing, he is on the Hogwarts Express with her — but his lines are minimal and he does not initiate any significant plot action. His function as a messenger on the battlements (telling McGonagall about wand needs) is a small active moment but not a characterisation-defining one.
narrative_role_agency.difference: Several of Dean's book agency moments are absent or transferred. His 'Says who?' challenge to Lockhart (Book 2) is omitted. His bold defence of Lupin to Umbridge (three exchanges, Book 5) is omitted — this is a moment where he drives a confrontation. His Book 7 question about Ginny, which functions as the mechanism for obtaining the sword intelligence, is omitted from the film (the Snatchers' camp scene is cut). His Muggle-born fugitive storyline is referenced only implicitly via his presence at Shell Cottage. The Ginny relationship, which in the books is an active source of tension that Dean navigates (the corridor confrontation with Ron, the breakup scene), is reduced in the films to background presence.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: Dean's narrative agency is reduced but he retains a presence in key ensemble scenes (DA, Battle of Hogwarts). His role is not fully reassigned to another character — it is simply diminished. The score falls in the 10–13 range: role and agency are clearly altered, with several defining agency moments absent.
narrative_role_agency.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for book baseline; directly evidenced for film portrayal; directly evidenced for specific absent agency moments.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Dean's motivations are not deeply foregrounded in the books — he is not a POV character — but observable patterns establish: (1) loyalty to Gryffindor and his friends, expressed through defending them publicly (against Lockhart, against Umbridge, against sceptics); (2) a pragmatic self-preservation instinct balanced against moral courage (he stays quiet about deaths at Hogwarts to his Muggle parents, but joins the DA and speaks up in class); (3) in Book 7, a survival motivation as a Muggle-born fugitive who nonetheless expresses faith in Harry ('I know Harry Potter. And I reckon he's the real thing'). His Book 6 romantic motivation vis-à-vis Ginny is present but not internally complex from his perspective — it is Harry's perspective that renders it significant. There is no deep internal conflict depicted.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The films provide no explicit motivational texture for Dean. He appears loyal and participatory, joins the DA and the Battle of Hogwarts, but no dialogue or action specifically establishes why. His Muggle-born identity and what it costs him under the regime is not addressed. His faith in Harry (Book 7) is not shown.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The motivations that are present in the books are either absent or too vague in the films to support the same characterisation. Most critically, his Muggle-born identity as a source of both vulnerability and pragmatic perspective is never explored in the films. His Book 7 declaration of faith in Harry is absent. These are not deep internal conflicts, but they are the closest the books come to establishing Dean's inner life, and they are lost.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: Because Dean's motivations in the books are themselves relatively surface-level — he is a supporting character — the bar for this dimension is lower. However, the films fail to establish even the observable motivational patterns the books provide. Score falls in the 8–10 range: motivations are partially flattened or underexplained rather than actively wrong.
motivations_internal_conflict.evidence_status: Reasonably inferred from book patterns; not enough evidence in the films to confirm or deny most motivational texture.

character_arc.book_baseline: Dean has a modest but genuine arc across the series. He begins as a background Gryffindor (Books 1–3), becomes more visible as a loyal DA member who challenges authority (Books 4–5), enters a relationship with Ginny that ends badly partly due to his own behaviour (he laughs at Harry being injured; he is overprotective toward Ginny in ways she resents) (Book 6), and in Book 7 undergoes a significant off-page transformation: he flees as a Muggle-born fugitive, joins Ted Tonks's group, maintains his moral compass under duress, and returns to fight at Hogwarts. The arc is from background presence to someone who has been tested by the regime and returns as a committed fighter. It is not a dramatic arc, but it is coherent and cumulative.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The films preserve the broad shape: Dean is present from Book 1 through to the Battle of Hogwarts, participates in the DA, and returns to fight. His Ginny relationship is depicted in HBP. His fugitive storyline is implied by his presence at Shell Cottage and in the Room of Requirement. The arc from student to fighter is intact in outline.
character_arc.difference: The middle of the arc — Dean's growth from passive presence to someone who challenges authority (Books 3–5) — is largely absent. His Book 6 arc (the relationship with Ginny, its deterioration due to his specific behaviour, the breakup) is reduced to background scenes without the texture that makes it meaningful. His Book 7 fugitive experience, which is the most dramatically significant phase of his arc, is almost entirely off-screen (the Snatchers' camp scene is cut from the film). What survives is the beginning and end of the arc, with the middle largely absent.
character_arc.penalty_logic: The arc exists and is not inverted. However, important steps are skipped or compressed to the point of near-absence, particularly the Book 7 phase which represents his most significant development. Score falls in the 11–13 range: arc is compressed but still traceable, though important steps are missing.
character_arc.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for both book and film; reasonably inferred that compression removes meaningful arc steps.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Dean's key relationships are: (1) Seamus Finnigan — his best friend, a warm, teasing dynamic built across all seven books through shared dormitory life, shared humour, and mutual support (Seamus's DA attendance is specifically noted as being 'brought along by Dean'); (2) Ginny Weasley — a romantic relationship in Book 6 that is significant not just for what it reveals about Dean (overprotectiveness, inability to let her be independent) but as a driver of Harry's emotional arc; (3) the broader Gryffindor dormitory group (Harry, Ron, Neville, Seamus) — a relationship defined by loyalty, casual friction (the Seamus argument in Book 5), and shared stakes. The Seamus friendship in particular is characterised by warmth and is one of the few peer friendships in the series depicted with genuine texture.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The Dean-Seamus friendship is present as a visual pattern — they are frequently shown together, they laugh together in the final Hall scene — but is given almost no dialogue that establishes its warmth or texture. The DA scene ('Blimey, Harry, I didn't know you could do that') shows them together. The Dean-Ginny relationship is depicted in HBP through background scenes and one kiss. The dormitory group dynamic is present structurally but not emotionally.
key_relationships.difference: The Dean-Seamus friendship is visible but its emotional texture (the teasing, the mutual support, Dean bringing Seamus to the DA for the first time) is absent from the films. The Dean-Ginny relationship is depicted but without the specific dynamic that defines it in the books: Dean's overprotectiveness, Ginny's frustration with it, and the specific ways in which the breakup happens. The film shows them together and then apart without the intermediate texture. Dean's relationship with Harry (as a sceptic, then a supporter, through the Book 5 Umbridge confrontations and Book 7 declaration) is absent from the films.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: The relationships are not falsified or replaced, but their emotional dynamics — particularly the Dean-Ginny dynamic and the Dean-Seamus friendship texture — are simplified. Score falls in the 5–6 range: important relationship dynamics are altered or weakened rather than absent or opposite.
key_relationships.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for book baseline; directly evidenced for film portrayal; reasonably inferred that absent dialogue and scenes constitute dynamic simplification.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: Dean's complexity in the books is modest but real: he is a Muggle-born who navigates both worlds with pragmatic good sense; he is artistically talented in a way that is noted approvingly by his peers; he is loyal but not blindly so (he stays quiet about deaths rather than alarming his Muggle parents); he challenges authority in specific, courage-requiring moments (Umbridge); he is capable of behaviour that ends a relationship (overprotectiveness of Ginny); he maintains his moral compass as a fugitive under genuine danger and returns to fight. These elements together create a character who is more than a background Gryffindor — he is a consistent moral agent with a specific social and cultural position.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The films preserve the surface identity (Gryffindor, Muggle-born background implied, Ginny's boyfriend, DA member, Battle of Hogwarts fighter) but remove almost all of the texture. The football identity is gone. The artistic talent is gone. The Muggle-born pragmatism is gone. The authority-challenging moments are gone. The Book 7 fugitive experience and faith-in-Harry declaration are gone. What remains is a recognisable but largely flat supporting figure.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The cumulative loss is significant: Dean's Muggle-born identity as a characterisation engine (not just a demographic fact), his artistic talent, his football passion, his willingness to confront authority, his specific relational failure with Ginny, and his Book 7 arc as a tested-but-faithful fugitive are all absent. This is not a case where compression merely shortens the portrayal — it removes the specific elements that gave the character richness and distinction from other background Gryffindors.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: The character is recognisable and not falsified, but the material that made him textured and distinct is almost entirely absent. This constitutes noticeable simplification where important nuances, agency, and relational complexity are missing. Score falls in the 8–10 range.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for book baseline; directly evidenced for film portrayal; directly evidenced for specific absent material.

score_caps_applied: Cap 4 applied (score above 70 not warranted): The films preserve Dean's broad identity but remove most of what defines his book characterisation — his football passion, artistic talent, Muggle-born perspective as a voice, authority-challenging moments, and Book 7 arc are all absent. Total kept at 65.
comparative.key_observations: Dean Thomas in the films is a faithful silhouette of the book character rather than a faithful portrayal. His broad identity — Gryffindor, Muggle-born, loyal friend, Ginny's boyfriend, DA member, Battle of Hogwarts fighter — is preserved, and he is never misrepresented or contradicted. However, the specific elements that gave him texture and distinction are almost entirely absent: his football passion (the most consistent characterisation device in Books 1–4), his artistic talent, his willingness to challenge authority (most dramatically in Book 5 against Umbridge), his pragmatic Muggle-born voice, and his Book 7 arc as a fugitive who returns as a tested fighter. The films treat him as a correctly-labelled background presence rather than a character with a specific personality. The score of 65 reflects a portrayal that is recognisable but substantially incomplete, with the cap at 70 triggered by the removal of most defining book material while the broad identity remains intact. Confidence is Medium throughout because Dean is a supporting character whose book presence, while consistent across 7 volumes, is diffuse enough that some interpretive judgement is required.

personality_voice.book_baseline: In the books, Grawp is a creature of extremely limited language and comprehension, dangerous and unpredictable through sheer size and animal impulse rather than malice. He is not hostile in a directed way — he grabs Hermione out of curiosity or instinct, knocks Hagrid over without apparent awareness of harm, and pulls trees for simple pleasure. His emotional range is narrow: displeasure (roaring at an empty nest), insistent longing for Hagrid ('HAGGER!', 'GRAWP WANT HAGGER!'), and a kind of dull, detached contentment. He is not tamed or teachable in any meaningful sense during OotP — Firenze's warning ('His attempt is not working') and Harry's internal observation that civilising Grawp is 'totally pointless' establish him as genuinely wild. By HBP he has improved somewhat, and by DH he attends Dumbledore's funeral docilely and fights Voldemort's giants in the Battle of Hogwarts, showing rudimentary loyalty. His speech is always minimal, broken, and mispronounced ('Hermy', 'Hagger').
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The film preserves the core physical presentation and the broken speech ('Hagger', 'Hermy'). He is dangerous and unpredictable on first meeting, grabs Hermione, and is managed with difficulty by Hagrid. In OotP he appears briefly in the forest scene and then again to grab Umbridge during the centaur confrontation. In DH Part 2 he fights Voldemort's giant. The basic personality — limited language, impulsive physicality, attachment to Hagrid — is present.
personality_voice.difference: The film softens Grawp's genuine menace and incomprehensibility. In the books, his grabbing of Hermione is terrifying and nearly fatal; Hagrid is knocked bleeding to the ground; Harry internally concludes the situation is hopeless. In the film, Hermione commands 'Put me down! Now!' and he complies, and she immediately concludes he 'just needs a firm hand' — a line that reframes him as manageable rather than genuinely dangerous. The film also adds a whimsical beat (Grawp giving Hermione a scooter bell) that has no book basis and softens his character toward comic-gentle rather than wild-unpredictable. The book's repeated emphasis on his detached, animal incomprehension ('it was hard to say whether he even recognised the sounds Hagrid was making as speech') is not conveyed.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The core traits are recognisable — broken speech, physical danger, attachment to Hagrid — but the film meaningfully softens the wildness and incomprehension that define him in OotP, and adds a whimsical gentleness (the bell) not present in the books. This is a noticeable reduction of an important trait, placing the score in the 14–17 range.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: In OotP, Grawp serves two narrative functions: (1) he is Hagrid's emotional burden and the reason Hagrid extracts a promise from Harry, Ron, and Hermione to look after him — creating plot obligation and foreshadowing; (2) he is the deus ex machina that disperses the centaurs when they have captured Harry and Hermione, enabling their escape. In the centaur scene, Grawp arrives independently, calls for Hagrid, and his presence causes the centaurs to scatter — he is the active agent of rescue. In DH, he fights Voldemort's giants at the Battle of Hogwarts, contributing to the defence of the school.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: In the film, Grawp's forest introduction scene is present and he retains the function of being Hagrid's reason for asking the trio to stay. In OotP, his rescue function is altered: he grabs Umbridge (who has already been taken by centaurs), and Harry and Hermione thank him and run. In DH Part 2, he fights a giant. The rescue function is partially present.
narrative_role_agency.difference: In the books, Grawp's arrival in the centaur clearing is the pivotal event that breaks the standoff — he arrives looking for Hagrid, the centaurs fire arrows at him, and in the chaos Harry and Hermione escape. His agency is clear: he causes the disruption that enables escape. In the film, Hermione has already lured Umbridge into the forest under a false pretext (Dumbledore's secret weapon), the centaurs take Umbridge, and Grawp then grabs Umbridge — a more passive, reactive role. The book's moment where Grawp bellows 'HAGGER!' and the centaurs scatter is replaced by a scene where Grawp is essentially a tool Hermione has positioned. The transfer of initiative from Grawp (arriving independently, causing chaos) to Hermione (engineering the situation) is a meaningful agency reduction.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: Grawp's most significant act of agency in OotP — arriving independently and disrupting the centaur standoff — is partially transferred to Hermione's scheme. He still physically acts (grabbing Umbridge), but the causal chain is different. This is a clear agency reduction, placing the score in the 10–13 range.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Grawp's motivations are simple but consistent: he wants Hagrid ('GRAWP WANT HAGGER!'), he acts on immediate physical impulse (grabbing things, pulling trees), and he has a rudimentary attachment to the people Hagrid associates him with (he remembers 'Hermy'). There is no internal conflict in a complex sense — he is too cognitively limited for that — but his longing for Hagrid is a genuine emotional driver that the books establish clearly.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The film preserves the attachment to Hagrid as the core motivation. Hagrid explains 'It's company he'll be needing when I'm gone' and Grawp's search for 'Hagger' is present in the centaur scene. The impulsive physicality is also present.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The motivations are simplified but not changed. The film does not develop the 'Grawp wants Hagrid' motivation as richly (the book's 'GRAWP WANT HAGGER!' scene in the centaur clearing is more emotionally legible than the film equivalent), but the core is intact.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: Motivations are simplified but correct. The longing for Hagrid is present in both. Minor compression but no meaningful change. Score in the 11–13 range.

character_arc.book_baseline: Grawp has a modest but real arc across OotP, HBP, and DH: he begins as a genuinely dangerous, uncivilisable wild giant (OotP) who cannot even pronounce his own name properly; by HBP Hagrid reports he is 'loads better behaved' and 'seemed right pleased' to see Hagrid, has moved to a cave in the mountains, and can hold a conversation with Hagrid; by DH he attends Dumbledore's funeral docilely, comforts Hagrid, and fights in the Battle of Hogwarts. The arc is one of very gradual domestication and loyalty — not transformation into a person, but a shift from wild animal to loyal, semi-tame creature.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The film corpus covers OotP (introduction) and DH Part 2 (battle). The HBP development — the cave, the improved behaviour, the reported conversations — is absent from the corpus. In DH Part 2 he fights and calls for Hagrid, which is consistent with the end-state of his arc. The intermediate steps are not shown.
character_arc.difference: The arc's middle stage (HBP improvement, relocation, growing attachment) is absent. The film jumps from dangerous-wild (OotP) to battle-participant (DH) without the intermediate development. This compresses the arc significantly, though the start and end points are roughly preserved.
character_arc.penalty_logic: The arc is incomplete — important intermediate steps are skipped. The HBP material that shows Grawp's gradual improvement is entirely absent. However, the start and end points are present, and for a minor character with a flat-ish arc, this is a meaningful but not catastrophic compression. Score in the 8–10 range.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Grawp's only meaningful relationship is with Hagrid — it is the entire basis of his characterisation. Hagrid brought him from the giant colony out of familial loyalty; Grawp's attachment to Hagrid ('GRAWP WANT HAGGER!') is his primary emotional driver. The relationship is asymmetric: Hagrid loves Grawp with the same uncritical devotion he gives all creatures; Grawp's attachment is more instinctive but genuine. By DH, Grawp comforts a sobbing Hagrid at Dumbledore's funeral — a moment of reversed care that shows the relationship has deepened. A secondary relationship exists with Hermione, whom Grawp remembers by name ('Hermy') and who he associates with Hagrid.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The Hagrid-Grawp relationship is present: Hagrid introduces him as 'my brother', explains he needs company, and Grawp's search for 'Hagger' in the centaur scene is preserved. The Hermione connection is also present (he remembers her name, gives her the bell). The DH funeral scene where Grawp comforts Hagrid is not in the film corpus provided.
key_relationships.difference: The core dynamic is preserved but the DH funeral moment — Grawp patting Hagrid hard on the head as Hagrid sobs, the reversal of the care dynamic — is absent from the film corpus. This is the most emotionally developed moment of their relationship in the books. The relationship is present but somewhat flattened.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: The relationship is mostly faithful in its basic dynamic, but the most emotionally resonant moment (DH funeral) is absent, and the film's whimsical bell scene slightly misrepresents the nature of Grawp's attachment to Hermione. Score in the 7–8 range.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: Grawp's complexity is limited by his nature, but the books give him specific texture: the genuine terror of his first appearance (Hagrid bleeding, Harry concluding the situation is hopeless, Hermione pale and shaking); the pathos of his longing for Hagrid in the centaur clearing; the dark comedy of his detached pleasure in pulling trees; the gradual, improbable improvement across books; the DH funeral scene where he comforts Hagrid. The books also use Grawp as a lens on Hagrid's self-delusion and unconditional love for creatures others find dangerous or hopeless.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The film retains the physical danger and the Hagrid attachment, but softens the genuine menace (Hermione's 'just needs a firm hand'), adds the whimsical bell scene, and omits the DH funeral moment. The function as a lens on Hagrid's self-delusion is present in Hagrid's dialogue but less developed.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The film loses: (1) the genuine hopelessness and terror of the first meeting as experienced by Harry and Hermione; (2) the pathos of the centaur scene ('GRAWP WANT HAGGER!') as an independent arrival rather than a positioned rescue; (3) the DH funeral scene; (4) the HBP development. It adds the bell scene, which softens his characterisation. The result is a Grawp who is recognisable but somewhat gentler and less textured.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: Noticeable simplification — the genuine wildness and the most emotionally resonant moments are reduced or absent. The character is not flattened to a single trait, but important nuances are missing. Score in the 8–10 range.

lost_or_transferred_material: Hermione's genuine terror and Harry's internal conclusion that civilising Grawp is 'totally pointless' — replaced by Hermione's 'just needs a firm hand'
Grawp's independent arrival in the centaur clearing calling for Hagrid as the active cause of the centaurs' dispersal — partially transferred to Hermione's scheme to lure Umbridge into the forest
The scooter bell scene — added in the film with no book basis, softening Grawp's characterisation
HBP development: Grawp's improved behaviour, relocation to a mountain cave, reported conversations with Hagrid
DH funeral scene: Grawp patting Hagrid hard on the head as Hagrid sobs, reversing the care dynamic
Harry's internal narration establishing Grawp as genuinely incomprehensible and uncivilisable (Firenze's warning, 'totally pointless attempts')
score_caps_applied: Cap 3 (score above 75 if a core book function or act of agency is transferred to another character): Grawp's agency in the centaur scene is partially transferred to Hermione's scheme; cap considered and reflected in the narrative_role_agency score and total.
comparative.key_observations: The film preserves Grawp's core identity — broken speech, physical danger, attachment to Hagrid — but meaningfully softens his wildness and incomprehensibility, partially transfers his most significant act of agency (disrupting the centaur standoff) to Hermione's scheme, omits the HBP arc development, and loses the most emotionally resonant moment of his relationship with Hagrid (the DH funeral). The addition of the whimsical bell scene actively misrepresents his characterisation. The result is a recognisable but simplified and somewhat gentled version of the book character, scoring in the mid-60s range. Confidence is medium throughout because Grawp is a minor character with limited material in both corpora, making some dimensions difficult to evaluate with full certainty.

personality_voice.book_baseline: In the books, Neville is defined by a precise combination of anxiety, clumsiness, and suppressed courage that builds across all seven years. His voice is timid and apologetic in early books — short sentences, frequent hesitation, self-deprecation ('I don't think you should be breaking any more rules!') — but it never disappears entirely behind fear. He shows brief flashes of determined assertion even in Year 1, notably standing in front of the portrait hole to physically bar Harry, Ron and Hermione ('I'll fight you!'). He is publicly humiliated by Snape and by Malfoy without fighting back verbally; he internalises shame rather than externalising it as anger. He is also quietly proud of his niche competence in Herbology and responds with visible pleasure to genuine praise, as seen when Moody relays Professor Sprout's compliment. His nervous comedy is consistent: breaking teacups in Divination, melting cauldrons, tripping over the trick stair, losing passwords. By Order of the Phoenix, a new register opens — nearly silent, white-knuckled determination in DA sessions after his parents' attackers escape — and in Deathly Hallows he speaks with compressed directness and a sardonic edge ('that's nothing, Seamus is worse'). His fearlessness in Year 7 is recognisably earned from the same character; the bluntness is new but not discontinuous.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The films preserve the surface symptoms of Neville's anxiety — he faints in Herbology, breaks teacups, is slow on a broom, forgets passwords — and Matthew Lewis plays the fearfulness with appropriate physical comedy. In Years 1–2, this is largely faithful. The boggart scene in Prisoner of Azkaban faithfully reproduces his fear of Snape and his dawning triumph over the wardrobe. In Deathly Hallows Part 2, the film delivers an authentic final Neville: gashed and battered but unbroken, with the 'it doesn't matter that Harry is gone' speech capturing his book voice reasonably well ('People die every day… They didn't die in vain'). However, several crucial aspects of the personality are thinned or lost in the middle films. The determined, self-asserting Neville of the common room scene (Years 1–6) who challenges authority when his moral code is crossed is only intermittently visible. The film does show him barring the portrait hole in Year 1 (via the Petrificus Totalus scene) but cuts the equivalent emotional work in later years: notably, the cut scene in which he defends Harry against Seamus removes a moment that shows proactive loyalty rather than reactive solidarity. His voice in Years 4–6 is reduced almost entirely to comic relief (fainting at Mandrakes, being seized by pixies, falling from the carriages in Goblet). The quiet, white-knuckled intensity that builds in OOTP after Bellatrix's escape — book-Neville barely speaking during DA sessions, simply working harder — is absent from the film, which provides no equivalent.
personality_voice.difference: The films preserve Neville's anxious, clumsy early persona and his triumphant late-series self largely intact. What is lost is the middle register: the Year 3–6 accumulation of small, specific assertions of will (the portrait-hole confrontation, the DA interior silence, the quiet pride in competence, the charged silence after St Mungo's). The film's Neville is more consistently comic and more consistently brave at the end, with less of the specific psychological texture — shame, suppressed anger, pride in small victories — that makes the character rich in the books. His voice in the films also loses the distinctive register of careful, slightly formal sentences when asserting himself ('You don't call me an idiot!') versus the inarticulate mumblings when he is distressed.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The character is recognisable and the arc endpoints are present, but important traits — the middle-period psychological complexity, the specific register shifts in voice, the accumulation of shame-and-pride moments — are reduced. This is not a wholesale alteration but a meaningful simplification. Score in the 14–17 range.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: Neville's narrative functions in the books are multiple and distinct. In Year 1, he is the moral counterweight — the friend who opposes Harry out of loyalty to Gryffindor and earns 10 points for it; he also initiates the confrontation at the portrait hole rather than being dragged into it. In Years 3–4, he is the key to the Gillyweed solution for the second task (Moody plants the book for him precisely because Neville is the one person guaranteed to give it to Harry) and is a barometer for the emotional cost of Voldemort's atrocities given what happened to his parents. In Order of the Phoenix, he is a co-leader of the DA with genuine teaching progress, and his agency reaches its peak in the Department of Mysteries, where he refuses to give Voldemort the prophecy even under Cruciatus torture ('DON'T GIVE IT TO HIM, HARRY!'), and physically rescues Harry from a Death Eater's chokehold by jabbing Hermione's wand through the mask. In Years 6–7, he becomes an active resistance leader within Hogwarts under the Carrows, organising the DA, taking physical punishment, and ultimately killing Nagini as the final Horcrux — a decision entrusted to him personally by Harry in the grounds. He is also, structurally, the prophetic alternate: the person Voldemort could have chosen instead of Harry, which gives him a unique thematic weight.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: The films retain Neville's Year 1 moral agency (the portrait hole confrontation, the 10 points), the boggart scene in Year 3, his presence in the Department of Mysteries, and his final-Horcrux killing of Nagini in Deathly Hallows Part 2. The speech he gives before the sword emergence is original to the film but broadly faithful in function. His role as a resistance leader in Year 7 is communicated through his battered appearance and his management of the Room of Requirement. However, several book-specific acts of agency are cut or transferred. The Gillyweed solution is transferred entirely to Dobby in the film of Goblet of Fire — Neville's role as the person Moody targeted precisely because of his connection to Harry is removed, eliminating a piece of plotting that rewards the character's relationships and competence. In the Department of Mysteries, Neville's specific acts of defiance under Cruciatus and his physical intervention to save Harry are not shown with equivalent weight in the film; the battle is compressed and chaotic and his individual moments of courage are harder to track. The OOTP cut scene removing his defence of Harry against Seamus — confirmed as a theatrical cut — also removes an act of proactive loyalty. The film also gives him little to no role in Years 5–6 outside of brief ensemble shots and comic beats.
narrative_role_agency.difference: Gillyweed transfer to Dobby is the most significant agency loss. Neville's specific combat agency in the DoM is partially preserved but reduced by the chaotic staging. The resistance-leader function in Year 7 is retained. The smaller acts of proactive loyalty (defending Harry against Seamus) are lost.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: One clear transfer (Gillyweed/Moody) penalised under the transfer rule. Role and agency are recognisable but clearly reduced in the middle films. Score in the 10–13 range.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Neville's motivations are unusually specific in the books. His early fear and passivity stem from two sources: genuine anxiety about magic (he was thought to be a Squib and had magic forced out of him by near-death experiences as a child) and the pressure of his grandmother's impossible comparison to his parents. These are not vague; Great Uncle Algie pushing him off a pier, the constant measure against Frank and Alice, Gran's letters demanding he uphold the family honour — all are established clearly. His deepest wound is the parents' situation: he visits them, keeps Alice's Drooble's wrappers, cannot bear to discuss them but cannot pretend they are fine. The revelation of his parents' fate and the escape of Bellatrix in Year 5 transforms his motivation from passive endurance to active resistance without any external push — it is entirely internal, making him work harder in DA silently. His conflict in Year 7 is between personal safety (the Carrows will kill him) and duty to Hogwarts: he chooses duty while acknowledging the reality ('I don't know whether they were planning to kill me or send me to Azkaban'). His pride is also a motivation — he works for the one area (Herbology) where he genuinely excels, and Moody's strategic compliment matters to him precisely because genuine praise is so rare.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The films preserve the grandmother-as-pressure figure (her letter praising him in Year 7 is referenced), the visit to his parents in OOTP (briefly glimpsed but present), and his resistance under the Carrows. However, the specific causal chain of his motivation — the childhood trauma with Great Uncle Algie, the Squib fear, the exact nature of his pride wound — is almost entirely absent from the films. The emotional logic of why a boy who nearly drowned as a child, was repeatedly told he had no magical ability, and grew up in the shadow of parents who cannot recognise him behaves with such a specific mixture of shame and surging courage is not communicated. The St Mungo's scene exists in the film (OOTP) but is compressed: we see Neville's mother, the wrapper, Neville's defiant expression, but the private complexity — that he has never told his Hogwarts friends about his parents, that this is his most guarded secret, that his grandmother's public correction humiliates him even as it speaks some truth — is reduced to a single beat rather than a sustained portrait. The motivation shift after Bellatrix's escape (Year 5 DA sessions) is entirely absent from the film, which shows nothing of his interior response to the escape.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The broad motivations are present (fear of inadequacy, loyalty to Hogwarts, parental shadow) but the specific causal texture is thinned. The critical interior shift after Bellatrix's escape is absent. The childhood backstory is not established.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: Motivations are simplified but still broadly correct. Not wholly replaced or wrong, but the specific emotional architecture that makes them coherent in the books is underexplained. Score in the 8–10 range.

character_arc.book_baseline: Neville's arc is one of the most clearly structured in the series. Starting point: a boy who is so afraid of his own magical inadequacy that he cannot mount a broom, who loses passwords, who melts cauldrons, who is publicly shamed by Snape without defence. Key turning points: (1) Year 1 end — earns ten points for standing up to his friends, recognised publicly as brave; (2) Year 3 boggart — defeats his greatest fear with help and is publicly validated by Lupin; (3) Year 4 Cruciatus scene — understands viscerally what happened to his parents for the first time in a classroom setting, leading directly to the St Mungo's revelation; (4) Year 5 — learns his parents' attackers have escaped, transforms silently into the hardest worker in the DA, fights in the DoM with broken nose and broken wand; (5) Year 7 — leads the Hogwarts resistance, refuses to submit under the Carrows, kills Nagini. The endpoint: he is named Herbology professor (epilogue), becoming the teacher who validates students' competence the way Moody and Lupin once validated his. The arc is not accelerated — each book adds a specific new layer — and the final steps depend on the earlier ones.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The arc's endpoints are preserved: the Year 1 ten-points moment and the Year 7 Nagini killing are both in the film, and the film Neville communicates the transformation convincingly at those points. The boggart scene is present and faithful. The DoM participation is present. However, several key turning points are either absent or underweighted. The Year 4 Cruciatus classroom revelation (Neville's white-knuckled reaction when Moody demonstrates the curse, his subsequent visit to Moody's office, his red eyes in the dormitory) is compressed: the film shows his reaction during the lesson but cuts the aftermath entirely, losing the explicit connection between the lesson and his parents. The St Mungo's scene in Year 5 is present but the interiority — Harry noticing Neville pocketing the wrapper, Harry's reflection on never having asked about Neville's parents in four years — is absent. Most significantly, the interior transformation in Year 5 after Bellatrix's escape, where Neville becomes the DA's hardest worker, is invisible in the film. Year 6 Neville is almost entirely absent from the films. The arc is therefore compressed rather than sequential: the film takes Neville from frightened Year 1 boy to resistant Year 7 leader without showing most of the steps in between.
character_arc.difference: Arc is present at both ends and at the Year 3 midpoint. Years 4–6 turning points (Cruciatus reaction, St Mungo's interiority, Bellatrix-escape transformation, Year 6 absence) are missing or reduced, making the arc feel less earned in the films.
character_arc.penalty_logic: Arc is compressed and missing important middle steps, but it is not false or opposite. The film communicates the transformation, just without the intermediate scaffolding. Score in the 11–13 range.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Neville's most defining relationships are: (1) with Harry — a friendship based on Harry's repeated specific kindnesses (the Chocolate Frog after the Leg-Locker Curse, 'you're worth twelve of Malfoys', the Dumbledore password conversation, the secret kept about his parents), which is mutual and generates real trust; (2) with his grandmother — a cold, demanding relationship in which praise is always comparative and inadequacy always implied, yet Gran's final letter praising him is one of the most important validations of his arc; (3) with Professor Snape — a relationship of pure terror and sustained public humiliation that is one of the most specific bully–victim dynamics in the series; (4) with the DA collectively — Neville rises to co-leadership in Year 7 partly because of what the DA meant to him in Year 5 ('I liked the DA! I learned loads with you!'); (5) with Hermione — she helps him frequently in Potions and is the one who performs the Body-Bind on him (apologetically), a small but telling moment of their dynamic.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The Harry–Neville friendship is the most visible in the films: the Year 1 ten-points moment, the Petrificus Totalus scene, the Deathly Hallows reunion. But the specific texture of Harry's private kindnesses — the chocolate frog, the 'worth twelve of Malfoys', the secret-keeping — is absent, so the friendship reads as broad ensemble solidarity rather than a specific bond. The Snape–Neville dynamic is present in Years 1 and 3 but largely disappears in Years 4–6 when Snape's sustained bullying of Neville is a recurring motif in the books. Gran is mentioned in Year 7 (Neville's pride at her letter) but her complex dynamic with him — the cold pressure, the inadequacy comparison — is not developed. The Hermione–Neville relationship (her helping him in Potions, the apology before the Body-Bind) is present but thin. The DA relationship is established in OOTP and briefly revisited in Deathly Hallows Part 2.
key_relationships.difference: The Harry–Neville friendship is reduced from specific mutual kindness to ensemble solidarity. The Snape relationship loses most of its Year 4–6 intensity. The Gran relationship is sketched. These losses change the emotional texture of Neville's characterisation, particularly the source of his shame and the meaning of his courage.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: Important relationship dynamics — Snape's sustained bullying as a source of Neville's specific shame, the specificity of Harry's private support — are weakened. Score in the 5–6 range.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: The books build Neville's complexity through repeated small scenes: the Remembrall as a portrait of forgetfulness and anxiety; the Chocolate Frog moment as a portrait of Harry's specific decency; the Leg-Locker Curse as a portrait of the cost of passive victimhood; the dream in which Harry imagines Ron using 'Neville' for the Quidditch team (trivial but revealing of how Neville is perceived); the detail that Neville asked Hermione to the Yule Ball (she kindly declined); his choice of Mimbulus mimbletonia as his pet plant — an ugly, underestimated thing with a powerful defensive mechanism, essentially a self-portrait; the keeping of Alice's sweet wrappers; his DA work as the one place he has no fear; his admission 'I'm not an idiot' (to Malfoy's taunt). The parents' situation is the richest seam of complexity: not a backstory but an active, present wound that Neville manages quietly and which Harry specifically promises to keep secret. The scene in St Mungo's — Neville's defiant expression when others see his parents, the wrapper pocketed quietly — is one of the most emotionally precise scenes in the series.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The Mimbulus mimbletonia is present in OOTP (brief train scene). The St Mungo's scene is present in the film of OOTP but reduced: the wrapper moment is visible but the full emotional complexity — Mrs Longbottom's public correction, Ron's embarrassed question, Harry's private resolution to keep the secret — is compressed. The Yule Ball subplot (Neville asking Hermione, taking Ginny instead, their stumbling dance) is retained in Goblet. The DA sessions as a space of competence and confidence are present. The sweet-wrapper detail is present. However, much of the specific texture is absent: the Leg-Locker Curse scene (Year 1 common room), which shows both Harry's private decency and Neville's shame, is cut from the film (only the Body-Bind survival scene remains). The Year 5 dormitory scene in which Neville's plant is lovingly placed on his bedside table while the others argue — a small but defining image of his interiority — is cut. The sustained Year 5 DA transformation (working harder than everyone, Patronus struggles, Shield Charm mastery) is described but not shown. The specific detail that Gran failed her Charms OWL and thus dismisses Charms as soft — and McGonagall's pointed letter to her — is absent. The prophetic alternate dimension (Dumbledore telling Harry that the prophecy could have referred to Neville) is entirely absent from the film of OOTP, removing a layer of thematic weight.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: Key complexity-building material lost: the prophetic alternate (OOTP), the Year 5 interior transformation, the sustained Snape bullying dynamic, the full St Mungo's complexity, the Leg-Locker/Harry kindness sequence, the McGonagall–Gran exchange, the specific self-portrait quality of the Mimbulus mimbletonia. What remains is the surface pattern of the character without much of the material that makes him feel textured and specific.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: The character is not flattened to one trait — he retains anxiety and courage — but much of what makes him rich and specific in the books is absent. This is a noticeable simplification, not a wholesale flattening. Score in the 8–10 range.

Year 1 Leg-Locker Curse scene and Harry's private kindness ('you're worth twelve of Malfoys') absent from films

comparative.key_observations: The films deliver a recognisable Neville Longbottom with intact arc endpoints — the frightened first-year earning ten points and the battered Year 7 resistance leader killing Nagini — and preserve some of the most distinctive individual scenes (boggart, St Mungo's, portrait-hole confrontation). The performance and broad emotional signature are faithful. However, the adaptation systematically removes or compresses the middle layers that make the books' Neville unusually rich: the specific psychological texture of shame rooted in his childhood and his parents' fate, the interior transformation after Bellatrix's escape, the sustained Snape bullying as a source of defined wound, the prophetic alternate dimension, and the small specific acts of private kindness (the chocolate frog, the secret-keeping) that define his friendship with Harry. The Gillyweed transfer to Dobby is the most concrete agency loss. The result is a Neville who is broadly correct but significantly simpler than the book version — courageous at both ends, anxious in the middle, but without much of the interior life that earns his transformation.
