personality_voice.book_baseline: Karkaroff in the books is defined by a layered, contradictory personality built from observable patterns across many scenes. His dominant register is unctuous flattery — 'How are you, my dear fellow' (Scene 4), his 'fruity, unctuous voice' (Scene 5) — but this surface warmth is consistently undercut by cold eyes that 'did not extend to his smile' (Scene 7) and 'remained cold and shrewd.' He is selectively warm: fawning over Viktor with offers of mulled wine, then snapping viciously at Poliakoff in the same breath — 'I wasn't offering it to you, Poliakoff... disgusting boy' (Scene 21). His voice shifts register depending on audience: unctuous with Dumbledore and judges ('you are our objective judges,' Scene 50), cold and steely when threatened ('his steely smile... his blue eyes were like chips of ice,' Scene 43), explosive when cornered ('in which Durmstrang will most certainly not be competing!' Scene 57), and barely controlled when frightened — his hands 'had balled themselves into fists' despite his attempt to sound disdainful (Scene 61). At his trial, even chained and terrified, the 'familiar unctuous note' in his voice persists (Scene 214). He is petty (twirling his goatee for photographs, Scene 84), vindictive (giving Harry a 4 during the first task, Scene 119), and capable of real cowardice — he fleeing at the end without a word. His speech patterns include rhetorical flourish ('Are we not right to be proud...,' Scene 131), abrupt hostility, and anxious repetition ('I have more!... No, no, no,' trial scenes). He is not a simple villain but a self-serving opportunist whose fear drives every action.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The film preserves several surface elements of Karkaroff's personality: the unctuous greeting to Dumbledore ('Albus' / 'Igor'), the cold competitive edge in the champions' chamber ('You seem to have given this a fair bit of thought, Mad-Eye,' Film Scene 4), the booming public support for Krum ('Come on! Krum! Krum! Krum!' Film Scene 8), and the trial scenes where the unctuous, desperate quality — 'No, no, no... I have more!' — is directly rendered (Film Scene 6). The selective favouritism toward Krum is visible in the arrival scene. His cowardice and fear are implied by Sirius's warning ('no one stops being a Death Eater,' Film Scene 5) and Moody's later confirmation of his flight (referenced in passing). However, the film loses his most revealing personality moments: the vicious snap at Poliakoff (cut — this scene is absent from film corpus), the moment his fists betray his fear during the Moody confrontation (no equivalent in film), the goatee-twirling nervous habit observed multiple times, his livid explosion at Krum's attack ('Treachery! It is a plot!'), his spitting at Dumbledore's feet, and his sustained rhetorical self-justification in the Yule Ball gardens scene (cut as non-theatrical). The film reduces him to two modes — cold competitor and desperate informant — without the texture of his cowardly self-preservation instinct expressed through small observable behaviors.
personality_voice.difference: The unctuous-yet-cold duality is partially preserved in the trial and champions' chamber. But the film removes: (1) the snap at Poliakoff showing his selective cruelty; (2) the physically observable signs of concealed fear (balled fists, burning face); (3) the rhetorical self-aggrandizement at the Yule Ball (non-theatrical); (4) the spectacular explosion and spitting at Dumbledore after Krum is attacked; (5) the nervous goatee-twirling as a repeated behavioral tell. The film Karkaroff is recognizable but stripped of the contradictory micro-behaviors that give him his book texture.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The character remains recognizable — unctuous, cold, competitive, cowardly — so no severe penalty applies. But several important behavioral patterns and contradictions (the Poliakoff snap, the physical fear tells, the Krum-attack explosion) are absent, and the voice is simplified to two modes rather than the multi-register book version. This warrants a score in the 14–17 range: recognizable but with reduced contradictions and tonal range.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: Karkaroff serves multiple active narrative functions in the books. (1) He is an active threat and suspect: Harry and Sirius spend significant time assessing whether he put Harry's name in the goblet; he spies on the first task in the forest at night (Scene 88–90); he gives Harry a biased score of 4 in the first task (Scene 119); he is the only judge not showing relief after Harry's second-task success (Scene 154). (2) He is the primary vehicle through which Voldemort's returning power is first concretely signaled to the reader: he shows Snape his darkening Dark Mark in Potions class (Scenes 170–178), and Snape's pensieve memory confirms both their Marks are burning (Scene 283). This moment is a key plot-and-thematic beat — the first physical proof of Voldemort's return visible to characters other than Harry. (3) He confronts and threatens in the champions' chamber (Scene 43–57), filing formal protests and demanding the goblet be reset. (4) His trial in the pensieve is a major exposition scene that reveals the Death Eater network and introduces Barty Crouch Jr. (5) His flight confirms Voldemort's return to the reader and to the characters at the end of Book 4. (6) He is used by Dumbledore in HBP (Scene 283–286) as a foil for Snape's courage.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: The film preserves: the champions' chamber protest (reduced in force); the trial scene which retains his informant role and his naming of Barty Crouch Jr. (a key plot function); his arrival and competitive presence; Sirius's warning about him as a Death Eater (Film Scene 5); the brief Snape corridor scene (Film Scene 7, though the arm-showing is off-screen and the scene is minimal). The film loses: his active nighttime spying on the first task (absent from film corpus); his biased score of 4 in the first task (absent — no scoring tableau shown in film); his pointed refusal to look relieved after the second task (absent); the full Potions classroom scene where he hovers for a double period, deliberately prevents Snape from leaving, and explicitly shows the Dark Mark (cut as non-theatrical). His flight is mentioned by Moody in the book denouement but is not dramatized or specifically confirmed in the theatrical film. His role as the primary signal of Voldemort's return through the Dark Mark is transferred or collapsed: the film's corridor scene (Film Scene 7) shows him opening his sleeve briefly but this is handled without the extended tension or Harry's active eavesdropping that makes it structurally meaningful.
narrative_role_agency.difference: The spying on the first task (active agency) is removed. The biased first-task score (active antagonism/agency) is removed. The extended Potions classroom scene where Karkaroff actively pursues Snape and demonstrates the Mark is non-theatrical (cut). His role as the primary in-story signal of Voldemort's return through the Dark Mark is substantially reduced. The trial scene retains his informant agency and the Barty Jr. reveal. The champions' chamber protest is retained but compressed. Overall, his active antagonist and plot-driver functions are significantly curtailed.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: Several of Karkaroff's active narrative functions — spying, biased scoring, the sustained Snape pursuit in Potions, the Mark revelation as a structural plot beat — are removed or heavily reduced. The trial scene retains meaningful agency (naming Barty Jr. is structurally important). His role as a suspect/threat is conveyed mainly through Sirius's dialogue rather than through his own actions. This is a clear reduction of both role and agency, warranting a score of 10–13.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Karkaroff's motivations are unusually consistent and clear across all his appearances: self-preservation above all else. Every action traces back to this. He named Death Eaters in court to escape Azkaban, calculating which names had already been caught (his visible panic when Dolohov and Rosier are already apprehended, Scenes 233–239). He competes viciously in the Tournament to win prestige and beat Dumbledore, feeding Viktor information about the first task (Scene 116). He gives Harry a 4 to damage his standing. He pursues Snape anxiously because he needs reassurance about the Dark Mark — he is afraid of what its darkening means, and specifically afraid of retribution from Voldemort if he returns (Scenes 140, 163–178, 283). His internal conflict is between his desire to appear loyal/respectable (as Durmstrang headmaster, as someone who 'turned his life around') and his deep cowardice and self-interest. When the Mark burns, he flees — consistent with every prior choice. He has no genuine moral conviction; his 'remorse' at the trial is performative and calculated.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The trial scene preserves his core motivation well: the desperation to escape Azkaban, the calculating way he offers names, the visible panic when his names are already known ('Dead?! I didn't know'), and the shift to naming Barty Jr. as a last resort are all present in Film Scene 6. Sirius's line in Film Scene 5 — 'no one stops being a Death Eater' — frames his motivation as ongoing self-interest rather than genuine reform. The corridor scene (Film Scene 7) shows him anxious and consulting Snape, preserving the fear-of-retribution motivation. However, the film does not develop his calculated self-interest across multiple scenes the way the books do — the biased scoring, the nighttime spying, the sustained pursuit of Snape in Potions. The motivation is present but underexplained across the narrative, relying heavily on a single Sirius exposition line.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The core motivation (self-preservation, fear of Voldemort's return) is present and correctly rendered in both the trial and the corridor scene. The film compresses rather than changes his motivations. The main loss is that the film does not dramatize his motivation playing out in active choices across multiple scenes — it tells rather than shows.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: Motivations are simplified and underexplained but not fundamentally changed. The self-preservation drive is intact and observable in the trial scene and in Sirius's framing. Compression is the main issue, not alteration. This falls in the 8–10 range: partially altered through flattening, not through distortion.

character_arc.book_baseline: Karkaroff's arc in GoF is a complete, internally logical coward's trajectory: (1) Arrival — performatively warm, competitive, calculating; (2) Escalating anxiety — the Dark Mark darkens, he pursues Snape obsessively, his fear grows visibly through the year; (3) Explosion — he accuses Dumbledore of treachery after Krum is attacked, spits at Dumbledore's feet; (4) Flight — he abandons his school and his champion the night Voldemort returns; (5) Death — confirmed in HBP, killed by Voldemort within a year. This arc is also retroactively illuminated by the pensieve trial: we see who he was before Azkaban (ruthless, calculating, self-serving under the Death Eaters), which makes his later anxious self-preservation legible as continuous character. Dumbledore's contrast in HBP ('You are a braver man by far than Igor Karkaroff,' Scene 286) serves as a retrospective capstone, using his arc to define Snape's courage by contrast. The arc is not one of redemption or growth — it is a sustained, revealed cowardice.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The film captures the beginning (competitive arrival, unctuous warmth) and the trial-era Karkaroff (calculating informant). The escalating anxiety arc during the year — the sustained Snape pursuit, the Potions classroom confrontation — is lost because that scene is non-theatrical. The explosion at Krum's attack ('Treachery! It is a plot!') and the spitting at Dumbledore are absent from the film corpus. His flight is confirmed verbally by Moody in the book denouement but the film's equivalent confirmation is not clearly present in the theatrical film corpus provided. The HBP contrast with Snape (Scene 283–286) has no film equivalent — this entire scene is absent from the film corpus. The arc's middle and end sections — the visible disintegration of composure through fear, the explosion, the flight, the death — are largely absent or unconfirmed.
character_arc.difference: The film has the arc's starting point (arrival, calculated warmth) and one major early beat (the trial). The escalating fear across the year, the explosion/breakdown, the flight, and the retrospective capstone in HBP are all absent or unconfirmed. The arc is present only in its first quarter.
character_arc.penalty_logic: This is more than compression — the arc's turning points (anxiety-to-explosion-to-flight) are missing, not just shortened. The audience cannot track his disintegration across the year. The HBP retrospective is entirely absent. This warrants a score of 8–10: arc is incomplete and missing important steps.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Karkaroff has two defining relationships in the books. (1) Karkaroff and Snape: This is the most important relationship for his characterization. They share a past as Death Eaters; Karkaroff tried to name Snape at his trial (Scene 250). During GoF, Karkaroff seeks Snape out anxiously, needing reassurance, treating Snape as his only peer who understands his fear. Snape is contemptuous and avoidant — 'Then flee. I will make your excuses. I, however, am remaining at Hogwarts' (Scene 141). The dynamic is one of Karkaroff's desperate dependence versus Snape's cold superiority. This relationship reveals Karkaroff's cowardice (he needs someone else to tell him what to do) and Snape's courage by contrast. (2) Karkaroff and Krum: Selectively paternal — fawning over Krum as his asset while being contemptuous of other Durmstrang students. Karkaroff uses Krum instrumentally (he told him about the first task; his only visible emotional investment in the Tournament is through Krum). (3) Karkaroff and Dumbledore: Performative warmth masking deep rivalry and resentment — 'we are all protective of our private domains' (Scene 131). Karkaroff blames Dumbledore bitterly when things go wrong.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The Karkaroff-Snape relationship in the film is reduced to a single brief corridor scene (Film Scene 7) where Karkaroff opens his sleeve and the two exchange a few words before Snape sees Harry and ends the scene. The anxious dependence, Snape's contemptuous 'Then flee,' and the sustained pursuit during Potions are all absent (the latter is non-theatrical). The Karkaroff-Krum relationship is shown only through surface moments: arrival together, Karkaroff cheering for Krum in the maze. The instrumental paternal quality exists but is not developed. The Karkaroff-Dumbledore relationship retains surface competitive tension in the champions' chamber but loses the Yule Ball conversational duel about secrets (non-theatrical) and the spitting incident.
key_relationships.difference: The Karkaroff-Snape relationship — the most characterization-rich relationship in the book — is reduced from a sustained, dramatically developed dynamic to a single wordless beat. The anxious-dependence/cold-contempt dynamic is not conveyed. Snape's defining 'I am not such a coward' line, which uses Karkaroff as a foil, is absent from the film (no HBP equivalent in corpus). The Krum relationship exists in outline only. The Dumbledore relationship loses its most revealing moments.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: The Karkaroff-Snape dynamic is central to understanding both characters and is largely lost. The film audience cannot perceive Karkaroff's anxious dependence on Snape or the power imbalance that reveals his cowardice most clearly. This is a significant loss — it changes how the character is understood — warranting a score of 5–6.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: Karkaroff in the books is a richly contradictory figure whose complexity operates on several levels: (1) The unctuous-yet-cruel contradiction, visible in the same scene (warm to Krum, vicious to Poliakoff); (2) The calculating coward who is still capable of genuine rage and explosion (the Krum attack scene); (3) The informant who tried to betray Snape in court but now desperately seeks his help — a relationship built on shared guilt and mutual calculation; (4) The performative reformer whose 'remorse so deep I can barely' is immediately undercut by his visible relief when his most useful names prove known; (5) The repeated behavioral tells — goatee-twirling as a nervous habit, fists balling under pressure — that give him physical specificity; (6) His function as thematic mirror: he represents the coward's path, against which Snape's choice to stay is measured (HBP). All of this creates a character who is petty, frightened, occasionally impressive in his cunning, and pathetic in his final flight.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The film retains: the trial-scene desperation and calculating quality, the competitive cold presence in the champions' chamber, the surface unctuous warmth at arrival. It loses: the Poliakoff snap (selective cruelty), the goatee-twirling nervous habit, the physical fear tells (balled fists), the sustained Snape-pursuit anxiety (non-theatrical), the Krum-attack explosion and spitting, the Yule Ball conversational duel (non-theatrical), the HBP retrospective function, and the full arc of disintegration. The film Karkaroff is recognizable but has been reduced primarily to 'cold competitor' and 'desperate informant' — two of his facets, without the contradictions between them.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: Substantial. The contradictions that make him complex — warm/cruel, calculating/panicking, self-serving reformer/genuine coward — are only partially visible in the film. The material that would show his complexity across the Tournament year (the sustained anxiety, the explosion, the physical tells) is mostly absent. His thematic function as coward-foil to Snape is entirely absent.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: The film preserves enough that he is not reduced to a single function, but the nuance, contradictions, and book-specific texture that make him more than a cold antagonist are largely gone. The absent material substantially changes the depth of the portrayal. Score in the 5–7 range: major flattening, character reduced to simpler functions.

lost_or_transferred_material: Karkaroff snapping at Poliakoff ('I wasn't offering it to you, Poliakoff... disgusting boy') — reveals selective cruelty and the unctuous/vicious contradiction; absent from film
Karkaroff spying on the first task in the forest at night — active agency as antagonist; absent from film
Karkaroff giving Harry a biased score of 4 in the first task — active antagonism; absent from film
Karkaroff as the only judge showing no relief after Harry's second-task success — subtle behavioral characterization; absent from film

Extended Potions classroom scene: Karkaroff hovers for a double period, explicitly shows Snape the darkening Dark Mark on his arm — primary in-story signal of Voldemort's return and key characterization of Snape-Karkaroff dynamic; cut as non-theatrical
Snape and Karkaroff argue in the Yule Ball gardens: Snape tells him to flee, Snape stays — key dynamic establishing Karkaroff's cowardice and Snape's courage by contrast; cut as non-theatrical
Karkaroff's explosion after Krum is attacked ('Treachery! It is a plot!') and spitting at Dumbledore's feet — key dramatic breakdown moment; absent from film
Karkaroff's flight confirmed and dramatized at end of GoF — arc endpoint; absent or unconfirmed in theatrical film
HBP Dumbledore-Snape scene using Karkaroff's desertion as a foil for Snape's courage ('You are a braver man by far than Igor Karkaroff') — retrospective thematic function; absent from film
Karkaroff's death reported in HBP ('found Igor Karkaroff's body in a shack up north') — arc completion; absent from film corpus
Repeated goatee-twirling nervous habit as physical behavioral tell — character texture; absent from film
Karkaroff's physically betrayed fear (hands balling into fists) during Moody confrontation — observable cowardice signal; absent from film
Karkaroff's sustained Yule Ball conversational duel with Dumbledore about school secrecy — relationship texture; cut as non-theatrical
score_caps_applied: Cap 3 (≤75): A core book function — the Dark Mark revelation scene in Potions, which is the primary in-story signal of Voldemort's return and the key beat of the Snape-Karkaroff dynamic — is absent (non-theatrical cut). This constitutes a transferred/lost structural beat of agency and function.

Cap 1 (≤85): The film removes major portions of Karkaroff's complexity, the sustained anxiety arc, key relationship dynamics, and the HBP thematic function. Even if remaining material were faithful, the overall cap applies.

Cap 5 (≤60): Karkaroff's arc and motivations are significantly underexplained across the film — the audience cannot track his disintegration through the year or understand his flight without the Potions and Yule Ball scenes. This cap is the binding constraint on the final score.
comparative.key_observations: The film's Karkaroff is a partial portrait: the trial scene is well-rendered and preserves his calculating desperation and the Barty Jr. revelation, and the champions' chamber protest retains his cold competitive quality. However, the theatrical cut loses or removes almost everything that happens between his arrival and the third task — the sustained anxiety arc, the defining Snape-Karkaroff dynamic in the Potions classroom, the Yule Ball argument, the biased scoring, the nighttime spying, and the explosion after Krum's attack. What remains is recognizable but thin: two facets (cold competitor, desperate informant) without the contradictions, behavioral texture, physical tells, or relational complexity that make him a rounded figure in the books. His most important narrative function — as the first in-story witness to Voldemort's Mark darkening, and as a cowardice-foil for Snape — is either cut or collapsed to a single brief shot. The score cap at 60 applies because his arc and motivations cannot be understood from the theatrical film alone, and Cap 3 applies because his primary agency beat (the Mark revelation) was transferred to a non-theatrical scene and is absent from the final film.

personality_voice.book_baseline: Petunia in the books is defined by a cluster of tightly interlocked traits: a ferocious desire for normalcy and respectability, obsessive domesticity (surgically clean kitchen, pride in her home), nosy surveillance of neighbors, sharp-tongued snappishness especially toward Harry, performative maternal gushing over Dudley, and a pattern of curt, dismissive, monosyllabic hostility when anything magical arises ('No,' 'So?', 'I suppose so,' 'Harry. Nasty, common name, if you ask me'). Her voice is characterized by pursed-lip iciness, brief declarative dismissals, and sudden shrieking alarm at any magical intrusion. Crucially, the books also reveal a deeply suppressed emotional interior: a longing she never acknowledges (she lingered on the flower closing its petals, she begged Dumbledore in a letter to let her into Hogwarts), resentment at being overshadowed by Lily, and a hidden but significant awareness of the wizarding world that she performs ignorance about. Her outburst at Hagrid ('Knew! Of course we knew!') is the books' single most revealing moment of her voice: it 'seemed she had been wanting to say all this for years,' combining bitterness, resentment, and barely contained grief. In OotP, her reaction to the Howler — trembling, near-fainting, obeying without explanation — and her startling knowledge of Dementors reveal a woman with an entire suppressed history.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The films preserve Petunia's surface traits clearly: the shrieking alarm at magical intrusions (zoo enclosure: 'My darling boy! How did you get in there?!'; letters chaos: screaming throughout Film 1; Weasley fireplace: shrieking and hiding behind Vernon; Dobby's pudding scene), the snappish commands to Harry ('Up! Get up! Now!'; 'Why don't you just cook the breakfast, and try not to burn anything'; 'Not yet, popkin'), the performative gushing over Dudley ('I want everything to be perfect for my Dudley's special day'), and the domestic competitiveness (the pudding masterpiece, the gleaming kitchen). The Hagrid reveal scene (Film 1) preserves her iconic outburst almost verbatim, including 'A freak! And then she met that Potter...' The PoA film retains her agitated one-word response about James ('Nothing. That is... he didn't work. He was — unemployed') which is faithful in tone. However, several important voice elements are absent or diluted: her nosy surveillance of neighbors is referenced obliquely but never dramatized with the book's specificity; her pursed-lip tea-sipping iciness and the pattern of deliberate monosyllabic deflection are present but compressed; and most significantly, the suppressed longing and emotional complexity underlying her hostility — the trembling with the Howler, the moment Harry perceives she is genuinely afraid of Voldemort, her eyes 'wide and fearful' for the first time — is entirely absent from the films.
personality_voice.difference: The films capture Petunia's dominant surface traits (snappishness, domestic obsession, shrieking alarm, Dudley-worship) but lose the emotional depth beneath them. The books' Petunia has a buried interior life — suppressed longing for magic, genuine fear of Voldemort, long-held grief about Lily — that occasionally breaks through and gives her voice a complexity and even pathos the films never render. The 'Knew! Of course we knew!' speech is preserved but stripped of its narrative framing ('she had been wanting to say this for years'). The OotP Howler sequence, her knowledge of Dementors, and the extraordinary moment where Harry sees her as his mother's sister for the first time are entirely cut, removing the most emotionally layered version of her voice. What remains is the hostile surface without the suppressed depth.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The dominant traits are preserved and recognizable, placing this solidly in the 14–17 range. The shrieking, the snappishness, the Dudley-gushing, and the hostility toward magic are all directly evidenced in the films. However, important secondary traits — the suppressed longing, the hidden awareness of the wizarding world, the rare moments of genuine fear and almost-grief — are absent. These are not minor ornaments; they are what makes Petunia a character with interiority rather than a flat antagonist. The loss of the Howler scene, the Dementor knowledge scene, and the OotP emotional revelation all remove material that distinguishes the book Petunia from a simple caricature. Score: 17.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: Petunia's narrative functions in the books are multiple and structurally significant. (1) She is Harry's primary domestic oppressor in his home life, consistently establishing the texture of his deprivation. (2) She is the active gatekeeper of magical knowledge: she shreds the Hogwarts letters (in the food processor), she enforces the household's denial of magic, she answers Vernon's questions about the Dursleys' decision-making. (3) In OotP, she becomes a pivotal plot agent: she alone causes Harry to stay at Privet Drive by choosing to obey the Howler, a decision that is entirely hers and that Harry (and the reader) cannot initially explain. This is an act of independent agency with major plot consequences — Harry's protection depends on it. (4) She is the keeper of a secret (Dumbledore's first Howler to her, 'Remember my last, Petunia') that is only revealed in DH, making her a holder of narrative information across the entire series. (5) In DH, the farewell scene gives her a moment of withheld emotion — she almost says something to Harry, then doesn't — that functions as a final closure beat for her arc. She also plays a reactive but present role in nearly every Privet Drive scene, often making small decisions (agreeing to take Harry to the zoo, deciding how to handle the letters, preparing the house for Vernon's dinner party).
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: In the films, Petunia retains her presence in most Privet Drive scenes but her agency is substantially reduced. She participates in the chaos of letters (Film 1, shredding is omitted — this is given to Vernon who burns them and boards up the mail slot), she appears at the zoo and the hut, she is present during Hagrid's visit. In Film 2, the Dobby/pudding scene retains her chasing the Masons outside and offering 'We have ice cream...' — a small but present action. In Film 3, her one line about James ('Nothing. That is... he didn't work') is retained. However, the entire OotP Howler sequence is cut, removing her single most consequential independent act in the series: the decision to let Harry stay. In Film 5, she appears briefly at the departure scene and at the station with the Order members, but the Howler, the Dementor knowledge revelation, and the decision to keep Harry are entirely absent from the theatrical film. In Film 7, she is given a wordless almost-moment ('Ready, Dudders?') but the near-farewell to Harry — her lingering look, her almost-spoken words — is reduced to a single silent exit.
narrative_role_agency.difference: The OotP Howler sequence is the most significant loss. In the books, Petunia actively decides to keep Harry — she overrides Vernon, she explains herself (badly, with a cover story about neighbors), and the decision is unambiguously hers. The film removes this entirely, meaning her most consequential act of independent agency across the entire series disappears. The letter-shredding is transferred to Vernon (burning rather than Petunia's food processor). Her role as a pivot point in Harry's protection is erased. What remains is a reactive presence rather than an occasionally decisive agent.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: Petunia retains a role and presence across the films, but her most significant act of agency (the Howler decision in OotP) is entirely cut. The transfer of the letter-destruction to Vernon (though minor) further diminishes her as an independent actor. Her narrative function as domestic oppressor and keeper of the household's magical denial is preserved, but her function as plot agent (the protection decision) and as keeper of secret knowledge (the Howler's content, Dumbledore's prior communication) is lost. Per the agency rule and transfer rule, this requires a clear penalty. Score: 12.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Petunia's motivations in the books are layered and, crucially, internally contradictory. The surface motivation is clear: maintain normalcy, protect the Dursley family's reputation, suppress all evidence of magic. But beneath this, the books reveal a much more complex picture: Petunia wanted magic herself. She begged Dumbledore to let her attend Hogwarts (Lily exposes this on Platform 9¾). She resented being 'ordinary' when her sister was special — and this resentment curdled into a defensive contempt for everything magical. Her suppression of magic is not simply bigotry but a wound: she was excluded, she was made to feel lesser, and her hostility to Harry is in part displaced grief and unresolved jealousy toward Lily. The OotP scenes make explicit that she has never stopped knowing about the magical world, that she retained a Dementor explanation Snape gave Lily years ago, and that she genuinely fears Voldemort. Her decision to keep Harry is also motivated (implicitly) by the old bargain she made when she took Harry in — she knows more than she admits. In DH, her near-goodbye to Harry hints at unresolved feeling she cannot bring herself to express.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The films present Petunia's surface motivation — protect normalcy, suppress Harry — clearly and repeatedly. In Film 1, 'We had to say something' (about the car crash lie) is present, and her Hagrid outburst preserves some of the resentment toward Lily. Film 3 retains a trace of her agitation about James. However, the films entirely omit the motivation layer that makes her interesting: her suppressed desire for magic, her written plea to Dumbledore, her retained knowledge of Dementors, the implicit bargain with Dumbledore underlying her decision to keep Harry, and the fear of Voldemort that briefly surfaces in OotP. Her internal conflict — hostility toward magic that is partly wish-fulfillment in reverse — is not visible in the films. She reads as someone who simply dislikes magic and resents Harry, rather than someone who wanted what Lily had and couldn't have it.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The surface motivation (protect normalcy, dislike magic) is preserved. The deeper motivation (suppressed longing, displaced jealousy, unresolved grief, the implicit bargain with Dumbledore) is absent. The films do not show us the Petunia who begged to go to Hogwarts, who retained Dementor knowledge from eavesdropping on Lily and Snape, or who felt something close to grief when she said 'She went and got herself blown up.' These are motivational layers that the films flatten into simple hostility.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: The surface motivation is present but the internal conflict and the deeper motivation are substantially absent. This is not a case of 'poorly explained but still the same' — the motivational complexity is genuinely different. The book Petunia is motivated by wounded exclusion and suppressed longing as much as by contempt; the film Petunia is motivated primarily by contempt and a desire for normalcy. This is a meaningful simplification that changes how her hostility toward Harry reads. Score: 9.
motivations_internal_conflict.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for surface motivation; reasonably inferred for the absence of deeper layers based on what is not present in the film corpus

character_arc.book_baseline: Petunia's arc across the books is subtle but present. She begins as a figure of pure hostile denial — pretending her sister doesn't exist, enforcing a wall between Harry and the magical world. The arc moves through: (1) the crack in OotP where her suppressed knowledge surfaces (Dementor explanation, Howler obedience) and she is revealed to have a secret history with Dumbledore; (2) the Dumbledore visit in HBP where she is present but silent while Dumbledore directly addresses the Dursleys' failure to care for Harry; (3) the DH farewell where she almost — but cannot — say something real to Harry. The arc does not end in reconciliation or redemption, but it does end with a gesture toward something unspoken, a withheld acknowledgment. The arc is from total denial to the threshold of acknowledgment, never crossed. This is a deliberately incomplete arc that reflects her character: she is a person who cannot let herself feel what she almost feels.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The films include Petunia at most key Privet Drive moments (Films 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7), but the arc is almost entirely absent. The OotP crack — where her suppressed history with the magical world surfaces — is cut. The HBP visit gives her a single line ('No' — correcting Dumbledore about Harry's age), which is faithful but isolated. The DH farewell is present (Film 7 Part 1) but compressed: she says 'Ready, Dudders?' avoids looking at Harry, and exits. The near-moment where she almost says something to Harry — which is the culmination of her entire arc — is absent. There is no accumulation of small revelations that would make the DH moment carry weight. The arc cannot be traced in the films because the pivotal middle steps (OotP crack, implicit bargain reveal) are missing.
character_arc.difference: The key turning points of Petunia's arc are missing from the films. The OotP Howler scene is cut entirely, removing the moment where her secret history with Dumbledore is first implied. The HBP scene retains only one line. The DH farewell exists in a compressed form but without the context that gives it meaning. The arc from denial to the threshold of acknowledgment cannot be traced in the films; she reads as static throughout.
character_arc.penalty_logic: The arc is incomplete in the films not because of compression but because its pivotal turning points are absent. The OotP crack is entirely cut. The DH near-acknowledgment exists as a scene but is stripped of the emotional weight that depends on what preceded it. This is an arc that is missing important steps, bordering on effectively absent given the removal of its central pivot. Score: 8.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Petunia's two most important relationships are: (1) with Harry — defined by a complex mix of genuine hostility, suppressed guilt, residual obligation, and a withheld almost-feeling that surfaces only at the very end; (2) with Lily (in memory and absence) — defined by envy, resentment, love she cannot admit, and the wound of exclusion; this relationship is the engine of Petunia's entire characterization. Secondary relationships include Vernon (she is his emotional anchor and co-conspirator, but she occasionally overrides him as she does with the Howler) and Dudley (performative adoration that borders on co-dependency). The Lily relationship is central: Petunia's treatment of Harry cannot be understood without understanding that he is the living embodiment of everything Lily had that Petunia didn't.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The Harry-Petunia relationship in the films retains the hostility and the surface dynamic of oppressor-ward, but loses the undertow of suppressed guilt and withheld feeling. The near-goodbye in DH is present but context-free. The Lily relationship is almost entirely absent: the films do not show the Platform 9¾ scene (book corpus shows Petunia calling Hogwarts a 'freak school' and her begging letter being exposed), and Snape's memory in DH (Film 7 Part 2, the Prince's Tale) shows young Petunia knocking away the flower and pulling Lily away, but gives her no dialogue. The film's Petunia-Lily dynamic is reduced to a brief wordless image rather than the layered jealousy-love-resentment of the books. The Vernon relationship is maintained at the surface (co-conspirators, her occasionally calming him) but her moment of overriding him (the Howler decision) is absent.
key_relationships.difference: The Lily relationship — the most important relationship in defining Petunia's character — is nearly invisible in the films. The Platform 9¾ argument, the begged letter, and the eavesdropping on Lily and Snape are not dramatized. The Prince's Tale sequence in Film 7 Part 2 gives young Petunia a brief wordless appearance that preserves only fear and disapproval. The Harry-Petunia relationship loses its suppressed complexity. The Howler decision (the one moment where Petunia's relationship with Dumbledore and her implicit obligation to Harry materially changes the plot) is absent.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: The most defining relationship (Petunia-Lily) is dramatically reduced in the films. The complexity of the Harry relationship loses its suppressed emotional undertow. The Dumbledore-Petunia relationship (implicit in the Howler) is entirely absent from the films. These are substantial alterations to the emotional dynamics that define the character. Score: 6.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: Petunia is one of the series' most carefully constructed secondary antagonists precisely because she is not simply cruel. The books build her through: (1) the suppressed longing scene (the flower, the 'how do you do it?' with 'definite longing in her voice'); (2) the begged letter to Hogwarts (revealed by Lily on Platform 9¾, and confirmed by Dumbledore's existence of prior correspondence); (3) the Dementor knowledge — she retained Snape's explanation to Lily about Azkaban for decades, an act of secret engagement with a world she claims to despise; (4) the OotP revelation where Harry sees her 'wide and fearful' eyes and, for the first time, understands she is his mother's sister — a moment of genuine empathy in the text; (5) the Howler decision, where she makes an independent choice that saves Harry's life based on a prior obligation she has never disclosed; (6) the DH near-farewell, where she stands at the threshold of saying something real and cannot do it. Together, these materials produce a character who is simultaneously petty, resentful, cowardly, and — buried very deep — grieving and guilty. The contradiction between her surface contempt and her buried history is what gives her nuance.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The films retain the surface texture (the screaming, the snappishness, the Dudley-gushing, the domestic perfectionism) but remove almost all of the material that produces her nuance. Items (3) through (6) above are entirely absent from the theatrical films. Item (2) is not dramatized (the Platform 9¾ argument is cut). Item (1) is partially present in the Prince's Tale but wordlessly, without the 'definite longing in her voice' narration. The result is a Petunia who reads as a straightforward hostile Muggle with no discernible interior life, rather than a woman whose entire presentation is a defense against something she can't admit.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The complexity material is almost entirely absent from the films. The suppressed longing, the begged letter, the retained Dementor knowledge, the Howler obedience, the moment of genuine fear and near-grief, and the DH near-acknowledgment — all removed or compressed to invisibility. What survives in the films is recognizable as Petunia but is missing the book's most important characterization layers.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: This is the dimension most severely affected by the adaptation. The films preserve Petunia as a recognizable surface type but remove the material that makes her a character with suppressed depth. She is reduced to her most functional traits (hostile Muggle, Dudley-gusher) without the contradictions that give those traits meaning. Per the scoring rubric, this is major flattening — she is reduced to a simpler function. Score: 7.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for what is present in films; directly evidenced for what is absent by comparing against the book corpus

lost_or_transferred_material: OotP Howler scene: Petunia receives a Howler from Dumbledore ('Remember my last, Petunia'), trembles, and independently decides to keep Harry — her single most consequential act of agency in the series — entirely cut from the films
Petunia's knowledge of Dementors (retained from eavesdropping on Lily and Snape decades earlier) — cut from Film 5
The moment Harry perceives Aunt Petunia as his mother's sister, seeing genuine fear in her 'wide and fearful' eyes for the first time — cut from Film 5
Platform 9¾ argument between Lily and Petunia, including Lily's revelation that Petunia begged Dumbledore to let her into Hogwarts — cut from the films (not dramatized)

Young Petunia's 'definite longing' while watching Lily perform magic with the flower (the 'how do you do it?' beat) — the Prince's Tale film scene shows Petunia knocking away the flower wordlessly, losing this nuance entirely
Young Petunia hiding behind a tree to eavesdrop on Lily and Snape, and her being struck by the falling branch — cut from Film 7 Part 2's Prince's Tale
Petunia shredding the Hogwarts letters in the food processor — transferred to Vernon (who burns them in the film)
Petunia's food-processor letter destruction on Saturday — not shown in films

Petunia's awareness that Voldemort has returned ('Back?' she whispers, in a moment where Harry fully appreciates for the first time that she is his mother's sister) — cut from Film 5

score_caps_applied: Cap 3 (score not above 75 if core book function/agency is transferred or eliminated): Petunia's most consequential act of agency — the Howler decision in OotP — is entirely absent, triggering this cap. Raw dimensional sum would be 59, which is already below 75, so this cap does not compress the score further but confirms the ceiling.

Cap 1 (score not above 85 if films remove a major part of complexity, agency, or key relationships): The removal of Petunia's suppressed longing, secret history with Dumbledore, Dementor knowledge, and near-acknowledgment of Harry constitutes removal of a major part of her complexity. Raw sum is 59, already well below 85.

Cap 5 (score not above 60 if motivations become substantially different): Petunia's deeper motivations (suppressed longing, displaced jealousy, implicit bargain with Dumbledore) are substantially absent, though her surface motivation is preserved. The raw sum of 59 touches the boundary of this cap; given that the surface motivation remains recognizable (even if the deeper layer is absent), a score of 59 is at the edge of — but consistent with — this cap.
comparative.key_observations: Petunia Dursley is a character whose surface — shrieking, snappish, domestically obsessive, Dudley-adoring — is faithfully reproduced in the films, but whose interior is almost entirely absent. The books construct her as a woman whose contempt for magic is a defense against the wound of having been excluded from it: she wanted it, begged for it, eavesdropped on it, retained knowledge of it for decades, and was bound to it through a secret obligation to Dumbledore that she honoured without ever admitting. The films render none of this. The Howler scene (her single most consequential independent act), the Dementor knowledge revelation, the OotP moment where Harry perceives her genuine fear and their shared loss, the Platform 9¾ argument exposing her begged letter, and the DH near-farewell are all absent or compressed to invisibility. What survives is a recognizable caricature of the character rather than the full person. The score of 59 reflects a portrayal that is superficially accurate — a viewer who has not read the books would recognise this as 'Petunia' — but which removes the complexity, the suppressed interiority, the pivotal agency, and the arc that make the book character memorable and psychologically coherent.

personality_voice.book_baseline: In the books, Seamus is a cheerful, curious, mildly impulsive Gryffindor with a persistent tendency to blow things up accidentally (the exploding cauldron, setting feathers on fire, the water-to-rum attempt). He is sociable and enthusiastic, quick to laugh and to show excitement (the boggart lesson, Nearly Headless Nick's demonstration, the Quidditch match). He has a distinct Irish identity and pride (his shamrock tent decorations, his Ireland rosette). He is also capable of genuine moral complexity: in OotP he becomes a credible skeptic who turns against Harry, repeating Ministry propaganda, escalating to a heated dormitory confrontation with real anger and standing fists raised against Harry. His eventual recantation (quietly stepping out of the queue to apologize to Harry, sending a copy of The Quibbler to his mother) shows moral growth. Throughout, his voice is direct, colloquial, and laced with sardonic humor.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The films preserve Seamus's defining surface trait — he blows things up. This is used consistently as a running gag: the water-into-rum attempt (Philosopher's Stone), setting feathers on fire (Philosopher's Stone), the pixie scene (Chamber of Secrets), knocking Professor Flitwick flat with a hose-jet spell (Half-Blood Prince tryout montage). His Irish identity is preserved in his accent and his half-blood background (Philosopher's Stone feast scene). In Goblet of Fire he has one notable observational quip ('Blimey, that's one big woman'). In Order of the Phoenix the dormitory confrontation is present: his accusation that Harry is lying, the escalation, his mother's influence from the Daily Prophet, and — crucially — his later apology ('I believe you. And I've sent a copy of that magazine to me mam'). In Deathly Hallows Part 2 the bridge-destruction scene is excluded per the non-theatrical ruling, but he appears in the Room of Requirement and in the Great Hall aftermath. His personality is recognizably present in short bursts, and his voice (direct, humorous, occasionally hot-headed) is broadly preserved.
personality_voice.difference: The main loss is texture and frequency. In the books Seamus functions as a consistent background voice across seven years: he asks questions, reacts, jokes, provides color across dozens of scenes. Many of those small moments are absent from the films, which compress him to a handful of signature appearances. The OotP confrontation is the one scene where his personality is tested at depth, and the films do include it (the dormitory argument and the apology), which preserves his most important personality beat. However, several secondary traits are reduced or absent: his broomstick-riding bravado (book 1), his enthusiasm for Defense Against the Dark Arts ('They might come in handy one of these days'), his commentary during the Quidditch match, and his ongoing comedic role as a sounding board in the dormitory across multiple years. The explosive gag becomes his only defining characteristic in the films, reducing a multi-trait character to a single recurring joke.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The core traits — impulsiveness, humor, hot-headedness, Irish identity, the pyrotechnic tendency — are preserved. The OotP arc's personality beats (skepticism, anger, apology) survive. The penalty reflects meaningful reduction of secondary traits and the flattening of a multi-dimensional personality into primarily one running joke, without the warmth, curiosity, and range of reactions that define him in the books.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: In the books, Seamus serves several narrative functions across the series. He is a dormitory companion who provides social texture and a measure of normal Gryffindor life. He is an early source of information (passing on Sirius Black's sighting in book 3, asking about the Inferius in book 6). In OotP he is a genuine narrative agent: he creates real conflict for Harry within the safety of Gryffindor tower, forcing Harry to confront the fact that his allies can become his accusers. His arc from doubter to believer mirrors the broader arc of the wizarding public. At the Battle of Hogwarts he is an active combatant who — in the theatrical cut — is credited with pyrotechnic expertise by McGonagall and appears fighting in the courtyard. He also functions as a recurring comic counterpoint in the classroom.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: In the films, Seamus retains the dormitory confrontation in OotP and the later apology — his most significant narrative contribution. He appears as a background presence at the Quidditch World Cup, in classrooms, and in the DA. In Deathly Hallows Part 2 he appears in the Room of Requirement and fights in the courtyard. However, the bridge-rigging scene (excluded per the non-theatrical ruling) was the one moment where Seamus was given a specific narrative task by McGonagall: his pyrotechnic expertise is referenced by McGonagall in the theatrical cut ('Mr. Finnigan — as I recall, he has a particular proclivity for pyrotechnics'), but the execution itself — where Seamus directs the charges and detonates the bridge — was cut. His appearance in the Great Hall aftermath confirms his survival but gives him no action. In OotP, the scene where Neville defends Harry after Seamus's accusation is also excluded, which removes a key beat in which Seamus's doubt generates a cascade of reactions from others.
narrative_role_agency.difference: The bridge scene's exclusion removes Seamus's most prominent individual moment of narrative agency in the entire film series — the one scene where he is given a specific task, competence, and consequence. McGonagall's line about his 'proclivity for pyrotechnics' survives in the theatrical cut but is now a setup without payoff, since the scene that delivers on it is cut. The Neville defense scene being excluded also reduces the narrative weight of the dormitory conflict: in the books, Seamus's accusation triggers Neville's declaration of faith in Harry, which matters. Without that beat, Seamus's role in OotP is incomplete as a narrative driver. Additionally, his function as an information conduit (Sirius Black sighting, Inferius question) is mostly absent from the films.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: The exclusion of the bridge destruction scene is a significant loss of agency — his only moment of individual narrative competence. His OotP conflict role is retained but its consequence (Neville's defense) is cut, weakening his narrative function as a conflict catalyst. He is substantially reduced to a background presence for most of the series.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Seamus's motivations in the books are mostly implicit but coherent. He is a loyal Gryffindor who wants to belong and to do the right thing. His most significant internal conflict occurs in OotP: his mother, a witch who reads the Daily Prophet, has convinced him that Harry is lying and Dumbledore is losing his mind. Seamus is caught between loyalty to a dormitory-mate he has known for four years and deference to his mother's authority and the Ministry-backed media consensus. His anger is real — he feels Harry's claims are dangerous and destabilizing — but so is his eventual recognition that his mother was wrong and that Harry deserves an apology. This is a small but genuine internal conflict: institutional trust versus personal loyalty.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The OotP dormitory scene in the film preserves the essential tension: Seamus cites his mother, the Daily Prophet, and the Ministry's position as the reason for his doubt. The film version of his accusation ('The Daily Prophet's been saying a lot of things about you, Harry') is compressed but coherent. His motivation — maternal influence, media pressure, institutional authority — is present. His apology ('I believe you. And I've sent a copy of that magazine to me mam') is also present, closing the arc. However, the film omits the texture of how this conflict develops: in the book, Seamus leaves the dormitory early the next morning to avoid Harry, is seen struggling in Potions, and his confusion and defiance are tracked across multiple scenes. The film collapses this to two scenes.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The core motivation is preserved but the internal conflict's development — its duration, its visible discomfort, Seamus's gradual shift — is compressed to near-absence. The book shows Seamus catching Harry's eye in the common room with a 'confused and defiant' expression, avoiding Harry over days, and only slowly coming around. The film moves directly from confrontation to apology with little tracking of the internal process.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: The motivations are essentially correct in the film but the internal conflict is underexplained and its development is largely lost. This is meaningful simplification, not wholesale change. The penalty reflects the flattening of a credible internal struggle into a two-beat sequence.

character_arc.book_baseline: Seamus has a minor but genuine arc, primarily in OotP. He begins as a cheerful, unquestioning dormitory companion across four books. In year 5 he becomes a doubter who turns against Harry under media and parental pressure, escalating to a confrontation. Over the course of the year he observes Harry and the DA's work and eventually recants — not dramatically, but quietly, stepping out of a queue to apologize. By DH he is fully committed to the resistance, having stayed at Hogwarts rather than go home when Dumbledore died (his mother wanted him to leave but he refused; they had a shouting match resolved when she agreed he could stay for the funeral). He fights at the Battle of Hogwarts, directing the bridge destruction. The arc is: reliable background figure → doubter shaped by external authority → quiet convert to personal conviction → active combatant.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The films preserve the OotP portion of the arc (doubt → confrontation → apology) and his presence at the Battle of Hogwarts. They omit the HBP beat of him refusing to go home after Dumbledore's death — a small but telling moment of commitment — and the bridge scene's execution is cut. The arc's shape is present but two of its steps (the refusal to leave Hogwarts and the bridge assignment) are missing or incomplete.
character_arc.difference: The arc exists in the films in its outline, but the post-OotP steps are either absent (the funeral scene, the refusal to leave Hogwarts) or cut from the theatrical release (the bridge). As a result, his journey from doubter to committed combatant loses its middle stages. The arc is present as a sketch but not as a complete sequence.
character_arc.penalty_logic: The arc is recognizable but key turning points are missing: his refusal to leave Hogwarts (a moment of independent conviction) and his role in the bridge destruction (the culmination of his competence and courage). The arc is incomplete and rushed.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Seamus's primary relationship is with Dean Thomas, his best friend and frequent dormitory companion. They share commentary on events, sit together, laugh together, and attend the Yule Ball together (Seamus goes with Lavender). His relationship with Harry is characterized by friendly familiarity that becomes temporarily hostile in OotP before being restored. His relationship with his mother is significant in OotP: she is the external voice that temporarily overrides his judgment. These relationships define the social world of the Gryffindor dormitory.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The Seamus-Dean friendship is consistently visible: they sit together, react together, and share comedic moments throughout the films. In Deathly Hallows Part 2, Seamus's reunion with Dean in the Room of Requirement ('Seamus gave a great roar of delight and ran to hug his best friend') is present as a brief warm beat. The Seamus-Harry tension and reconciliation in OotP is preserved as described above. The maternal relationship is referenced in dialogue but not otherwise developed.
key_relationships.difference: The Seamus-Dean friendship is present but thin — they are seen together but rarely given moments that develop the friendship's emotional texture. The book shows them sharing dormitory life in detail (reacting together to events, going to the World Cup, discussing Quidditch). The films treat them primarily as a visual pair rather than an individuated friendship. The relationship with his mother is preserved only as a plot device in the OotP argument.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: The key relationships are recognizable and functionally present, but the Seamus-Dean friendship is compressed and the maternal relationship is underexplored. No relationship is fundamentally altered or transferred, but the emotional texture of the friendships is reduced.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: Seamus's complexity in the books comes from several sources: the running pyrotechnic gag that gives him a specific identity; his genuine enthusiasm and curiosity in multiple settings; his willingness to laugh at authority (pretending to vomit at Snape-Malfoy sycophancy); his role as a semi-skeptic who can be swayed by institutional pressure; his genuine anger in OotP; his eventual moral clarity; his refusal to leave Hogwarts after Dumbledore's death; his willingness to use his particular skill (pyrotechnics) in the final battle. He is a minor character but one whose repeated presence creates texture — he is never just background noise; he always has a reaction, a joke, a question.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The films preserve the pyrotechnic identity, the OotP conflict, and his presence at the Battle of Hogwarts. They largely remove: his curiosity and enthusiasm across classroom scenes; his specific reactions to events (his commentary at the Boggart lesson is reduced to 'That's a Boggart, that is'; his enthusiasm about the Dueling Club is absent; his question about the Inferius in HBP is absent in the theatrical cut); his refusal to leave Hogwarts; his bridge role; several dormitory moments. The cut of the bridge scene is particularly significant because it removes the one moment that synthesizes his arc's thematic point: his particular flaw (blowing things up accidentally) becomes his most useful quality.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The films reduce Seamus to two characteristics: the explosive gag and the OotP conflict. Everything else — his curiosity, his humor across multiple settings, his loyalty, his moral complexity, his arc-resolving moment of agency — is either absent or cut from the theatrical release. The pyrotechnic running joke was always present in the books but surrounded by additional texture; in the films it becomes his sole defining trait.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: Significant simplification. The character is reduced to one running joke plus one dramatic arc. The nuance, the texture, and the synthesis of his arc in the bridge scene are all lost. This is not merely compression — the material removed changes how the audience understands who Seamus is and what his journey means.

lost_or_transferred_material: Bridge destruction scene (Deathly Hallows Part 2, theatrical cut): Seamus's most significant act of individual agency — directing the rigging and detonation of the wooden bridge — was cut. McGonagall's reference to his 'proclivity for pyrotechnics' survives but without the payoff scene.

Seamus refusing to leave Hogwarts after Dumbledore's death (HBP→DH): In the books, Seamus stays at Hogwarts against his mother's wishes, with a shouting match resolved when she allows him to remain for the funeral. This moment of independent conviction is absent from the films.

Neville defending Harry after the dormitory confrontation (OotP): Excluded per non-theatrical ruling. Seamus's accusation loses its narrative consequence — the moment where Neville's declaration of faith in Harry demonstrates the effect of Seamus's conflict on the wider dormitory.

Seamus's curiosity and classroom agency across books 1–6: Multiple scenes where Seamus asks questions, reacts to events, or initiates exchanges (the Quirrell zombie story, the Chamber of Secrets question in History of Magic, the Inferius/Mundungus question in HBP) are absent or cut, reducing him from an active presence to a background figure.
Seamus's enthusiasm about the Dueling Club and Defense Against the Dark Arts: His excitement ('They might come in handy one of these days') is absent from the films.

Seamus attending the Quidditch World Cup with his mother and his patriotic Irish decorations: Present only briefly in the background of the film; the mother's characterization as an opinionated, politically-engaged witch is absent until OotP.

Seamus's ongoing dormitory-life texture across seven years: Sleeping in the background, reacting to events (Sirius Black break-in, Levicorpus incident, Christmas presents), sharing commentary with Dean — these small moments accumulate in the books to create a consistent and warm presence that is largely absent from the films.
Seamus pretending to vomit at Snape's praise of Malfoy (CoS): A moment of silent satirical commentary that shows his irreverence toward authority, absent from the films.
score_caps_applied: Cap 5 considered but not strictly applied: Motivations are not incoherent or opposite — they are simplified and underexplored. The score of 59 is below 60, consistent with the spirit of Cap 5 given the reduced motivation development.

Cap 3 considered: The bridge scene represents a transferred/removed act of agency. The theatrical cut removes the execution of that agency while retaining the setup (McGonagall's line). This partial removal — agency referenced but not shown — is penalized in narrative role/agency and complexity dimensions, keeping the total below 75.
comparative.key_observations: The films preserve Seamus Finnigan's most important single dramatic moment — the OotP dormitory confrontation and his subsequent apology — along with his defining comic identity as someone who accidentally blows things up. These two elements together ensure he remains recognizable. However, the theatrical cut of the bridge destruction scene removes the one moment in which his flaw becomes his strength, collapsing his arc's thematic payoff. Beyond those two anchors, seven years of accumulated personality texture, curiosity, humor, classroom agency, and dormitory presence are compressed away. The result is a character who is recognizable as a sketch but substantially impoverished as a full portrait: a running gag plus a single dramatic beat, where the books gave a warm, curious, impulsive, occasionally flawed, ultimately loyal Gryffindor whose journey from reluctant doubter to committed combatant had genuine shape and meaning.

personality_voice.book_baseline: In the books, Greyback is defined by a rasping, animalistic voice, physical filth (matted hair, yellow nails, blood-smeared mouth, stench of dirt and sweat), predatory menace directed especially at children, and a gloating, sadistic pleasure in his own savagery. He is verbally threatening and taunting but also calculating - he interrogates Harry methodically, reads the situation for personal gain, and asserts dominance over his Snatcher gang. He is not mindlessly feral; he is cunning enough to redirect the prisoners to Malfoy Manor rather than the Ministry when he senses greater reward. His speech is rasping, short, commanding, and laced with relish ('delicious, delicious', 'I'd say I'll get a bite or two, wouldn't you, ginger?'). He also shows resentment at being excluded from the Dark Mark inner circle.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The film corpus shows Greyback in three scenes. In HBP Film Scene 1 (Burrow attack), he is a largely silent physical threat - he sniffs Ginny ('Don't you smell clean'), pursues Harry and Ginny, and retreats on Bellatrix's signal. He has one line of dialogue at the Astronomy Tower: 'He doesn't have the stomach. Like his father. Let me finish him. In my own way.' In DH1 Film Scene 3, he is physically present but almost entirely silent - he punches Ron and presses his boot to Ron's neck, while Scabior takes over the interrogation role entirely.
personality_voice.difference: The rasping, gloating, verbally sadistic voice is almost entirely absent from the film corpus. The methodical interrogation of Harry and the gang, the taunting of Hermione and Ron about biting, the resentment at being excluded from the Dark Mark - none of this appears. The Burrow attack scene is invented for the film and has no book equivalent. In DH1, Scabior absorbs nearly all of Greyback's dialogue and personality functions. The physical menace is preserved in broad outline, but the verbal texture, cunning, and sadistic relish are largely transferred or absent.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The core trait of physical predatory menace is preserved - the corpus shows him as dangerous, animalistic, and threatening. However, the verbal dimension of his personality (rasping taunts, gloating interrogation, sadistic commentary) is almost entirely transferred to Scabior in the film. The cunning and resentment are absent. This is a meaningful reduction of a character whose voice and verbal sadism are central to his book characterization. Score sits in the 14-17 range: recognizable but with important traits reduced.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: In the books, Greyback serves multiple narrative functions: (1) he is the instrument of Lupin's werewolf condition and thus a key piece of Lupin's backstory and motivation; (2) he is Voldemort's primary tool for terrorizing the wizarding population through the threat of werewolf attacks on children; (3) at the Astronomy Tower he actively attempts to kill Dumbledore and is only stopped by another Death Eater; (4) in the Snatchers sequence he leads the gang, conducts the interrogation, makes the decision to go to Malfoy Manor rather than the Ministry, and physically delivers Harry to Voldemort's base; (5) at Malfoy Manor he asserts his claim to reward and threatens Hermione; (6) in the Battle of Hogwarts he attacks Lavender Brown. He is an active agent throughout.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: In the film corpus: the Burrow attack is invented and gives him a physical role but no book narrative function. At the Astronomy Tower he has one line and is otherwise passive. In the Snatchers scene, Scabior leads the interrogation, delivers the key lines about the list, makes the decision about not going to the Ministry, and is the dominant personality. Greyback punches Ron and presses his boot to his neck but does not speak the interrogation dialogue.
narrative_role_agency.difference: The most significant agency transfer is in the Snatchers sequence: in the books, Greyback leads, interrogates, decides, and delivers Harry to Malfoy Manor. In the film, Scabior does all of this. Greyback is reduced to physical muscle. The Lupin backstory connection is not present in the film corpus at all. The Malfoy Manor confrontation with Bellatrix over the sword and the reward claim is absent from the film corpus shown.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: This is a clear case of agency transfer. Greyback's role as interrogator, decision-maker, and gang leader is given to Scabior. His narrative function as the werewolf threat underpinning Lupin's arc is not present in the film corpus. He retains physical menace but loses the agency that defines his book role. Score in the 10-13 range: role and agency clearly altered.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Greyback's motivations are explicit and layered: (1) ideological - he wants to create more werewolves, bite children, and raise them to hate wizards, building a werewolf army; (2) mercenary - he works for Voldemort in exchange for prey and operates as a hired savage for gold (the Snatchers sequence shows him calculating reward); (3) resentful - he is excluded from the Dark Mark inner circle and is aware of his second-class status among Death Eaters, which produces visible resentment; (4) predatory appetite - he has developed a taste for human flesh even outside the full moon. These motivations are distinct and create a character who is both ideologically driven and personally self-interested.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The film corpus shows almost none of this. The ideological motivation (werewolf army, biting children) is absent. The mercenary calculation is absent - Scabior handles the reward discussion. The resentment at being excluded from the inner circle is absent. Only the predatory appetite is faintly present through physical behavior (sniffing Ginny, punching Ron).
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The motivational complexity is almost entirely absent from the film corpus. What remains is a generic physical threat with no articulated motivation. The ideological dimension (his mission to spread lycanthropy) is the most significant loss.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: Motivations are not merely simplified - they are absent. The film corpus does not establish why Greyback does what he does beyond generic menace. This is a meaningful flattening. Score in the 8-10 range: motivations partially altered and largely underexplained to the point of functional absence.

character_arc.book_baseline: Greyback has a flat arc in the books - he is consistently savage, predatory, and mercenary from his first mention to his defeat in the Battle of Hogwarts. There is no redemption, no change, no internal development. His arc is intentionally flat: he is a force of nature and a tool of Voldemort. The only trajectory is his increasing prominence as Voldemort's power grows, and his final defeat. A flat arc faithfully preserved scores full points.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The film corpus shows a flat arc as well - Greyback is consistently threatening across HBP and DH1. There is no invented redemption or change. The Burrow attack (invented) and the Snatchers scene both show the same character.
character_arc.difference: The arc is flat in both books and films. However, the film invents the Burrow attack scene which has no book equivalent, adding a narrative beat that does not exist in the source. This does not change the arc's flatness but does introduce non-canonical material. The Battle of Hogwarts defeat (book) is not in the film corpus provided.
character_arc.penalty_logic: A flat arc faithfully preserved should score full points per the rules. The arc is flat in both. Minor penalty for the invented Burrow scene which adds non-canonical material, though it does not contradict the arc. Score 11-13: arc is compressed but still faithful, with one invented scene.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Greyback's key relationships in the books are: (1) Lupin - Greyback bit Lupin as a child deliberately, making him the direct cause of Lupin's condition and a source of deep personal significance; (2) Voldemort/Death Eaters - he is a hired savage, permitted to wear Death Eater robes but excluded from the Dark Mark, creating a relationship of use and resentment; (3) Bellatrix - at Malfoy Manor she disarms and humiliates him, asserting her superiority, and he is forced to submit while showing defiance ('Release me, woman!'); (4) Malfoy family - Draco uses his name as a threat against Borgin, establishing him as a tool of the Malfoys.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The film corpus shows: Greyback responding to Bellatrix's signal at the Burrow (subordinate relationship preserved in broad outline). At the Astronomy Tower he is one of several Death Eaters with no distinct relational dynamic shown. In the Snatchers scene he is physically present but Scabior dominates. The Lupin relationship is entirely absent from the film corpus. The Bellatrix humiliation at Malfoy Manor is absent from the film corpus provided.
key_relationships.difference: The Lupin relationship - the most personally significant relationship Greyback has in the books - is entirely absent from the film corpus. The Bellatrix dynamic (humiliation, forced submission, defiance) is absent. The Malfoy family relationship as established through the Borgin threat is not shown in the film corpus. Only a generic subordination to Bellatrix is faintly present.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: The most important relationship (Lupin) is absent. The most dramatically rich relationship (Bellatrix at Malfoy Manor) is absent from the corpus. What remains is generic. This significantly changes how the character is understood relationally. Score 5-6: important relationship dynamics are altered or absent.
key_relationships.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for what is present; reasonably inferred for what is absent based on corpus scope

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: Greyback's complexity in the books comes from several sources: (1) he is not mindlessly feral - he is calculating, cunning, and self-interested; (2) he has an ideology (werewolf supremacy, revenge on wizards) that gives him a political dimension beyond mere savagery; (3) he is aware of and resentful about his exclusion from the Death Eater inner circle, giving him a social position that complicates his role; (4) he attacks outside the full moon, which even Dumbledore finds disturbing, suggesting a character who has crossed a line even within the logic of his own condition; (5) his verbal sadism (the taunting of Hermione and Ron about biting) adds a layer of psychological cruelty beyond physical threat; (6) his defeat at Malfoy Manor by Bellatrix shows him capable of defiance even when powerless.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The film reduces Greyback almost entirely to physical menace. The cunning, the ideology, the resentment, the verbal sadism, and the social complexity are absent. The Burrow attack scene (invented) adds a non-canonical beat that replaces book material with action-sequence filler. Scabior absorbs the verbal and intellectual dimensions of the Snatchers sequence.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The character is reduced from a multi-layered predator with ideology, cunning, resentment, and verbal sadism to a largely silent physical threat. The most nuanced material - his awareness of his own exclusion, his ideological mission, his verbal taunting - is absent or transferred.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: This is a significant flattening. The character is recognizable as dangerous and animalistic but the book's complexity is largely removed. The transfer of verbal agency to Scabior is the most damaging single change. Score 5-7: major flattening, character reduced to a simpler function.
