Greyback's rasping, gloating verbal sadism across multiple scenes - largely transferred to Scabior or absent
The Burrow attack scene is invented for the film with no book equivalent
score_caps_applied: Cap 3 (score above 75): Greyback's core book function as interrogator and decision-maker in the Snatchers sequence is transferred to Scabior in the film

Cap 4 (score above 70): The films preserve only Greyback's broad identity as a dangerous werewolf while removing most of what defines his book characterization - ideology, cunning, verbal sadism, resentment, key relationships
comparative.key_observations: The film reduces Greyback from a calculating, ideologically driven, verbally sadistic predator with a distinct social position among Death Eaters to a largely silent physical threat. The most damaging single change is the transfer of his interrogation role and verbal personality to Scabior in DH1, which strips the character of the agency and voice that define him in the books. His ideological motivation (spreading lycanthropy, building a werewolf army), his resentment at exclusion from the Dark Mark inner circle, his connection to Lupin, and his confrontation with Bellatrix at Malfoy Manor are all absent from the film corpus. The invented Burrow attack scene adds non-canonical material without compensating for what is lost. What remains - physical menace, animalistic appearance, and a subordinate role to Bellatrix - is recognizable but represents only the surface of the book character. Confidence is Medium throughout because the film corpus is limited to three scenes, but the pattern of reduction is consistent and clear.

personality_voice.book_baseline: In the books, Dudley is established across multiple volumes with a consistent and layered behavioral profile. He is spoiled, entitled, and physically intimidating, but also cowardly when magic is involved. His dominant mode is aggressive confidence around peers and family who enable him, and panicked retreat when confronted with anything supernatural. He performs emotions strategically — the famous birthday tantrum (Scene 36: 'he wasn't really crying... but he knew that if he screwed up his face and wailed, his mother would give him anything') exemplifies calculated manipulation rather than genuine feeling. His speech is characterized by short, blunt commands ('Make it move,' 'Pass the frying pan,' 'I want to read that letter') and taunts ('Today's your birthday. And nobody cares,' 'Don't kill Cedric! Who's Cedric, your boyfriend?'). He is not stupid in a simple way — he can read situations, and by Book 5 he has developed a genuine physical menace (junior boxing champion). Crucially, he is not a cartoon villain: the books show him to be a product of appalling parenting, capable of rudimentary empathy by Book 7 when he expresses, with agonizing difficulty, that he does not think Harry is a waste of space and acknowledges Harry saved his life.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The films preserve Dudley's surface traits accurately: the overweight, blond, aggressive bully who manipulates his parents. The birthday present counting scene (Film Scene 2: '36?! But last year, last year I had 37!!') faithfully reproduces the book's entitlement. His cowardice around magic is shown effectively in the Hagrid scene (Film Scene 7: 'I'm-I'm not Harry'). The dementor encounter in Film Scene 14 retains his taunting voice well ('Don't kill Cedric! Who's Cedric, your boyfriend?') and his terror during the dementor attack is shown. His physical presence as a bully is noted. However, the films lose important texture: the calculating fake-crying is absent (replaced by simple bratty complaining), his evolving menace as a boxer is not established, his strategic intelligence in manipulating situations is not demonstrated, and his speech loses the patterned short-command rhythm that marks him in the books. The films reduce him to a reliable sight gag and threat prop.
personality_voice.difference: The core personality type — entitled, cowardly, bullying — is preserved. What is lost is the layering: the deliberate emotional manipulation (fake crying established explicitly in the books), the trajectory from fat child bully to genuinely formidable teenage boxer, and the subtle intelligence that makes him something more than a cartoon bully. The books also give him memorable, rhythmically distinctive taunting dialogue (the Dementor exchange in Book 5 being the most complex — 'I heard you last night, talking in your sleep. Moaning.') which the films approximate but compress. His voice in Film Scene 14 retains the cruelty but loses the sustained cat-and-mouse rhythm of the alleyway confrontation.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The character remains clearly recognizable as Dudley, and the main traits are intact. However, important secondary traits — the deliberate emotional manipulation, the arc of physical menace, and the speech texture — are reduced or absent. This places him in the 14–17 range: recognizable but with noticeable loss of important traits. A score of 17 reflects that the core is faithfully rendered even if the textural layers are missing.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: Dudley serves multiple narrative functions across the books. (1) He is Harry's primary domestic antagonist and the embodiment of Muggle cruelty and enabled entitlement, which contextualizes why Hogwarts is a liberation. (2) He is a plot driver: his reaction to Harry's Hogwarts letter (Scene 83: 'Dad! Dad, Harry's got a letter!') and his fight for the letter are active narrative contributions. (3) In Book 5, he functions as Harry's first civilian victim of a Dementor attack, which directly triggers the Ministry hearing and the Order's response — a major plot pivot. (4) In Book 7, his goodbye scene is the culmination of a years-long secondary arc about whether any Dursley is capable of humanity; his question 'Why isn't he coming with us?' and his final handshake are narrative acts that force acknowledgment of Harry's worth even from his abuser.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: In the theatrical films, Dudley retains function (1) clearly. He participates in function (2) at a reduced level (he notices Harry's letter, Film Scene 4, but the fight for it is compressed and his role is brief). His role in function (3) — the dementor attack — is preserved as a plot trigger in Film Scene 14. However, function (4) — the farewell scene — is explicitly excluded from theatrical scoring per the non-theatrical material note; the 'Dudley's goodbye' scene was cut. This removes his most significant narrative act of agency entirely from the theatrical film.
narrative_role_agency.difference: The loss of the farewell scene (cut from theatrical release) is the most significant agency loss. In the books, Dudley's choice to ask about Harry, acknowledge being saved, and offer a handshake is an active narrative moment that closes a character arc and morally functions as a small counterpoint to the Dursleys' cruelty. In the theatrical film, Dudley simply departs with his parents. His role in the dementor plot is retained but his agency within that scene is reduced — he is largely a passive victim rather than someone whose terror and subsequent testimony (at the kitchen table, Scene 473–484) drives the scene's conflict. His letter-spotting moment is retained but brief.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: The dementor plot function is preserved, which keeps him from a very low score here. But the loss of the farewell's agency, and the compression of his active role in the letter scenes and post-dementor kitchen confrontation, represent a meaningful reduction. He is still functional as a domestic antagonist, but his capacity to initiate, confront, or change narrative direction is substantially reduced compared to the books. Score of 13 reflects clear alteration of role and agency while acknowledging the dementor pivot is intact.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Dudley's motivations in the books are clear if shallow for most of the series: he wants maximum material comfort, peer dominance, and parental validation. He bullies because he can, because it is rewarded, and because Harry's existence is an affront to his status. The more interesting motivational layer emerges in Book 5 and 7: the dementor encounter forces him to confront something real — his own worst memories — and the books explicitly raise the question of what a pampered bully's worst memories actually are (Scene 478: 'What would spoiled, pampered, bullying Dudley have been forced to hear?'). His Book 7 behavior suggests that the dementor experience created genuine internal conflict between his conditioned contempt for Harry and some nascent awareness of Harry's humanity and the reality of danger.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The films establish Dudley's surface motivations (entitlement, bullying) effectively. The dementor scene in Film Scene 14 shows his terror, but the film does not develop or explore what memories the dementor surfaced. The post-dementor kitchen scene (Book scenes 473–484) where Dudley slowly, haltingly describes what he experienced ('All went dark. And then I h-heard... things. Inside m-my head.') is present in abbreviated form in the theatrical film — Vernon asks what happened, Dudley responds minimally. The internal conflict this implies — the dawning awareness of genuine darkness beyond his comfortable world — is shown only superficially. The theatrical cut of the farewell scene removes the culmination of any motivational evolution entirely.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The films show the dementor's effect on Dudley but do not develop what this does to him internally. The book's careful attention to what Dudley might have worst memories about (Scene 478) is entirely absent. The motivational evolution from unthinking bully to someone capable of expressing gratitude is lost in the theatrical cut. What remains is the stimulus (dementor attack) without the response arc (changed behavior, gratitude).
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: The surface motivations are intact, but the deeper motivational layer — the internal conflict generated by the dementor encounter — is partially shown but not developed, and its culmination is cut. This is a partial alteration and flattening, placing the score in the 8–10 range. Score of 9 reflects that some motivational texture survives but the internal conflict is underexplained to the point of changing the characterization.
motivations_internal_conflict.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for surface; reasonably inferred for internal conflict loss

character_arc.book_baseline: Dudley has a clear arc across the seven books, even if it is a minor one. Starting point: a five-year-old spoiled child whose parents worship him (Book 1). Midpoint development: an increasingly physically menacing teenage bully enabled by his parents, who begins to realize Harry has genuine power over him (Books 2–4). Turning point: the dementor attack in Book 5, which is the first time Dudley is confronted with real consequences — not punishment from adults, but genuine existential horror. His halting description of what he heard/felt (Scenes 476–484) suggests genuine psychic exposure. Resolution: the farewell in Book 7, where Dudley — against everything his upbringing has made him — asks about Harry, acknowledges being saved, says he doesn't think Harry is a waste of space, and shakes his hand. This is not a transformation into a good person, but it is a genuine, hard-won, minimal act of recognition that closes the arc meaningfully.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The films show the early-period Dudley (Books 1–2) with reasonable fidelity. The dementor encounter is shown in Film Scene 14. However, the arc's culminating moment — the farewell — is cut from the theatrical release per the non-theatrical material note. Without that scene, there is no resolution to any arc. The dementor attack appears as an isolated event rather than a turning point with consequences. Dudley simply disappears from the films after Book 5 without any acknowledgment of change.
character_arc.difference: The arc's starting and middle points are present. The turning point (dementor encounter) is present but underplayed as an arc moment rather than a catalyst. The resolution — the only moment in which Dudley's arc achieves any kind of completion — is entirely absent from the theatrical release. This means the arc exists in setup but has no payoff.
character_arc.penalty_logic: An arc that is set up but has its resolution entirely removed is significantly altered. The books' arc has a clear, meaningful, emotionally earned endpoint; the theatrical films have none. The dementor encounter loses its narrative weight as a turning point when it has no visible consequence. This is a 'significantly altered' arc per the scoring rubric, placing it in the 5–7 range. Score of 5 reflects that the resolution is not merely compressed but absent.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Dudley's most important relationships: (1) With Harry — a relationship of sustained cruelty and power imbalance that is the defining context of Harry's Muggle life, with a final, fragile pivot to acknowledgment in Book 7. (2) With Vernon and Petunia — a relationship of total indulgence and enabling that explains his character: he is the product of parenting that has never said no. (3) With his gang (Piers, Malcolm, Gordon, etc.) — he is a leader who relies on numbers, which speaks to his cowardice; he needs the gang to feel powerful. The Harry relationship is the most dramatically important, and its arc from bully/victim to an awkward, minimal recognition is irreplaceable. The parental relationship functions as both comedic and explanatory — every scene of Petunia calling him 'Ickle Dudleykins' or Uncle Vernon saying 'Little tyke' contextualizes who Dudley is and why.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The Harry-Dudley dynamic of cruelty and power imbalance is preserved through Books 1–2 film adaptations (birthday, zoo, letters, dementor). The parental enabling relationship is shown clearly in Film Scenes 2–7, particularly in Petunia's coddling and Vernon's pride. The dementor scene preserves the physical dynamic. However, the final pivot in the Harry-Dudley relationship — the only moment in which the dynamic meaningfully changes — is cut. The gang relationship is mostly absent from the films (Piers appears briefly in Film Scene 3 but the gang dynamic is not developed). The Harry-Dudley relationship therefore ends, in the theatrical film, in its default state of mutual hostility and fear, without any acknowledgment of the arc.
key_relationships.difference: The dominant dynamic of the Harry-Dudley relationship is preserved through the bulk of the story. The loss of the farewell scene means the relationship ends without the pivot that makes it meaningful in retrospect. The gang relationship, which in the books contextualizes Dudley's cowardice (he only attacks with backup), is mostly absent.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: The main dynamic is preserved but the emotional endpoint is removed, and a secondary relationship (the gang) is absent. The relationship is mostly faithful through most of the story but loses its most important moment of change. Score of 6 reflects important relationship dynamics that are altered at their culmination and weakened overall.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: Dudley in the books is richer than a simple bully. The books include: (1) His deliberate emotional performance — the fake crying is explicitly noted as calculated (Scene 36). (2) The tantrums over food during his diet, where his parents navigate around him, which is both comic and revealing about family dysfunction. (3) The alleyway confrontation in Book 5 (Scenes 393–431), where Dudley gets under Harry's skin by taunting him about Cedric — showing he is perceptive enough to identify Harry's real vulnerabilities. (4) His snoring as a recurring background detail that anchors him as a physical presence in Harry's domestic world. (5) Harry's specific contempt and occasional dark amusement at Dudley (Scene 282: 'He suppressed a laugh as he imagined the look that would spread over Dudley's piggy face'). (6) The diet subplot in Book 4, which is both funny and a study in how the Dursleys respond to any external constraint with denial. (7) Dumbledore's observation in Book 6 (Scene 538) that Dudley has been 'appallingly' damaged by his parents' treatment — which reframes Dudley as a victim of his own upbringing, not merely a perpetrator.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The films retain the surface humor (birthday presents, zoo, letters) and the dementor threat. Lost: the fake-crying detail, the diet subplot and its comedy, the alleyway confrontation's full psychological texture (the Cedric taunting and Harry's near-violent response), Dumbledore's observation about Dudley as a victim of his parents, and the farewell scene's humanizing moment. The films also lose the recurring small details that build texture — the snoring, the PlayStation, the five chins, the deliberate descriptions of his size and appetites that make him vivid.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The films give Dudley his signature scenes — birthday, zoo, letters, pig tail, dementor — and he is recognizable and often funny. But he functions primarily as a reliable antagonist and comedic target rather than a character with internal contradiction. The nuance that he is both a bully and a damaged child, that his cruelty is enabled by pathological parenting, and that he is capable of a minimal form of moral growth, is almost entirely absent from the theatrical release.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: The films preserve the character's broad identity and some of his most memorable moments, but remove most of what gives him complexity: the arc resolution, the psychological texture of the alleyway scene, the reframing via Dumbledore, and the farewell. What remains is a flattened version of Dudley that works as comic relief and a threat but not as a character with internal life. This is major flattening, placing the score in the 5–7 range. Score of 7 reflects that the core is recognizable but the complexity is largely missing.

lost_or_transferred_material: Dudley's farewell scene (Book 7: 'I don't think you're a waste of space' / handshake with Harry) — cut from theatrical release

The alleyway confrontation's full psychological texture (Book 5): Dudley's sustained taunting about Cedric, Harry's near-violent response, the extended cat-and-mouse dynamic before the Dementor attack
Dudley's deliberate fake-crying, explicitly described as calculated manipulation (Book 1, birthday scene)
The diet subplot (Book 4): Dudley's tantrums over food restrictions, smuggling doughnuts, throwing PlayStation out the window — the family dysfunction comedy
Dumbledore's observation (Book 6) that Dudley has been 'appallingly damaged' by his parents — the reframing of Dudley as victim
Dudley's arc as junior boxing champion (Book 5) — the evolution of his physical menace and the neighborhood terror he causes

Post-dementor kitchen scene: Dudley's halting description of what he heard/felt ('All went dark. And then I h-heard... things. Inside m-my head.') is present in abbreviated form but loses the sustained psychological texture
The gang dynamic: Piers and the gang as context for Dudley's cowardice (he attacks only in numbers)
Harry's interiority about Dudley in Books 4–5: the complex mixture of contempt, dark humor, and tactical calculation Harry applies to their interactions
Book 7 departure scene: Dudley asking 'But where's he going to go?' and the extended, agonized effort to express gratitude
score_caps_applied: Cap 5 (score above 60 if motivations or arc become unclear, incoherent, or substantially different): Applied. The character arc has no theatrical resolution and motivational evolution is cut, keeping the total at or below 60.

Cap 4 (score above 70 if films preserve only broad identity but remove most of what defines book characterization): Applied as a cross-check — the theatrical films preserve broad identity but remove arc resolution, complexity, and most nuanced material.
comparative.key_observations: Dudley Dursley's theatrical film portrayal is recognizable and faithful in its broad strokes — the spoiled, cowardly, physically imposing bully whose parents enable everything is clearly present across the franchise. The surface humor and the key set-pieces (birthday presents, zoo, letters, pig tail, Dementor attack) are all retained. However, the films systematically lose the layers that make Dudley a character rather than a type: his deliberately calculated emotional manipulation, his arc from child bully to something approaching human recognition, and above all the farewell scene that closes his story. The theatrical cut of 'Dudley's goodbye' is the single most damaging adaptation decision for this character, as it removes the only moment of arc resolution and leaves his relationship with Harry ending in its default state of mutual hostility. The alleyway confrontation in Book 5, though partially present, loses its psychological texture. Dumbledore's reframing of Dudley as a victim of his own upbringing is entirely absent. What survives is a functional comedic antagonist who generates laughs and threat as needed, but not the minor-arc character that Rowling constructed across seven books.

personality_voice.book_baseline: Frank is established as stubborn, quietly courageous, and defiant under pressure. He is a war veteran with a deep distrust of authority (especially police), a loner who endures community hostility without yielding, and a man who acts on his own judgment. His voice in the confrontation scene is direct, rough, and combative: 'I don't think much of your manners, My Lord. Turn round and face me like a man, why don't you?' He bluffs ('my wife knows I'm up here'), shows fear physically (sweating, trembling hands) but does not break verbally. He is not passive - he processes what he hears, forms a plan, and chooses to stay and listen rather than flee. His internal monologue shows a man reasoning under terror.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: Frank appears only in brief, mostly silent action: he sees the light, enters the house, overhears voices, is spotted by Nagini, and is killed. His only spoken line in the film is 'Bloody kids' - directed at the Weasley twins offscreen, not at Voldemort. The defiant confrontation with Voldemort is entirely absent. He is killed without speaking a word to his killer.
personality_voice.difference: The film removes Frank's entire verbal confrontation with Voldemort - the scene that most directly establishes his personality. His defiance, his bluffing, his rough directness, his war-veteran courage under pressure, and his stubborn refusal to be intimidated are all absent. 'Bloody kids' is a throwaway line that establishes only that he is a grumpy old man. The film retains his physical action (going to investigate) but strips the voice and personality that define him.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The confrontation scene is not incidental - it is the only scene where Frank's character is directly expressed through dialogue. Without it, the film shows a man who walks into a house and is killed silently. The core traits (defiance, rough courage, verbal stubbornness) are not preserved. The character remains recognizable as 'old man who investigates and dies' but the defining personality traits are removed. Score falls in the 14-17 range: recognizable but important traits are reduced.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: Frank's narrative role is dual: (1) he is the vehicle through which the reader witnesses the Voldemort/Wormtail scene and learns critical plot information, and (2) he is a humanizing victim whose death gives moral weight to Voldemort's return. His agency within the scene is active: he decides to investigate, he chooses to stay and listen rather than flee, he processes the information and forms a plan to go to the police, he confronts Voldemort directly and verbally challenges him. He is not merely a passive observer - he makes decisions throughout.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: Frank retains his structural function as the POV witness to the Voldemort scene and as the victim whose death opens the film. However, his agency within the scene is almost entirely removed. He does not confront Voldemort, does not speak to him, does not challenge him, does not form a plan. He is spotted by Nagini and killed immediately. He is a passive observer who becomes a passive victim.
narrative_role_agency.difference: The film preserves the structural role (witness/victim) but removes the active agency. In the books, Frank decides to stay, decides to confront, chooses to bluff, chooses to challenge. In the film, he simply walks in and is killed. The decision-making and confrontation that constitute his agency are absent.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: The transfer rule applies partially: Frank's agency (confronting Voldemort, speaking defiantly) is not transferred to another character - it is simply removed. This is an agency loss. The structural role as witness/victim is preserved, which prevents a lower score, but the active dimension of his role is gone. Score falls in the 10-13 range.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Frank's motivations are layered: (1) civic duty and suspicion of vandalism drive him to investigate; (2) distrust of police means he acts alone rather than calling authorities; (3) once inside, he stays because he recognizes criminal activity and feels compelled to gather information; (4) he is torn between the impulse to flee to the police and the compulsion to keep listening. His internal conflict - wanting to leave but being unable to - is explicitly narrated: 'He wanted more than anything to be back in his bed with his hot-water bottle. The problem was that his legs didn't seem to want to move.'
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The film shows Frank investigating (motivation: sees a light, assumes intruders) but does not show any internal conflict. There is no moment where he considers leaving, no moment where he processes what he hears and decides to stay. The motivation to investigate is preserved; the internal conflict between fear and compulsion is absent.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The primary motivation (investigate the light) is preserved. The secondary motivations (distrust of police, civic duty) are implied by his solo action. The internal conflict - the paralysis between fleeing and staying, the moral weight of what he overhears - is entirely absent from the film.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: The core motivation is present but the internal conflict is removed. This is a partial alteration - the motivation is simplified to 'old man investigates light' without the layered reasoning and paralysis that the books establish. Score falls in the 8-10 range: motivations partially present but flattened.

character_arc.book_baseline: Frank's arc within GoF is compact but complete: he begins as a man unjustly suspected of murder who has endured decades of community hostility with stubborn dignity; he ends as a man who, in his final moments, demonstrates the same courage and defiance that defined his wartime self. The arc is not one of change but of revelation - the final scene confirms who he has always been. Dumbledore's eulogy at the end of the book ('he has not been seen since last August') frames him as a forgotten victim, adding a final note of injustice.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The film preserves the beginning (isolated old man, unjustly suspected) and the end (killed by Voldemort). The revelation arc - the confirmation of his character through his final confrontation - is absent because the confrontation is absent. He dies without the moment that would have confirmed his courage.
character_arc.difference: The arc's endpoint is structurally present (he dies) but the meaning of that endpoint is changed. In the books, he dies having faced Voldemort defiantly. In the film, he dies having said nothing. The arc is compressed to the point where the defining moment is lost.
character_arc.penalty_logic: The arc is compressed but the structural shape (suspected man dies as forgotten victim) is present. However, the key turning point - the confrontation that reveals his character - is missing. This is an incomplete arc rather than a false one. Score falls in the 11-13 range.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Frank's key relationship in the corpus is his adversarial confrontation with Voldemort. This is not a relationship in the ongoing sense, but it is the defining dynamic of his appearance: Frank as the defiant, morally clear ordinary man facing an incomprehensible evil. The power imbalance is absolute, but Frank refuses to be diminished by it. His relationship with the village (community hostility, his stubborn refusal to leave) is also established, though no individual relationship is developed.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The film shows Frank in proximity to Voldemort but without any exchange. Voldemort says 'Nagini tells me the old Muggle caretaker is standing just outside the door' and 'Avada Kedavra' - Frank never responds. The dynamic of defiance against power is entirely absent. The village relationship is not shown at all.
key_relationships.difference: The confrontation dynamic - the only relationship the corpus develops - is removed. Frank does not speak to Voldemort, does not challenge him, does not register as anything other than an obstacle to be eliminated. The emotional and dramatic function of the relationship (ordinary human dignity vs. inhuman evil) is lost.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: The relationship's dramatic function is changed: in the books it reveals Frank's character and gives moral weight to Voldemort's cruelty; in the film it is a one-sided execution with no exchange. The dynamic is not preserved. Score falls in the 5-6 range.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: Frank's complexity comes from several sources: (1) the injustice of his situation - a decent man destroyed by community suspicion; (2) his stubborn dignity in the face of that injustice; (3) his war-veteran psychology (courage under fire, distrust of authority, physical limitation); (4) his internal reasoning process as he listens to Voldemort; (5) his defiant verbal confrontation; (6) the pathos of his death as a forgotten Muggle victim. He is a minor character but a fully realized one - his complexity is concentrated in a single chapter.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The film retains: isolated old man, investigates light, is killed. It removes: the community backstory, the war veteran psychology, the internal reasoning, the defiant confrontation, the verbal challenge to Voldemort, and Dumbledore's eulogy. 'Bloody kids' is the only line that characterizes him, and it characterizes him only as a grumpy old man.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The majority of what makes Frank a complex minor character is removed. What remains is a functional placeholder: old man who witnesses the scene and dies. The nuance, the backstory, the defiance, the pathos of his specific situation - all absent.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: This is a major flattening. The film reduces Frank to a single function (witness/victim) and a single trait (grumpy old man). The complexity that makes him memorable in the books - his dignity, his courage, his unjust history - is almost entirely absent. Score falls in the 5-7 range.

lost_or_transferred_material: Frank's verbal confrontation with Voldemort ('Turn round and face me like a man, why don't you?') - removed entirely
Frank's defiant bluff about his wife knowing where he is - removed
Frank's internal reasoning process while listening to Voldemort's conversation - removed
Frank's decision to stay and listen rather than flee - removed (shown only as passive observation)
Frank's war-veteran psychology: courage under fire, distrust of police, physical limitation as character texture - removed
The community backstory: decades of unjust suspicion, stubborn refusal to leave Little Hangleton - removed
Frank's physical fear responses (sweating, trembling) contrasted with verbal defiance - removed
Dumbledore's end-of-book eulogy framing Frank as a forgotten Muggle victim - removed (not in film corpus)
Frank's recognition that Voldemort is a murderer and his moral decision to act - removed
score_caps_applied: Cap 4 (score above 70 not applicable): the film preserves only Frank's broad identity - old man who investigates and dies - while removing most of what defines his book characterization
Cap 3 (score above 75 not applicable): Frank's defining act of agency - the verbal confrontation with Voldemort - is removed entirely
comparative.key_observations: The film preserves Frank Bryce's structural function (POV witness to the Voldemort scene, first victim of the restored Voldemort) and his broad identity (isolated old man, caretaker of the Riddle House) but removes almost everything that makes him a character rather than a plot device. The single most important scene in his book portrayal - his defiant verbal confrontation with Voldemort - is entirely absent. Without it, his defining traits (rough courage, stubborn dignity, war-veteran defiance) are invisible. The film reduces him to a silent figure who walks into a room and is killed, characterized only by 'Bloody kids.' The injustice of his situation, his internal reasoning, his community backstory, and the pathos of his death as a forgotten Muggle are all lost. He is recognizable as the same person in the same situation, but the characterization that makes that situation meaningful is gone.

personality_voice.book_baseline: The books construct James Potter through two distinct temporal layers. As a teenager (Snape's Worst Memory, Deathly Hallows flashbacks), he is arrogant, casually cruel, performative, and attention-seeking — he bullies Snape unprovoked, plays to an audience, rumples his hair to look cool, steals a Snitch, and is only stopped by Lily's intervention. He is also genuinely talented, brave, and loyal to his friends. As an adult (Lily's letter, Sirius's accounts, the Resurrection Stone scene), he is described as having 'deflated his head,' showing warmth, humor, and protectiveness — making colored smoke for baby Harry, getting frustrated being cooped up but trying not to show it, dying wandlessly trying to hold off Voldemort. His voice in the Pensieve is sharp, mocking, and performative ('All right, Snivellus?', 'Who wants to see me take off Snivelly's trousers?'). His posthumous voice via the Resurrection Stone is brief but tender and encouraging.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The films give James almost no direct characterization. In Philosopher's Stone, he appears only as a silent reflection in the Mirror of Erised, smiling and nodding. In Order of the Phoenix, the Pensieve scene is drastically compressed: James disarms Snape and says 'Right. Who wants to see me take off Snivelly's trousers?' — preserving the bullying behavior but stripping the extended performative cruelty, the Snitch-playing, the hair-rumpling, the audience-playing, and the complex reaction to Lily. In Deathly Hallows Part 2, James appears via the Resurrection Stone and says 'You're nearly there, son' and 'Until the end.' The teenage arrogance and the adult warmth-under-pressure are both present in fragments, but the film never builds either into a coherent personality.
personality_voice.difference: The film preserves the surface markers (bullying Snape, tender Resurrection Stone moment) but removes the behavioral texture that makes James legible as a character: the performative showing-off for Wormtail, the hair-rumpling vanity, the complex reaction to Lily's rejection, the casual theft of the Snitch, the way he only stops for Sirius. The adult James — frustrated but trying to hide it, playful with baby Harry, writing to Sirius — is entirely absent. The film James is a collection of two or three gestures rather than a personality.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The core traits are recognizable but substantially thinned. The teenage arrogance survives in one line; the adult warmth survives in two lines. The contradictions, the performative vanity, the specific social dynamics, and the emotional texture are all missing. This is a 14–17 range: recognizable but important traits, tone, and contradictions are reduced.
personality_voice.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for both book and film material present in the corpus.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: James functions across multiple narrative roles: (1) as a posthumous moral reference point whose legacy Harry must interrogate and complicate (the Pensieve revelation destabilizes Harry's idealization); (2) as an active agent in his own death scene — he tries to hold off Voldemort wandlessly, buying Lily time; (3) as a structural presence in the Marauder backstory, where his choices (becoming an Animagus to help Lupin, insisting on Pettigrew as Secret-Keeper, saving Snape from the Shrieking Shack) directly drive plot; (4) as a guide figure in the Resurrection Stone scene. His agency in the books is substantial even in death: his decisions caused the betrayal, his sacrifice enabled Harry's survival, and his character forces Harry to grow up morally.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: In the films, James is almost entirely passive and symbolic. He appears as a silent reflection (PS), a brief Pensieve bully (OotP), a name on a gravestone (DH1), and a two-line guide figure (DH2). His active role in the Marauder backstory — the Animagus transformation, the Secret-Keeper decision, saving Snape — is either cut entirely or transferred to Lupin's narration in PoA (which is itself cut from the film). His wandless attempt to hold off Voldemort is narrated in the books but not dramatized in the films; the film version of Voldemort's attack on Godric's Hollow (DH1) shows James only as a body falling.
narrative_role_agency.difference: The Marauder backstory is largely absent from the films, removing James's most significant acts of agency. The Secret-Keeper decision, the Animagus transformation, and the Snape rescue are all cut. The Pensieve scene is compressed to a single bullying moment without the broader context of James's social power and choices. His role as a moral complication for Harry — forcing Harry to question his idealization — is present in OotP but severely truncated.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: James's narrative agency is substantially reduced. His key decisions and actions are either cut or transferred to narration that doesn't appear in the films. His role as a moral complication for Harry is present but compressed to the point where it cannot fully function. This is a 10–13 range: role and agency are clearly altered.
narrative_role_agency.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for what is present; reasonably inferred for what is absent based on the corpus showing no film scenes corresponding to major book agency moments.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: James's motivations are layered. As a teenager: desire for status, peer approval (especially Sirius's), and attraction to Lily — all visible in the Pensieve. As an adult: love for Lily and Harry, loyalty to friends (which leads to the fatal trust in Pettigrew), and a protective instinct that costs him his life. His internal conflict is implicit rather than explicit: he is arrogant but capable of growth; he trusts too completely; he is brave to the point of recklessness (dying wandlessly). Lily's letter shows a man frustrated by confinement but suppressing it for his family's sake.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The films provide almost no access to James's motivations. The Pensieve scene shows the bullying impulse but not the attraction to Lily or the peer-approval dynamic. The Resurrection Stone scene shows paternal love and pride but without the context of who James was or what he sacrificed. The letter, the Godric's Hollow backstory, and the Secret-Keeper decision — all of which illuminate his motivations — are absent or reduced to set dressing.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The motivational complexity (arrogance coexisting with love, trust leading to betrayal, bravery shading into recklessness) is almost entirely absent from the films. What remains is a sketch: he bullied people, he loved his son.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: Motivations are partially present but so underexplained that they cannot support the same characterization. The internal conflict between arrogance and love, between trust and vulnerability, is not visible. This is an 8–10 range.
motivations_internal_conflict.evidence_status: Reasonably inferred from the corpus; the film corpus is too limited to directly evidence motivational complexity.

character_arc.book_baseline: James has a clear arc across the books: from arrogant, bullying teenager (Pensieve) to a man who 'deflated his head' (Sirius, Lupin), married Lily, became a father, and died protecting his family. The arc is confirmed by multiple sources: Sirius ('once James had deflated his head a bit'), Lupin ('he would have saved Pettigrew'), Dumbledore ('he would have saved Pettigrew too'). The arc is not shown in real time but is reconstructed through testimony and flashback. It is essential to understanding James as a character — without it, the Pensieve scene leaves him simply as a bully.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The films show the teenage James (OotP Pensieve) and the posthumous James (DH2 Resurrection Stone) but do not connect them with any arc. The growth from arrogant teenager to loving father is never established in the films. Sirius's comment about James 'deflating his head' is absent. The film audience sees a bully and then a tender ghost, with no bridge.
character_arc.difference: The arc exists in the books as a reconstructed trajectory confirmed by multiple characters. In the films, the two endpoints are present but the arc itself — the change, the growth, the reasons Lily eventually loved him — is entirely missing. The film cannot convey the arc because the testimony that establishes it (Sirius, Lupin, Dumbledore) is cut.
character_arc.penalty_logic: The arc is incomplete and missing its most important step: the evidence of change. Without it, the film James is incoherent — a bully who is also a loving father, with no explanation. This is an 8–10 range: arc is incomplete and missing important steps.
character_arc.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for the book arc through corpus testimony; directly evidenced for the film's failure to connect the arc.

key_relationships.book_baseline: James's key relationships are: (1) Lily — complex, evolving from her contempt to eventual love, central to his growth; (2) Sirius — best friend, 'like brothers,' the relationship that defines his social world and leads to the Secret-Keeper decision; (3) Lupin — deep loyalty, the Animagus transformation done for Lupin's sake; (4) Pettigrew — misplaced trust that causes his death; (5) Snape — mutual hatred rooted in jealousy and cruelty, with the complicating fact that James saved Snape's life. Each relationship reveals something essential about James.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The films preserve almost none of these dynamics. The Lily relationship is reduced to a silent mirror reflection and a gravestone. The Sirius friendship is mentioned in PoA but the film cuts the scenes that dramatize it. The Lupin relationship (Animagus transformation) is cut from the PoA film. The Pettigrew relationship and the fatal trust are referenced but not dramatized. The Snape relationship survives in the OotP Pensieve but without the saving-Snape's-life complication.
key_relationships.difference: The emotional dynamics of all five key relationships are either absent or reduced to references. The Lily relationship — the most important — is never shown developing. The Sirius friendship loses its depth. The Lupin loyalty is cut. The Pettigrew betrayal loses its emotional weight because the trust was never established.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: Key relationship dynamics are substantially altered or absent. The loss changes how James is understood — without the Lily arc, his growth is invisible; without the Sirius/Lupin/Pettigrew dynamics, his fatal trust is unmotivated. This is a 5–6 range.
key_relationships.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for what is present and absent in the corpus.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: James's complexity in the books rests on several tensions: he is a bully who becomes a good man; he is brave but reckless; he is loyal but his loyalty kills him; he is arrogant but capable of love; he saves the life of the man who hates him. The Pensieve scene is specifically designed to complicate Harry's idealization, and the subsequent testimony from Sirius, Lupin, and Dumbledore restores a more complete picture. The letter from Lily adds domestic warmth and suppressed frustration. The Godric's Hollow death scene (from Voldemort's POV) shows him dying wandlessly, trying to protect his family.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The films preserve the bullying moment and the tender ghost, but remove almost all the material that makes James complex: the saving of Snape, the Animagus transformation, the Secret-Keeper decision, the letter, the domestic scenes, the testimony from Sirius and Lupin about his growth. The OotP Pensieve scene is present but compressed, and crucially, the film does not include Harry's subsequent moral reckoning with what he saw — the scene that makes the Pensieve moment narratively meaningful.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The contradictions, the growth, the fatal loyalty, the domestic warmth, and Harry's moral reckoning are all absent. What remains is a simplified figure: bully-as-teenager, loving-ghost-as-adult. The material that made James rich — his flaws, his growth, his relationships, his specific acts of agency — is almost entirely lost.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: Major flattening. James is reduced to two gestures without the connective tissue that makes him a complex character. The lost material is not incidental — it is the substance of his characterization. This is a 5–7 range.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for what is present; reasonably inferred for what is absent based on the corpus.

comparative.key_observations: James Potter is one of the most significantly reduced characters in the film adaptations relative to his book importance. The films preserve two data points — teenage bully and loving posthumous father — but remove almost everything that connects and complicates them: the growth arc, the key relationships, the fatal loyalty, the domestic warmth, and Harry's moral reckoning with his father's flaws. The result is a character who is recognizable in outline but hollow in substance. The OotP Pensieve scene is the films' most substantive engagement with James, but even there the compression removes the behavioral texture and the crucial aftermath. The Resurrection Stone scene is faithful in tone but too brief to carry characterization. The score of 56 reflects a portrayal that is superficially present but substantially incomplete.

personality_voice.book_baseline: Book Moody is defined by paranoid vigilance ('CONSTANT VIGILANCE' as a repeated verbal tic), a gravelly growling voice, blunt directness, dark humor, and a willingness to operate outside rules when he judges it necessary. He is simultaneously intimidating and unexpectedly kind — he takes Neville aside after the Cruciatus demonstration, lends him a book, and notices Harry's distress. He is sardonic with authority figures (Karkaroff, Fudge, Snape), openly contemptuous of cowardice and disloyalty, and speaks in short, declarative sentences with occasional harsh laughs. He is also genuinely perceptive — he reads situations quickly, notices Harry under the Invisibility Cloak, spots Crouch on the Marauder's Map, and identifies Snape's arm-grab. His paranoia is presented as both a flaw and a professional asset.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The film preserves the surface markers: the growling voice, the hip flask, the magical eye, 'CONSTANT VIGILANCE,' the ferret incident, the Unforgivable Curses lesson, and the general atmosphere of menace. However, the film Moody is almost entirely the impostor (Barty Crouch Jr.), and the corpus shows that the film collapses the distinction between the real Moody's personality and the impostor's performance. The real Moody appears only briefly in GoF (end scene, twitchy at the feast) and more substantially in OotP. In OotP the film preserves his gruffness, his operational command during the flight from Privet Drive, and his protectiveness of Harry. However, the quieter, more humane dimensions — the Neville kindness, the Marauder's Map conversation, the career advice, the sardonic wit in the Pensieve flashback — are absent.
personality_voice.difference: The film loses the interior texture of Moody's voice: the sardonic asides ('Another old friend,' his commentary on Karkaroff in the Pensieve), the unexpected gentleness with Neville, the dry humor about his own paranoia, and the extended conversational register that shows him as a complex thinker rather than just a menacing presence. The 'CONSTANT VIGILANCE' catchphrase is preserved but the philosophical weight behind it — his extended classroom speeches about preparation, the nature of Dark magic, the Imperius Curse resistance lesson — is compressed. His speech in the film is almost entirely reactive commands and growls; the book's Moody also lectures, reasons aloud, and reveals his worldview.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The core traits (paranoia, gruffness, vigilance, physical distinctiveness, dark authority) are preserved well enough that the character is recognizable. However, important secondary traits — unexpected warmth, sardonic wit, the reasoning mind behind the paranoia — are reduced. The film also conflates the impostor's performance with the real Moody's personality for most of GoF, which means the 'personality' on screen is partly Barty Crouch Jr.'s interpretation. Score sits in the 14-17 range: recognizable but with meaningful reduction of secondary traits and emotional register.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: Book Moody serves multiple narrative functions across GoF and OotP: (1) Defense teacher who genuinely prepares students for Dark magic; (2) active investigator — he searches Snape's office, uses the Marauder's Map to hunt Crouch, confronts Snape on the stairs, and pieces together the conspiracy before anyone else; (3) protector of Harry — he guides Harry toward the Summoning Charm solution, covers for him on the stairs, and patrols the maze; (4) Order veteran who contextualizes the first war through the photograph and Pensieve scenes; (5) the dramatic irony engine — his apparent loyalty and competence make the reveal devastating. In OotP he commands the escort mission, briefs the Order, and is the operational leader of the guard.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: The film preserves his role as Defense teacher (Unforgivable Curses lesson) and the ferret incident. In GoF, his investigative agency is almost entirely removed: the Marauder's Map scene is cut, the Snape confrontation on the stairs is cut, his piecing together of the conspiracy in the teachers' meeting is reduced to one line ('You seem to have given this a fair bit of thought, Mad-Eye' — present in the book but the film version of this scene is compressed). His guidance of Harry toward the Summoning Charm is retained but shortened. In OotP, his operational command of the escort is preserved and he is shown briefing the group, which is faithful. However, his role in the Department of Mysteries battle is minimal on screen — he appears and fights but has no distinct agency. The photograph/Order history scene is transferred to Sirius in the film.
narrative_role_agency.difference: The Marauder's Map scene (where Moody investigates Crouch, covers for Harry, and reveals his obsession with Death Eaters who walked free) is entirely cut. This is a major agency loss: in the book it is the scene that most clearly shows Moody as an active investigator and foreshadows the reveal. The Snape staircase confrontation is cut. His role as the person who most clearly identifies the conspiracy ('Someone put Potter's name in that goblet knowing he'd have to compete') is present in the film but compressed. The photograph scene — where he contextualizes the first war and shows emotional investment in the fallen — is given to Sirius.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: Multiple specific acts of agency are removed or transferred. The Marauder's Map scene is the single most important cut: it is where the real Moody's investigative mind is most visible and where the dramatic irony is sharpest (the impostor is hunting himself). The transfer of the photograph scene to Sirius removes Moody's function as living memory of the first Order. These are not mere compressions — they change what the character does in the story. Score falls into the 6-9 range.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: The real Moody's motivations are: genuine hatred of Dark wizards and those who escaped justice; loyalty to Dumbledore and the Order; a professional ethic that distinguishes him from Death Eaters ('he never killed if he could help it, always brought people in alive'); and a deep, almost obsessive investment in preparedness born from decades of trauma. His internal conflict is subtle: his paranoia is both his greatest strength and a liability that makes him easy to impersonate and isolate. He is also shown to have genuine affection for students like Neville and Harry, which sits in tension with his harsh pedagogical methods.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The film establishes his vigilance and hatred of Dark magic through the classroom scenes and his operational behavior. His protectiveness of Harry is shown. However, his professional ethic (never killing when capture is possible) is never articulated. His emotional investment in the fallen Order members — which in the book motivates his obsessive surveillance of Snape and Karkaroff — is not shown in the film (the photograph scene is Sirius's). His motivation for being at Hogwarts (a favor to Dumbledore, one year only) is mentioned briefly in the classroom scene and is present.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The film does not articulate the distinction between Moody's methods and Death Eater methods, which in the book is a key part of his moral identity. His obsession with Death Eaters who walked free — the motivation that makes the Barty Crouch Jr. reveal so ironic — is not established for the real Moody in the film (it appears only in the impostor's confession). The emotional weight of his investment in the first war's casualties is transferred to Sirius.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: Motivations are partially present (vigilance, loyalty to Dumbledore, protectiveness of Harry) but the deeper layer — the moral code that distinguishes him, the obsession with justice for escaped Death Eaters, the trauma-driven paranoia — is underexplained. This is a meaningful flattening, not just compression. Score in the 8-10 range.

character_arc.book_baseline: Moody's arc across the series is relatively flat in terms of internal change — he is consistently the battle-scarred, paranoid veteran — but has a structural arc: introduced as a legend (GoF pre-Hogwarts), revealed as an impostor (GoF climax), restored as the real person (GoF end, OotP), and killed in action (DH). The arc is about the gap between reputation and reality, and ultimately about a man whose vigilance was not enough to save him. His death in DH is framed as a genuine loss — 'the consummate survivor' who could not survive. The real Moody's brief appearances after the reveal (twitchy at the feast, OotP escort, DH Seven Potters) show a man shaken but still operational.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The film follows the same structural arc: legend → impostor reveal → real Moody in OotP → death in DH. The GoF end scene (real Moody twitchy at the feast) is present. OotP shows him operational. DH shows his death reported by Bill. The arc is compressed but structurally intact.
character_arc.difference: The film compresses the restoration arc — the real Moody's brief GoF appearance is very short, and his OotP presence, while present, omits the photograph scene and the quieter moments that show him processing his imprisonment. His death in DH is handled faithfully (reported off-screen, mourned, toast raised). The arc is present but some of the texture of the post-reveal recovery is missing.
character_arc.penalty_logic: The arc is structurally faithful and the key beats are present. Compression is noticeable but does not fundamentally alter the trajectory. Score in the 11-13 range.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Moody's key relationships: (1) Dumbledore — deep mutual trust, Moody defers to him but also challenges him ('Alastor!' as a warning); (2) Harry — genuine investment in Harry's survival and potential, expressed through the Summoning Charm hint, the career advice, the Marauder's Map scene, and the OotP escort; (3) Snape — open contempt and suspicion, active surveillance, the staircase confrontation is a key scene; (4) Neville — unexpected tenderness, the post-lesson kindness is one of the most humanizing moments for Moody; (5) the Order — he is a founding member, his photograph contextualizes his place in the community of the fallen.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The Dumbledore relationship is present but reduced to brief exchanges. The Harry relationship is shown through the classroom, the Summoning Charm hint, and the OotP escort — partially faithful. The Snape relationship is almost entirely absent: the staircase confrontation is cut, and Snape's wariness of Moody (a key dynamic in the book) is not shown. The Neville relationship is reduced to a brief post-lesson moment without the book's depth (no lending of the book, no extended kindness). The Order relationship loses the photograph scene.
key_relationships.difference: The Snape-Moody dynamic is a significant loss: in the book it establishes Moody as the one person Snape is visibly afraid of, and it drives the subplot about who is surveilling whom. The Neville relationship loses its most humanizing beat. The Order history relationship is transferred to Sirius.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: Two of Moody's five key relationships are substantially weakened (Snape, Neville) and one is transferred (Order history to Sirius). The Harry and Dumbledore relationships are partially preserved. Score in the 5-6 range.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: Book Moody's complexity comes from: the tension between his harshness and his unexpected kindness (Neville); his sardonic self-awareness about his own paranoia ('they say old Mad-Eye's obsessed... but I'm nothing compared to Barty Crouch'); his moral code that distinguishes him from the people he hunts; the dramatic irony of the impostor being more 'Moody-like' in some ways than the real man; his role as living memory of the first war; the Marauder's Map scene where his investigative mind is fully on display; and the OotP photograph scene where his grief for the fallen is visible.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The film preserves the surface complexity (the eye, the leg, the paranoia, the gruffness) but loses most of the interior complexity. The Neville kindness is reduced. The sardonic self-awareness is absent. The moral code is not articulated. The Marauder's Map scene is cut entirely. The photograph scene is transferred. What remains is a vivid but somewhat one-dimensional figure: the scary, paranoid Auror.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The film loses the material that made Moody more than his surface: the unexpected warmth, the self-aware humor, the moral distinctions, the investigative intelligence shown in extended scenes, and the emotional weight of his connection to the first war's dead. These are not incidental — they are what prevent him from being merely a grotesque.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: The character is reduced to a simpler function: intimidating veteran/protector. The contradictions (harsh but kind, paranoid but perceptive, rule-breaking but principled) are mostly lost. Score in the 5-7 range.

comparative.key_observations: The film preserves Moody's iconic surface — the magical eye, the wooden leg, the hip flask, the growling voice, 'CONSTANT VIGILANCE,' the ferret incident, the Unforgivable Curses lesson — well enough that he is immediately recognizable. However, the adaptation loses almost everything that made him complex beneath that surface. The two most damaging cuts are the Marauder's Map scene (his single greatest moment of active agency and investigative intelligence in GoF, and the scene that most sharpens the dramatic irony of the impostor) and the Snape staircase confrontation (which established the only relationship in which Snape was visibly afraid). The transfer of the Order photograph scene to Sirius removes Moody's function as living memory of the first war. The Neville kindness is reduced to a gesture. What remains is a vivid but flattened figure: the scary, paranoid veteran. The film also faces a structural problem unique to this character — for most of GoF, the 'Moody' on screen is Barty Crouch Jr.'s performance, and the film does not clearly distinguish between the impostor's exaggerated version of Moody and the real man's more nuanced personality. The real Moody's brief post-reveal appearances are too short to compensate. The total score of 55 reflects a character who is recognizable and partially faithful in personality and arc, but substantially diminished in agency, relationships, motivation depth, and complexity.

personality_voice.book_baseline: In the books, Alecto is introduced as a stocky, grinning Death Eater who jeers at Dumbledore with contemptuous mockery ('Think your little jokes'll help you on your death bed, then?'). She is cruel, eager, and gleeful in the presence of power over others. As Muggle Studies teacher under Snape's regime, she is an instrument of terror and ideological enforcement. Her pressing the Dark Mark to summon Voldemort when she catches Harry is a cold, decisive act of loyalty and threat.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The single film scene shows Alecto threatening a small girl (Maisy Reynolds) with a visit to her father - a menacing, sadistic taunt delivered with casual cruelty. The tone is consistent with her book characterization: she uses fear and implied violence against the vulnerable.
personality_voice.difference: The film captures her cruelty and her role as an enforcer of terror, but the corpus is far too limited to assess voice, speech patterns, emotional range, or the full texture of her personality. The jeering, eager quality from the Astronomy Tower scene is not directly evidenced in the film corpus.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The one film scene is consistent with her book personality - cruel, threatening, enjoying power over the weak. No contradictory traits are introduced. However, the corpus is too thin to confirm preservation of her full voice and behavioral pattern. Score reflects consistency of what is shown, penalized for insufficient evidence to confirm broader preservation.
personality_voice.evidence_status: Directly evidenced (cruelty, intimidation of students); Not enough evidence (speech patterns, emotional range, eagerness/gleeful quality from book scenes)

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: In the books, Alecto has two distinct narrative functions: (1) as one of the Death Eaters who breaches Hogwarts and enables Dumbledore's death - she is part of the group that corners Dumbledore on the Astronomy Tower; (2) as Muggle Studies teacher under the Death Eater regime at Hogwarts in Deathly Hallows, enforcing ideological terror, and crucially, she is the one who catches Harry in Ravenclaw Tower and summons Voldemort by pressing her Dark Mark - a pivotal plot action that triggers the final battle.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: The film corpus shows only one scene: Alecto herding Ravenclaw students and threatening a child. This is a background enforcement role. The pivotal act of summoning Voldemort - her most significant narrative agency in the books - is not present in the film corpus provided.
narrative_role_agency.difference: Her most important act of agency (pressing the Dark Mark to summon Voldemort, triggering the endgame of Deathly Hallows) is absent from the film corpus. Whether this was transferred to another character or simply cut cannot be confirmed from the corpus alone, but its absence represents a major loss of narrative function.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: The corpus shows her only in a minor enforcement role. Her book function as the trigger of the final battle's commencement is not evidenced in the film corpus. This is a significant agency loss. Score reflects that she retains a functional (if reduced) enforcement role but loses her most consequential plot action.
narrative_role_agency.evidence_status: Directly evidenced (student enforcement role); Not enough evidence (Astronomy Tower presence, Dark Mark summoning in films)

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Alecto's motivations are straightforward: fanatical Death Eater loyalty to Voldemort, belief in pure-blood supremacy, and enjoyment of cruelty and power. There is no internal conflict - she is ideologically committed and acts without hesitation. Her pressing the Dark Mark the instant she catches Harry confirms total, reflexive loyalty.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The film scene shows her threatening a student with a visit to the child's father - implying she has already used violence against the family. This is consistent with pure-blood enforcement ideology and enjoyment of power over the vulnerable.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: No internal conflict exists in the books, and none is introduced in the films. Motivations are consistent. The corpus is too limited to confirm full preservation, but nothing contradicts the book baseline.

The arc is intentionally flat.

character_arc.difference: No arc exists in the books; none is shown in the films. This is appropriate.

The sibling dynamic with Amycus is the most distinctive relational element.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The film corpus shows no interaction with Amycus. She appears alone, interacting only with students she is herding. The sibling pair dynamic - which is how she is introduced and defined in the books - is absent from the corpus.
key_relationships.difference: The Amycus-Alecto pairing, which is the most characteristically defining relational element in the books, is not evidenced in the film corpus. Her relationship with students as terrorizer is present but minimal.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: The absence of the sibling dynamic from the film corpus is a notable loss of her most distinctive relational texture. Whether it exists elsewhere in the films cannot be confirmed. Score reflects this gap.
