personality_voice.book_baseline: In the books, Justin is established with a distinct, layered personality across multiple encounters. He is friendly, socially confident, and eager to belong: he introduces himself warmly to Harry, Hermione, and Ron by name in Herbology (Scene 3–4), demonstrates class-conscious pride in his Muggle background (references Eton, his mother's expectations, his family wanting a trained wizard), and shows enthusiastic if credulous admiration for Lockhart (Scene 6–7). He is also capable of fear-driven hostility: when he believes Harry is dangerous, he avoids him (Scene 9), storms out of the Duelling Club angrily after the snake incident (Scene 30), and hides in his dormitory on Ernie's advice (Scene 48). His voice is direct, sociable, and lightly upper-class in register ('My name was down for Eton, you know'). He can hold a grudge (avoiding Harry for weeks, laughing at him in Herbology in Book 3 over the Bouncing Bulbs), but also apologises sincerely and at length once cleared (Scene 84). He is not passive: he reacts, confronts, and then reconciles on his own terms.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: In the theatrical film, Justin's self-introduction scene before the Duelling Club has been cut per the non-theatrical exclusion instruction. This removes the only film moment where Justin speaks proactively, introduces himself, references Lockhart enthusiastically, and exhibits his sociable, class-tinged voice. What remains in the theatrical cut is: Justin standing near Harry at the Duelling Club where the snake is directed at him (he says one line: 'What are you playing at?' before backing away in terror), and a brief non-speaking appearance in the final feast scene where he rejoins the Hufflepuffs. The single retained line — 'What are you playing at?' — does preserve the fear-and-hostility response that is present in the books, but it strips it of the preceding context (the warm self-introduction, the Lockhart enthusiasm, the class pride) that gives it emotional texture. The film Justin is a near-silent victim figure with one reactive line.
personality_voice.difference: The books establish Justin as friendly, socially assertive, credulous about Lockhart, and class-conscious before he becomes fearful of Harry. The film removes all of this proactive personality and reduces him to a single frightened reaction. His voice, humor, social ease, Muggle-world pride, and Lockhart enthusiasm are entirely absent from what reaches the screen. The sustained pattern of avoidance followed by sincere reconciliation (Book 2 ending) and later the cold-shoulder behavior in Book 3 (Herbology scene) are also absent.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The loss of the self-introduction scene (cut from theatrical release) removes the primary evidence for Justin's personality and voice — his directness, warmth, class-conscious humor, and Lockhart credulity. What remains is one frightened reactive line. This is a substantial personality reduction: the character is recognisable as 'a Muggle-born student who fears Harry' but the traits that defined him beyond that function are absent. Score placed in the 10–13 range: personality is substantially altered in several important scenes, though 'What are you playing at?' does preserve at minimum his confrontational fear response from the books.
personality_voice.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for book baseline across multiple scenes. Film portrayal directly evidenced by what remains in the theatrical cut (one line, one silent appearance). The cut introduction scene is excluded per instruction.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: Justin serves several distinct narrative functions in the books. First, he is a named, individualised Muggle-born student whose fear of Harry makes the Chamber of Secrets threat personal and socially costly for Harry: Justin's avoidance after the snake incident (Scene 9), Ernie's conversation about him hiding in the dormitory (Scene 48), and Harry's active effort to find and clear his name with Justin (Scenes 44–55) all give Justin agency as a social antagonist whose suspicion Harry must navigate. Second, Justin is a victim of the Basilisk whose Petrification is a major plot beat (Scene 58–73) and whose eventual revival is a marker of the story's resolution (Scene 84). Third, in later books (Order of the Phoenix), Justin is a named DA member who participates in the defence against Malfoy, Crabbe and Goyle on the Hogwarts Express (Scene 97), demonstrating active loyalty and agency as a trained fighter. Justin also provides Harry's connection to the broader Hufflepuff social world and to Muggle-born vulnerability as a theme.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: In the theatrical cut, Justin's narrative role is reduced to: (1) being the person the snake is aimed at during the Duelling Club, triggering the Parseltongue revelation — a plot function he retains but does not actively drive; (2) lying Petrified in the corridor (a visual beat, no speech or agency); (3) silently rejoining the Hufflepuffs at the end-of-year feast. The DA subplot (Book 5) is absent from the film corpus provided, so the Order of the Phoenix material cannot be credited or evaluated here. The key agency loss is that Justin's role as a social obstacle Harry actively tries to resolve — the scenes where Harry seeks him out, confronts the Hufflepuffs, and tries to repair his reputation — is largely stripped. Ernie's conversation about Justin hiding is present in the film corpus (Scene 73 of the film), but Justin himself has no agency in any of these sequences in the theatrical cut.
narrative_role_agency.difference: The book Justin is both a passive victim and an active social agent whose suspicion Harry must work to overcome. The film Justin is only a passive victim and an incidental trigger for the Parseltongue revelation. His role as a figure Harry pursues and must clear his name with is present in the screenplay but entirely through Ernie's dialogue — Justin himself never appears in those scenes with any lines or action.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: Justin's core plot function (Petrification victim, Parseltongue trigger) is preserved. However, his agency as a social antagonist — the scenes requiring Harry to seek him out and address his suspicion — is absent from what Justin himself does on screen. The role is partially present through other characters' dialogue about him (Ernie), but Justin's own agency in that dynamic is gone. This is a meaningful reduction: the character's narrative role is recognisable but materially weakened. Score in the 10–13 range.
narrative_role_agency.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for book baseline. Film portrayal directly evidenced by absence of Justin's lines/actions in relevant scenes.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Justin's motivations are clear and consistent in the books. He is a Muggle-born who is proud of his background and has actively chosen the wizarding world (Eton reference, converting his mother), but that background also makes him vulnerable: once the Chamber of Secrets attacks begin, fear for his safety motivates his hostility toward Harry. His internal conflict is mild but present: he wants to belong to the wizarding world and trust its heroes (he was friendly with Harry before), but his fear and the plausible-seeming evidence (Parseltongue, Slytherin's heir) override that. This conflict resolves in his sincere apology at the feast. He also has a brief social-pressure dimension: Ernie's group gossip shapes his behavior, suggesting susceptibility to peer influence alongside his personal fear.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: In the theatrical cut, Justin's motivations are inferrable only from his one line and his Petrification. The fear motivation is present in 'What are you playing at?' but the fuller picture — his pride in being Muggle-born, the specific conflict between his earlier friendliness toward Harry and his subsequent fear, the peer-pressure element, and the resolution through apology — is absent. The film never shows why Justin in particular fears Harry beyond being the person the snake approached.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The motivation (fear as a Muggle-born) is partially present by implication but is not developed or complicated. The internal conflict between prior friendliness and current fear, and the resolution of that conflict, are absent. What remains is fear without texture.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: The core motivation (Muggle-born fear of the heir) survives in implication, but it is underexplained and the internal conflict (prior warmth vs. current fear, personal resolution) is absent. This is a partial alteration — the motivation is not opposite or absent, but it is flattened significantly. Score in the 8–10 range.
motivations_internal_conflict.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for book baseline. Film portrayal: reasonably inferred from the single line and Petrification scene.

The arc is compact but complete: he begins trusting, becomes suspicious, and ends apologetic. The arc is therefore truncated at both ends: no warm beginning, no reconciliation. What remains is only the fearful middle.

character_arc.penalty_logic: The arc is missing its beginning and its resolution. The character's journey from trust to fear to reconciliation — which is the entirety of his meaningful arc in Book 2 — is reduced to fear only. This is an incomplete, rushed presentation that removes important steps. Score in the 8–10 range.

This relationship is important because it shows Harry's social cost during the Chamber of Secrets crisis and humanises Justin as someone who must overcome fear to do the right thing. Justin's relationship with Ernie Macmillan is also relevant: Ernie shapes Justin's fear response and speaks for him, suggesting Justin is part of a peer group where he defers to Ernie's more extreme suspicion. In Order of the Phoenix, Justin's relationship with Harry takes a positive turn as a DA member who fights alongside him.

The apology — which is the emotional resolution of their relationship — is absent. The Ernie dynamic exists in the film (Ernie talks about Justin hiding) but Justin himself has no lines in that context. The relationship is present only as a one-sided fear reaction.
key_relationships.difference: The dynamic, arc, and resolution of the Harry-Justin relationship are absent from the theatrical film. What survives is only the fear beat. The reconciliation that defines the relationship's final state is gone. The Ernie peer-group dynamic is partially present but entirely mediated through Ernie, not Justin.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: The emotional dynamic of the Harry-Justin relationship — warm start, fearful middle, reconciling end — is reduced to the fearful middle only. This substantially changes how the relationship reads. The peer-group dimension with Ernie is technically present but entirely off-screen from Justin's side. Score in the 3–4 range: key relationships are heavily flattened.
key_relationships.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for book baseline. Film portrayal directly evidenced.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: Justin's complexity in the books comes from several layered elements: (1) the class-conscious Muggle pride (Eton reference, converting his mother) that makes him a specific, textured individual rather than a generic Muggle-born; (2) the Lockhart enthusiasm that shows his credulity and social optimism; (3) the specific shame and social pressure of hiding in the dormitory rather than confronting Harry directly; (4) his eventual courage in apologising publicly and sincerely at the feast; (5) the brief Book 3 relapse into coldness (Bouncing Bulbs scene) that shows residual embarrassment rather than clean resolution; (6) his active DA participation and loyalty in Order of the Phoenix. Together these give Justin a personality that exceeds his plot function.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: In the theatrical cut, almost all of this material is absent. The Eton reference and class pride are gone (introduction scene cut). The Lockhart credulity is gone (same scene cut). The hiding-in-dormitory dynamic is present in the film corpus through Ernie's dialogue but Justin himself is absent from that sequence. The public apology is gone. The Book 3 Herbology relapse is not in scope here. The DA material is not in the provided film corpus. What survives is one frightened line and a silent background appearance.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The entirety of what makes Justin a character beyond 'Muggle-born victim' has been removed from the theatrical cut: his social voice, his class-conscious humor, his credulity about Lockhart, his peer-group dynamics, and his reconciliation. The lost introduction scene was the primary carrier of almost all his personality texture.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: The character is reduced to a near-silent victim function. The material that distinguished Justin as an individual — rather than an interchangeable Muggle-born student — is almost entirely absent. This is major flattening into a single function. Score in the 5–7 range.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for book baseline. Film portrayal directly evidenced by theatrical absence of key scenes.

score_caps_applied: Cap 4 (score above 70 not applicable): The film preserves only Justin's broad identity as a Muggle-born student who fears Harry; most of what defines his book characterisation — personality, voice, arc resolution, relational dynamic, nuance — is removed.

comparative.key_observations: Justin Finch-Fletchley is a case where a single scene excision — his Herbology/Duelling Club self-introduction, excluded from the theatrical release — strips away almost everything that made him a distinct character in the books. What survives theatrically is one frightened reactive line ('What are you playing at?') and a silent appearance at the end-of-year feast. His book characterisation rests on several interlocking elements: the warm, class-conscious, Lockhart-credulous personality established in Herbology; his role as a social obstacle Harry must actively pursue and reconcile with; the arc from trust through fear to apology; and the peer-group dynamics with Ernie. All of these are absent or reduced to near-zero in the theatrical film. The Petrification plot function and the Parseltongue-trigger function are both retained, but these are structural uses of Justin rather than characterisation of him. The result is a character who is recognisable in broad outline (Muggle-born student, afraid of Harry, Petrified) but has been functionally hollowed out. The score of 51 reflects that the core plot role is intact but the character beneath it has been almost entirely lost.

personality_voice.book_baseline: In the books, Tonks is established across OotP as a vivid, irreverent personality defined by several consistent traits: infectious enthusiasm and cheerfulness (she volunteers eagerly, exclaims 'Wotcher Harry!', entertains at dinner by morphing her nose), self-deprecating humor about her clumsiness and domestic incompetence ('I'm dead clumsy'), directness and informality (insisting on 'Tonks' over 'Nymphadora'), and physical expressiveness (her Metamorphmagus ability mirrors her emotional state as a literal visual cue). She is also sharp and situationally aware — she warns the Knight Bus conductor with menace ('If you shout his name I will curse you into oblivion'), argues confidently with Moody mid-flight, and engages substantively with Order intelligence. In HBP, her voice changes completely and deliberately: she becomes withdrawn, silent, mousy-haired, and emotionally hollow — a portrait of grief and survivor's guilt rendered with great specificity. In DH she is radiant again ('simply radiant') upon reconciliation with Lupin, and her final appearances show a woman of conviction and courage. The voice across all three books is consistently individuated — colloquial, energetic in health, visibly broken in grief, specific in diction ('Wotcher,' 'dead clumsy,' 'I owe Bellatrix').
personality_voice.film_portrayal: In the films, Tonks's personality is present but severely compressed. In OotP (Film 1 in the corpus), she gets one exchange establishing her name aversion ('Don't call me Nymphadora') and one line of reassurance to Harry ('Don't worry, Harry, we'll explain everything'). The cheerfulness, clumsiness, self-deprecating humor, nose-morphing mealtime entertainment, and enthusiastic volunteerism that define her book personality in OotP are entirely absent from the film corpus. In HBP (Film 2 corpus), she appears briefly at a Christmas scene where she supports Harry's suspicion about Snape ('Perhaps Harry's right, Remus'), and leaves the Burrow — contextually suggesting her depression, though no mousy hair, no hollow expression, no explicit grief characterization appears in the film corpus text. In DH Part 1 (Film 3 corpus), she announces her pregnancy at Privet Drive ('My husband, the joker. By the way, wait until you hear the news! Remus and I are —') in a bright, warm moment, and praises Ron warmly ('Deserves that. Brilliant, he was'). At the wedding she whispers to Mrs. Weasley about her pregnancy with visible happiness. The theatrical Battle of Hogwarts scene (DH Part 2) has her only as a visual presence in the Great Hall — fingers intertwined with Lupin's in death. The scene of Tonks arriving at the Battle to fight beside Lupin is explicitly cut and excluded from scoring. The result is that the film preserves the broad markers of her personality (informal address, warmth, occasional directness) but eliminates the texture: the clumsiness comedy, the nose-morphing personality, the specific wit and irreverence, and critically, the entire HBP arc of depression and its distinctive voice.
personality_voice.difference: The most significant loss is the HBP personality register: the withdrawn, grey, emotionally devastated Tonks who speaks in flat monosyllables, avoids eye contact, and wanders the castle in misery. This is not a minor compression — it is the dominant characterization of Tonks across an entire book. The OotP personality is also flattened: the clumsiness jokes, dinner table morphing, mid-flight arguments with Moody, and volunteer enthusiasm are absent. What remains is a pleasant, warm background presence without the comic energy, specific voice, or emotional depth the books give her.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The book establishes two distinct and well-evidenced personality phases: vivid, clumsy, irreverent (OotP) and grief-hollowed, subdued, almost unrecognizable (HBP). The film preserves the first in outline only (name aversion survives, warmth survives) and eliminates the second almost entirely. The clumsiness — a defining physical-comedic trait across dozens of OotP scenes — has no film presence. The HBP voice transformation, explicitly described in the book as affecting her Metamorphmagus ability and speech patterns, is absent from the scored film corpus. This is not compression that preserves character; it is compression that removes defining traits. Score placed at 14 (character remains recognizable, important traits and tone reduced).

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: Tonks serves multiple distinct narrative functions across the books. In OotP: she is an active escort and protector (she leads the broomstick formation, carries Harry's trunk, lures the Dursleys away with the fake lawn competition letter — an act of initiative and wit she personally devises), she is an informant about Ministry politics (explains Fudge's fear of Voldemort), she is a source of warmth and humor within Grimmauld Place, and she fights meaningfully at the Department of Mysteries (firing spells at Death Eaters, being felled by Bellatrix). In HBP: she is a mystery — her changed Patronus, her visits to Hogwarts, her emotional collapse — and functions as a living signal of how the war affects individuals personally. Her agency is real: she takes initiative in visiting Dumbledore, she engineers her own emotional confrontation with Lupin at Bill's bedside. In DH: she partners with Ron during the Seven Potters escape (her pair escapes Death Eaters and she praises Ron's Stunner), she is part of the Order's active resistance, and most critically she abandons her infant son to fight at the Battle of Hogwarts — an act of autonomous moral decision-making that costs her life. Her death is narratively significant precisely because she made that choice.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: In OotP (film), Tonks's narrative role is reduced to a member of the rescue party with minimal individual function. She says 'Don't worry, Harry' and 'Don't call me Nymphadora' — her most significant OotP action, luring the Dursleys away, is absent. She plays no distinct role in the Department of Mysteries battle as captured in the film corpus. In HBP (film), she appears at the Christmas dinner briefly, supporting Harry's theory about Snape, and departs — no agency beyond a conversational contribution. In DH Part 1 (film), she announces her pregnancy, praises Ron's bravery after the Seven Potters escape, and appears at the wedding. Her most significant DH agency moment — the decision to leave Teddy and fight at Hogwarts — is explicitly a cut scene and cannot be credited. In DH Part 2 (film), she appears only as a corpse in the Great Hall with fingers intertwined with Lupin's. The agency of her final choice (leaving her infant to fight) is completely removed from the scored film.
narrative_role_agency.difference: The luring of the Dursleys (OotP agency) is absent. The Department of Mysteries fighting is not individually rendered in the film corpus. The HBP visits to Hogwarts and confrontation with Lupin are compressed to near-invisibility. The DH Battle of Hogwarts arrival — her most consequential autonomous act — is a cut scene. What remains is a supportive background presence who praises others (Ron), announces pregnancies, and dies offscreen.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: Multiple specific acts of agency are absent or transferred: the Dursley ruse (her initiative), the Lupin confrontation at Bill's bedside (her emotional forcing of the relationship resolution), and the Battle of Hogwarts arrival (her moral choice). The golden rule applies: her most defining act of agency in DH — choosing to fight over staying with her child — is cut entirely. Her narrative function collapses from active protector, intelligence source, and moral agent to a peripheral Order member who dies between scenes. Score at 10 (role and agency clearly altered).

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Tonks's motivations are layered and evolve across the series. In OotP, she is driven by loyalty to Dumbledore and the Order, professional pride as an Auror, and genuine warmth toward Harry. In HBP, her motivations become dominated by two intersecting forces: survivor's guilt (she blames herself for Sirius's death because she failed to stop Bellatrix) and unrequited love for Lupin (she has fallen for him and he refuses the relationship on grounds of age, poverty, and werewolf status). These two motivations compound each other — she is depressed, her Metamorphmagus ability is failing, she is isolated. Her internal conflict is explicit: she wants Lupin to accept her love and acknowledge the relationship is not doomed by his condition. In DH, her motivation is reconciled (they marry) but a new conflict emerges: she must balance protection of her newborn son against her loyalty to the Order and her desire to fight. The corpus confirms she resolves this conflict by leaving Teddy with her mother to join the battle — a decision explicitly described as anguished ('I couldn't stand not knowing').
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: In the films, Tonks's survivor's guilt is entirely absent — there is no scene in the film corpus where this motivation is established or explored. Her love for Lupin is established obliquely in HBP (she appears at the Christmas dinner and there is clearly something between them) and confirmed in DH Part 1 (she announces their marriage and pregnancy). The tension of Lupin resisting the relationship — his stated reasons of being 'too old, too poor, too dangerous' — has some film presence in the HBP dinner scene context, but the depth and specificity of the internal conflict is not established. The DH conflict between motherhood and duty is cut (the Battle of Hogwarts arrival scene is excluded), so her final and most acute motivation — the anguished choice to fight — does not exist in the scored film.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: Survivor's guilt is entirely absent. The specific texture of Lupin's resistance and Tonks's persistence across HBP is reduced to implication. The DH anguish of leaving Teddy is eliminated by the scene cut. What remains is a woman who loves Lupin, marries him, and has his baby — the motivational skeleton without the flesh of conflict.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: The survivor's guilt motivation is not poorly explained — it is absent. This is a change, not a compression. The DH motivational conflict (mother vs. fighter) is eliminated entirely by the cut scene. The love-for-Lupin motivation survives in outline but without the internal conflict that gives it dramatic weight. Score at 8 (motivations partially altered and flattened).

character_arc.book_baseline: Tonks's arc across the books is clearly defined and spans three phases: (1) OotP — introduction as a vivid, clumsy, enthusiastic young Auror who is fully functional and joyful; (2) HBP — emotional collapse driven by survivor's guilt and unrequited love, manifesting in changed appearance, altered Patronus, withdrawal, and diminished Metamorphmagus ability; (3) DH — partial restoration via marriage and pregnancy, but culminating in the ultimate expression of her values: sacrificing her life by choosing to fight beside her husband rather than stay safe with her infant. The arc moves from vitality → grief → reconciled sacrifice. Key turning points are: Sirius's death (triggering the collapse), Lupin's acceptance at Bill's bedside (triggering restoration), and the decision to enter the Battle of Hogwarts (completing the arc with her death). The arc is complete and structurally deliberate.
character_arc.film_portrayal: In the films: Phase 1 (OotP) is present only as a sketch — Tonks is introduced as a young, friendly Auror, but the defining characterization that would make Phase 2 meaningful is absent. Phase 2 (HBP collapse) is almost entirely absent from the film corpus — her depression, changed Patronus, and emotional withdrawal are not depicted in any scored film scene. The HBP film has her briefly in the Christmas dinner scene appearing to support Harry, with no depiction of the grief arc. Phase 3 (DH reconciliation) is partially present — the pregnancy announcement and the wedding scene communicate happiness — but the culminating act of sacrifice that completes the arc is the cut Battle of Hogwarts arrival scene. She dies in the film, but the arc that gives her death meaning — the conscious choice to leave her child — is removed.
character_arc.difference: The entire middle phase of the arc (HBP grief) is missing. The culminating act of the arc (DH choice to fight) is cut. What remains is introduction and death, without the transformation that connects them. The arc cannot be described as compressed — it is structurally absent.
character_arc.penalty_logic: A character arc requires its turning points to exist. The HBP phase is the emotional core of Tonks's arc — it is what makes her DH happiness meaningful and her death devastating. Its absence means the films portray a character who is introduced, marries, has a baby, and dies, without any of the internal journey that the books construct. The cut Battle of Hogwarts scene removes the arc's final beat. Score at 7 (arc significantly altered — the middle phase is missing and the culminating beat is cut).

key_relationships.book_baseline: Tonks's two most important relationships are: (1) Tonks and Lupin — the central emotional relationship of her arc, defined by her persistent love, his guilt-driven resistance, their eventual reconciliation, marriage, and joint death; it is the relationship that drives her HBP depression, changes her Patronus, and gives her DH arc its meaning. (2) Tonks and the Order (especially Mad-Eye Moody) — Mad-Eye is described as her mentor and the person who trained her, she is his 'favourite and his protégée at the Ministry.' Her grief at his death is singled out as specific and personal. Secondary: her relationship with Sirius (distant cousins, she cares about him and feels guilt for his death) and her relationship with Harry (warm, slightly teasing, genuinely protective).
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The Tonks-Lupin relationship exists in the films but is dramatically compressed. The tension and resistance that defines HBP — Lupin's stated reasons, Tonks's seizing of his robes and shaking him, the public confrontation witnessed by Harry, Mrs. Weasley, and Mr. Weasley — is entirely absent from the scored film corpus. The film establishes their marriage and pregnancy but skips the conflict that made the relationship dramatically textured. Their shared death (fingers intertwined) is an emotionally resonant image in the film, but it is the conclusion of a relationship that was never fully dramatized. The Tonks-Moody relationship is not present at all in the scored film scenes — her grief at his death, her being his protégée, are not depicted. The Tonks-Harry relationship is present but minimal (one reassuring line in OotP, one rescue at the train station in HBP which is not in the film corpus).
key_relationships.difference: The Tonks-Lupin relationship survives as a fact (they are married, she loves him) but the emotional dynamic — specifically the conflict, her persistence, and his resistance — is absent. The Tonks-Moody mentorship relationship is entirely absent from the scored film. The grief at Sirius that drives her HBP characterization is absent.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: The relationship that defines Tonks's character across HBP and DH (Lupin) is present in outline but its dynamic is removed. The secondary relationship that defines a key emotional beat in DH (Moody as mentor) is absent entirely. Per the scoring rubric, penalizing because the emotional dynamic and function of these relationships is altered or absent, not simply because there are fewer scenes. Score at 5 (important relationship dynamics altered or weakened).

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: Tonks's book complexity rests on several interlocking elements: (1) The comedic-physical texture of clumsiness and Metamorphmagus play that makes her charming and individuated in OotP; (2) The counterintuitive HBP portrait of a skilled Auror reduced to emotional wreckage — contradicting her OotP competence and revealing the cost of war on individuals; (3) The specificity of her survivor's guilt (not general grief but the specific belief that she should have stopped Bellatrix); (4) The Patronus as a living symbol of internal state — its transformation to a werewolf shape is one of the book's subtler pieces of characterization; (5) The DH tension between her role as new mother and her identity as a fighter; (6) Her relationship with her family background (half-blood, Andromeda's daughter, Black family tapestry connection); (7) Her death as the consequence of a deliberate moral choice, not random battle casualty. These layers make her a character who is simultaneously comic, tragic, professional, in love, politically embedded, and morally purposeful.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The films preserve: her name, her Auror status, her love for Lupin, her pregnancy, her death in battle. They eliminate: the entire clumsiness comedy texture of OotP, the HBP grief arc and its specific cause, the Patronus symbolism (never depicted in film as a changed werewolf shape), the Moody mentorship, the survivor's guilt, the Black family connection, and the DH choice to fight over staying with Teddy. The image of Tonks and Lupin with intertwined fingers is genuinely moving but it is the residue of complexity rather than complexity itself — the audience cannot know what it costs her unless the prior characterization exists.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The films retain Tonks's identity and broad function (Order member, Lupin's wife) while removing most of what makes her a fully realized individual. The comedy texture of OotP, the tragedy texture of HBP, and the moral texture of DH are all substantially absent.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: The simplification is major. The surviving film portrayal reduces Tonks to: warm, married-to-Lupin, dies in battle. This is the outline of the character without her substance. The HBP arc — arguably the most complex portrayal of how war damages an individual in the entire series, told through a secondary character — is absent. The DH moral choice is cut. The OotP personality texture is present only in trace form. Score at 7 (major flattening; character reduced to simpler function). Cap rule 1 applies: a major part of complexity, agency, and narrative function is removed.

comparative.key_observations: Tonks is one of the most substantially altered major supporting characters in the adaptation. The films preserve her identity — her name, her Auror status, her love for Lupin, her marriage, her pregnancy, her death — but almost entirely remove the characterization that makes her interesting: the vivid, clumsy, irreverent OotP personality; the devastating HBP grief arc driven by survivor's guilt and unrequited love; the Patronus symbolism; her mentor relationship with Moody; and critically, her final act of autonomous moral agency — leaving her newborn son to fight beside her husband. Her death in the film is visually poignant (fingers intertwined with Lupin's) but narratively hollow because the arc that would make it devastating has not been built. The film portrayal is recognizable but not faithful: it is the skeleton of a character rather than the character herself.

personality_voice.book_baseline: Percy is defined by a dense, consistent cluster of traits across all seven books: pomposity, rule-obsession, ambition, self-importance, and a deep need for external validation through titles and authority. His voice is verbose, formal, and self-congratulatory. He lectures, corrects, and moralizes. He is also capable of genuine warmth (pride in Ron at chess, concern for Ginny), vulnerability (the Penelope secret, his breakdown over Fred), and self-awareness (his return in DH where he explicitly calls himself 'a pompous prat'). His speech patterns are distinctive: long sentences, formal register, frequent invocation of his titles ('I am a prefect,' 'I'm Head Boy'), and a tendency to repeat himself for emphasis. He is also the target of sustained mockery from Fred and George, which he endures with stiff dignity. His flaw is not cruelty but a catastrophic misjudgment of where loyalty should lie, driven by insecurity about his family's poverty and his own need to be taken seriously.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The films preserve Percy's pomposity and rule-enforcement in Years 1-2 (leading first years, confronting Malfoy as prefect, the Polyjuice corridor scene). His formal register and title-invocation are present. However, the films strip away almost all of his interior life: his ambition, his career arc, his relationship with Penelope, his idolization of Crouch, his political betrayal of his family, and his eventual breakdown and return. In the Deathly Hallows Part 1 film corpus, Percy appears only as a background Ministry functionary with no dialogue of substance. His DH return and reconciliation — including his explicit self-condemnation ('I was a pompous prat') and his dueling of Thicknesse with the line 'Did I mention I'm resigning?' — are absent from the film corpus provided, though they occur in DH Part 2 (not represented here). The film Percy is recognizable as pompous and rule-bound but is reduced to a recurring background figure whose defining traits are present only in surface form.
personality_voice.difference: The films preserve the surface personality (pomposity, formality, title-obsession) but remove the depth: the ambition that drives him, the insecurity beneath the pomposity, the capacity for genuine emotion (pride, love, grief), and the self-awareness that culminates in his return. His voice is present in early films but becomes functionally absent from GoF onward. The Weatherby humiliation scene — one of the richest comic-character moments in the books — is absent. His sanctimonious laugh at Dumbledore's expense in OotP (film corpus scene 11 shows him only as a silent background figure at the Ministry hearing) removes a key moment of his moral compromise.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The surface traits are preserved in Years 1-2, justifying a score above the lowest bands. However, the removal of his interior life, the loss of his distinctive voice in the later films, and his reduction to a background extra from GoF onward constitute significant simplification. The score sits in the 14-17 range: recognizable but with important traits, contradictions, and emotional texture reduced.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: Percy serves multiple narrative functions across the series: (1) comic foil to Fred and George, (2) authority figure and rule-enforcer for Harry and Ron, (3) a structural warning about institutional loyalty vs. family loyalty, (4) a plot-relevant figure in GoF (his proximity to Crouch, his role in the Ministry's cover-up), (5) a source of genuine dramatic tension in OotP (his letter to Ron, his appearance at Harry's hearing, his public alignment with Fudge against Dumbledore), and (6) a redemption figure in DH (his return, his dueling of Thicknesse, his grief over Fred). He initiates actions, makes consequential choices, and changes the emotional landscape of scenes. In GoF, his idolization of Crouch and his dismissal of Winky are active positions that reveal his character and foreshadow his later betrayal. In OotP, his letter to Ron is a direct act of agency — he chooses to try to separate Ron from Harry and align with the Ministry.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: In Years 1-2, Percy retains some agency: he leads first years, enforces rules, confronts Malfoy. In the Polyjuice scene (film corpus scene 9), he challenges Harry and Ron (as Crabbe and Goyle) and asserts his authority. However, from GoF onward, Percy's narrative role is almost entirely eliminated. His GoF function — proximity to Crouch, his role in the Ministry's response to the World Cup attack, his promotion to Crouch's personal assistant, his appearance at the Yule Ball — is absent from the film corpus. His OotP role — the letter to Ron, his appearance at Harry's hearing as a silent note-taker, his public endorsement of Umbridge — is reduced to a background presence. His DH return and the 'Did I mention I'm resigning?' moment are not in the provided film corpus. The film Percy does not initiate, decide, or change events in any meaningful way after Year 2.
narrative_role_agency.difference: Percy's agency is almost entirely removed from GoF onward. His most consequential narrative acts — the family betrayal, the letter to Ron, the Ministry alignment, the return and reconciliation — are either absent or reduced to silent background appearances. His function as a structural warning about institutional loyalty is lost. The transfer of narrative weight to other characters (Fudge, Umbridge, Scrimgeour) means Percy's specific contribution to the Ministry storyline disappears.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: This is a severe agency loss. Percy's role in Years 1-2 is partially preserved, but his entire GoF-DH narrative function is eliminated or reduced to decoration. The score falls in the 10-13 range: role and agency are clearly altered, with his later functions essentially removed.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Percy's motivations are layered and consistent: (1) a desperate need to escape the stigma of his family's poverty and his father's low status at the Ministry; (2) a genuine belief in rules and institutions as the path to a better world; (3) ambition — he explicitly wants to be Minister of Magic; (4) a need for external validation through titles and authority; (5) an internal conflict between family loyalty and institutional loyalty that culminates in his betrayal and eventual return. His internal conflict is made explicit in OotP: he accuses his father of having 'no ambition,' of dragging the family down, and chooses the Ministry over his family. This is not simple villainy — it is a recognizable human failure, driven by shame and ambition. His return in DH is motivated by the same self-awareness: he explicitly acknowledges he was wrong.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The films establish Percy as ambitious and rule-obsessed but never explain why. His motivation to be Minister of Magic (established in CoS book, scene 100) is absent. His internal conflict over family vs. institution is entirely absent — the family betrayal arc is not depicted in the films at all. The film Percy has no discernible internal conflict: he is simply pompous and rule-bound, without the shame, ambition, or institutional loyalty that drive his book counterpart. His motivations are reduced to 'he likes rules and titles,' which is a surface reading that misses the psychological core.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The motivations are present only in their most superficial form. The shame about his family's poverty, the ambition to be Minister, the internal conflict between family and institution — all absent. The films show what Percy does (enforces rules, defers to authority) but not why, and the 'why' is what makes him a complex character rather than a comic type.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: Motivations are partially altered and substantially underexplained. The surface behavior is preserved but the psychological engine is missing. Score falls in the 8-10 range.

character_arc.book_baseline: Percy has one of the most complete arcs in the series: (1) starting point — ambitious, pompous prefect, proud of his achievements; (2) development — increasing institutional loyalty, idolization of Crouch, growing distance from family; (3) crisis — the family betrayal in OotP, the letter to Ron, the public alignment with Fudge; (4) stasis — years of estrangement, the Christmas visit with Scrimgeour as a political tool, the returned Christmas jumper; (5) resolution — his return at the Battle of Hogwarts, his explicit self-condemnation, his grief over Fred, his continued fighting. This arc is about the cost of choosing institutional loyalty over family, and the possibility of redemption. It is one of the series' most carefully constructed secondary arcs.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The films depict Percy in Years 1-2 as a pompous prefect and Head Boy. The entire arc from GoF onward — the family betrayal, the estrangement, the return — is absent from the film corpus. The DH Part 1 film corpus shows Percy only as a silent Ministry functionary. His return and reconciliation (DH Part 2) are not in the provided corpus, but even if they were, the preceding arc that gives the return its emotional weight is absent. Without the betrayal, the estrangement, the letter, the Christmas visit, and the years of silence, any reconciliation scene would be dramatically inert.
character_arc.difference: The arc is almost entirely absent from the films. Only the starting point (pompous prefect) is depicted. The development, crisis, stasis, and resolution are all missing or reduced to background noise. This is not compression — it is elimination.
character_arc.penalty_logic: The arc is significantly altered — the starting point exists but the entire trajectory is absent. Score falls in the 5-7 range. Cap 3 applies (core decisions and emotional beats transferred or removed).

key_relationships.book_baseline: Percy's key relationships are: (1) Fred and George — sustained comic antagonism, with Percy as the straight man who is mocked but occasionally asserts himself; (2) Ron — a complex dynamic of sibling rivalry, mutual irritation, and eventual estrangement followed by reconciliation; (3) Mr. and Mrs. Weasley — Percy's betrayal of his father is the emotional core of his arc, and his mother's grief over the estrangement is a recurring motif; (4) Penelope Clearwater — a secret relationship that humanizes Percy and reveals his capacity for genuine feeling; (5) Crouch — an idolization that mirrors and foreshadows Percy's later institutional loyalty; (6) Harry — a minor but consistent dynamic of authority vs. rule-breaking.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The films preserve the Fred-and-George mockery in Years 1-2 (the sweater scene, the prefect badge jokes). The Ron relationship is present in surface form. However, Penelope Clearwater appears only briefly in the CoS film (scene 8 in the film corpus, a single lunch scene with no dramatic function). The Crouch idolization is entirely absent. The family betrayal and estrangement — the most important relational development — are absent. The reconciliation with his father and the grief over Fred are absent from the provided corpus.
key_relationships.difference: The Fred-and-George dynamic is partially preserved. All other key relationships are either absent (Crouch, the family betrayal dynamic) or reduced to cameos (Penelope). The emotional core of Percy's relational life — his betrayal of his father and his eventual return — is missing.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: Important relationship dynamics are altered or absent. The Penelope relationship, which humanizes Percy, is reduced to a background appearance. The family betrayal arc, which defines his relationship with his parents and Ron, is absent. Score falls in the 5-6 range.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: Percy's complexity comes from the tension between his comic surface (pomposity, self-importance) and his genuine emotional depth (love for Penelope, pride in his family when it suits him, grief over Fred, eventual self-awareness). He is not simply a buffoon — he is a character who makes a recognizable human mistake (choosing status over family) and pays for it. His complexity also comes from his contradictions: he enforces rules rigidly but is capable of bending them (his secret relationship with Penelope, his eventual defection from the Ministry). The Weatherby humiliation — Crouch repeatedly calling him the wrong name — is a rich comic-dramatic moment that reveals both Percy's obliviousness and his pathetic eagerness. His letter to Ron in OotP is one of the series' most chilling secondary-character moments: a pompous, self-righteous document that reveals how far he has fallen.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The films preserve Percy's comic surface but remove almost all of his complexity. The Weatherby scenes are absent. The letter to Ron is absent. The Penelope relationship is reduced to a background appearance. The family betrayal arc is absent. The grief over Fred is absent from the provided corpus. The film Percy is a recurring comic extra — pompous, rule-bound, occasionally funny — but without the contradictions, vulnerabilities, and moral failures that make him a genuinely complex character.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The complexity is almost entirely removed. What remains is the surface type (pompous prefect) without the psychological depth, the moral arc, or the relational texture. The character is recognizable but flattened into a single trait.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: Major flattening. The character is reduced to a comic type. Score falls in the 5-7 range. Multiple caps apply.

comparative.key_observations: Percy Weasley is one of the most severely compressed secondary characters in the Harry Potter film series. The films successfully establish his surface type — pompous, rule-obsessed, self-important — in Years 1 and 2, and this surface is recognizable and occasionally well-executed (the prefect badge jokes, the corridor confrontation in Polyjuice). However, from Goblet of Fire onward, Percy is functionally absent as a character. His entire arc — the most important thing about him — is never depicted: the idolization of Crouch, the family betrayal, the estrangement, the letter to Ron, the political alignment with Fudge, and the eventual return and reconciliation. What the films preserve is a comic type; what they lose is a character study about the cost of choosing status over family and the possibility of redemption. The score of 49 reflects a character who is superficially recognizable but whose defining characterization — everything that makes Percy more than a pompous joke — is absent.

personality_voice.book_baseline: Kreacher speaks in third person, mutters audible insults under his breath as a form of passive resistance, performs exaggerated bows while simultaneously insulting the recipient in undertones, and uses a distinctive croaking voice. He is sycophantic on the surface and venomous underneath — a split register that is his defining speech pattern. He is deeply loyal to the Black family ideology, contemptuous of Muggle-borns and blood traitors, and expresses grief and devotion toward his dead mistress and Regulus. He is not simply malicious: he is a traumatized, enslaved creature whose cruelty is inseparable from his suffering. In OotP he is hostile and subversive; in HBP he remains resentful but compliant; in DH, after Harry treats him with respect and invokes Regulus, he transforms into a devoted, even affectionate servant — cooking elaborate meals, bowing with genuine feeling, and leading the house-elves into battle.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: In OotP (film Scene 2), Kreacher appears briefly in Sirius's room, mutters 'Nasty brat... Mudblood and werewolves and traitors and thieves... If my poor Mistress only knew...' and is dismissed by Sirius. In DH Part 1 (film Scene 3), he is dragged in by one ear, mutters foul oaths, calls Hermione a 'Filthy Mudblood', calls Ron a 'Blood-traitor Weasley', and is briefly interrogated before being ordered to find Mundungus. In film Scene 4, he returns with Mundungus and formally announces 'As requested, Kreacher has returned with the thief Mundungus Fletcher.' The third-person speech is preserved. The muttered insults are present. The croaking voice and bow are referenced in stage directions.
personality_voice.difference: The surface speech pattern — third person, muttered insults, bowing — is preserved. However, the full emotional register is absent. The film never shows the split between surface compliance and seething resentment across multiple scenes; it is compressed into one or two moments. The transformation in DH — the devoted cooking, the warmth toward Harry after the Regulus conversation, the 'Master has not finished his soup' tenderness, the steak-and-kidney pie, the battle cry — is entirely absent from the film corpus. The film Kreacher goes from hostile to obedient with no visible emotional shift. The grief over Regulus, the self-punishment, the sobbing on the floor — none of this appears in the film corpus. The OotP film reduces his presence to a single brief scene with no muttering pattern across the household.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The core speech mechanics are preserved (third person, insults, bowing), which prevents a heavier penalty. But the emotional complexity of the voice — the grief, the devotion, the transformation into warmth — is absent. The film Kreacher is recognizable but flattened to his hostile register only. The tender, devoted post-Regulus voice is a major part of his book characterization in DH and is entirely missing.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: Kreacher serves multiple structural functions: (1) In OotP, he is an active saboteur — he exploits Sirius's careless order, contacts Narcissa and Bellatrix, manipulates Harry into going to the Ministry, injures Buckbeak, and lies to Harry's face with gleeful triumph. He is a direct cause of Sirius's death. (2) In HBP, he is Harry's intelligence asset — assigned to tail Malfoy, he provides surveillance reports and engages in a physical altercation with Dobby. (3) In DH, he is the key to the Horcrux hunt — he holds the history of the locket, reveals Regulus's sacrifice, finds Mundungus, and leads the house-elves into the Battle of Hogwarts. He is not a passive figure; he initiates, deceives, reports, retrieves, and fights.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: In OotP, Kreacher appears in one brief scene and is dismissed. His role as saboteur — contacting Bellatrix, manipulating Harry, injuring Buckbeak — is entirely absent from the film corpus. In DH Part 1, he is interrogated, provides information about the locket and Mundungus, and is sent to retrieve Mundungus. He returns with Mundungus in Scene 4. His agency in the interrogation scene is reactive: he answers questions under compulsion. The Battle of Hogwarts appearance (book Scene 351) is absent from the film corpus provided.
narrative_role_agency.difference: The OotP saboteur role — his most consequential act of agency in the entire series — is completely removed from the films. The film never shows Kreacher as the architect of Sirius's death. In DH, his role is compressed: he provides information and retrieves Mundungus, but the emotional weight of the Regulus story (which in the books transforms his narrative function from obstacle to tragic figure to ally) is stripped down to a brief interrogation. The Battle of Hogwarts leadership is not present in the film corpus. The HBP surveillance role is absent entirely.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: The transfer/removal of his OotP saboteur role is a major agency loss — this is the single most consequential thing Kreacher does in the books, and it is absent. His DH role is partially preserved (information, retrieval) but the emotional and narrative weight is gutted. The Battle of Hogwarts moment, where he leads house-elves crying Regulus's name, is his culminating act of agency and is absent from the film corpus.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Kreacher's motivations are layered and coherent: (1) Loyalty to the Black family ideology and his dead mistress — he preserves her portrait, hoards family relics, venerates Bellatrix's photograph. (2) Devotion to Regulus specifically — deeper than his general Black loyalty; Regulus was kind to him, and Kreacher's entire existence in DH is shaped by his failure to fulfill Regulus's final order. (3) Resentment of Sirius — not mere hostility but a specific grievance: Sirius treated him with contempt and indifference, which Dumbledore explicitly identifies as the cause of Kreacher's betrayal. (4) The internal conflict between his compulsion to obey and his desire to serve his 'true' masters (the Blacks, Bellatrix, Narcissa). This conflict is what makes him dangerous and ultimately pitiable. (5) In DH, his motivation shifts: Harry's kindness and the invocation of Regulus give him a new master worth serving.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The film shows Kreacher's hostility toward Harry and his loyalty to the Black family ideology (muttering about his mistress, calling Hermione a Mudblood). In DH, he confirms the locket belonged to Regulus and that Regulus ordered him to destroy it. But the internal conflict — the grief over failing Regulus's order, the self-punishment, the specific resentment of Sirius rooted in neglect, the transformation triggered by Harry's kindness — is absent. The film Kreacher has surface motivations (loyalty to Blacks, hostility to Harry's group) but no internal conflict.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The film removes the motivational complexity that makes Kreacher comprehensible rather than simply villainous. Dumbledore's explanation in OotP (book Scenes 138-144) — that Kreacher was made what he is by wizard neglect, that indifference does more damage than hatred — is absent. The DH revelation that Kreacher's betrayal of Sirius was driven by specific emotional deprivation, not pure malice, is not present in the film corpus. The shift in motivation triggered by Harry's treatment of him is absent.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: The film preserves the surface motivation (Black family loyalty) but removes the internal conflict entirely. The distinction between Kreacher as villain and Kreacher as victim — which is the entire point of his character — is lost. This is a substantial motivational flattening.

character_arc.book_baseline: Kreacher has one of the most complete arcs of any secondary character in the series. Starting point: hostile, subversive, actively dangerous house-elf who betrays Sirius. Turning point 1 (OotP end/HBP): passes to Harry's ownership, is sent to Hogwarts, returns resentful but compliant. Turning point 2 (DH): Harry treats him with respect, invokes Regulus's memory, gives him the fake locket as a gift. This triggers a complete transformation — Kreacher becomes devoted, cooks elaborate meals, bows with genuine warmth, refers to Harry as 'Master Harry.' Culmination: leads house-elves into the Battle of Hogwarts crying Regulus's name, wearing the locket. The arc is explicitly about what kindness does to a creature shaped entirely by how it has been treated.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The film shows Kreacher hostile in OotP, hostile in early DH, and then compliant after being ordered to find Mundungus. There is no emotional transformation. The Regulus conversation — the engine of the arc — is compressed into a brief interrogation with no emotional weight. Harry does not give Kreacher the fake locket. Kreacher does not cook for Harry. The Battle of Hogwarts moment is absent from the film corpus. The arc from betrayer to devoted ally to battle leader does not exist in the films.
character_arc.difference: The arc is almost entirely absent. The film shows a static hostile character who becomes briefly useful. The transformation — which is the entire point of Kreacher's presence in DH — does not occur. The culminating moment (Battle of Hogwarts) is absent.
character_arc.penalty_logic: This is a near-complete arc removal. The film preserves only the starting point (hostile) and a fragment of the middle (provides information). The transformation and culmination are gone. This is not compression — it is elimination.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Three key relationships define Kreacher: (1) Kreacher/Sirius — mutual contempt and neglect, with Kreacher's resentment rooted in Sirius's indifference; this relationship directly causes Sirius's death and is the moral center of Kreacher's OotP arc. (2) Kreacher/Regulus — deep devotion, grief, and a sense of failed duty; this is the emotional core of Kreacher's DH arc and the reason he transforms. (3) Kreacher/Harry — begins with hostility and betrayal, transforms into genuine loyalty after Harry treats him with respect and honors Regulus's memory; this relationship is the vehicle for the arc's resolution.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: Kreacher/Sirius: one brief scene in OotP where Sirius dismisses him ('That's enough of your bile. Away with you.'). No history, no mutual contempt developed across scenes, no sense that this relationship has consequences. Kreacher/Regulus: mentioned in DH interrogation — Kreacher confirms the locket was Regulus's and that Regulus ordered him to destroy it — but the emotional depth (Kreacher's grief, his devotion, the cave story) is absent. Kreacher/Harry: Harry orders him to find Mundungus; Kreacher obeys. No transformation, no warmth, no loyalty developed.
key_relationships.difference: All three relationships are present in outline but gutted of their emotional dynamics. The Sirius relationship loses its consequence (no betrayal shown). The Regulus relationship loses its grief and devotion. The Harry relationship loses its transformation. The power dynamics and emotional textures that define these relationships in the books are absent.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: The relationships are not merely compressed — their dramatic functions are removed. The Sirius relationship's consequence (Sirius's death caused by Kreacher's betrayal) is absent. The Regulus relationship's emotional weight (the cave, the grief, the failed order) is reduced to a plot summary. The Harry relationship's arc (hostility to devotion) does not occur.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: Kreacher is one of the most morally complex secondary characters in the series. His cruelty is inseparable from his suffering. He is simultaneously villain and victim. His complexity includes: the split between surface compliance and seething resentment; the magpie-like hoarding of family relics; the photograph of Bellatrix mended with Spellotape; the nest of dirty blankets; the self-punishment; the sobbing over Regulus; the cave story (being used as bait by Voldemort, watching Regulus die, carrying the grief for years); the transformation triggered by kindness; the battle cry invoking Regulus. Dumbledore's speech about indifference doing more damage than hatred is the thematic capstone of Kreacher's complexity.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The film shows a hostile, muttering house-elf who provides plot information and retrieves a character. The nest, the hoarding, the Bellatrix photograph, the self-punishment, the cave story, the transformation, the cooking, the battle — all absent. The film Kreacher is a functional plot device: he confirms the locket's history and finds Mundungus. His complexity is reduced to surface hostility.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The vast majority of what makes Kreacher a complex character is absent from the films. What remains is the hostile surface and the basic plot function (locket information, Mundungus retrieval). The moral and emotional texture — the victim/villain duality, the grief, the transformation, the thematic weight — is gone.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: This is major flattening. The character is reduced to a single trait (hostile house-elf) and a single function (information source). The complexity that makes Kreacher one of the series' most interesting secondary characters is almost entirely absent.
